Conclusion: Demonstrates effectiveness of anisotropic, deformable sampling plus fuzzy multi-scale context in industrial defect segmentation; potential impact on quality inspection with compact models; future work could explore broader defect types and cross-domain generalization.

Abstract: Steel surface defect segmentation is critical for industrial quality inspection, yet existing methods struggle with elongated, anisotropic defects such as cracks and scratches due to the isotropic receptive fields of standard convolutions and rigid sampling grids that cannot adapt to irregular defect boundaries. To address these limitations, we propose Strip-based Predictor for Deformable Convolutional Networks (SPDCN) with two key innovations. The \textbf{Fuzzy-enhanced Multi-scale Context Module (FMCM)} employs group-wise multi-branch convolutions with an intuitionistic fuzzy channel attention mechanism to adaptively capture multi-scale contextual information across varying defect sizes. The \textbf{Adaptive Direction-Aware Deformable Convolution (ADADC)} replaces the conventional offset predictor with decoupled horizontal and vertical strip convolutions, enabling the deformable sampling grid to anisotropically align with the principal orientation of elongated defects. Extensive experiments on public steel surface defect benchmarks demonstrate that SPDCN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 89.60\% mIoU on NEU-Seg with only 3.54M parameters. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/DWlzm .

</details>


### [77] [CLUIE: Clustering-Aware Recurrent Propagation with Local Structural Compensation for Underwater Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21467)
*Kui Jiang,Zefan Feng,Laibin Chang,Yan Luo,Junjun Jiang,Xiaopeng Fan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A novel CRWKV framework for underwater image enhancement that makes RWKV recurrent propagation content-adaptive through semantic clustering and local propagation modulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underwater imaging suffers from depth- and condition-dependent degradations (color distortion, loss of contrast, detail) that vary across regions, necessitating region-adaptive restoration. Existing RWKV models have fixed, content-agnostic traversal, limiting non-uniform restoration.

Method: Introduce Clustering-aware Semantic Dynamic Reordering (CSDR) to create a content-driven token trajectory by clustering semantically similar tokens and deriving traversal via inter-cluster relations. Employ Dark-response Modulated Local Propagation (DMLP) to preserve local continuity by computing depth-wise conv-based local responses and modulating propagation with a neighborhood-aware pseudo-dark map, enabling compensatory local cues before recurrent aggregation.

Result: Empirical evaluation on multiple underwater image enhancement benchmarks shows state-of-the-art quantitative performance and superior visual quality.

Conclusion: CRWKV enables content-adaptive long-range modeling for underwater image enhancement by combining semantic clustering-informed traversal with local propagation modulation, addressing non-uniform degradation.

Abstract: Underwater image enhancement remains challenging due to wavelength-dependent light absorption, scattering, and backscattering, which jointly cause color distortion, contrast degradation, and detail loss. Since these degradations vary with scene depth and imaging conditions, different regions within the same image often exhibit heterogeneous degradation patterns and thus require region-adaptive restoration. Although visual RWKV models offer an efficient linear-complexity solution for long-range dependency modeling, their predefined scanning orders are content-agnostic and therefore fail to adapt recurrent state propagation to spatially non-uniform restoration demands. To address this limitation, we propose a Clustering-aware RWKV framework, termed CRWKV, which reformulates the fixed recurrent propagation path of conventional RWKV into a content-adaptive token trajectory. Specifically, we introduce Clustering-aware Semantic Dynamic Reordering (CSDR), which groups tokens according to semantic feature similarity and derives a dynamic traversal order from inter-cluster contextual relations. This design enables WKV states to be accumulated along semantically correlated regions rather than fixed spatial or spectral orders. Since dynamic reordering may disrupt the local continuity of original spatial neighborhoods, we further propose Dark-response Modulated Local Propagation (DMLP), which extracts local structural responses via depth-wise convolution and adaptively modulates their propagation strength using a neighborhood-aware pseudo-dark response map. In this way, local structural cues are compensated before recurrent aggregation while preserving content-adaptive long-range modeling. Extensive experiments on multiple underwater image enhancement benchmarks demonstrate that CRWKV achieves state-of-the-art quantitative performance and superior visual quality.

</details>


### [78] [Future Rendering $\neq$ Future Surface: A Benchmark and Dataset for Dynamic Surface Reconstruction Beyond the Observed Window](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21471)
*Yukun Shi,Minglun Gong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FutureSurf provides a benchmark/dataset to evaluate future-time surface reconstruction with exact future ground truth, revealing non-trivial geometry gaps not captured by standard rendering metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is no standard benchmark to assess geometry beyond the observed window; deployment contexts (AR, robotics, planning) require accurate future surfaces and falsification controls to test robustness.

Method: Train on the first 75% of sequences; evaluate per-frame future surface via Chamfer distance on held-out future; use eight controlled motions including falsification controls; include exact per-frame ground-truth meshes and a ground-truth recoverability oracle; release splits, scoring code, and metadata; test across multiple backbones (DG-Mesh, Deformable-3DGS).

Result: Future gaps are substantial: 2.7–4.1x gap for predictable futures with DG-Mesh (four of five recoverable cases); falsification controls behave as intended (surface-invariant motion shows no gap); across six additional scenes and another backbone (2.0–6.6x); future rendering metrics decouple from future-surface accuracy; error concentrates where the surface moves.

Conclusion: The benchmark exposes a measurable, structured future-geometry gap not captured by existing metrics, provides data/tools for robust future-time evaluation, and suggests that future geometry tracking remains challenging even when optical rendering appears plausible.

Abstract: Dynamic-scene reconstruction is almost always evaluated inside the observed time window, yet deployment settings such as AR overlays, robot interaction, and anticipatory planning need the future surface: the geometry at times beyond those captured. No standard benchmark measures this. We introduce FutureSurf, a controlled diagnostic benchmark and dataset for future-time surface reconstruction that trades scene diversity for exact future ground truth and falsification controls. A method trains on the observed first 75% of a sequence; we score its extracted per-frame surface on the held-out future by Chamfer distance, reporting absolute future CD as the primary score and the future/observed gap as a diagnostic. The dataset contains eight analytically defined controlled motions, including three falsification controls, with exact per-frame ground-truth meshes. We also provide a ground-truth-side recoverability oracle. The release includes split files, scoring code, a benchmark card, and Croissant metadata. On the controlled motions, the DG-Mesh backbone leaves a 2.7-4.1$\times$ gap even for futures predictable in principle (four of five recoverable from observed motion by a fixed rule), while the falsification controls behave as designed (the surface-invariant motion shows no gap). Beyond the contributed dataset, the gap persists across six animated DG-Mesh asset scenes and a second backbone, Deformable-3DGS (2.0-6.6$\times$; both share a deformation-MLP temporal model). The benchmark also shows that future rendering quality and future-surface accuracy are statistically decoupled, so the novel-view-synthesis metrics the field reports do not track future geometry. The future error is structured, concentrating where the surface moves. The dataset, evaluation toolkit, and scoring code are available on Hugging Face and GitHub (https://github.com/Ricky-S/futuresurf).

</details>


### [79] [Recurrent Sinusoidal INRs for Efficient High-Fidelity Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21485)
*Hyunmin Cho,Jaejun Yoo,Kyong Hwan Jin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Sinusoidal recurrence in INRs yields harmonic spectra and spectral enrichment, enabling a shared sinusoidal block that iteratively refines representations; achieves higher RGB fidelity with fewer parameters/steps and transfers well to SR, NeRF, and SDF.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide a spectral explanation for how sinusoidal activations and recurrent unrolling can expand an implicit representation's spectral support, enabling parameter-efficient and cross-domain improvements.

Method: Introduce a shared sinusoidal block that is iteratively unrolled to refine the latent representation; compare against feed-forward INRs, non-sinusoidal recurrent variants, and equilibrium-style sinusoidal models; evaluate on image and 3D representation tasks.

Result: Sinusoidal activations induce a harmonic line spectrum; recurrent unrolling enriches the spectral content, improving fidelity on RGB images with fewer parameters and optimization steps; demonstrates favorable transfer to super-resolution, NeRF, and SDF tasks.

Conclusion: Sinusoidal recurrence provides a spectrally grounded, effective mechanism for enriching INRs, achieving improved performance and cross-domain transfer while reducing model complexity and training effort.

Abstract: We study sinusoidal recurrence as an iterative mechanism for harmonic spectral enrichment in implicit neural representations (INRs). Our analysis reveals that sinusoidal activations induce a harmonic line spectrum, providing a spectral account of how recurrent unrolling enriches the effective spectral support. We realize this principle with a shared sinusoidal block that iteratively refines the latent representation. We empirically validate the resulting spectral behavior against feed-forward INRs, non-sinusoidal recurrent variants, and equilibrium-style sinusoidal models. Complementing this analysis, we evaluate the proposed architecture across image and 3D representation tasks. On RGB image benchmarks, our method achieves higher fidelity than feed-forward baselines with fewer parameters and fewer optimization steps, and it further transfers favorably to super-resolution, NeRF, and SDF tasks.

</details>


### [80] [Texture++: Elevating 3D Asset Texture Resolution with a Region-Aware Diffusion Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21504)
*Shuaiwei Wang,Shi Li,Jieting Xu,Yuchi Huo,Qi Wang,Wenting Zheng,Rengan Xie*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Texture++ adaptively super-resolves textures by cross-view diffusion in UV space, using adaptive view selection and a quadtree-based region fusion to produce coherent, high-quality textures across multiple viewpoints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many 3D assets have low-resolution textures; existing SR methods focus on natural images and ignore texture maps, leading to limited utility for 3D assets. A texture-specific SR framework is needed to revive aging assets across industries.

Method: Reformulate SR in UV space by rendering multiple views, adaptively aggregating textures from dispersed UV patches; employ a quadtree-based organization to merge super-resolved regions with masks indicating areas needing improvement; apply a diffusion-based SR model to masked regions and seamlessly blend with surroundings.

Result: Comprehensive evaluations show substantial improvements in texture detail and coherence over existing methods across varied assets, indicating effective texture restoration for aging assets.

Conclusion: Texture++ provides a generalizable texture super-resolution framework that enhances texture resolution while maintaining cross-view consistency, enabling revitalization of low-resolution textures in 3D assets.

Abstract: Numerous 3D assets are discarded due to low texture resolution, while current super-resolution models ignore texture maps and focus on natural images. An efficient and generalizable texture super-resolution model can revitalize a large corpus of aging yet valuable assets across industries such as film and video games. We present Texture++, a novel framework for texture super-resolution, which enhances the low-resolution textures of assets to produce high-resolution, high-quality results. Specifically, we reformulate the task of super-resolution in UV space into performing it across multiple rendered views and merging the outputs. Firstly, to achieve more complete and continuous textures in the view space, we propose an adaptive view selection strategy to integrate textures dispersed across UV texture patches. Furthermore, we introduce a quadtree-based texture region organization method for combining super-resolved textures from different viewpoints, providing masks to distinguish regions that require improvement. Finally, we design a diffusion-based super-resolution model that enhances the texture resolution for specified masked regions, seamlessly integrating with surrounding regions. Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that our approach yields textures with substantially improved detail and coherence over existing methods.

</details>


### [81] [Boosting Robustness for All-Weather Self-Supervised Depth Estimation in Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21526)
*Mengshi Qi,Xiaoyang Bi,Xianlin Zhang,Huadong Ma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A robust self-supervised depth estimation approach for all-weather conditions using unpaired real data, via (1) uncertainty-weighted multi-teacher distillation to handle adverse condition-induced errors, and (2) camera–radar fusion across POV and BEV via ray-based constraints to leverage denser radar data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adverse weather degrades pixel correspondences and self-supervised losses for depth estimation; radar data, while useful, is sparse in POV, complicating fusion. A robust, data-efficient self-training framework for safe autonomous driving is needed.

Method: 1) Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Teacher Distillation: train diverse teacher models with various adverse condition inputs; weigh distillation losses by uncertainty to reduce the influence of unreliable teachers. 2) POV-BEV Radar Fusion: use camera-pixel ray constraints to align POV (image space) with BEV (radar space), enabling denser radar point utilization and cross-view fusion.

Result: Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments on all-weather datasets demonstrate robustness and achieve state-of-the-art performance in depth estimation under adverse conditions.

Conclusion: The proposed framework enhances depth estimation robustness in adverse weather via self-training with multi-teacher distillation and cross-view radar fusion, and provides code for replication.

Abstract: Self-supervised depth estimation is challenging for safe autonomous driving under various adverse weather conditions due to sensor perception degradation. These challenges arise from two main aspects. Firstly, adverse conditions can distort pixel correspondences and violate the assumptions embedded in the self-supervised loss function, leading to erroneous depth predictions. Secondly, while radar is a widely adopted sensor in adverse weather conditions, the sparse distribution of radar points in the Point of View (POV) poses challenges for self-supervised fusion. To address these issues, we introduce a novel self-training pipeline using unpaired real all-weather data through multi-teacher distillation and robust radar fusion. We propose the Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Teacher Distillation method to generate diverse teacher models with different adverse condition inputs, and then employ uncertainty modeling to weigh the knowledge distillation loss. Additionally, we design the POV-BEV Radar Fusion approach, which leverages camera-pixel ray constraints to establish connections between the camera's Point of View (POV) and the radar's Bird's-Eye View (BEV). This approach enables the utilization of denser radar points, effectively capturing the complementary perspectives of both POV and BEV. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the robustness of our proposed method on all-weather datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/MICLAB-BUPT/RobustDepth.

</details>


### [82] [ElasticTTT: Prior-Preserving Test-Time Tuning for Video Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21529)
*Yueyi Liu,Chi Zhang,Sen Cui,Miao Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ElasticTTT preserves the generative prior in diffusion-based test-time tuning for video editing, addressing Prior Collapse and delivering state-of-the-art one-shot editing results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A fundamental mismatch exists between the distribution-mapping nature of pretrained diffusion models and the single-point optimization of standard Test-Time Tuning (TTT). This mismatch can cause Prior Collapse, where the model ignores text conditions and latents or entangles region-specific features, degrading editing quality.

Method: ElasticTTT introduces a framework that preserves the base model's generative prior and restores generative elasticity through: (1) Target Distribution Regularization to avoid sharp memorization minima, (2) Contrastive CFG to steer inference away from source-region biases, and (3) Asynchronous Noise Schedule to maintain unedited regions during editing.

Result: Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments demonstrate that ElasticTTT preserves the model’s generative prior and achieves state-of-the-art performance in one-shot video editing.

Conclusion: ElasticTTT offers a principled solution to the Prior Collapse problem in TTT for diffusion video editing by maintaining the base model’s prior and improving editing fidelity, supported by theory and empirical results.

Abstract: Test-Time Tuning (TTT) on pretrained diffusion models has emerged as a powerful paradigm for video editing. However, there exists a foundational mismatch between the distribution-mapping nature of generative models and the single-point optimization of standard TTT. In this paper, we demonstrate that this mismatch triggers \textit{Prior Collapse}, a degenerate state where the model discards the text conditions and spatial latents, collapsing generations to the source video, or entangling the features of distinct regions. To resolve this, we propose \textbf{ElasticTTT}, a novel framework that preserves the prior generative distribution and rescues generative elasticity. Specifically, we propose \textit{Target Distribution Regularization} to prevent sharp memorization minima, \textit{Contrastive CFG} to guide inference away from source biases, and \textit{Asynchronous Noise Schedule} to preserve unedited regions. Extensive evaluations, supported by theoretical analysis, demonstrate that ElasticTTT successfully preserves the generative prior of the base model, achieving state-of-the-art performance on one-shot video editing.

</details>


### [83] [Towards Robust Iris Recognition Through Occlusion Identification and Conditional Diffusion-Based Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21545)
*Kamrul Hasan,Mylene C. Q. Farias,Oleg V. Komogortsev*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: An occlusion-aware iris recognition pipeline with three stages: occlusion-type identification via a residual 2D CNN, diffusion-based reconstruction conditioned on mask and occlusion type, and a VGG19-HPMNet-based recognizer; evaluated on CASIA-Iris-Thousand with synthetic occlusions, showing gains from explicit occlusion handling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Iris texture is degraded by occlusions (eyelids, eyelashes, reflections, etc.). Existing methods either operate on degraded samples or rely only on visible iris, which can fail when textures are heavily corrupted. An explicit occlusion-aware approach aims to improve robustness by identifying occlusion type, restoring corrupted regions, and re-evaluating with a strengthened recognizer.

Method: Three sequential modules: (1) occlusion-type identification using a residual 2D CNN to classify images as non-occluded or into controlled occlusion categories; (2) a denoising diffusion probabilistic model that reconstructs the corrupted region using the occluded image, a binary mask, and the predicted occlusion type as conditioning; (3) recognition with VGG19-HPMNet (a modified VGG19 with horizontal pyramid mapping) to extract global and part-wise local iris features for final recognition.

Result: Experiments on CASIA-Iris-Thousand under a controlled synthetic-occlusion protocol report improved iris recognition by incorporating occlusion-type identification, region reconstruction, and re-evaluation of restored samples.

Conclusion: The proposed occlusion-aware framework effectively handles occlusions by (i) identifying occlusion type, (ii) reconstructing masked regions via diffusion models, and (iii) re-running recognition on restored images, yielding improved robustness to occlusions.

Abstract: Iris recognition is a reliable biometric approach that identifies individuals using the distinctive and stable texture of the iris. However, recognition performance can degrade when discriminative iris texture is partially occluded by eyelids, eyelashes, specular reflections, or other acquisition artifacts. Existing approaches often perform recognition directly on degraded samples or rely only on the remaining visible iris region, which may be inadequate when substantial texture is corrupted. To address this limitation, we propose an occlusion-aware iris recognition framework with three sequential modules: occlusion-type identification, diffusion-based reconstruction, and deep-learning-based recognition. First, a residual 2D CNN-based network determines whether an iris image is non-occluded or belongs to one of the controlled occlusion categories. Second, the occluded image, binary mask, and predicted occlusion type condition a denoising diffusion probabilistic model to reconstruct the corrupted region. Finally, VGG19-HPMNet, a modified VGG19 model with horizontal pyramid mapping, extracts discriminative global and part-wise local iris features for recognition. Experiments on the CASIA-Iris-Thousand dataset under a controlled synthetic-occlusion protocol show that the proposed framework improves iris recognition performance by identifying the occlusion type, reconstructing masked regions, and re-evaluating the restored iris samples.

</details>


### [84] [UnDA: Unpaired Domain Alignment for Cross-Modal Knowledge Transfer in Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21546)
*Rafsan Jany,Shadab Tanjeed Ahmad,Ahsan Bulbul,Tahsinul Islam,Md Azam Hossain,Abu Raihan Mostofa Kamal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UnDA is an anchor-guided, backbone-agnostic unpaired cross-modal distillation framework, featuring an alignment module, uncertainty-weighted optimal transport, and per-class ProtoNCE to transfer semantic structure across unpaired modalities, improving segmentation accuracy and boundary precision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multimodal learning, paired data often scarce; modality gaps and noisy predictions hinder cross-modal knowledge transfer; a robust unpaired distillation method is needed to preserve semantic structure across modalities.

Method: Introduce UnDA: (1) backbone-agnostic Alignment Module with attention-based pooling to produce semantically structured class tokens; (2) Uncertainty-Weighted Optimal Transport (UCT-OT) to weight feature-level alignments by prediction confidence to suppress noise; (3) per-class ProtoNCE objective to maintain stable prototypes across unpaired batches for global discriminability.

Result: On representative segmentation tasks under strictly unpaired settings, UnDA yields consistent improvements in accuracy and boundary precision in the target modality, demonstrating effective structural knowledge transfer across heterogeneous sources without paired datasets.

Conclusion: UnDA enables robust, structure-aware cross-modal knowledge transfer in unpaired settings, mitigating modality gaps and noisy supervision while improving segmentation performance.

Abstract: Multimodal based approaches often outperform single modality approaches in downstream tasks as the different modalities provide complementary information, yet acquiring paired clinical data remains a significant challenge in real world scenarios. While cross-modal knowledge distillation addresses this, existing methods often struggle with large modality gaps and the propagation of noise from uncertain source-domain predictions. To overcome these challenges, we propose UnDA, an anchor-guided framework for unpaired cross-modal distillation. Our approach introduces a backbone-agnostic Alignment Module that extracts semantically structured class tokens via an attention based pooling mechanism. To ensure robust knowledge transfer, we propose Uncertainty-Weighted Optimal Transport (UCT-OT), which dynamically weights feature-level alignment based on prediction confidence, effectively suppressing noisy supervision. Furthermore, a per-class ProtoNCE objective maintains stable prototype memories to enforce global discriminability across unpaired batches. Evaluations on representative segmentation tasks under strictly unpaired settings show consistent improvements in accuracy and boundary precision in the target modality, demonstrating that meaningful structural knowledge can be transferred across heterogeneous data sources without paired datasets.

</details>


### [85] [SANA-Video 2.0: Hybrid Linear Attention with Attention Residuals for Efficient Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21553)
*Junsong Chen,Jincheng Yu,Yitong Li,Shuchen Xue,Haozhe Liu,Jingyu Xin,Yuyang Zhao,Tian Ye,Zhangjie Wu,Zian Wang,Daquan Zhou,Ping Luo,Song Han,Enze Xie*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Hybrid linear-softmax video diffusion with 5B/14B scales enabling 720p on a single GPU; matches full-softmax quality with long-sequence efficiency; introduces Hybrid Linear-Softmax Attention and AttnRes, plus optimized Sol-Engine; achieves 84.30 VBench at 480p and 13.2s on H100; 3.2x faster than full-softmax baseline; ~120x faster than Wan 2.2-A14B.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the computational cost of full-softmax attention in video diffusion while preserving expressiveness and enabling long-sequence processing and high-resolution generation on commodity hardware; aim for end-to-end training from scratch rather than distillation.

Method: Introduce Hybrid Linear-Softmax Attention (combining gated linear attention for O(N) mixing with periodic gated-softmax anchors at a 3:1 ratio); employ Block Attention Residuals (AttnRes) to propagate refreshed representations across depth; train from scratch; use reduced-resolution proxy studies to select ~25% softmax as optimal quality-efficiency trade-off; 40-step sampling; apply full-stack Sol-Engine optimizations (kernel fusion, caching, sparse attention).

Result: Achieves VBench 84.30 at 480p in 13.2s on a single H100 at 40-step sampling; competitive with larger softmax video DiTs at lower latency; DiT forward is 3.2x faster than a matched full-softmax baseline at 720p/60s; Sol-Engine optimization adds ~3.58x, reaching 13.06s at 720p/5s; claimed 120x faster than Wan 2.2-A14B on one H100.

Conclusion: The hybrid attention design recovers softmax-level expressiveness at substantially reduced cost, enabling scalable long-range, high-resolution video generation on a single GPU and suggesting a practical path for efficient diffusion video models.

Abstract: We introduce SANA-Video 2.0, a hybrid video diffusion transformer instantiated at 5B and 14B scales under a unified architecture. Designed to generate high-quality video up to 720p on a single GPU, SANA-Video 2.0 matches full-softmax video DiTs in quality while retaining the favorable long-sequence scaling of linear attention. To avoid quadratic attention throughout, Hybrid Linear-Softmax Attention combines gated linear attention for O(N)-dominated mixing with periodic gated-softmax anchors at a 3:1 ratio, restoring the full-rank token interactions that pure linear attention lacks. To propagate these refreshed representations across depth, Block Attention Residuals (AttnRes) route completed block summaries into later linear layers, enabling anchor-feature reuse and boosting deep-layer effective rank by ~12%. Through from-scratch training, SANA-Video 2.0 learns the complete hybrid directly rather than linearizing pretrained models, with reduced-resolution proxy studies establishing 25% softmax as the optimal quality-efficiency trade-off. With 40-step sampling, SANA-Video 2.0 achieves a VBench score of 84.30 in 13.2s at 480p on a single H100, remaining competitive with far larger softmax video DiTs at a fraction of the latency. Its compiled DiT forward pass is 3.2x faster than a matched full-softmax baseline at 720p/60s, a gap that expands with video duration. Furthermore, full-stack Sol-Engine optimization (kernel fusion, caching, and sparse attention) accelerates this hardware-friendly backbone by a further 3.58x, bringing the 5B pipeline to 13.06s at 720p/5s and making it 120x faster than Wan 2.2-A14B on one H100. Overall, our hybrid design recovers softmax-level expressiveness at substantially reduced cost, unlocking scalable long, high resolution video generation.

</details>


### [86] [Visual Contrastive Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21556)
*Yijun Liang,Yunjie Tian,Yijiang Li,Yuqi Jia,Furong Huang,Tianyi Zhou,Di Fu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VCSD introduces a purely input-conditioned, on-policy self-distillation method that uses a contrast between two EMA teacher distributions (original image vs content-erased) to provide a self-supervised learning signal, eliminating external teachers and privileged information while showing consistent gains on ViRL39K across Qwen3-VL/3.5 models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for asymmetric information in on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). The authors propose removing external teachers, privileged answers, and visual evidence signals, and investigate whether a simple, input-conditioned mechanism suffices to drive effective self-distillation.

Method: At each student-generated prefix, an EMA teacher yields two next-token distributions under the same prompt: one conditioned on the original image, the other on a content-erased control. The token-wise log-probability difference highlights tokens whose likelihood increases due to instance-specific visual content. This contrast sharpens the teacher's original-image distribution within its plausible support, and the resulting full distribution target is distilled into the student. The approach, named Visual Contrastive Self-Distillation (VCSD), uses no external teacher, privileged signals, reasoning traces, or extra inference cost. Evaluations are performed on ViRL39K with Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 models.

Result: VCSD consistently outperforms matched OPSD on the ViRL39K benchmark across model scales: for Qwen3-VL, aggregate seven-benchmark accuracy improves from 62.27% to 67.04% at 2B, from 71.30% to 73.16% at 4B, and from 72.51% to 76.26% at 8B. Similar gains are reported for Qwen3-VL/3.5 configurations (exact numbers per model/size in the abstract).

Conclusion: A purely input-conditioned OPSD approach (VCSD) can surpass traditional OPSD without external teachers or auxiliary signals, and without additional inference-time costs, offering a simpler and effective self-distillation paradigm for vision-language models.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is promising as it removes the external teacher required by on-policy distillation (OPD), yet it still needs asymmetric information between teacher and student to ensure that the self-teacher provides a stronger learning signal than the student. Existing methods create this asymmetry either through privileged answers or visual evidence. We ask whether both can be removed, yielding a simpler form of OPSD driven purely by input conditioning. For this purpose, we propose Visual Contrastive Self-Distillation, namely VCSD, which converts image-content removal into an on-policy self-distillation signal. At each student-generated response prefix, the EMA teacher produces two next-token distributions under the same prompt and prefix -- one conditioned on the original image and the other on a content-erased control. Their token-wise log-probability difference highlights candidates whose likelihood is specifically increased by the instance-level visual content. We use this contrast to sharpen the teacher's original-image distribution within its plausible support, and distill the resulting full-distribution target into the student. Using ViRL39K dataset, VCSD consistently outperforms matched OPSD across Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 models. For example, on Qwen3-VL, it improves the seven-benchmark aggregate from $62.27\% \rightarrow 67.04\%$ at 2B, $71.30\% \rightarrow 73.16\%$ at 4B, and $72.51\% \rightarrow 76.26\%$ at 8B. Furthermore, VCSD requires no external teacher, privileged answers, visual evidence signals, reasoning traces, or additional inference-time cost.

</details>


### [87] [Scene Parameter Saliency via Differentiable Light Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21562)
*Linas Beresna,Eugene Fiume*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Gradient-based saliency extends to differentiable rendering: metric saliency maps show how scalar image metrics depend on scene elements via gradient propagation through the image formation process, yielding metric-specific explanations that differ across objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and compare how different image-based metrics rely on scene parameters when the image is produced through a differentiable renderer, and to demonstrate that saliency is not intrinsic to the scene but to the chosen metric.

Method: Compute per-parameter gradients of a scalar metric with respect to scene parameters by reverse-mode differentiation through a differentiable renderer. Apply to multiple metrics (psychovisual glare indices, mean luminance, neural perceptual scores) and analyze gradient fields (metric saliency maps) for different scenes and metrics.

Result: Gradient fields identify which scene elements most influence each metric. Saliency rankings vary across metrics for the same scene, indicating parameter influence is metric-dependent. The gradient maps propagate through the image formation process (including multi-bounce light transport) and can reveal dependencies semi-opaque to manual inspection.

Conclusion: Differentiable renderers yield derivative images (metric saliency maps) that are as informative as primal renders for scene understanding, but the saliency is inherently tied to the metric. This provides a new, objective way to interpret how different objectives prioritize scene parameters.

Abstract: Gradient-based saliency methods reveal which input features most influence a neural network's output, and are a standard tool for model interpretability. We observe that differentiable renderers, which are conventionally used for parameter optimisation, produce an analogous form of saliency: given any scalar metric evaluated on a rendered image, a single reverse-mode differentiation pass yields per-parameter gradients that identify which scene elements most influence the metric. We call these gradient fields metric saliency maps. Unlike neural saliency, which propagates attribution through learned weights, metric saliency propagates through the image formation process itself, including multi-bounce light transport, capturing parameter dependencies that are semi-opaque to manual inspection. We compute metric saliency maps for qualitatively different objectives: psychovisual glare indices, mean scene luminance, and neural perceptual scores. The saliency rankings differ substantially across metrics for the same scene, with parameters that dominate one objective being negligible for another. The saliency map is specific to the metric, not an intrinsic property of the scene. Our results suggest that differentiable renderers produce derivative images that are as informative for scene understanding as the primal images they were designed to generate.

</details>


### [88] [Self-Supervised Learning of Structured Dynamics from Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21576)
*Lukas Knobel,Andrew Zisserman,Yuki M. Asano*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A structured dynamics model (SDM) reuses frozen vision-transformer features to separate camera- and object-motion via future-feature prediction, yielding robust, learned motion representations that outperform baselines with weaker supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle camera motion from object motion in video representations, addressing the entanglement of dynamics and the lack of supervision for structured motion; aims to leverage pretrained image models to learn robust, interpretable motion factors.

Method: Introduce SDM which explicitly separates the dominant source of temporal change from residual dynamics by predicting future features. Uses frozen features from a pretrained image ViT, avoids entangled latent or dense transition tokens, and trains with self-supervision on real video plus weak supervision on synthetic Kubric data; evaluation on ProbeMotion across synthetic and real videos with varying dynamics.

Result: SDM outperforms backbone baselines that rely on global CLS or average-pooled features and compares favorably to strongly supervised representations like VGGT on several probes, despite weaker supervision; demonstrates that pretrained image models can be repurposed into structured video-dynamics representations.

Conclusion: Pretrained image models provide a useful inductive bias for learning and analyzing latent video dynamics; structured dynamics representations are feasible and beneficial for disentangling camera and object motion in video.

Abstract: Understanding motion in video is a fundamental challenge for visual learning, as frame-to-frame change entangles two sources of dynamics: camera motion and object motion. This decomposition has remained underexplored in representation learning, partly because these factors are tightly coupled in natural videos and difficult to supervise separately. Yet recovering it is important for learning robust motion representations that separate meaningful object dynamics from camera-induced variation. We study whether such structured motion representations can be recovered from frozen features of a pretrained image vision transformer. We propose the Structured Dynamics Model (SDM), which explicitly separates the dominant source of temporal change from residual dynamics through future-feature prediction, rather than representing video change with a single entangled latent or with unstructured, spatially dense transition tokens. Training combines self-supervised learning on real video with weak supervision of scene dynamics on synthetic Kubric data. We evaluate SDM on ProbeMotion, a new evaluation suite spanning synthetic and real videos with camera motion, object motion, and combined dynamics. SDM outperforms backbone baselines using global CLS or average-pooled features, and compares favorably to strongly supervised representations such as VGGT on several probes, despite using substantially weaker supervision. These results suggest that pretrained image models can be readily repurposed into structured video-dynamics representations, providing a useful inductive bias for learning and analyzing latent video dynamics.

</details>


### [89] [Synthetic data generation framework for quality control automation in gravure printing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21577)
*Korota Arsène Coulibaly,Mohamed Hamlich,Khalid Hmali,Andrea Trombin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Synthetic data pipeline for rotogravure defect detection; trains RFDETR; achieves 80.9% mAP on real samples; enables zero-cost, rapid deployment without requiring large real-dataset collection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the scarcity of real-world industrial defect images and the high cost of manual labeling, hindering robust deep-learning-based defect inspection in rotogravure printing.

Method: A pipeline that automatically generates high-fidelity images of specific defects (creases, streaks, misregistration, etc.) with corresponding bounding boxes and annotations; produces a synthetic dataset of 7,533 images; trains the RFDETR object detector; evaluates on real industrial testing samples.

Result: Model trained on synthetic data achieves a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 80.9% on real testing samples, indicating good transfer from synthetic to real data.

Conclusion: The proposed framework provides a zero-cost, rapid-deployment solution for automated defect inspection in printing lines, reducing reliance on large-scale manual data collection.

Abstract: Quality control in printing, particularly in rotogravure printing, still depends on slow, costly, and subjective manual inspection. Automated surface defect detection is critical for maintaining high-quality standards in rotogravure printing. Deep learning models give prospects for automation. However, training robust deep learning models, such as YOLO or Vision Transformers, is heavily hindered by the extreme scarcity of real-world industrial defects images. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a novel synthetic data generation framework tailored for rotogravure printing quality control. The proposed pipeline automatically generates high-fidelity images of specific printing defects (creases, streaks, misregistration, etc.) and outputs corresponding bounding boxes and annotations. To validate the framework, a synthetic dataset of 7533 images was generated and used to train the state-of-the-art object-detection model RFDETR. Experimental results demonstrate that the model trained on our synthetic data achieves a Mean Average Precision (mAP) of 80.9\% on real industrial testing samples. This framework provides a zero-cost, rapid-deployment solution for automating defect inspection in printing lines without requiring massive manual data collection.

</details>


### [90] [GraphVid: Interactive Graph-Controllable Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21580)
*Vedant Shah,Onkar Susladkar,Tushar Prakash,Kiet Nguyen,Tianjio Yu,Adheesh Juvekar,Muntasir Waheed,Ismini Lourentzou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GraphVid introduces a graph-conditioned image-to-video model with an interaction-graph interface and GraphVid-Bench dataset to enable interactive, precise multi-subject control, achieving superior controllability and quality with less data/parameters than prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the limitations of text- or trajectory-based controls for multi-object interactions, which are brittle under occlusion/overlap and do not scale well with scene complexity.

Method: Proposes GraphVid, a graph-conditioned video generation framework that uses structured interaction graphs for controllable video synthesis; introduces GraphVid-Bench with relational annotations for training interaction-aware models; demonstrates data- and parameter-efficiency relative to prior Motion-I2V methods.

Result: Achieves substantial improvements: FID reduced by up to 39.9% and FVD reduced by 37.6%; PSNR improves from 9.87 to 15.98; SSIM improves from 0.38 to 0.61, indicating better perceptual quality and stability.

Conclusion: Structured semantic interfaces based on interaction graphs offer a powerful paradigm for controllable video generation, enabling flexible yet precise multi-subject control with efficient training.

Abstract: Controllable video generation remains challenging due to the difficulty of specifying precise multi-object interactions using text prompts or motion-control inputs that primarily constrain pixel movement. In practice, trajectory-based control often requires users to draw accurate tracks for multiple objects, which scales poorly with scene complexity and becomes ambiguous under occlusion or overlap. To enable flexible yet precise multi-subject control, we introduce $\textbf{GraphVid}$, a graph-conditioned image-to-video generation model that enables interactive control through structured interaction graphs. We further curate $\textbf{GraphVid-Bench}$, a large-scale interaction-centric video dataset with structured relational annotations to enable training of interaction-aware video generation models. Despite using substantially less training data and fewer trainable parameters than prior motion-control methods, GraphVid delivers strong controllability and video quality. Compared with Motion-I2V, GraphVid reduces FID by up to 39.9% and FVD by 37.6%, while improving PSNR (9.87=>15.98) and SSIM (0.38=>0.61). Our results highlight the potential of structured semantic interfaces as a powerful paradigm for controllable video generation.

</details>


### [91] [Inference-Time Scaling of Diffusion Models via Progressive Seed Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21591)
*Rogerio Guimaraes,Pietro Perona*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Progressive Seed Pruning (PSP) introduces an inference-time scaling axis for diffusion/flow-matching models by front-loading seed exploration, scoring intermediate denoised estimates, and aggressively pruning seeds to fit a fixed compute budget. This yields better prompt-alignment and GenEval/human scores compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference for diffusion and flow-matching models is highly sensitive to the initial noise seed, and existing approaches often waste compute under fixed memory. A principled method to allocate compute across seeds could improve final quality under a fixed budget.

Method: Evaluate many seeds early to explore trajectories; score intermediate denoised outputs; progressively prune the candidate set so only promising seeds proceed to full denoising; maintain a fixed total number of model evaluations. Validate across diffusion and flow-matching backbones; compare to best-of-N, importance sampling, and tree-search baselines; use GenEval and human evaluations for prompt-alignment.

Result: PSP consistently improves reward-guided seed selection and achieves higher GenEval scores and better human alignment on prompt prompts than the baselines at matched compute.

Conclusion: Front-loading seed exploration with aggressive pruning is an effective inference-time scaling axis for diffusion/flow-matching models, generalizing across backbones and enabling better prompt-alignment under fixed compute budgets; code and project page provided.

Abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching models dominate conditional image generation, yet inference-time scaling for these models is far less developed than for autoregressive language models. Because final quality is highly sensitive to the initial noise seed, many approaches spend extra compute on seed search or resampling under a black-box reward, but typically maintaining a constant memory footprint throughout inference. We show that relaxing this constraint enables an underexplored inference-time scaling axis: by front-loading exploration, evaluating many seeds early, and pruning aggressively, we can use a fixed compute budget more effectively. \emph{Progressive Seed Pruning} (\PSP) scores intermediate denoised estimates and progressively narrows the candidate set so that only promising trajectories are fully denoised, while keeping the total number of model evaluations fixed. Across diffusion and flow-matching backbones, \PSP \ consistently improves reward-guided selection and achieves higher GenEval scores (automated) and better human evaluation on prompt-alignment than best-of-$N$, importance-sampling, and tree-search baselines at matched compute. Project page: https://www.vision.caltech.edu/psp. Code: https://github.com/rogerioagjr/psp.

</details>


### [92] [Unified Video Dense Prediction from Disjoint Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21592)
*Yihong Sun,Seoung Wug Oh,Jiahui Huang,Bharath Hariharan,Joon-Young Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UniD: a unified video model that predicts eight dense scene properties from disjoint, domain-specific datasets using distillation and diffusion-prior bridging, achieving strong generalization and temporal consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Annotations for scene understanding are fragmented across incompatible datasets; full co-annotation or pseudo-labeling is costly. A unified model should leverage disjoint sources to learn multiple properties.

Method: Train per-task experts on their respective datasets; supervise a single unified backbone via lightweight task projectors (distillation); use priors from a pretrained diffusion model to bridge domain gaps across datasets.

Result: UniD is competitive with per-task specialists and multi-task baselines; exhibits strong generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios and improved temporal and cross-task consistency; code/video results available.

Conclusion: A distillation-based UniD framework can learn eight dense scene properties from disjoint sources, leveraging diffusion priors for robust cross-task generalization without overlapping annotations.

Abstract: Scene understanding requires simultaneous prediction about geometry, appearance, and semantics. However, existing task-specific annotations are fragmented across incompatible, domain-specific datasets. Current unified systems circumvent this by restricting training to fully co-annotated data, or by incurring the large computational cost of pseudo-labeling. To mitigate this, we introduce UniD, a unified video model that jointly predicts eight dense scene properties-depth, surface normals, semantic segmentation, boundaries, human parts, albedo, shading, and materials-all learned from disjoint, domain-specific datasets. We propose a simple yet effective distillation step in which per-task experts supervise a unified backbone through lightweight task projectors, eliminating the need for annotation overlap or pseudo-labeling. Our key insight is that the strong visual priors of a pretrained diffusion model are sufficient to bridge the domain gaps introduced by disjoint training sources, enabling robust generalization to scene-task combinations never seen during training. UniD achieves competitive performance against per-task specialists and multi-task baselines, with strong generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios and enhanced temporal and cross-task consistency. Code and video results are available at https://unid-video.github.io/.

</details>


### [93] [Streaming Multi-Agent Autoregressive Diffusion Model with World State Registers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21594)
*Sicheng Mo,Yuheng Li,Ziyang Leng,Krishna Kumar Singh,Bolei Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WorldWeaver (W^2) is a streaming multi-agent video diffusion model that maintains shared world state across agents via learnable tokens updated after each generated chunk, improving consistency in two-agent Minecraft video generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive video diffusion pipelines condition on past observations, making cross-agent world state hard to maintain in multi-agent/multi-view settings; explicit world-state modeling is needed for consistency and coherence.

Method: Introduce world state registers (learnable tokens) that store shared world information and track agent status, dynamically updated per chunk; ground registers with supervision signals over individual agent status, global views (including bird's-eye views) and scene text; employ a Mixture-of-Transformers design with separate weights for world state modeling and visual frame modeling.

Result: Experiments on two-agent Minecraft video generation show that explicit world-state modeling improves logical consistency and generation quality.

Conclusion: Explicit world-state modeling via WorldWeaver enables persistent cross-agent state and improves multi-agent video generation quality and coherence.

Abstract: Multi-agent interactive world models should not only generate consistent observations, but also maintain world states that persist across agents and evolve across views. Existing autoregressive video diffusion pipelines carry forward observation history as conditioning context, which makes shared state difficult to maintain in multi-agent and multi-view settings. We present WorldWeaver (W^2), a streaming multi-agent video diffusion model that augments rollout with cross-agent world state registers: learnable tokens that store shared world information, track individual agent status, and are dynamically updated after each generated chunk. We ground these registers with supervision signals spanning individual agent status, global state views including bird's-eye views, and scene text. We further improve the architecture with a Mixture-of-Transformers design that uses separate weights for world state modeling and visual frame modeling. Extensive experiments in two-agent Minecraft video generation show that explicit world-state modeling improves logical consistency and generation quality.

</details>


### [94] [3D-Aware VLMs with Implicit and Explicit Geometries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21595)
*Wenhao Li,Xueying Jiang,Quanhao Qian,Deli Zhao,Ran Xu,Shijian Lu,Gongjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified RGB-only VLM-IE3D framework that injects implicit and explicit 3D geometry into vision-language models to improve 3D spatial reasoning, via Implicit Geometry Tokens (IGTs), Explicit Geometry Tokens (EGTs), and a 3D-aware adapter; achieves strong performance on 3D tasks and code is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 2D-based VLMs struggle with tasks requiring fine-grained 3D spatial understanding. To close the gap, it is desirable to inject 3D inductive biases learned from RGB videos without extra 3D inputs.

Method: Proposes Implicit Geometry Tokens (IGTs) capturing high-level geometric priors from videos and Explicit Geometry Tokens (EGTs) encoding detailed geometric structures from reconstructed 3D attributes. A 3D-aware adapter fuses 2D cues with both geometric representations. The approach is RGB-only and learns geometric priors from video data.

Result: Extensive experiments show consistent superior performance across 3D tasks: 3D video detection, 3D visual grounding, 3D dense captioning, and spatial reasoning. Code and models are released at the given repository.

Conclusion: The combination of implicit priors and explicit geometric information, integrated via a 3D-aware adapter, provides strong 3D inductive biases for VLMs using only RGB input, enabling improved 3D understanding and reasoning.

Abstract: Despite rapid progress, most existing vision-language models (VLMs) built from 2D visual inputs often struggle when handling various 3D tasks that require fine-grained spatial understanding and reasoning. To bridge this gap, we present VLM-IE3D, a unified framework that enhances the 3D spatial awareness of VLMs by equipping them with both implicit and explicit 3D geometries learned from RGB videos. Our VLM-IE3D introduces Implicit Geometry Tokens (IGTs) that capture high-level geometric priors from input videos, as well as complementary Explicit Geometry Tokens (EGTs) that encode detailed geometric structures from reconstructed 3D attributes. On top of that, VLM-IE3D comes with a 3D-aware adapter that effectively fuses the two types of geometric representations with 2D visual cues. This RGB-only design injects strong 3D inductive biases for fine-grained spatial understanding and reasoning without requiring any additional 3D inputs. Extensive experiments show that VLM-IE3D achieves superior performance consistently across various 3D tasks including 3D video detection, 3D visual grounding, 3D dense captioning, and spatial reasoning. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Vegetebird/VLM-IE3D.

</details>


### [95] [Deblurring in the Wild: A Real-World Image Deblurring Dataset from Smartphone High-Speed Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19445)
*Syed Mumtahin Mahmud,Mahdi Mohd Hossain Noki,Prothito Shovon Majumder,Abdul Mohaimen Al Radi,Sudipto Das Sukanto,Afia Lubaina,Md. Mosaddek Khan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A large real-world smartphone-based long-exposure deblurring dataset with 42k blur-sharp pairs derived from 240-frame sequences; demonstrates SOTA deblurring models underperform on realistic data; provides a challenging benchmark to improve robustness and generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap between synthetic/short-exposure deblurring datasets and real-world blur, which is driven by diverse scenes, camera/object motion, and sensor characteristics; existing datasets are limited in size and variety.

Method: Constructed by recording 240-frame slow-motion clips per scene; blur is simulated by averaging frames across the sequence to create a long-exposure blur, using the temporally centered frame as the sharp reference; collected over 8x more scenes and over 42k image pairs, covering indoor and outdoor environments; benchmarked multiple state-of-the-art deblurring models on this dataset.

Result: State-of-the-art deblurring models show significant performance degradation on the new dataset, indicating higher complexity and diversity than prior benchmarks.

Conclusion: The dataset provides a challenging, realistic benchmark to promote robust and generalizable deblurring models and highlights gaps in current SOTA methods when faced with real-world motion blur.

Abstract: We introduce the largest real-world image deblurring dataset constructed from smartphone slow-motion videos. Using 240 frames captured over one second, we simulate realistic long-exposure blur by averaging frames to produce blurry images, while using the temporally centered frame as the sharp reference. Our dataset contains over 42,000 high-resolution blur-sharp image pairs, making it approximately 10 times larger than widely used datasets, with 8 times the amount of different scenes, including indoor and outdoor environments, with varying object and camera motions. We benchmark multiple state-of-the-art (SOTA) deblurring models on our dataset and observe significant performance degradation, highlighting the complexity and diversity of our benchmark. Our dataset serves as a challenging new benchmark to facilitate robust and generalizable deblurring models.

</details>


<div id='cs.CG'></div>

# cs.CG [[Back]](#toc)

### [96] [Beyond Degree Four: Near-Orthogonal Planar Drawings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21305)
*Patrizio Angelini,Sabine Cornelsen,Giordano Da Lozzo,Seok-Hee Hong,Ignaz Rutter*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: Hardness and algorithmic landscape for planar polyline drawings close to orthogonal. NP-complete to decide if at most h faces are non-orthogonal, even for triconnected graphs; in fixed embedding, linear-time FPT algorithms parameterized by outerplanarity or by h; FPT by treewidth and a PTAS; in variable embedding, FPT by treewidth for biconnected graphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend orthogonal planar drawings (maximum degree 4) to unrestricted-degree graphs by allowing a bounded number of non-orthogonal faces, balancing drawing clarity with computational tractability; analyze complexity and develop parameterized and approximation algorithms.

Method: Prove NP-completeness of the decision problem under a fixed number h of non-orthogonal faces (even for triconnected inputs). Develop linear-time FPT algorithms in the fixed-embedding setting parameterized by outerplanarity index and by h. Provide an FPT algorithm parameterized by treewidth and a polynomial-time approximation scheme. In the variable-embedding setting, give an FPT algorithm parameterized by treewidth for biconnected graphs.

Result: Establishes NP-hardness of near-orthogonal planar polyline drawings and offers a spectrum of tractable algorithms: fixed-embedding FPTs by outerplanarity and by h, treewidth-based FPT, PTAS; variable-embedding FPT by treewidth for biconnected graphs.

Conclusion: The problem is computationally hard in general, but becomes tractable under relevant structural parameters and with approximation schemes. This delineates a clear complexity boundary and guides practical algorithm design for near-orthogonal drawings, while highlighting avenues for future work on other parameters and embedding settings.

Abstract: Orthogonal planar drawings constitute a classical and mainstream research topic in graph drawing due to their clarity and wide applicability. In an orthogonal planar drawing of a graph, each face is represented as an orthogonal polygon, that is, a polygon whose edges are either horizontal or vertical. Yet a planar graph admits such a representation if and only if its maximum degree is at most four.
  In this paper, we consider planar polyline drawings of graphs with unrestricted maximum degree. We focus on drawings that are ``close to orthogonal'', where closeness is measured by the number of faces that are not orthogonal polygons. We show that, even when the input graph is triconnected and thus has a unique planar embedding, the problem of testing whether there exists a planar polyline drawing with at most $h$ non-orthogonal faces is NP-complete. Motivated by this computational hardness, we study parameterized and approximation algorithms. In the fixed-embedding setting, we prove that the problem admits linear-time FPT algorithms parameterized by (i) the outerplanarity index and (ii) the natural parameter $h$. In addition, we provide an FPT algorithm parameterized by the treewidth and a polynomial-time approximation scheme. In the variable-embedding setting, we give an FPT algorithm parameterized by treewidth for biconnected graphs.

</details>

### [97] [AINTMA: Agentic AI Architecture for Autonomous Test Management with Generative Intelligence, Secure Cloud Communication and Adaptive Quality Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20452)
*Vinil Pasupuleti,Shyalendar Reddy Allala,Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu,Shrey Tyagi,Srinivasateja Songa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes AINTMA, an agentic AI system for autonomous test management in cloud-scale environments, achieving high prioritization accuracy, efficiency, defect reduction, and ROI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for autonomous, scalable QA orchestration in distributed cloud environments to reduce manual toil and improve software quality.

Method: Six specialized agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, RL Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, Cloud Security Monitor) coordinate via a secure multi-agent framework atop cloud-native microservices. RL uses a Markov Decision Process with 47 features over a 36-month window; Generative Intelligence uses LLMs for plain-language narratives and recommendations. Security uses zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation.

Result: Empirical evaluation across 12 projects over 18 months: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD) vs 51.2% random and 82.1% best commercial baseline; 43% reduction in test cycle time; defect escape reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback; scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time; generative module rated 4.3/5 by developers.

Conclusion: The agentic AI architecture demonstrates feasibility and potential to transform cloud-scale software quality management, highlighting benefits of autonomous coordination, generative insights, and secure connectivity, while inviting examination of deployment challenges, scalability, governance, and integration in real-world settings.

Abstract: Modern software quality assurance demands intelligent, autonomous systems capable of adaptive decision-making across distributed cloud environments. This paper presents AINTMA (Agentic Intelligent Test Management Architecture), a multi-agent agentic AI system that transforms traditional test management into an autonomous quality intelligence ecosystem. AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, Reinforcement Learning Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, and Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated through a secure multi-agent communication framework over a cloud-native microservices infrastructure. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent employs large language models to produce plain language quality narratives, defect risk summaries, and data-augmented test recommendations. The RL Prioritization agent models test selection as a Markov Decision Process, learning contextual policies from large-scale historical test execution data (47 features, rolling 36-month window). Secure cloud communication is enforced through a zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT authentication, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation. Evaluation across 12 heterogeneous software projects over 18 months demonstrates: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD, vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback. The agentic architecture scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time, and the generative intelligence module achieves 4.3/5.0 developer usefulness rating. AINTMA demonstrates that agentic AI, combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence and secure smart connectivity, can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

</details>


### [98] [Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20462)
*Melanie Rieff,Robin Staab,Thibaud Gloaguen,Stefan Hegselmann,Martin Vechev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Domain-specific evaluation shows LLM watermarks can substantially degrade medical performance across multiple failure modes, highlighting the need for expert-audited, domain-tailored benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing watermark evaluations rely on general-purpose benchmarks and overlook medicine-specific risks, where small token perturbations can cause large semantic shifts and misinterpretation of findings. The study argues for domain-aware auditing to ensure safe deployment of watermarked models in clinical settings.

Method: Benchmarked 5 watermarking schemes on 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs across unimodal and multimodal clinical tasks. Introduced a human-expert-validated pipeline to audit medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and hallucinations, assessing lexical integrity, terminology accuracy, and image finding attribution.

Result: Watermarking induces substantial degradation in medical performance across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and misattribution/omission of image findings. Aggregate metrics can mask domain-specific failures absent in standard benchmarks; domain-specific analyses are necessary to reveal practical degradations.

Conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is essential for the safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine; relying solely on general benchmarks can mask clinically consequential failures.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, stressing the need for reliable traceability of model-generated output with watermarking. Yet, most watermarks are evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks, leaving domains like medicine, where small token-level perturbations can result in significant semantic changes, underexplored. In this work, we present the first rigorous study of how LLM watermarks affect medical performance, benchmarking 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on various tasks spanning unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning. Importantly, we complement existing evaluations by introducing a human-expert-validated pipeline for systematically auditing medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and induced hallucinations. Our results reveal that watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings. Notably, we find that the absence of domain-specific analyses, combined with aggregate metrics that miss failures inherent to clinical text, can systematically obscure practical watermark-induced degradations. Our findings establish domain-specific evaluation as a prerequisite for the safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine, where current benchmarks can otherwise mask clinically consequential failures.

</details>


### [99] [ClickGuard: Detecting and Spoiling Clickbait News with Informativeness Measures and Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20463)
*Wojciech Michaluk,Tymoteusz Urban,Mateusz Kubita,Soveatin Kuntur,Anna Wróblewska*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid AI approach for clickbait detection via a browser extension achieving F1 0.91 on an open dataset; provides pre/post warnings, explanations, and a spoiler summary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address pervasive clickbait and improve user protection by moving beyond traditional detectors; enable real-time warnings and transparent explanations within a browser extension.

Method: Hybrid architecture: transformer-based embeddings, linguistically motivated features, and a custom 'baitness' score; evaluation across classic vectorizers and LLM embeddings; final model is XGBoost-based; uses open combined dataset; extension warns before/after article access, outputs a probability, explains predictions using developed metrics, and provides a one-to-two-sentence spoiler of the article.

Result: F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset; real-time warnings before and after article access; post-access likelihood score; explanation based on analyzed metrics; spoiler text; demo video provided.

Conclusion: Demonstrates practical feasibility of real-time clickbait detection in a browser extension; hybrid feature set and XGBoost yield strong performance; supports user guidance and transparency through explanations and spoilers.

Abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven browser extension that identifies clickbait to help users avoid misleading Internet articles. Moving beyond traditional detection, the application employs a hybrid machine learning architecture that combines transformer-based embeddings with linguistically motivated features and a custom "baitness" score. After evaluating various natural language processing techniques -- from classic vectorizers to large language model (LLM) embeddings -- an XGBoost-based model was developed that achieves an F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset. Most importantly, the tool can warn users before and after they access a clickbait article. After opening an article, the user receives a percentage score indicating the likelihood that it is clickbait. The prediction is explained based on the analyzed metrics, including those specifically developed within the proposed system. The browser extension also provides a clickbait spoiler -- a one- to two-sentence summary of the entire article. Demo video:https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4}{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4

</details>


### [100] [Stochastic Sampling is Epistemically Shallow: The Dimensionality Gap Between Temperature Variation and Model Diversity in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20464)
*Izhar Ali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-consistency isolates per-question uncertainty but fails to reveal cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble reveals cross-question gaps in model knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether repetition-induced variation in LLM responses contains cross-question structure and assess whether self-consistency or a diverse ensemble better surfaces what a model does not know; use random-matrix tests to separate signal from noise.

Method: Two regimes on the same questions: (1) 100 runs of a single model at τ=1; (2) an ensemble of 24 LLMs run once each at τ=0. Apply Marchenko–Pastur random-matrix test to separate signal from sampling noise. Evaluate across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K). Include a matched-difficulty Bernoulli null with Monte Carlo draws to set noise. Compare per-question uncertainty vs cross-question structure.

Result: Within a single model, at most one dimension rises above noise across the tested families/benchmarks. Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues exceed the noise edge, while the Bernoulli null yields at most one in 500 Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency provides accurate per-question uncertainty but shows no detectable cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces cross-question knowledge gaps.

Conclusion: Self-consistency is effective for per-question uncertainty estimation; to reveal cross-question structure and inter-question dependencies, use a diverse ensemble of models.

Abstract: When a language model gives different answers on repeated runs, does that variation reveal what it does not know? Self-consistency turns the variation into a per-question uncertainty estimate via majority voting. But does the same variation reveal cross-question structure -- related questions flipping together, the way a diverse ensemble does? We compare two regimes on the same questions: one model run $100$ times at $τ=1$ versus an ensemble of $24$ LLMs run once each at $τ=0$. A Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix test separates signal from sampling noise on both sides. Within any single model, at most one dimension rises above noise across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K). Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge, while a matched-difficulty Bernoulli null produces at most one in $500$ Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency gives accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces what a model does not know.

</details>


### [101] [JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20466)
*Arya Tschand,Charles Hong,Julian Walker,Nina Cai,Shangkun Wang,Suvinay Subramanian,Sundar Dev,Vijay Janapa Reddi,Amir Yazdanbakhsh,Sethu Sankaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JAXBench is a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs, featuring 50 JAX workloads, 17 production operators from public architectures, 33 translated KernelBench operators, eight hand-tuned Pallas kernels, and evaluation of four feedback-driven generation methods; results show target-specific context and documentation significantly boost correctness and speedups, with Autocomp and beam-search approaching or exceeding XLA baselines; the work releases benchmark and harness for open source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the absence of standardized TPU kernel optimization benchmarks analogous to GPU benchmarks, enabling reproducible evaluation of AI-driven kernel generation methods and toward optimized TPU performance.

Method: Construct JAXBench with 50 JAX workloads; extract 17 production operators from MaxText-architectures (Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, AlphaFold2); translate 33 KernelBench operators with new problem sizes to achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization; include 8 hand-tuned Pallas kernels from Tokamax; evaluate four feedback-driven methods for generating Pallas kernels on Gemini 3 Flash; measure per-sample correctness and speedups relative to XLA; analyze impact of target context vs model scale; release benchmark and evaluation harness.

Result: Conditioning on curated TPU documentation increases per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks with 1.28x geometric mean speedup; a search-structure approach (Autocomp with beam-search) yields 1.36x geometric mean speedup over XLA; on eight hand-tuned kernels Autocomp achieves 1.60x over XLA, nearly matching the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but lagging on specialized paged and ragged attention; overall, high-quality TPU kernel optimization remains challenging.

Conclusion: JAXBench provides an open-source benchmark suite and evaluation framework to drive and compare TPU kernel optimization approaches, highlights the importance of target-specific context and accessible TPU documentation, and invites community contributions.

Abstract: Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel performance optimization by establishing a shared target to hillclimb on, but no equivalent exists for TPUs. We present JAXBench, a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs. JAXBench comprises 50 JAX workloads that are both relevant and provide headroom for optimization. We extract 17 production ML operators from architectures in the public MaxText library such as Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, and AlphaFold2, and translate 33 operators from KernelBench that are validated for correctness and set with new problem sizes that achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight of the 17 production operators ship with hand-optimized Pallas kernels from the public Tokamax library and block-size tuned to establish an expert upper-bound baseline. We evaluate four feedback-driven methods on generating candidate Pallas kernels for JAXBench. Across the full suite with Gemini 3 Flash, we find that target-specific context matters more than model scale on a sparsely-documented DSL like Pallas. Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks at a 1.28x geomean speedup. Search structure yields significant gains once correctness is achieved, with Autocomp's beam-search pipeline reaching a 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on the specialized paged and ragged attention operators. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains a challenging task, and we release the JAXBench benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results to support open source contributions.

</details>


### [102] [DC-Leap: Training-Free Acceleration of dLLMs via Draft-Guided Contiguous Leaping Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20467)
