*Yanhua Jiao,Tianyi Wu,Xiaoxi Sun,Yulin Li,HuiLing Zhen,Libo Qin,Baotian Hu,Zhuotao Tian,Min Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DC-Leap is a training-free framework enabling reliable, fast parallel decoding for diffusion LLMs in moderate-confidence regimes by addressing JPDE with Dynamic Contiguous Verification and draft-guided look-ahead, achieving large speedups with comparable quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current parallel decoding suffers from Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE) due to conservative confidence thresholds, hindering speedups; a training-free solution is desirable to accelerate dLLMs without fine-tuning.

Method: Introduce Dynamic Contiguous Verification (DCV) to enforce strictly ordered causal constraints during parallel decoding, progressively validating token dependencies to neutralize JPDE; integrate draft-guided decoding to extend context by leaping forward across multiple tokens while preserving bidirectional attention; option to combine with KV-Cache.

Result: Experiments show substantial speedups: up to 53.19x on MBPP long-sequence generation; up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache; generation quality remains comparable to baseline.

Conclusion: DC-Leap offers training-free, reliable acceleration for diffusion LLMs in moderate-confidence regimes by mitigating JPDE through dynamic verification and enabling look-ahead with drafts, with public code available.

Abstract: While parallel decoding is central to the efficiency of Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs), current strategies are often hindered by overly conservative confidence thresholds. These thresholds, necessitated by the Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE), result in redundant denoising iterations and suboptimal inference speeds. To overcome this, we propose DC-Leap, a training-free framework that enables reliable acceleration of dLLMs in the moderate-confidence regime. DC-Leap introduces a Dynamic Contiguous Verification strategy that integrates strictly-ordered causal constraints into the parallel decoding process. By progressively validating token dependencies, this mechanism effectively neutralizes the JPDE, enabling reliable acceleration with comparable performance. Furthermore, DC-Leap incorporates the draft-guided decoding mechanism, where the draft helps extend the context by leaping forward across multiple tokens, providing look-ahead context and retaining the structural benefits of bidirectional attention during inference. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that DC-Leap achieves substantial speedups, up to 53.19x on MBPP for long-sequence generation, and up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache with comparable generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/ffh-wyls/DC-Leap .

</details>


### [103] [InferenceBench: A Benchmark for Open-Ended LLM Inference Optimization by AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468)
*Jehyeok Yeon,Ben Rank,Maksym Andriushchenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InferenceBench tests AI agents in optimizing the speed of OpenAI-compatible LLM inference under time constraints, revealing gains over naive baselines but limited by lack of exploration of diverse configurations; memorization remains a barrier in open-ended AI engineering tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmarks often reward memorized recipes or narrow action spaces, making it hard to assess genuine optimization. There is a need to evaluate agents in open-ended AI engineering tasks that require proposing and testing diverse configurations.

Method: Four optimization scenarios targeting prefill latency, decode latency, concurrent throughput, and a balanced combination; 15 frontier agent configurations; one H100 GPU; a two-hour wall-clock budget; task: deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize inference speed.

Result: Agents improve over a naive PyTorch baseline (up to 8.08×); often match or exceed default-config serving engines (e.g., vLLM at 4.05×); however, a simple hyperparameter search within the same budget can reach up to 11.53×, exceeding the best agent performance; qualitative analysis shows convergence on a single inference framework and limited exploration of configurations, with much budget spent on re-measurement and hyperparameter tuning rather than exploring diverse strategies.

Conclusion: Open-ended AI engineering tasks are constrained by limited diversity in proposed configurations; genuine progress requires agents to generate and systematically evaluate a broader set of configurations, rather than relying on memorized solutions.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly used to automate research and development tasks, yet existing benchmarks typically evaluate them on prescribed workflows or narrow action spaces. Even nominally open-ended tasks can often be solved by retrieving a well-known recipe and tuning a few hyperparameters, making it unclear whether strong results reflect genuine optimization or memorized solutions. We introduce InferenceBench, where an agent must deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize the speed of LLM inference. Each agent receives a target LLM, one H100 GPU, an optimization scenario, and a wall-clock time budget of two hours. Three optimization scenarios isolate distinct bottlenecks of inference (prefill latency, decode latency, and concurrent request throughput) and a fourth balances all three at the same time. Across 15 frontier agent configurations, agents reliably improve over a naive PyTorch baseline (up to $8.08\times$) and often match or exceed serving engines with default settings ($4.05\times$ for vLLM), but still fall below a simple hyperparameter search under the same time budget (up to $11.53\times$). Qualitative analysis of agent trajectories shows that although agents enumerate many relevant optimization techniques, they overwhelmingly converge on a single inference framework. They test only a few distinct configurations and spend the remaining budget re-measuring, repairing, or optimizing hyperparameters rather than exploring substantially different strategies. This suggests the bottleneck is not domain knowledge, but the ability to propose diverse configurations, evaluate them systematically, and submit the best identified solution. Overall, InferenceBench reflects the ability of agents to operate in an open-ended AI engineering setting, where memorized solutions lead to limited improvements.

</details>


### [104] [DecodeShare: Tracing the Shared Subspace of LLM Decode-Time Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20469)
*Zishan Shao,Lixun Zhang,Kangning Cui,Yixiao Wang,Ting Jiang,Hancheng Ye,Qinsi Wang,Zhixu Du,Yuzhe Fu,Fan Yang,Danyang Zhuo,Yiran Chen,Hai Helen Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DecodeShare identifies a shared, low-dimensional subspace in decode-time hidden states across tasks in KV-cached LLMs. Removing this subspace during decoding degrades performance far more than removing subspaces derived from prefill or random baselines, indicating a task-general decode-time channel. Projection of this subspace separates decode-time functional roles from prefill effects, and decoding-time activation steering signals yield more reliable downstream signals than prefill proxies. Code is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To uncover whether a task-general, decode-time structure governs decision making in KV-cached LLMs and to establish a causal link between a decode-time subspace and task performance, with implications for interpretability and deployment.

Method: Identify a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states. Test causality by removing that subspace only during decoding (not prefill). Compare against removals of subspaces derived from prefill or random baselines under equal intervention budgets. Examine overlap with the decode-time channel and steering directions. Evaluate impact on task performance and on downstream deployment reliability, and study the benefits of decoding-time rather than prefill-based steering.

Result: Disturbing the decode-time shared subspace degrades task performance far more than disturbing prefill-derived or random subspaces under the same budget. The shared subspace aligns with the decode-time channel and enables high-leverage causal control. Projecting it out separates the functional roles of decode-time and prefill components. Activation steering signals evaluated at decode time provide more reliable downstream signals than prefill proxies. Code implementing DecodeShare is released.

Conclusion: There exists a compact, high-leverage decode-time causal channel shared across tasks. DecodeShare offers a practical method to identify and manipulate this channel, with implications for interpretability, steering, and robust deployment in KV-cached LLM workflows.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) handle many tasks with one set of parameters, but under KV-cached inference it is unclear what task-general structure, if any, is used at decode time rather than during prefill. We propose DecodeShare, a protocol that identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, and then tests its causal role by removing that subspace only during decoding. In our experiments, disturbing the discovered shared subspace degrades decision performance far more than disturbing either a prefill-derived or random subspace under the same intervention budget. We further show this decode-shared subspace has practical consequences for activation steering: common steering directions can overlap the task-general decode channel. Projecting out this shared subspace directly separates the functional roles of the two components, while evaluating steering vectors at decode-time yields more reliable signal for downstream deployment than prefill-based proxies. Despite its compactness, the shared subspace can serve as a high-leverage causal channel at decode time. Code is available at: https://github.com/Zishan-Shao/decodeshare.git.

</details>


### [105] [PlanE: Meta Planning of Data, Tuning, and Inference for Extractive-based LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20470)
*Jiacheng Wang,Weiyan Zhang,Guangya Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PlanE: A planning framework with data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference to build task-tuned LLMs, plus a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner that selects the best base-LLM and DTI configuration for a dataset; validated across datasets and base models; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce annotation costs and optimize task-specific LLM adaptation by introducing a planning-based data decomposition, tuning, and inference approach.

Method: Propose PlanE framework (data decomposition, instruction tuning, prompt inference) and the DTI planner to choose optimal base-LLM and DTI configurations for given datasets; comprehensive experiments across datasets and base LLMs; assess generalizability under varying objectives; provide open-source code.

Result: PlanE yields improved construction efficiency and task-specific performance across different datasets and base LLMs; the DTI planner demonstrates generalizability to different optimization objectives.

Conclusion: PlanE and the DTI planner offer a scalable, generalizable approach to efficient, data-aware LLM tailoring with reduced annotation costs; code is publicly available.

Abstract: Enhancing the task-specific capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily requires substantial instruction-tuning datasets. However, the sheer volume of such data imposes a considerable annotation cost, and a lack of optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks. To address the above issues, we propose a \textbf{Plan}ning framework for constructing \textbf{E}xtractive-based LLMs called \textbf{PlanE}, which includes data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner, aimed at selecting the optimal base-LLM and its DTI combinations for specific datasets to improve construction efficiency. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our PlanE from two views: (1) across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. Furthermore, we validate the generalizability of the proposed DTI planner under different optimization objectives. The codes are publicly available at https://github.com/gugugu-469/PlanE.

</details>


### [106] [Benchmarking the Personalization Capabilities of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20471)
*Ashutosh Srivastava,Siddharth Yedlapati,Vinay Aggarwal,Yaman Kumar Singla,Shashwat Dixit,Jitendra Ajmera,Balaji Krishnamurthy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Bayesian Persuasion is extended to generative agents in sales to study true two-party personalization; introduces SDR-Bench/Arena; reveals a plateau in personalization across models and practical usefulness validated by field reps; datasets released for reproducible research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To rigorously evaluate genuine two-party personalization by generative models, addressing the gap between sender-side personalization and actual influence on a target receiver, and to provide reproducible benchmarks using a Bayesian persuasion framework.

Method: Adapt Bayesian Persuasion to generative agents; build SDR-Bench: 6,279 customer success stories across 22 industries, ~200 enterprises, with a temporally constrained simulation to prevent data leakage; evaluate across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents; log receiver actions; field test with 12 sales reps; publish SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench for reproducibility.

Result: Consistent personalization plateau across models; no Fortune 100 tech cohort model distinguishes successful vs unsuccessful outreach; field deployment: 48% of model content rated immediately useful; senior-expert agreement (Pearson r=0.82); results support releasing resources for reproducible analysis.

Conclusion: Generative personalization remains limited under the current evaluation framework; two-party persuasion measurements align with a plateau in actionable impact; public data releases (SDR-Arena/SD-Bench) enable broader, reproducible scrutiny and method refinement.

Abstract: Personalization, the act of varying a message to induce action from a specific receiver while keeping sender, channel, and time fixed, has a long tradition in psychology and marketing as a two-party problem in which sender and receiver have independent objectives. Large language models remove the bounded-inventory constraint of classical retrieval-and-ranking approaches by generating a continuum of message variants conditioned on inferred receiver state, raising the question of how well current models perform personalization in the classical sense. Existing LLM personalization benchmarks measure sender-side adaptation, in which the receiver is the same user the model is serving. The two-party question, whether a generated message induces its intended action in a third party, has been investigated only through A/B tests and small-scale human studies that cannot be re-run against a new model on demand. We adapt the Bayesian Persuasion framework of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) to generative agents and instantiate the formulation in sales, where receiver actions are routinely logged against the outreach that induced them. We release SDR-Bench, a public corpus of 6,279 customer success stories spanning 22 industries and approximately 200 enterprises, served through a temporally constrained simulation that prevents future-data leakage. Across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, we observe a consistent personalization plateau and on a Fortune 100 tech cohort no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach. A field deployment with 12 professional sales representatives validates the framework, with 48 percent of model-generated content rated immediately useful and senior-expert agreement at Pearson 0.82. We release SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench publicly to support reproducible study of generative personalization at scale.

</details>


### [107] [Robust Critics: Defending LLMs Against Multi-Turn Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20472)
*Roman Belaire,Arunesh Sinha,Pradeep Varakantham*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DCGS is an intent-aware, critic-guided sampling framework for safer multi-turn dialogue. It infers user intent at every turn, uses token- and utterance-level critics to score responses, and optimizes via exponential-tilting-like reweighting to improve safety. It outperforms baselines on adversarial dialogue benchmarks and transfers to frontier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ambiguity in user intent (harmful vs. harmless) and evolving intent across turns makes safety hard; fixed rules are brittle and context-insensitive; a trajectory-aware method with theoretical guarantees is needed.

Method: Model adversarial dialogue as an MDP; learn value and regret-based critics at token and utterance levels; employ an action-value critic to score candidate responses; perform inference-time reweighting (exponential tilting-like) to bias responses; evaluate on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, Harmbench; demonstrate transferability to frontier models.

Result: DCGS outperforms robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks; improves robustness of frontier models without fine-tuning across multiple benchmarks.

Conclusion: Intent-aware, critic-guided sampling enhances safety in adversarial dialogue; provides theoretical guarantees via exponential tilting approximation; demonstrates practical transfer to other models without retraining.

Abstract: When a user asks a language model something harmful, is it a genuine attack or a misunderstood but well-meaning question? This ambiguity is one of the central challenges of LLM safety. A model that assumes the worst harms legitimate users; one that assumes the best is easily exploited. The problem is compounded in multi-turn dialogue, where an attacker's true intent may only reveal itself gradually across many exchanges, yet existing safety frameworks apply a contextual bandit treatment, ignoring the trajectory of the conversation.
  To that end, we propose Dialogue Critic Guided Sampling (DCGS), a framework that addresses this by inferring user intent at every turn of dialogue. Instead of applying a fixed rule about what is or is not safe, DCGS learns what the user's intent is likely to be based on the full conversational history and generates responses accordingly. Formally, we model adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process and learn value and regret-based critics at both the individual token and utterance (full response) levels, scoring candidate responses via an action-value critic. We prove that this inference-time reweighting approximates exponential tilting of the base policy, guaranteeing improvement in expected return for any finite candidate pool, a property that group-relative objectives do not exhibit. Evaluated on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench, DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks. DCGS also transfers to frontier models, improving their robustness without fine-tuning.

</details>


### [108] [Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20473)
*Yeonjea Kim,Bumjin Park,Jaesik Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Incomplete prompts can trigger harmful continuations in open-weight LLMs; training refusals alone fails to generalize across domains; identifies termination and continuation neurons as avenues for precise defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Formalize incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ), systematically characterize when/how incomplete prompts elicit harmful outputs, and understand model defenses at behavioral and neuronal levels.

Method: Empirical analysis across attractor types for incomplete sentence continuations; measure refusal timing; evaluate parameter-tuning defenses across content domains and attractor types; analyze internal neurons to identify termination and continuation neurons.

Result: LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination; incomplete prompts can induce harmful continuations; naive defense via parameter tuning lacks cross-domain/generalization; two functional neurons (termination and continuation) implicated in sentence completion; neuron-level interventions proposed as a path to robust IPJ defenses.

Conclusion: A neuron-level perspective offers targeted IPJ defenses; generalization across domains remains a challenge; future work should explore precise interventions at termination/continuation pathways to improve robustness.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly released as open-weight models with safeguards against harmful requests. Nevertheless, sentence completion remains vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts. In this work, we formalize this phenomenon as incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ) and provide a systematic empirical characterization of when and how incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations. We analyze diverse attractor types associated with incomplete sentence continuation and show that LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination. We further demonstrate that training models to refuse incomplete harmful prompts via parameter tuning is insufficient, failing to generalize across both content domains and attractor types. To enable fine-grained control, we identify two functional neurons: termination and continuation neurons. By clarifying their roles in sentence completion, we highlight the potential of neuron-level interventions for more precise and robust IPJ defenses.

</details>


### [109] [VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20474)
*Sumaya Abdul Rahman,Seckhen Ariel Andrade Cuellar,Ghani Raissov,Mohammad Raza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriSimpl leverages simplification-based verification in a solver-backed LLM loop to translate natural language into optimization formulations with higher accuracy and a high-precision self-verification signal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NL-to-optimization methods risk generating incorrect formulations that may execute but fail to implement the intended task; robust verification is needed to align formulations with task descriptions.

Method: Introduce simplification-based verification: use an optimization solver to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation; the LLM reasons about correctness under fixed global context; develop strategies across constraints and decision variables to enable local reasoning; operates in an iterative verification framework.

Result: Empirical evaluations on optimization benchmarks show consistent accuracy gains over prior methods; also yields a novel high-precision self-verification signal for the candidate formulations.

Conclusion: VeriSimpl provides a robust framework for NL-to-optimization formalization, improving correctness and trust by integrating solver-driven diagnostics and LLM-based reasoning, with a reliable self-verification mechanism.

Abstract: Natural language interfaces can greatly benefit the accessibility and usability of optimization modeling, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) show promise in automatically translating textual problem descriptions into executable solver formulations. However, a key challenge for existing approaches is to ensure that the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, even if it may execute without errors. We introduce VeriSimpl, a solver LLM framework for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization. Our approach is based on the idea of simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver is leveraged to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation to allow the LLM to tractably reason about the correctness of the formulation with respect to the task description. We present such simplification strategies along different dimensions with respect to problem constraints and decision variables, which allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks show how our approach provides consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, while also providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

</details>


### [110] [SonicSampler: Unified Tile-Aware Kernels for LLM Sampling and Speculative Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20475)
*Pragaash Ponnusamy,Shivam Sahni,Jue Wang,Tri Dao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A unified, tile-aware Triton kernel suite (SonicSampler) that fuses the full LLM sampling pipeline into a single batched kernel, enabling dynamic per-request decoding and CUDA Graph compatibility, achieving up to 10x–16x speedups over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM sampling pipelines are fragmented across multiple kernels and often assume homogeneous batch behavior, hindering dynamic serving workloads and efficient CUDA Graph execution.

Method: Introduce SonicSampler with tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuse logit processing, token selection, and verification into a single batched kernel. Support dynamic per-request sampling behaviors (grammar-constrained decoding, repetition and penalties, logit bias, temperature, top-k/top-p/min-p filtering, speculative verification). Employ a hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm that exploits low-entropy output to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies. Ensure CUDA Graph compatibility and operate within a fixed, workload-aware execution model.

Result: Achieves up to 10x speedup over competitive baselines for top-k processing; up to 16x speedup across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads compared to state-of-the-art baselines; maintains flexible batched execution and CUDA Graph compatibility.

Conclusion: SonicSampler delivers a unified, high-performance, and flexible end-to-end sampling solution for LLM inference, enabling dynamic per-request decoding patterns through a fused kernel design, a novel top-k strategy, and graph-friendly execution.

Abstract: Sampling in LLM inference comprises a combinatorial set of logit processing, token selection, and verification operations for speculative decoding. However, existing implementations either accelerate only subsets of this pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling behavior across a batch, limiting support for dynamic serving workloads and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution. We present $\textbf{SonicSampler}$, a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Our kernels support dynamic per-request sampling behaviors, including grammar-constrained decoding, repetition, frequency and presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-$k$ / top-$p$ / min-$p$ filtering, and speculative verification - within a single batched kernel while remaining fully CUDA Graph-compatible. Central to our approach is a novel hierarchical two-stage top-$k$ algorithm that achieves up to $\textbf{10x speedup}$ over competitive baselines and exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to $\textbf{16x speedup}$ over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.

</details>


### [111] [Benchmarking Large Language Models on Multi-Sensor Physical Hazard Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20476)
*Faizan Iqbal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Five LLMs fail to issue precautionary warnings in multi-sensor hazard settings below individual limits, but perform well on single-sensor thresholds; formatting (tabular vs prose) generally does not improve detection, though ChatGPT-4o benefits from prose; implications for safety-monitoring deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmark multisensor physical hazard assessment by LLMs to identify safety gaps and risk of missed precautions in real-time monitoring systems.

Method: Evaluate five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) across 60 scenarios spanning three categories (multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, pattern disambiguation) with 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0; compare formatting (prose vs structured) and report category-wise scores and a statistical comparison (p=0.001) for prose vs tabular performance.

Result: Category A multi-sensor scenarios yield near-zero warning/decision scores (Q2: 0.000–0.208; Q3: 0.000–0.592) across all five models; Category B single-sensor threshold violations yield high accuracy (Q1: 0.975–1.000). Tabular vs prose formatting shows no consistent advantage; ChatGPT-4o shows significantly better performance with prose (p=0.001). Overall, models failed to emit precautionary signals when multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated but below individual safety limits, raising safety concerns for physical monitoring deployments.

Conclusion: There is a critical safety risk in multisensor hazard assessment by current LLMs when sub-threshold, multi-sensor elevations occur. Deployments should incorporate explicit guardrails, sensor-fusion-aware prompting, or secondary verification, and further research should focus on improving multi-sensor risk-signal recognition and calibration across model families.

Abstract: We present an empirical benchmark evaluating how five large language models assess multisensor physical hazard data. Testing 60 scenarios across three categories - multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation - with 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0, we find that all tested models consistently produced no precautionary warning signal across the tested scenarios where multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below their individual safety limits, while achieving near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations. All five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) score near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) compared to strong performance on single-sensor scenarios (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Structured tabular formatting shows no consistent advantage over plain prose; ChatGPT-4o performs significantly better under prose (p = 0.001). These findings have direct implications for practitioners deploying the tested models in physical safety monitoring systems.

</details>


### [112] [Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20477)
*Yurui Lai,Samir Moustafa,Renchi Yang,Tsz Nam Chan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes algo, a Wasserstein Distance-guided semi-supervised framework for Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) that handles scalability issues with LLMs via a graph-text collaborative encoding, dual-pathway encoders, and WSD-based graph sketching plus an LLM-based text synthesis module, achieving strong performance with high compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TAGs combine graph topology with rich text, but existing representation learning methods struggle with scalability when interfacing with LLMs, face label scarcity in semi-supervised settings, and fail to produce human-readable textual attributes for downstream LLM tasks. A data-centric, scalable solution is needed that captures graph-text interplay and yields readable summaries for condensed nodes.

Method: Introduce a graph-text collaborative encoding module with dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and graph-free) operating within a collaborative self-training loop to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. Develop a theoretically grounded Wasserstein Distance (WSD)-based graph sketching algorithm. Implement a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module that uses cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes.

Result: Experimental results on benchmark TAG datasets show state-of-the-art performance with a favorable performance-compression trade-off for both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, demonstrating effective and efficient TAG learning/analytics under the proposed framework.

Conclusion: algo enables scalable, LLM-friendly TAG learning by integrating WSD-based graph sketching and text synthesis with collaborative self-training, yielding accurate pseudo-labels and readable summaries that facilitate downstream tasks.

Abstract: {\em Text-Attributed Graphs} (TAGs) have emerged as an expressive data model for integrating graph topology with rich textual semantics. Existing representation learning methods over TAGs suffer from severe scalability bottlenecks, particularly together with {\em Large Language Models} (LLMs). While data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution, existing methods fail to capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, struggle with the label scarcity inherent in semi-supervised settings, and lack the ability to produce the human-readable textual attributes required for downstream LLM-based tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose \algo{}, a unified semi-supervised framework guided by the {\em Wasserstein Distance} (WSD). Grounded in our empirical findings on real TAGs, \algo{} introduces a graph-text collaborative encoding module that utilizes dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and -free) within a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. Furthermore, we develop a theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm and a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module, which leverages cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that \algo{} achieves a state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off in terms of both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning or analytics.

</details>


### [113] [Beyond Liars' Bench: The Impact of Lie Typology, Depth, and Sparsity on Deception Detection in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20479)
*Amr Moustafa,Max Feser,Florian Mai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Detection probes for LLM deception are highly dataset- and representation-dependent; training data type crucial for detectability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why deception-detection probes fail out-of-domain and identify factors influencing performance.

Method: Augment benchmark data with diverse deception (fabrication, omission, exaggeration); assess seven probe types across factors: representation depth, expressivity, sparse features, lie typology.

Result: Depth optimal varies by dataset; expressive probes provide limited gains beyond linear baselines; sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense features; training data and lie typology significantly affect detection performance.

Conclusion: Deception detection is highly dependent on representation and training data; robust detection requires careful consideration of lie typology and dataset composition; cross-domain generalization remains challenging.

Abstract: Training probes to detect deceptive outputs from large language models is still an open problem. Recent work has demonstrated that detection probes fail especially in out-of-domain scenarios -- training on one type of lie does not transfer well to deception scenarios involving other types of lies. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on how various factors impact detection performance: representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations, and the lie typology of the training data. To this end, we augment standard benchmark training data with a supplementary dataset containing diverse types of deception, including fabrication, omission, and exaggeration examples. Analyzing these factors across seven probe types, our experimental results show that the optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent, more expressive probes provide only selective gains over linear baselines, and sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the choice of training data and lie typology substantially changes detectability, highlighting that deception detection is a highly representation-dependent problem.

</details>


### [114] [Enabling Scalable Topology Inference in Distribution Systems via Constrained Multi-Source Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20480)
*Haoran Li,Lihao Mai,Muhao Guo,Jiaqi Wu,Yang Weng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Constrained inference to refine a base distribution topology using heterogeneous evidence and physical constraints, achieving high accuracy with localized reconnections and a falsification-driven reliability metric; scalable and robust in dense feeders compared to correlation-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable topology records are difficult due to heterogeneous/imperfect utility data; existing methods relying on electrical similarity or spatial data underperform in dense feeders; a scalable, feasible topology identification framework is needed.

Method: Formulate topology identification as constrained inference that refines a base topology. Detect inconsistencies, perform localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods, and iteratively enforce physical feasibility. Leverage heterogeneous evidence (electrical measurements, spatial metadata, operational constraints). Introduce a falsification-driven reliability metric to quantify support for each inferred link while guiding verification priority.

Result: Validated on three feeders with over 8,000 AMI meters; topology reconstruction accuracy >95%; significant reduction in computation compared with global inference. Correlation-based methods alone yield ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders; integrating electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints yields robust, scalable topology recovery under realistic deployments.

Conclusion: The framework yields operationally consistent topology estimates at scale, with a reliability metric to prioritize field verification. The study demonstrates that combining measurements with spatial/operational constraints outperforms purely correlation-based approaches, enabling robust topology recovery in challenging deployment conditions.

Abstract: Accurate distribution system topology is essential for outage localization, voltage analytics, and operation of distribution grids, yet maintaining reliable connectivity records remains challenging in practice due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing topology identification methods often rely primarily on electrical similarity or spatial records alone, which become unreliable in dense feeders and under inconsistent metadata conditions. This paper formulates distribution topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines a utility-provided base topology using heterogeneous evidence while enforcing spatial feasibility and physical operational constraints. Instead of reconstructing connectivity from scratch, the proposed framework detects inconsistent assignments, performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods to ensure scalability, and iteratively enforces physical feasibility to produce operationally consistent topology estimates. In addition, a falsification-driven reliability metric evaluates how strongly each inferred connection is supported relative to alternative feasible assignments, enabling utilities to prioritize verification efforts while preserving system-wide observability. The framework is validated using operational data from three feeders comprising more than $8{,}000$ AMI meters in collaboration with a large U.S. utility. Results demonstrate over $95\%$ topology reconstruction accuracy while significantly reducing computational effort compared with global inference approaches. The study further shows that correlation-based methods alone produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, whereas combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust and scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions.

</details>


### [115] [Routing Without Training: Controllable-Ratio LLM Offloading via Reliability Gating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20481)
*Evan Chen,Shiqiang Wang,Kevin S Chan,Su Wang,Christopher Brinton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A training-free routing framework (CARGO) uses the local model's inference-time agreement across prompt-varied samples to decide when to offload to cloud, with Bayesian early stopping and deployment-time calibration, outperforming training-free baselines and, in some cases, supervised routers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Eliminate the need for trained routers or finetuning to enable local-cloud collaboration for LLMs, by leveraging the local model's own response consistency as a signal for when to defer to cloud models.

Method: Prompt-varied sampling to estimate agreement between local responses; Bayesian early stopping to control uncertainty with few samples; deployment-time calibration to support arbitrary target collaboration ratios; designed to work across diverse tasks, model families, and both pretrained and finetuned locals.

Result: CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and, in several settings, surpasses supervised learned routers across multiple tasks, model scales, and local model types.

Conclusion: Effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge from the local model's intrinsic response behavior without requiring an externally trained router.

Abstract: Local-cloud collaboration is a practical way to deploy large language models under resource constraints, but existing methods often rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware finetuning that tie routing behavior to a particular operating regime. In this work, we show that such training may be unnecessary: the local model's own inference-time agreement across sampled responses already provides a strong signal for deciding when to trust local execution and when to offload to a stronger cloud model. We propose CARGO, a training-free routing framework that estimates this agreement through prompt-varied sampling, applies Bayesian early stopping for sample-efficient uncertainty control, and supports arbitrary target collaboration ratios through lightweight deployment-time calibration. Across diverse reasoning and question-answering tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales, and both pretrained and finetuned local models, CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and in several settings surpasses supervised learned routers. These results suggest that effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from the local model's intrinsic response behavior, without requiring an additional trained router.

</details>


### [116] [PersonaTrail: Benchmarking Personalized Web Agents through Browsing Trails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20482)
*Seungbin Yang,Chaewoon Ki,Dohyun Lee,Jaegul Choo,ChaeHun Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces PersonaTrail, a benchmark for personalized web agents using realistic browsing histories, and PACMem, a memory framework that separates factual session summaries from user preference patterns; demonstrates PACMem outperforms baselines on personalized web tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the gap in personalization when user prompts are underspecified; agents must infer user preferences and recall past browsing context in a managed open web environment.

Method: Proposes PersonaTrail as a realistic browsing-history-based benchmark; introduces Preference-Aware Contextual Memory (PACMem) that decomposes histories into factual memories (session summaries) and preference memories (recurring patterns); uses retrieval of relevant memories to guide personalized navigation; evaluates against memory-based baselines.

Result: PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks (personalization/navigation).

Conclusion: Structured memory of factual and preference information enhances personalized web navigation and enables evaluation of user-specific inference and recall capabilities in agents.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled web agents to autonomously execute complex tasks. In practice, users frequently provide underspecified instructions, requiring agents to infer the missing context from their raw browsing histories. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this form of personalization, as they either restrict tasks to fully explicit prompts or abstract web interaction history into simplified forms. To bridge this gap, we introduce PersonaTrail, a benchmark for personalized web agents operating in a managed open web environment. By leveraging realistic browsing trajectories as user history, PersonaTrail evaluates an agent's ability to infer user preferences and recall information from past browsing sessions. We further propose Preference-Aware Contextual Memory (PACMem), a framework that decomposes raw browsing histories into two types of structured memory: factual memories that summarize individual sessions and preference memories that distill recurring behavioral patterns. At inference time, the agent retrieves the most relevant entries from these memories to guide personalized navigation. Extensive experiments show that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks.

</details>


### [117] [Tractable Hierarchical Control of Autoregressive Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20483)
*Max Scribner,Antonio Vergari,Vaishak Belle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Polynomial-time satisfaction of LR(k) grammars enables efficient constraint-based steering of autoregressive LLMs to guarantee syntactic validity, improving integration with formal systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To ensure generated outputs (e.g., code, data) are syntactically valid and parsable by formal systems, addressing the gap between powerful LLM generation and strict syntax constraints.

Method: Distill the LLM into a tractable probabilistic model and steer/mask generation using the probability of satisfying LR(k) grammar constraints; prove that satisfaction of any finite-duration LR(k) grammar can be computed in polynomial time; integrate this into generation to constrain outputs.

Result: The paper proves a polynomial-time method for checking satisfaction of finite-duration LR(k) grammars, enabling efficient constraint steering of LLM outputs to satisfy formal syntactic constraints (theoretical result; enables practical implementation).

Conclusion: Provides a viable mechanism to enforce formal syntactic constraints during autoregressive generation, facilitating generation of valid code/data outputs and smoother integration with formal systems.

Abstract: Constraining the generation of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) is an important component of integrating language models into formal systems. In the generation of code and data for tasks like program synthesis, ensuring that language models produce syntactically valid output is a prerequisite for processing such output. These languages (such as SQL or JSON) are often designed as $LR(k)$ context-free grammars. By distilling the LLM to a tractable probabilistic model, its autoregressive generation can be steered and masked to incorporate the probability of satisfying logical constraints, ensuring high quality output that is guaranteed to be valid. This paper demonstrates that the satisfaction of any $LR(k)$ grammar of finite duration can be calculated in polynomial time, an improvement over the exponential time of applying previous methods to such grammars. This result enables efficient constraint and steering of LLM generation towards output that better satisfies formal syntactic constraints.

</details>


### [118] [The Devil is in the Spectrum: Mitigating Representation Collapse in LLMs via Topologically Regularized Side-Path](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20484)
*Yiheng Tao,Kaiwen Cheng,Yao Lu,Chang Liu,Jie Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRSP introduces a non-invasive topological regularization for attention in LLMs to balance spectral mixing and information capacity, addressing representation collapse and long-context degradation without changing core attention mechanisms; it uses a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism with a length-aware gate, proximal coupling, and distal propagation, achieving improved long-context performance (e.g., NoLiMa 8x length) and releasing code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context performance in LLMs is limited by representation collapse, manifesting as homogenization (attention sinks, rank deficiency) or isolation (local attention, context disconnection). Existing mechanisms struggle to balance spectral mixing (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank). A non-invasive architectural intervention that stabilizes the transition operator without altering core attention is needed.

Method: Introduce Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP) with a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a light, length-aware gate. Regularizes token interaction topology via proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation to maintain non-degenerate mixing, achieving spectral balance without modifying core attention.

Result: Empirical results show improvements in general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. Notably, on NoLiMa at 8x training length, TRSP retains 83% accuracy and surpasses Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by ~30 and ~50 percentage points, respectively.

Conclusion: TRSP provides a non-invasive architectural intervention that regularizes attention topology to balance mixing and capacity, improving long-context performance while preserving the core attention mechanism; code available at the provided repository.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are fundamentally limited by representation collapse, a bottleneck that severely degrades long-context performance. We identify that existing approaches risk drifting into one of two pathological extremes: homogenization collapse (e.g., attention sinks causing rank deficiency) and isolation collapse (e.g., local attention causing context disconnection). Through spectral analysis of attention dynamics, we derive an intrinsic trade-off between mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank) that standard mechanisms struggle to balance. To resolve this dilemma, we propose the Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP), a non-invasive architectural intervention that achieves spectral balance. TRSP employs a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight, length-aware gate, to regularize the token interaction topology. By integrating proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation to support non-degenerate mixing, TRSP promotes a geometrically healthier transition operator without altering core attention. Experiments show significant improvements across general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. Notably, on NoLiMa at $8\times$ the training length, TRSP retains $83\%$ accuracy and surpasses the Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by approximately 30 and 50 percentage points, respectively. Code available at: https://github.com/Eziotao-tyd/TRSP.

</details>


### [119] [Expectation Alignment of Language Models for Real-World User Expectations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20485)
*Miaomiao Li,Yang Wang,Bin Liang,Shudong Liu,Zhiwei Zhang,Kam-Fai Wong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions; introduces ExpectBench and LENS to align LLMs with user needs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation methods do not capture the diversity and subtleties of real user expectations, leading to misalignment.

Method: Proposes a principled procedure to extract semantically rich user expectations, introduces ExpectBench benchmark, and presents LENS as a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework.

Result: Analyses show current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate user expectations; LENS yields consistent improvements in expectation satisfaction.

Conclusion: Explicit modeling of user expectations is critical for realistic human-AI alignment; ExpectBench and LENS demonstrate the value of this approach.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on standard benchmarks, yet it remains largely unexplored whether they truly meet user expectations. Existing evaluation approaches, relying on model heuristics, expert rubrics, or user simulation, fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of real human expectations, causing models to appear competent while misaligning with what users actually seek. We present the first systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions, proposing a principled procedure to extract semantically rich expectations and introducing ExpectBench, a benchmark grounded in real user expectations. Analyses reveal that current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate what users hope to obtain, highlighting a fundamental source of misalignment. Building on these observations, we propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework. LENS enables models to internalize user expectations and generate better-aligned responses, consistently improving expectation satisfaction and underscoring the importance of explicitly modeling user expectations for realistic human-AI alignment.

</details>


### [120] [OPTScientist: Multi-Agent Discovery of Typed Optimizer Programs for Transformer Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20486)
*Zhongzheng Li,Tiancan Feng,Wenhao Li,Qingsong Ran,Shikun Feng,Xiaoyuan Zhang,Yue Wang,Xiaoguang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPTScientist is a theory-guided, multi-agent DSL-based framework for automatic optimizer discovery, integrating evolutionary search with small DSL extensions, yielding the RS-MR optimizer and demonstrating improvements in transformer pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of existing automated optimizer discovery methods, balancing flexibility, interpretability, stability, and novelty while enabling theory-guided, compiler-validated optimization programs.

Method: A four-agent orchestration (Theorist, Designer, Engineer, Reviewer) operates in a guided search loop within a typed DSL. Optimizers are built from modular components (direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, grouping). The search uses evolutionary methods with a second-stage mechanism to extend the DSL when bottlenecks appear, plus compiler validation and closed-loop evaluation.

Result: Discovery of RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer, which improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines under the native evaluation protocol.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a viable path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and experiment-driven refinement; suggests broader applicability of DSL-based, collaborative search for optimizer design.

Abstract: Designing optimizers for modern deep learning remains a challenging scientific problem, requiring the joint consideration of optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, implementation constraints, and empirical generalization. Existing automated optimizer discovery methods typically search either over unconstrained code spaces or within narrowly parameterized optimizer families. The former is flexible but often produces invalid or uninterpretable programs, while the latter is stable but limits novelty. We introduce OPTScientist, a theory-guided multi-agent framework for optimizer discovery in a typed domain-specific language (DSL). OPTScientist formulates optimizer design as a constrained scientific search process, where candidate updates are expressed through direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, and grouping modules. Four role agents, Theorist, Designer, Engineer, and Reviewer, collaborate within a single orchestration loop to propose hypotheses, synthesize DSL candidates, compile and evaluate optimizers, and critique results. To overcome the limitations of a fixed search space, OPTScientist combines evolutionary search over optimizer programs with a second-stage mechanism that proposes small DSL extensions when repeated failures reveal representational bottlenecks. Using this framework, we discover RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines under our native evaluation protocol. Our results suggest a path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.

</details>


### [121] [Directional Hallucinations: Ideological Drift in News-Grounded LLM Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20487)
*Chendi Wang,Liam Cunningham,Tom Yishay,Jieying Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A reproducible framework treats hallucinations in document-grounded QA by LLMs as signals of ideological drift in political content, using 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. articles to quantify model-driven biases; finds leftward bias in hallucinated content and entropy-driven uncertainty, with model- and source-variation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand how LLMs may distort political information and exhibit ideological drift, especially in election-adjacent contexts, to enable auditing and safeguards for AI-mediated political content.

Method: Build a reproducible pipeline: (i) use 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from QBias across left/center/right; (ii) generate article-specific questions; (iii) collect document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model; (iv) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison; (v) classify hashed ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier; (vi) analyze output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and ideological drift.

Result: Hallucination rates vary by model and concentrate on contentious topics; source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest; however, hallucinated content shows robust leftward drift, even when sources are right-leaning; logit analysis indicates hallucinations occur in high-entropy generation contexts, with uncertainty predicting leftward drift in some models (an “uncertainty to guessing” mechanism).

Conclusion: The framework enables auditing AI-mediated political information by treating hallucinations as diagnostic signals of ideological drift; results highlight left-leaning biases in hallucinations and the need for safeguards and further research on how uncertainty drives drift in election-relevant deployments.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about political information, including in election-adjacent information settings where factual errors and ideological distortions are high-stakes. We present a reproducible measurement framework that treats hallucinations, unsupported statements in document-grounded QA, as diagnostic signals of ideological drift. Using 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from QBias spanning left, center, and right sources, we (i) generate an article-specific question, (ii) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, (iii) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison, (iv) classify the ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier, and (v) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and drift. Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious topics, while source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. In contrast, hallucination content exhibits robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, including among hallucinations generated from right-leaning sources. Logit-level analysis shows hallucinations arise in high-entropy generation contexts, and in some models uncertainty also predicts leftward drift, consistent with an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism. We discuss implications for auditing AI-mediated political information and for designing safeguards in election-relevant deployments.

</details>


### [122] [Autonomous Topology Mutation: Safe Runtime Restructuring for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Capability, State, and Shadow Invariants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20488)
*Bronislav Sidik,Chaya Levi,Nizzan Kimhi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATM enables runtime topology mutation in multi-agent LLM frameworks using telemetry-driven overload detection and safety invariants, yielding large improvements in task success and privacy with minimal latency; the approach is open-sourced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed team topologies at boot time hinder scalability and adaptability; runtime overloads (e.g., excessive action categories, tool errors, queuing) require dynamic reconfiguration to maintain performance and safety.

Method: ATM uses a six-signal Bottleneck Index (queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, cross-agent wait time) for overload detection. When thresholds breached for consecutive ticks, an overloaded agent is factorised into specialized sub-agents and the parent becomes a coordinator. Privacy-level-aware routing controls state transfer, routing memory atoms only to permitted child sets or logging the drop. A shadow-validation window gates live traffic, and three safety invariants—capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, shadow-before-live—gate each structural change.

Result: On 720 DeepSeek-V3-driven tasks with deterministic tool stubs across four ablations and three workloads, the code-task success improved from 3.3% to 61.7%. A related privacy system reduced high-privacy memory exposure events per task from 2.0 to 0.0 (regex classifier). The ATM runtime adds under 500 microseconds of p99 latency on the hot path. An external live-tool probe with real Python execution supports external validity. The implementation, benchmark harness, and traces are open-sourced.

Conclusion: ATM demonstrates safe, telemetry-driven runtime topology mutation that enables dynamic specialization of agents with minimal overhead and improved privacy safeguards. The approach offers robust handling of overload while preserving task quality, but further validation across diverse domains and long-term stability considerations would strengthen generalizability.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM frameworks typically fix their team topology at boot time. When an individual agent becomes overloaded at runtime, for example by mixing too many action categories, accumulating tool errors, or queueing behind too many calls, the system has no mechanism to restructure itself. We introduce Autonomous Topology Mutation (ATM), a runtime team-mutation mechanism for multi-agent LLM frameworks. ATM combines telemetry-driven overload detection with three safety invariants that gate each structural change: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation.
  ATM monitors a six-signal Bottleneck Index that includes queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, and cross-agent wait time. When a warmup-calibrated threshold is breached for multiple consecutive ticks, ATM factorises the overloaded agent into specialised sub-agents and hot-swaps the parent into a coordinator role while preserving its external identity. State transfer is controlled by privacy-level-aware routing: each memory atom is routed only to a permitted child set, or explicitly dropped with a logged reason. No candidate topology receives live traffic until it has passed a shadow validation window.
  On 720 DeepSeek-V3-driven task runs with deterministic tool stubs across four ablation conditions and three workloads, the ATM factoriser split lifts code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. The full rail-and-distillation system reduces detected high-privacy memory exposure under a regex classifier from 2.0 to 0.0 events per task while preserving task quality. The runtime rails carrying ATM's invariants add less than 500 microseconds of p99 latency on the agent hot path. A small live-tool probe with real Python execution is included as an external-validity check. The implementation, benchmark harness, and traces are open-sourced.

</details>


### [123] [EvoSQL: Memory-Augmented Critic-Generator Co-Evolution for Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20489)
*Jiawei Zhou,Jianwei Wang,Chenyu Zhou,Chaojian Shi,Ming Dong,Kai Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoSQL introduces a memory-grounded co-evolution framework for Text-to-SQL where a generator and a critic iteratively refine SQL via execution signals and LLM critique, augmented by a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) stage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: to overcome limitations of one-shot generation in complex SQL synthesis by leveraging iterative interaction, execution feedback, and memory to enable multi-step reasoning and correction.

Method: A generator–critic pair co-evolves with contextualized candidate memory. It verifies SQL candidates with execution signals and LLM-based critique, updating memory via utility-guided aggregation. A Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) stage injects execution-aware supervision into modern coding LLM backbones.

Result: On Spider and BIRD datasets, EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines, with large gains on BIRD-Dev (e.g., +1.37% to +9.19% depending on model). SDPO initialization also boosts performance on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev.

Conclusion: Memory-grounded co-evolution is a promising approach for more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems; code is publicly available.

Abstract: Text-to-SQL has advanced rapidly with large language models, but complex database queries still require reasoning beyond one-shot generation, including multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction. We present EvoSQL, a co-evolution framework that formulates SQL synthesis as an iterative interaction between a generator and a critic. EvoSQL maintains a contextualized candidate memory, verifies SQL candidates with both execution signals and LLM-based critique, and updates its memory through utility-guided aggregation. To strengthen the underlying generator-critic pair, we further introduce a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) fine-tuning stage that injects execution-aware supervision into modern coding LLM backbones. Experiments on Spider and BIRD show that EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines, with particularly large gains on BIRD-Dev, ranging from +1.37% for Qwen3-4B to +9.19% for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. SDPO initialization further improves selected backbones on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev. These results suggest that memory-grounded co-evolution is an effective path toward more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/EvoSQL.

</details>


### [124] [CRAWO: Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20490)
*Eugênio Santos,Daniel Maia,Stefano Loss,José Manoel Silva,Aluizio Rocha Neto,Thais Batista,Everton Cavalcante,Nélio Cacho,Eduardo Nogueira,Daniel Araújo,Frederico Lopes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes CRAWO, a hardware-aware adaptive workload orchestration framework for distributed edge AI pipelines, implemented on K3s with CRDs and a custom operator to improve workload distribution and reduce cloud dependence in latency-sensitive edge environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge AI deployment faces heterogeneity and dynamic resource constraints across devices, making static or centralized orchestration inefficient. There's a need for adaptive, hardware-aware placement and state management to meet real-time requirements.

Method: A control-loop architecture that separates allocation from execution, with a hardware-aware allocator and a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer using real-time infrastructure metrics. Implemented as a microservices-based system on lightweight Kubernetes (K3s), using Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for domain modeling and a dedicated operator for state reconciliation to coordinate placement, data flows, and service instantiation across edge nodes.

Result: Vehicle surveillance with license plate recognition demonstrates improved workload distribution and reduced cloud dependence, achieving lower latency by keeping processing closer to edge devices.

Conclusion: CRAWO enables adaptive, edge-wide orchestration of AI pipelines by decoupling decision-making from execution, leveraging hardware-awareness and real-time metrics, and is validated in a latency-sensitive, heterogeneous edge scenario.

Abstract: Edge Intelligence has emerged as a key paradigm for enabling real-time applications in smart cities by shifting computation from centralized cloud data centers to the network edge, thereby reducing latency and bandwidth consumption. However, deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) pipelines across heterogeneous edge infrastructures remains challenging due to the wide range of device capabilities, from low-power microcontrollers to accelerator-equipped systems. Existing edge orchestration platforms primarily focus on deployment automation and infrastructure management, but these approaches are often inefficient and limit the ability to adaptively allocate resources under dynamic conditions. To tackle these issues, this paper introduces CRAWO (Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration), an architectural framework for coordinating AI pipelines across distributed edge environments. CRAWO follows a control-loop-based model that separates allocation intelligence from execution by managing placement decisions, state management, and inter-stage data flows while instantiating services on edge nodes. The framework incorporates a hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer that leverages real-time infrastructure metrics to enable adaptive workload placement. The reference implementation adopts a microservices architecture deployed on a lightweight Kubernetes distribution (K3s), using Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for domain modeling and a dedicated operator for state reconciliation. Evaluation in a vehicle surveillance scenario using license plate recognition demonstrates improved workload distribution and reduced reliance on centralized cloud processing in latency-sensitive environments.

</details>


### [125] [DFAH-Bench: Benchmarking Observable Agent Instability in Financial Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20491)
*Raffi Khatchadourian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DFAH-Bench exposes observable behavioral instability in financial agents by replay benchmarking across tool-use, evidence, and decision-concentration channels, revealing strong divergence in decision processes even when outcomes align.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard outcome-only benchmarks miss process-level instability that can threaten reliability and robustness of tool-using agents. There is a need to measure how decisions are reached, not just what the decision is.

Method: DFAH-Bench is a replay benchmark that tracks three observable channels: tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration. It analyzes 8,127 replay episodes across 10 models and 3 financial tasks to compare outcome agreement with two forms of process-level agreement (tool-path and evidence-trajectory alignment), categorizing models into pattern matchers, stable executors, and trajectory divergents. Benchmark artifacts (code, logs, README, etc.) are released.

Result: Key findings: (1) Outcome agreement among frontier models is high (95%), but agreement on tool paths is much lower (77%), an 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: 0.14–0.22) that outcome-only tests miss. (2) Among high outcome-agreement groups, over 55% show meaningful trajectory divergence. (3) Identified three behavioral profiles: pattern matchers (high outcome, collapsed outputs), stable executors (consistent tool-use), trajectory divergents (same conclusions via different tool paths/evidence). (4) Release includes code, scripts, logs, and dataset README.

Conclusion: Outcome-focused benchmarks can overstate stability; measuring observable process channels reveals substantial internal variability. DFAH-Bench provides a practical framework and data to assess and understand stability in tool-using agents, with implications for safer and more robust AI systems.

Abstract: Standard evaluation benchmarks measure what a tool-using agent decides, not whether it arrives at that decision through the same process each time. We introduce DFAH-Bench, a replay benchmark that measures observable behavioral instability in financial agent decision-making across three channels -- tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration -- none of which require access to hidden reasoning text. Across 8,127 replay episodes spanning 10 models and 3 financial tasks, we find that outcome agreement alone is an incomplete stability signal: frontier models can agree on decisions 95% of the time while following the same tool path only 77% of the time -- an 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]) that outcome-only evaluation misses entirely. Among frontier-model case groups with high decision agreement, over 55% exhibit meaningful trajectory divergence. We identify three behavioral profiles: pattern matchers that achieve near-perfect agreement by collapsing to a single output regardless of input, stable executors with relatively consistent tool-use processes, and trajectory divergers that reach the same conclusions through materially different tool paths and evidence contacts. The benchmark code, metric scripts, replay logs, benchmark card, dataset README, and release manifest are released in the accompanying repository.

</details>


### [126] [Attention-based Experience Replay Framework for Continual Learning of Agnostic Time Series Forecasting Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20493)
*Quentin Besnard,Nicolas Ragot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A continual time-series forecasting framework using Experience Replay guided by Attention to adapt to changing contexts while mitigating forgetting, reducing retraining and data needs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address non-stationary, evolving data distributions in real-world time series and to balance stability and plasticity under limited computation.

Method: Extends static forecasting models with an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention mechanisms to enable dynamic adaptation while preserving prior knowledge.

Result: Evaluated on standard forecasting benchmarks and a piezometric time series; demonstrates maintained or improved predictive performance over time with reduced retraining costs and data requirements.

Conclusion: Presents a practical continual forecasting framework capable of handling dynamic environments; shows potential for broader deployment and suggests directions for scalability and testing on more datasets.

Abstract: Deep learning has led to remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, particularly in robotics, imaging and sound processing. However, a major limitation of neural networks remains their strong dependence on large and stationary datasets. In many real-world applications, these conditions are rarely met due to evolving and dynamic environments where data distributions change over time. Continual learning aims to address this challenge by developing models capable of adapting incrementally while maintaining a balance between stability and plasticity under computational constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for continual time series forecasting, designed to extend existing static forecasting models commonly used in the literature by incorporating an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention mechanisms. This approach allows the model to adapt dynamically to new contexts while preserving prior knowledge, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting. The framework is evaluated on standard forecasting benchmarks as well as on a piezometric dataset exhibiting diverse temporal behaviors. Results show that our approach effectively increases or maintains predictive performance over time while reducing retraining costs and data requirements, thus facilitating the deployment of forecasting models in dynamic and real-world settings.

</details>


### [127] [Isolating LLM Alignment from Regex: Zero Coverage and Metric-Dependent Divergence Under Adversarial Mutation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20494)
*Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: L5-no-regex shows no increase in blocking rate under a substring-based detector when the regex is disabled, but an LLM-judge metric detects substantial blocking on adversarial probes; alignment’s benefit is metric-dependent and modest for natural-language harmful requests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reassess whether alignment-layer safeguards add value beyond static regex protection when the corpus is specifically designed to bypass the regex, addressing prior findings of no measurable coverage gain behind a live Gemini backend.

Method: Construct L5-no-regex (L4-real with nine-pattern filter disabled). Evaluate against N=45 adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified with Gemini paraphrase and PAIR to ~1,555 probe-run pairs across N=5 replications. Use a primary substring classifier (OWASP LLM Top-10 categories) and a secondary LLM-judge metric on PAIR variants to assess block rates. Statistical tests report H1 outcomes and interaction effects across sub-corpora.

Result: Primary substring classifier yields 0% block rate across all five OWASP categories (Wilson upper bound <5%), refuting H1. The LLM-judge metric shows 56–100% block rates for PAIR variants (p<0.01), indicating alignment responds to adversarial framing but refuses are nuanced beyond substring matching. Sub-corpus differential predictions are not supported (p=1.00).
