Alignment’s contribution is metric-dependent: zero for natural-language harmful probes beyond the regex, but detectable refusals by an LLM judge on adversarial probes that substring matching misses.

Conclusion: Alignment’s value is contingent on evaluation metric. When the regex is disabled, coverage from alignment depends on the detection method; for natural-language harms, regex suffices, while for adversarial framing, judgment models reveal refusals beyond substring detectors. Replication materials (locked corpus, mutation artifacts, export scripts) are released.

Abstract: Production LLM applications commonly stack a regex filter in front of model-side alignment; prior work found no measurable coverage gain from adding a live Gemini backend behind an active regex filter. We ask whether that ceiling holds when the corpus is \emph{designed to bypass the regex}. We introduce $L_5$-no-regex -- identical to $L_4$-real (Gemini-2.5-flash, token-budget cap, rate limit, output scrub) but with the nine-pattern filter disabled -- and evaluate it against $N{=}45$ adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified by Gemini paraphrase and PAIR to ${\sim}1{,}555$ probe-run pairs over $N{=}5$ replications. Under the primary substring classifier, H1 is refuted: $L_5$ block rate is $0,%$ across all five OWASP LLM Top-10 categories ($Δ\text{pp}{=}0$ vs.\ $L_0$, $p{=}1.00$; Wilson upper bound ${<}5,%$). A secondary LLM-judge metric on PAIR variants shows $56$--$100,%$ block rates ($p{<}0.01$), revealing alignment does respond to adversarially-framed probes -- but produces refusals too nuanced for substring matching. The sub-corpus differential prediction is not supported ($p{=}1.00$). Alignment's contribution is \emph{metric-dependent}: on natural-language harmful-request probes, it adds zero observed coverage beyond the regex; on adversarially-framed variants, an LLM judge detects refusals the substring classifier misses. The locked corpus, mutation artifacts, and export scripts are released for replication.

</details>


### [128] [Workload-Aware Caching for Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20495)
*Anas Mohamed,Kaizan Haque,Azal Ahmad Khan,Chetan Sharma,Shuwen Ge,Ali Anwar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A workload-aware eviction policy for caching intermediate results in DAG-based multi-agent executions, combining recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency to retain valuable entries under memory constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing caches treat cached entries uniformly by access history, ignoring structural/workload signals unique to agentic DAG executions; improved eviction can reduce latency.

Method: Introduce a unified scoring function combining recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency to rank cache entries and evict lower-scoring items under memory limits; evaluate on three benchmarks.

Result: Latency reductions up to 64.7% vs uncached baseline; average 31.1% reduction over the best finite-capacity baseline; performance approaches unbounded cache; maintains accuracy compared to finite-capacity methods.

Conclusion: Workload-aware caching complements other agentic optimizations (plan-level caching, parallel execution); each targets distinct bottlenecks; results demonstrate improvements and compatibility.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems decompose complex tasks into directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of specialized agent executions, creating natural opportunities for caching intermediate results across queries. However, existing cache eviction policies treat all cached entries uniformly based on access history, ignoring structural and workload signals uniquely available in agentic execution environments. We present a workload-aware eviction policy that combines three signals, namely recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency, into a unified scoring function that retains the most valuable entries under memory constraints. Evaluated across three multi-agent benchmarks spanning diverse reuse regimes, our policy reduces latency by up to 64.7% relative to the uncached baseline and achieves on average a 31.1% latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, while approaching the performance of an unbounded cache and maintaining accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. We further show that workload-aware content caching is complementary to other agentic system optimization methods, including plan-level caching and parallel agent execution, with each technique targeting a distinct efficiency bottleneck in multi-agent pipelines.

</details>


### [129] [From Errors to Rules: Iterative Prompt Optimization for Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20497)
*Yueying Cui,Renhao Xue,Yi Zhang,Mukul Prasad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Comprehensive empirical study of prompt optimization for text classification showing no single paradigm dominates; introduces ERGO, an error-driven method with a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite loop that excels on boundary-learnable tasks and provides a complementary framework for paradigm selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand strengths/limitations of demonstration-, exploration-, and error-driven prompt optimization paradigms, and to guide practitioners in choosing the right approach based on task structure.

Method: Large-scale empirical study across diverse benchmarks (2–150 classes) comparing demonstration-based ICL, exploration-based search, and error-driven diagnosis; qualitative analysis of optimization traces; development of ERGO with full-batch error diagnosis and rule-based prescription and rewrite.

Result: No single method dominates; each paradigm excels on structurally different tasks. ERGO achieves best accuracy on boundary-learnable tasks (e.g., TREC 90.0%, CLINC150 94.4%), converges in 3–5 iterations, and yields interpretable decision rules; demonstrates complementary strengths to ICL and exploration-based methods.

Conclusion: Proposes a complementarity framework linking task characteristics to optimal paradigm selection, providing practical guidance for practitioners on selecting prompt optimization strategies based on task structure.

Abstract: Prompt optimization for text classification spans diverse approaches, from demonstration selection to exploration-based search to error-driven diagnosis, each with known but incompletely characterized strengths and limitations. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study across diverse classification benchmarks (2 to 150 classes) comparing these paradigms through both quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis of optimization traces, revealing that each paradigm excels on structurally different task types and that no single method dominates. Guided by these insights, we propose Error-Guided Optimization (ERGO), an error-driven method that iterates over the full training set in non-overlapping batches, diagnoses classification failures, and generates targeted decision rules through a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite feedback loop. ERGO achieves the best accuracy on tasks where errors concentrate in specific confused label pairs (which we term boundary-learnable tasks): TREC: 90.0%, CLINC150: 94.4%, converges in 3-5 iterations, and produces interpretable decision rules. While ERGO does not achieve the highest overall average, it fills a complementary role: demonstration-based ICL wins on coverage-dependent tasks, exploration-based search wins on many-class intent, and ERGO wins where decision boundaries are learnable from error patterns. We provide a complementarity framework linking task characteristics to optimal paradigm selection, offering practical guidance for practitioners.

</details>


### [130] [AISE-Bench: A Full-Cycle Curated Benchmark for Information Seeking on Academic Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20498)
*Fanjin Zhang,Zhengyang Wang,Ruixuan Huang,Kefan Zhang,Amy Xin,Yuanchun Wang,Shu Zhao,Evgeny Kharlamov,Jie Tang,Juanzi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AISE-Bench introduces a real-world, full-cycle benchmark for information seeking on academic knowledge graphs with 1,133 QA pairs, annotated API workflows, and grounding; current LLMs show only moderate performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address gaps in existing tool-using benchmarks that rely on synthetic templates and narrow tasks, and to provide a rigorous testbed for real-world, multi-step API planning, execution, grounding, and evaluation in academic KG information seeking.

Method: Constructed AISE-Bench with 1,133 QA pairs including query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with references; designed an annotator workflow for planning, executing, and revising complex API workflows; developed a comprehensive evaluation protocol assessing answer quality, grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success; evaluated 14 methods (best: PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro).

Result: Even the strongest model achieves only moderate performance and often struggles with API planning and execution, highlighting the benchmark’s difficulty and its usefulness for evaluating stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning in multi-step API-using LLM agents.

Conclusion: AISE-Bench provides a challenging testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving multi-step, grounded tool-use in LLMs; code and data are publicly available at the project site.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with tools are emerging as autonomous agents capable of using Web engine, APIs, and code to solve complex, long-horizon tasks. Current tool-using benchmarks for information seeking on academic graphs rely on synthetic templates, simplified solution spaces, or narrow tasks such as paper-centric tasks, leaving key challenges underexplored - realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, rich parameter filling for APIs, grounded answers with references, and comprehensive evaluation of both the process and the outcome. We introduce AISE-Bench, a real-world, full-cycle annotated benchmark for information seeking on academic knowledge graphs. AISE-Bench release contains 1,133 QA pairs, including query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. To support high-quality annotation, we design a customized agent workflow to enable annotators to plan, execute, and revise complex API workflows efficiently. We develop a comprehensive evaluation protocol measuring answer quality, reference grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success. Among the 14 evaluated methods, even the strongest model (PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro) achieves only moderate performance and often struggles with API planning and execution. AISE-Bench establishes a challenging new testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving the stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning of multi-step API-using LLM agents. Our code and data are available at https://aise-bench.github.io/.

</details>


### [131] [ExecuGraph: A Multi-Agent, Execution-Grounded Framework for Reliable Backend Code Synthesis with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20499)
*Sai Deekshith Lekkala,Jothi Prabha Appadurai,Rohith Reddy Bellibatlu,Manpreet Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ExecuGraph is a multi-agent framework for backend code synthesis that uses execution-based validation, showing performance gains especially when base models are stronger; provides a methodological, configurable codebase to measure marginal contributions of each lever (agents, retries, ablations).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-pass LLM code generation can produce plausible but unreliable code; need execution-based validation and controlled experiments to quantify where multi-agent decomposition helps and how benefits scale with model capability.

Method: Six specialized agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, Explainer) operate within a typed directed workflow with a bounded retry budget, implemented on LangGraph with Ollama-hosted models and an optional retrieval layer. Execution is sandboxed with wall-clock timeouts. Compared against: (i) one-shot single-agent baseline, (ii) single-agent execution-retry baseline. Evaluated on internal-30, HumanEval, and APPS-intro; includes per-agent ablations, retry-budget sweep, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit.

Result: On internal-30, the three configurations show no significant differences (paired Wilcoxon; p-values not significant); 95% CIs include zero for all pairwise mean differences. On HumanEval, multi-full edges ahead by +3.1 percentage points. Cross-model: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, graph-category accuracy rises from 57.5% (oneshot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp uplift, supporting a scaling hypothesis that benefits grow with base-model capability.

Conclusion: The framework's primary contribution is methodological: a single codebase that can be configured into one-shot, execution-retry, and per-agent ablation modes, enabling controlled measurement of each lever's marginal contribution. It reports per-agent ablations, retry-budget sweeps, error taxonomy, and test-source audits to support causal inference about multi-agent governance in code synthesis.

Abstract: Large Language Models generate plausible backend code, but a single-pass paradigm provides no guarantee of correctness or runtime reliability. We present ExecuGraph, a multi-agent framework that places execution-based validation at the center of backend code synthesis. Six specialized agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, and Explainer) are coordinated by a typed directed workflow with a bounded retry budget, implemented on LangGraph with locally hosted models (Ollama) and an optional retrieval layer for algorithmic technique recall. A subprocess-isolated sandbox with a wall-clock timeout guards every evaluation. We evaluate on a curated 30-problem DSA suite (internal-30), HumanEval (n=64), and an APPS-introductory subset, contrasting ExecuGraph against a single-agent one-shot baseline and a single-agent execution-retry baseline (a Reflexion-style ablation that isolates the contribution of multi-agent decomposition). On internal-30, the three conditions are statistically indistinguishable (n=30; paired Wilcoxon p=0.59 MF vs. SO, p=0.08 SR vs. SO); 95% bootstrap confidence intervals on all pairwise mean differences include zero. On HumanEval, multi-full edges ahead by +3.1 pp. The strongest signal is cross-model: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, graph-category accuracy improves from 57.5% (oneshot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp jump that supports a scaling hypothesis: the value of multi-agent decomposition grows with base-model capability. The framework's primary contribution is methodological: a single codebase that collapses by configuration into one-shot, execution-retry, and per-agent ablation conditions, enabling controlled measurement of each lever's marginal contribution. A per-agent ablation, retry-budget sweep, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit are reported.

</details>


### [132] [FlowEdit: Information-Theoretic Control of LLM Reasoning Flows for Ill-posed Problems Involving Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20500)
*Sizhe Tang,Guangyu Jiang,Yu Li,Rongqian Chen,Ioannis G. Kevrekidis,Tian Lan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FlowEdit introduces an information-theoretic framework to enable branch-aware, multi-hypothesis reasoning in LLMs for ill-posed problems, with dual objectives to maximize hypothesis-to-outcome information and minimize cross-branch overlap, achieving diverse, informative responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-world ill-posed problems often yield conflicting requirements; standard LLMs struggle due to single-token-primary next-token prediction. There is a need to surface hidden conflicts, maintain multiple hypotheses, and generate alternative responses in one pass.

Method: FlowEdit enforces branch-aware reasoning via two dual information-theoretic objectives on internal representations: (1) maximize information flow from each hypothesis to the branch outcome, (2) minimize overlap/conditional dependence across sibling branches. It uses tractable variational bounds under ε-sufficient boundary embeddings to optimize conditional mutual information, producing a full set of alternative responses under valid hypotheses.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, with +68% improvement in exact-set-match accuracy and +24% increase in overall response informativeness. Flow-regulation effects observed in token streams include redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates within branches, spikes at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of required flows.

Conclusion: FlowEdit demonstrates a viable framework for explicit conflicts and diverse reasoning in LLMs, linking internal information flows to observable token-level dynamics and offering a path toward robust multi-hypothesis reasoning for ill-posed tasks.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on well-specified reasoning tasks with a feasible answer. However, problems encountered in the open world can become ill-posed due to inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements, admitting no valid responses. We argue that reasoning of such ill-posed problems involving conflicts require novel LLM capabilities to make hidden conflicts explicit, maintain competing hypotheses via multiple reasoning branches, and generate alternative responses in a single pass, all of which are challenging due to the limitation of the next-token prediction mechanism in LLMs. To this end, we propose FlowEdit, a novel framework that leverages information-theoretic principles to quantify and regulate internal reasoning flows of LLMs, for generating a full set of alternative responses under valid hypotheses. FlowEdit can be viewed as enforcing a branch-aware reasoning process using two dual information-theoretic objectives on the model's internal reasoning representations: maximizing the information flow from each selected hypothesis to the branch outcome, while minimizing the overlap and conditional dependence across sibling branches, to provide a diverse, informative set of responses with broad coverage. We show that this is achieved through tractable variational bounds under boundary embeddings being ε-sufficient, optimizing the underlying conditional mutual information in LLM reasoning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68%, while boosting overall response informativeness by 24%. We further show that flow regulation surfaces in the token stream as a redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates inside each branch, amplifies at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of flows the problem requires.

</details>


### [133] [MKEvolve: A Modular Multi-Agent Framework for Kernel Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20501)
*Jason Yoo,Rajarshi Saha,Shaowei Zhu,Tao Yu,Wei Tang,Youngsuk Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A modular, co-evolving kernel synthesis framework (MKEvolve) that decomposes PyTorch modules into subkernels, uses LLM-guided beam search to optimize each subkernel, and combines them into configurable, interpretable kernels; shows improved correctness and speed with reduced LLM token usage on KernelBench/Triton. 


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The bottleneck is writing correct, performant kernels for hardware accelerators in modern ML workloads; end-to-end kernel synthesis is inefficient and hard to debug. A modular, co-evolving approach aims to improve correctness, performance, tractability, and interpretability by decomposing workloads into subkernels whose implementations can be independently optimized and swapped.

Method: MKEvolve iteratively co-evolves a modular decomposition of PyTorch modules and a kernel for each submodule. It refines the decomposition by splitting/fusing submodules across iterations and uses LLM-driven beam search to independently improve each subkernel. The resulting kernel is a composition of independently verified subkernels; subkernel implementations are swappable, allowing configurability and traceability of errors and speedups to specific components.

Result: Empirical evaluation with Triton on KernelBench L2/L3 across multi-operator sequences and full model architectures shows that MKEvolve achieves higher correctness and speedups compared to end-to-end direct synthesis baselines, while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%.

Conclusion: A modular, verifiable, and adaptable kernel synthesis framework can outperform end-to-end approaches, offering traceable performance gains and token efficiency, with potential applicability to related model architectures.

Abstract: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based code generation, writing correct and performant kernels for hardware accelerators remains a key bottleneck in scaling modern ML workloads. We present MKEvolve (Modular Kernel Evolve), a framework that iteratively co-evolves a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and the LLM-generated kernel for each submodule, refining the decomposition by splitting and fusing across iterations while independently improving each subkernel via LLM-driven beam search. The resulting kernels are programmatic compositions of independently verified subkernels, making them configurable (subkernel implementations are swappable), interpretable (errors and speedups are traceable to specific subkernels), and readily adaptable to related model architectures. Experiments with Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3, spanning multi-operator sequences and full model architectures, show that MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%.

</details>


### [134] [Inducing Comparability of Factorised Probability Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20502)
*Jan Speller,Malte Luttermann,Marcel Gehrke,Tanya Braun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a principled extension framework to compare probabilistic graphical models on non-identical variable sets by lifting to a common measurable space using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions; preserves semantics, enables discrepancy measures, and provides deterministic algorithms for minimal common structure and projection-invariant joints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable principled, semantically faithful comparison of probabilistic graphical models defined on different variable spaces; current measures require a common space.

Method: Extend unmatched components with conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions to form joint distributions that differ from originals only by multiplicative constants and project to the originals; prove joint-invariance under projection; develop deterministic algorithms for minimal structural extension to the smallest common measurable space and to a common graph structure; discuss measure-theoretic properties.

Result: Demonstrates invariance of the induced joint under projection; provides algorithms for minimal and common extensions; analyzes properties and outlines criteria for effective comparison methodologies.

Conclusion: The framework enables principled, semantics-preserving comparison of PGMs across non-identical variable sets and lays a foundation for robust distributional discrepancy-based methodologies.

Abstract: To allow for principled comparison between two probabilistic graphical models defined over non-identical variable sets, they have to be lifted to a common measurable space. To this end, we propose an extension scheme for any two given models and establish the formal foundation: Unmatched components are completed using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions such that the resulting joint distributions differ from the original ones only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. This preserves the probabilistic semantics while enabling the application of well-defined distributional discrepancy measures. We establish the invariance of the induced joint under projection and use the extensions to provide a minimal structural extension of two factor graphs to the smalles common measurable space as well as to a common graphical structure by a deterministic algorithm. In addition, we discuss structural and measure-theoretic properties and identify promising criteria for comparison methodologies.

</details>


### [135] [LeanFlow: A Case Study in Workflow-Driven Lean Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20503)
*Lazar Milikic,Simon Guilloud,Khanh Nguyen,Viktor Kuncak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LeanFlow is a specialized LLM agent system for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects, with ablation studies showing runtime mechanisms affecting completion, auditability, and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the challenge of converting formalizable mathematical documents into executable Lean projects and understanding how runtime choices (models, workflows, toolsets) impact completion and cost.

Method: Case studies on two unformalized math papers (number theory and measure theory) using LeanFlow with Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5, including model/workflow/toolset ablations; reporting task outcome, API calls, input/output tokens; budget-constrained completion.

Result: Kimi2.6 enables completing both document-level Lean projects within a 2000-call budget; no-queue variants reach the budget. GPT5.5 variants complete all documents; full workflow achieves lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost. LeanFlow attains 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in GPT5.5 runs.

Conclusion: LeanFlow demonstrates effective translation of papers to Lean with favorable efficiency and auditability profiles under studied runtimes, though generalization to broader corpora requires further evaluation and scalability work.

Abstract: We present and evaluate LeanFlow, an LLM agent system specialized for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Recent verifier-in-the-loop systems show that large formal artifacts can be produced, but it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms affect completion, auditability, or efficiency in document-to-project formalization. We study this question through case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers in number theory and measure theory, using model, proof-workflow, and toolset ablations with Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5; we report task outcome, API calls, input tokens, and output tokens. With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget, while no-queue variants reach the budget limit; with GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow has the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. As complementary calibration, LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in our GPT5.5 runs.

</details>


### [136] [Optimizing Hypergraph-Based RAG: Toward Better Fact Extraction and Chunk Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20506)
*Houda Khrouf,Pedro Fillastre,Sebastiao Correia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-consistency improves extraction quality; Personalized PageRank over hypergraphs enhances chunk retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GraphRAG struggles with n-ary facts; HyperGraphRAG adds richer semantics but suffers from error-prone LLM extraction and slow chunk retrieval.

Method: Use self-consistency prompting to stabilize extraction from LLMs; apply Personalized PageRank on the hypergraph to rank and retrieve chunks more efficiently.

Result: Anticipated improvement in extraction accuracy and chunk retrieval efficiency, enabling deeper reasoning.

Conclusion: Combining self-consistency prompts with PPR over hypergraphs mitigates extraction errors and retrieval bottlenecks, strengthening HyperGraphRAG for complex reasoning.

Abstract: GraphRAG enables deeper reasoning by structuring knowledge as graphs but struggles with n-ary facts. HyperGraphRAG uses hypergraphs for richer semantics, improving accuracy, yet relies on error-prone LLM extraction and inefficient standard chunk retrieval. We address this by employing self-consistency prompting to improve the extraction, and Personalized PageRank algorithm over hypergraph to enhance chunk retrieval.

</details>


### [137] [MiniCache: Reusable Program Caching with Small Model Interfaces for Efficient LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20507)
*Jingquan Chen,Jinghua Piao,Jie Feng,Shaogang Hu,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MiniCache enables reusable computation for PoT-based tasks via parameterized caches and small-interface models, achieving significant latency reductions and throughput gains while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs for program-aided reasoning and agentic tasks incur high inference costs; there is value in reusing computation across structurally similar requests to improve efficiency.

Method: Transform Program-of-Thought programs into parameterized cache objects. On cache hits, a small model performs semantic variable extraction; during target-LLM generation, the system uses speculative drafting to reduce expensive invocations while preserving task quality.

Result: Across WebShop, Formula, and CodeTAT-QA datasets, MiniCache improves latency, cache reuse, and accuracy, achieving up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving.

Conclusion: Small models serve best as lightweight interface models that enable reliable, reusable program caching rather than as direct replacements for large models.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for program-aided reasoning, agentic decision making, and structured task execution, but these applications often incur high inference cost. We present MiniCache, a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects, enabling reusable computation across structurally similar requests. MiniCache reuses the same small model for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests and speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, reducing expensive target-LLM invocations while preserving task quality. Experiments on shopping-style request datasets, WebShop, Formula, and CodeTAT-QA demonstrate that MiniCache improves the trade-off between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy, achieving up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving. These results show that small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching.

</details>


### [138] [Telco-GAIA: Bilingual Benchmark for Agents in Telecom Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20510)
*Dmitrii Khizbullin,Zaid Alyafeai,Abdelrahman Eldesokey,Nourah AlSultan,Raghad Alshalan,David R. Pugh,Bernard Ghanem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Telco-GAIA is a bilingual (English/Arabic), multi-modal benchmark with 100 tasks to evaluate tool-using agents on real telecom operator data. Tasks require multi-hop reasoning across HTML site data, a synthetic SQL database, and external web archives, spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. Delivered in a Docker sandbox and evaluated by normalized exact string matching. Across 12 LLMs, strong performance is limited (best ~71%), with significant headroom in visually grounded tasks (scores <30%). Provides a reproducible enterprise testbed and a template for closed-domain benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a need for closed-domain, reproducible benchmarks to evaluate tool-using agents across multiple modalities and real-world data sources in enterprise settings. Existing benchmarks often rely on LLMs as judges or lack realistic multi-source, multi-modal tasks that require multi-hop reasoning, hindering progress on practical tools and data integration.

Method: Construct 100 bilingual tasks (English/Arabic) requiring about 4.2 hops of reasoning on average. Data sources include a static website snapshot (HTML, images, PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives, with text, image, and tabular content. Provide the benchmark in a sandboxed Docker environment and score using normalized exact string matching for objective, deterministic evaluation. Evaluate a reference agent across twelve commercial and open LLMs.

Result: Telco-GAIA proves challenging for current models: the strongest model solves 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, performance drops to ~40%. Visually grounded tasks are the weakest category, with average backend scores below 30%, indicating substantial headroom in document and image understanding.

Conclusion: Telco-GAIA offers a rigorous, reproducible enterprise testbed for evaluating tool-using agents in a closed-domain, multi-modal setting and provides a blueprint for constructing future benchmarks that emphasize real-world data integration and multi-source reasoning.

Abstract: We introduce Telco-GAIA, a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on the data of a real-world telecommunications operator. Telco-GAIA comprises 100 human-verified question-answering tasks, in English and Arabic, that each demand multi-hop reasoning (4.2 hops on average) over three heterogeneous sources: a static website snapshot (HTML, images, and linked PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives, spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment and scored by normalized exact string matching, making evaluation objective, deterministic, and reproducible over time without any LLM-as-a-Judge. Evaluating a purpose-built reference agent across twelve commercial and open LLMs, we find Telco-GAIA challenging: even the strongest model solves only 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, this falls to about 40%, and the visually grounded categories remain the weakest, where the average backend scores below 30%, leaving substantial headroom in document and image understanding. Telco-GAIA offers a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise agents and a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks.

</details>


### [139] [SiGMA: Sign-Guided Merging and Adaptation for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20511)
*Keonhee Park,Gunhee Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SiGMA introduces sign guided merging and adaptation for MTIM LLMs to address negative interference in continual multimodal instruction tuning, achieving better task consolidation than prior MCIT methods on UCIT and DCL benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal LLMs struggle with negative interference and forgetting when learning a sequence of tasks; existing MCIT methods (MoE, expansion-merge) reduce forgetting but degrade performance via new updates overwriting prior knowledge; a simple, effective mechanism to preserve past knowledge during both training and inference is needed.

Method: Two components: (1) sign guided adaptive tuning during training to reduce collisions with past tasks and minimize drift while learning the current task; (2) sign guided merging at inference to selectively scale salient parameters, preserving and amplifying useful task-specific knowledge.

Result: Empirical evaluation on UCIT and DCL benchmarks shows SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state-of-the-art MCIT methods.

Conclusion: SiGMA offers a simple, effective framework for mitigating negative interference in multimodal continual instruction tuning, improving knowledge consolidation across tasks; code is released for reproducibility.

Abstract: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) is crucial for adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to evolving a sequence of downstream tasks. Prior methods mostly utilize Mixture of Experts or expansion merge approach, primarily focusing on catastrophic forgetting, yet they still suffer from negative interference during inference, where newly learned updates overwrite useful prior knowledge and degrade overall performance. To address this, we propose SiGMA (Sign Guided Merging and Adaptation), a simple yet effective framework that mitigates negative interference with two components: sign guided adaptive tuning during training and sign guided merging at inference. Sign guided adaptive tuning reduces collisions with past knowledge and learns the current task with minimal drift, mitigating severe forgetting. Sign guided merging further improves consolidation by selectively scaling salient parameters to preserve and amplify useful task specific knowledge. Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks show that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state of the art MCIT methods. Our code is available at SiGMA.

</details>


### [140] [Reliability-Aware LLM Alignment from Inconsistent Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20515)
*Jingyi Huang,Ruohan Zong,Yujun Feng,Liran Ma,Lanyu Shang,Yang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A robust RLHF framework RGPO that estimates annotator reliability, infers latent ground truth, and applies reliability-aware consistency optimization to prioritize high-consensus supervision, improving LLM alignment over standard RLHF baselines; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human preference data for RLHF are noisy and inconsistent. Treating disagreement as equal guidance leads to overfitting to noise. There is a need to model annotator reliability and leverage robust signals.

Method: 1) Estimate annotator reliability; 2) Infer latent ground-truth labels from noisy feedback to identify robust preferences; 3) Use reliability-aware consistency optimization that modulates the training objective based on annotation consensus level to emphasize high-consensus supervision signals.

Result: Empirical evaluation on LLM alignment benchmarks shows RGPO reduces inconsistency/noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared with widely used RLHF baselines.

Conclusion: RGPO effectively mitigates noisy/inconsistent human feedback in RLHF and improves alignment quality; code and configurations are released at the provided GitHub link.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is critical for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its efficacy is often compromised by the inherent inconsistency and subjectivity of human annotations. Existing preference optimization frameworks, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), typically treat ambiguous pairs with high annotator disagreement identically to those with unanimous consensus, forcing models to overfit to inconsistent supervision signals and leading to suboptimal alignment. In this work, we propose Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization (RGPO), a robust framework designed to mitigate the impact of inconsistent human feedback. RGPO estimates annotator reliability and infers latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences. Furthermore, we introduce a reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on the consensus level of annotations, ensuring the model prioritizes high-consensus supervision signals. Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks demonstrate that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/GenieHuang/RGPO.

</details>


### [141] [CANN Bench: Benchmarking Agent Generated Kernels against Real NPU and Algorithmic Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20518)
*Xue-Jian Gao,Deng Pan,Yueming Su,Jiasheng Li,Bin Du,Fengming Zhu,Chengdi Ma,Junyi Fan,Qichen Liao,Chengqiu Hu,Xinxian Chen,Lingchao Zheng,Jun Li,Jiwei Yang,Yuwei Fan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CANN Bench is an open benchmark for AI-generated operator kernels on Huawei Ascend NPU, covering 53 operators and 1060 test cases across four difficulty tiers and multiple precisions, evaluated with a three-dimensional weighted score over compilation, correctness, and performance, benchmarked against a PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and hardware-anchored performance limits to discourage reward hacking; integrated in the official CANN repo for community maintenance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarking focuses on CUDA/Triton; Ascend and other hardware ecosystems lack a standardized, reproducible baseline for evaluating AI-generated operator code, hindering fair comparison and progress.

Method: Construct 4 difficulty tiers (elementwise to MoE/FlashAttention), 53 operators, 1060 test cases across FP16, BF16, FP32, INT8; define a three-dimensional weighted composite score with independent axes for compilation, functional correctness, and performance; compare against an out-of-the-box PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and a hardware-anchored performance (HAP) limit on real hardware; design the harness to resist reward hacking; versioned within the official CANN repository for long-term community co-construction.

Result: Release covers 53 operators and 1060 test cases; introduces a 3D weighted score combining compilation, correctness, and performance; evaluation against PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and HAP limits ensures meaningful headroom measurement and reduces artifacts.

Conclusion: CANN Bench provides a reproducible, scalable, and sustainable yardstick for AI operator-authoring on Ascend, enabling long-term community-driven improvement and benchmarking of AI-generated kernels within the official CANN ecosystem.

Abstract: AI agents are now capable of writing, compiling, and iteratively optimizing low-level operator kernels on different hardware platforms. Existing benchmarks, however, focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware ecosystems with less-exposed programming models without a common evaluation baseline. We present CANN Bench, an open benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei's Ascend NPU. The current release covers 53 operators and 1060 test cases organized into four difficulty tiers -- from simple elementwise primitives to MoE dispatch and FlashAttention kernels -- spanning FP16, BF16, FP32, and INT8 precision formats. Evaluation adopts a \textbf{three-dimensional weighted composite score} that treats compilation, functional correctness, and performance as independent axes, providing a principled reward signal for kernel-generation agents. Performance is graded against an out-of-the-box PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical per-case Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit on real NPU hardware, ensuring scores reflect genuine optimization headroom rather than measurement artifacts. The evaluation harness is designed to resist reward hacking from the ground up. CANN Bench is versioned within the official CANN repository and is designed for long-term community co-construction, providing the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible, and sustainably maintained yardstick for AI operator-authoring capability.

</details>


### [142] [Representation Robustness Under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20520)
*Sagnik Nath,Edith Aurora Graf,Liang Zhang,Diego Zapata-Rivera*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Represenational robustness is poor; LLMs are sensitive to problem surface form; code-based reasoning reveals latent abilities but doesn't fully fix brittleness; advocate treating representation as a core interface variable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether equivalently structured math problems are treated equivalently by LLMs and whether representation affects reasoning outcomes; assess robustness under multiple surface forms and isomorphic paraphrases.

Method: Create a curated dataset of mathematically equivalent problems across representations: story problems, word equations, symbolic equations, and paraphrases; evaluate five contemporary LLMs with direct answer generation; then test a code-augmented setting where models emit executable Python to validate solutions; measure correctness, flip rates, robustness, and types of errors.

Result: High sensitivity to surface form: correctness often flips across different representations; word/story variants vs equations show nontrivial misalignment; isomorphic paraphrases cause regressions; code-augmented reasoning reveals latent capabilities in some models but does not uniformly improve robustness; failures shift to protocol/execution errors; brittleness persists even with reasoning scaffolds.

Conclusion: Treat representation as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment; need to balance correctness, reliability, latency, and cost; future work should design interface-aware evaluation and robust multi-form problem-solving systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on mathematical problem solving, yet prior work often treats representationally equivalent formulations as interchangeable and conflates reasoning errors with interface failures. This paper investigates representation robustness in LLM-based mathematical problem solving by systematically varying surface representations of the same underlying problems, including story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, and isomorphic paraphrases. Using a curated dataset of mathematically equivalent problems, we evaluate five contemporary LLMs under a direct answer generation condition. We find substantial representational sensitivity: models frequently change correctness across equivalent formulations, with nontrivial flip rates across story, symbolic, and word-equation variants. We also observe systematic regressions under isomorphic reformulations, showing that even subtle paraphrase-level changes can degrade performance despite preserved mathematical structure. We then evaluate a code-augmented condition in which models externalize reasoning as executable Python code that is run locally for validation. This interface reveals strong latent reasoning capability in some models that perform poorly under direct prompting, but it does not uniformly improve robustness. Instead, failures shift across interaction layers, from opaque reasoning errors to protocol violations and execution failures. Even when executable reasoning succeeds, representation sensitivity often persists. Overall, our results show that reasoning scaffolds do not eliminate representational brittleness, but expose new tradeoffs among correctness, reliability, latency, and cost. We argue that representation should be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment, especially for AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

</details>


### [143] [Attention Degradation, Function Token Anchoring, and the Limits of Attention-Based Intervention in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20524)
*Sagar Dangal,Manoj Shakya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mean cross-positional attention degradation across transformers is largely descriptive; causal manipulation shows mixed or negligible effects on retrieval; function tokens influence predictions via hidden states, not attention mass, with model-specific variations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether mean cross-positional attention degradation causally limits contextual retrieval and whether attention patterns can be used for interpretability or inference optimizations.

Method:  Six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. Characterize short-term attention degradation (5-100 tokens), analyze layer-wise entropy, examine function-token anchoring (architecture-dependent), test syntactic boundary effects via comma insertion, apply Relay-Aware Attention to bias attention toward function tokens, and perform multi-fact retrieval probes.

Result:  Found an exponential-then-plateau degradation pattern whose rate inversely correlates with depth and exhibits architecture-specific entropy signatures. Function-token anchoring differs by architecture: OPT uses absolute positional encoding with distance-dependent specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA with RoPE shows long-distance reversal. Inserting commas at clause boundaries reduces degradation in the 40-80 token window, linked to boundary alignment rather than token density. Relay-Aware Attention raises attention mass by 16-24% but yields null or mixed effects on prediction across models (neutral for GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, prelim harm for LLaMA-3B, near-zero for OPT-1.3B). Multi-fact retrieval probes show degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy. 

Conclusion: Mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive: function tokens influence predictions through their hidden states rather than the attention they receive, with implications for interpretability methods and attention-score-based inference optimizations (e.g., KV-cache eviction).

Abstract: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is widely reported in transformer interpretability, yet whether it causally limits contextual retrieval remains untested. We present six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. We first characterise short-term (5-100 token) attention degradation, finding a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern whose rate is inversely correlated with depth, with distinct layer-wise entropy signatures per architecture. Function token anchoring proves architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B (absolute positional encoding) shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. Strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries causally reduces prediction degradation in the 40-80 token range, with the benefit tied to syntactic boundary alignment rather than token density. We then test the mechanism causally: Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), which biases attention logits toward function token positions, verifiably increases attention mass by 16-24% yet yields null effects on GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm on LLaMA-3B, and a mixed effect on OPT-1.3B that nets to approximately zero. Multi-fact retrieval probes further show that degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy across models. We conclude that mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive: function tokens contribute through what their hidden states compute, not through the attention they receive -- with implications for interpretability methodology and attention-score-based inference optimisations such as KV-cache eviction.

</details>


### [144] [Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ with GPT-5.5 Pro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20525)
*Yichen Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GPT-5.5 Pro-based agent autonomously produced correct disproofs of the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over R in 7/8 trials using a three-stage prompting pipeline; one trial had an unresolved gap; highlights AI-assisted mathematical discovery and reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Demonstrate feasibility and mechanics of autonomous AI-assisted proof discovery in high-level mathematics and provide a reproducible case study for proof generation and verification.

Method: Problem-agnostic three-stage prompting: proof-plan proposal, proof construction, review; 8 independent trials; diverse strategies (including unit-based and L^p-type regions of algebraic integers); average 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial; code and intermediate outputs released.

Result: Disproved Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over R in 7/8 trials; one trial identified an unresolved gap; proofs varied and included novel approaches; provides a reproducible dataset for autonomous proof generation.

Conclusion: AI can contribute to deep mathematical proof/disproof workflows; emphasizes reproducibility and transparency; invites independent verification; one gap suggests need for improved verification.

Abstract: OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marked a milestone for AI in mathematics. It also inspired another breakthrough: a human disproof of the Erdős--Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$. In this paper, we present a simple agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro. Using a problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline -- proof-plan proposal, proof construction, and review -- the agent autonomously generated correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over $\mathbb R$ in 7 of 8 independent trials; in the remaining trial, it identified an unresolved gap in its argument. The seven proofs are diverse: some are close to existing unit-based constructions, while others avoid units by using $L^p$-type regions of algebraic integers. The system used an average of 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial. We release the code, intermediate outputs, and generated proofs, providing a reproducible, data-contamination-free case study in autonomous proof generation.

</details>


### [145] [ConfidenceBench: Evaluating Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20526)
*Matthew ffrench-Constant,Daniel Yang,Xinmeng Huang,Sanyam Kapoor*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ConfidenceBench evaluates verbalized confidence in 15 frontier LLMs using the Brier score on 200 private MCQs across four domains; best models (Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview) achieve Brier ~0.103, outperforming calibrated-random baseline 0.1875; Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite ~0.367; accuracy and calibration diverge, showing confidence calibration is a distinct axis of reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In high-stakes settings, accuracy alone is insufficient; models must also reliably indicate when they are likely wrong. The work introduces a calibration benchmark to quantify this via verbalized confidence.

Method: Prompt-based elicitation of confidence without access to model logits; compute Brier score using predicted probability for the chosen answer; evaluation on 200 private MCQs across four categories; 15 frontier LLMs; three independent runs.

Result: Best-performing models achieve low Brier scores (~0.103), outperforming calibrated-random baseline (~0.1875); Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite performs poorly with ~0.367; accuracy and calibration diverge across model families; confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important axis beyond accuracy.

Conclusion: Verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct reliability axis for LLMs; prompting yields usable calibration signals without logits access; the benchmark supports using Brier score to incentivize truthful probability reporting.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where fluent but incorrect answers can be costly. In these settings, accuracy alone is insufficient: models must also know when they are likely to be wrong. We present ConfidenceBench, a calibration benchmark that evaluates verbalized confidence estimates in 15 frontier LLMs using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule that incentivises truthful probability reporting. Confidence is elicited via prompting, requiring no access to model logits and making the framework applicable to both closed-source and open-source systems. The benchmark comprises 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories: spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Across three independent runs, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the lowest Brier scores, both reported as 0.103. Both substantially outperform the calibrated-random baseline of 0.1875, while Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverge substantially across model families: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, and several models perform worse than the calibrated-random Brier baseline despite reasonable accuracy. These results show that verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important axis of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy-based evaluation.

</details>


### [146] [Evaluating and Guarding Citation Faithfulness in Agentic Scientific Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20527)
*Taewan Goo,Junsik Kim,Kyulhee Han,GwonYul Jo,Jong-Soo Kim,Tae-Hyung Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A protocol and guard for evaluating verifier reliability in citation checks by agentic LLMs, revealing wide variation in unsupported-citation rates across verifiers and poor cross-verifier agreement on which citations to flag. Introduces a gold-anchored evaluation protocol, split-conformal bound, and a deployable guard to measure and bound unsupported citations, with an open single-GPU kit and validation across multiple models and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current citation-verification in agentic LLMs is unreliable and lacks a standard protocol. Different verifiers (fixed models or human graders) produce inconsistent flagging, undermining trust and cross-paper comparisons. A named verifier and protocol are needed for trustworthy evaluation.

Method: Propose a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard. Use a swappable verifier calibrated to human gold, deterministic BM25-based re-attribution for citations, and a split-conformal layer to bound truly unsupported citations irrespective of individual flags. Validate across four open LLMs in 27-35B range and three agentic pipelines on SciFact, QASA, PubMedQA. Provide confidence intervals and an open-GPU kit.

Result: Found that the unsupported-citation rate ranges 3%–18% depending on verifier strictness; verifiers agree on supported citations but disagree on which to flag (negative-specific agreement 0.27–0.30). The authors present a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard that yield a distribution-free finite-sample bound on missed unsupported citations. Bound holds on held-out gold; calibration transfer discussed with a recalibration recipe. Kit: open single-GPU and held-out benchmarks.

Conclusion: A standardized, auditable evaluation framework (protocol + guard) addresses variability in verifier judgments, enabling trustworthy cross-paper comparisons and measurable guarantees on citation reliability in agentic LLM systems.

Abstract: Agentic LLM systems such as OpenScholar and PaperQA2 read the scientific literature and return cited answers, and both they and their benchmarks already check whether those citations hold, with a fixed attribution model or human graders. Neither audits the reliability of that check itself. We show it is not reliable, and that this matters. On identical agent outputs the measured unsupported-citation rate ranges from about 3% to about 18% depending only on the verifier's strictness, and although verifiers agree on which citations are supported, they disagree on which to flag (negative-specific agreement 0.27 to 0.30), so no single flag set is trustworthy and cross-paper comparison is invalid without a named verifier and protocol.
  We present a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard that make this behavior measurable and bounded. The protocol validates the verifier, measures re-attribution, and calibrates a guarantee against human gold rather than another model's verdict; the verifier is a swappable instrument chosen on cost (recall 0.94 on the supported class, held out), and re-attribution is a commodity step where a deterministic BM25 matches the best open generator. The guard adds a split-conformal layer placing a distribution-free, finite-sample bound on truly unsupported citations that slip past a chosen flagging rule, a guarantee on catch rate rather than conclusion correctness. The bound holds on held-out gold, and we identify and quantify the condition governing its transfer to deployment, calibration-negative difficulty, with a concrete recalibration recipe, left untested by prior conformal-factuality work.
  Validated across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on public benchmarks (SciFact, QASA, PubMedQA), with confidence intervals on every headline number, the protocol and guard ship as an open single-GPU kit.

</details>


### [147] [PromptPack: Scaling LLM Annotation Agents for Online Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20528)
*Sebastian Koralewski,Merwan Barlier,Yulia Stolin,Blaž Škrlj*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PromptPack reduces LLM annotation cost for ad creatives by batching with a shared system prompt and strict XML structure, enabling scalable, high-throughput feature extraction while maintaining performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online recommendation platforms rely on costly per-creative prompts for LLM-based feature extraction; scaling to large creative sets requires cheaper, higher-throughput methods that preserve signal quality.

Method: In-context batching using a shared system prompt, a strict XML envelope for outputs, and a post-output correction layer to ensure deterministic, pipeline-ready features across multiple creatives. Evaluation via offline retrieval benchmark with a downstream logistic-regression ranker and a new VWAL metric for signal quality.

Result: Batch size 20 yields 89% reduction in LLM input cost and 2.5x throughput increase, with AUC fully preserved compared to the production baseline.

Conclusion: Batching with a shared prompt and structural output envelope can substantially cut costs and increase throughput without sacrificing predictive performance, demonstrating a scalable approach for LLM-based feature extraction in live recommendation systems.

Abstract: Online recommendation platforms increasingly use Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract structured features from ad creatives. While deploying a single-call LLM annotation agent yields significant Click-Through Rate (CTR) improvements in our live production environment, per-creative prompting is prohibitively expensive to scale. The redundant system instructions sent in every request account for 94% of billed input tokens. To break this cost bottleneck, we introduce PromptPack, a scalable, high-throughput LLM annotation agent. PromptPack achieves this scale via in-context batching, combining a shared system prompt, a strict XML structural envelope, and an output correction layer to ensure deterministic, pipeline-ready feature extraction across multiple creatives simultaneously. We evaluate PromptPack via an offline retrieval benchmark using a downstream logistic-regression ranker. To deeply profile the agent's behavior, we measure AUC and introduce Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL), a novel metric capturing the signal quality of the generated features. Compared to our live, unbatched production baseline, PromptPack at batch size 20 cuts our LLM costs by 89% and accelerates throughput by 2.5x while fully preserving AUC.

</details>


### [148] [DynamicMCPBench: A Trace-Grounded, Effect-Scored Benchmark for LLM Agents over Live MCP Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20531)
*Jerzy Kamiński,Ilya Galyukshev,Artem Kuznetsov,Sergey Chuprin,Kirill Redko,Aidar Shumbalov,Anna Kalyuzhnaya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DynamicMCPBench introduces a reusable, live benchmarking framework for LLM agents on MCP servers, focusing on reproducing agentic effects rather than final answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks are brittle in live settings; need reproducible, live evaluation across practitioner-owned servers to measure general agentic ability and tool-use proficiency.

Method: Generate live goals, execute trajectories on each server-model pair, distill into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, score based on reproduction of effects (pass^3), scale across many models/servers/tasks; validate scoring with human raters.

Result: Across 24 models, 121 servers, 750 tasks in 15 categories, only ~50% of tasks solved; 31% unsolved by all models; task success declines with longer tool chains; human agreement on automatic scoring is solid (chance-corrected 0.76).

Conclusion: DynamicMCPBench provides a practical, repeatable benchmark for evaluating long-horizon agentic abilities on live MCP servers and exposes current limitations of agents in multi-step, tool-using tasks.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed over Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, yet the benchmarks used to evaluate them score the final answer or a fixed "ground-truth" list of tools, both of which are fragile once the underlying data is live and stateful. We present DynamicMCPBench, a reusable framework rather than a fixed dataset. A practitioner can run it on their own MCP servers to test models on their own tasks, or let it collect servers automatically to measure a model's general ability to solve agentic tasks. Given the servers and any set of models, it generates realistic goals, pursues each one live to record a successful trajectory, distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scores an agent on whether it reproduces those effects, never on the final answer. To show what the framework reveals, we run it at scale: 24 models over 121 servers and 750 tasks spread evenly over 15 task categories (50 each), where each category targets a distinct tool-use challenge of the generated questions. Each task is scored by pass^3: it counts as solved only if all three independent attempts succeed. Even the strongest agents solve only about half of the tasks, 31% of tasks are solved by no model at all, and accuracy collapses as the required tool chain grows longer (from 39% on the shortest chains to 13% on the longest). A human validation study confirms the automatic scoring is reliable (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76). DynamicMCPBench thus turns benchmark construction into something practitioners can rerun on their own servers and models, while exposing a consistent inability of current agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks.

</details>


### [149] [AppWorld-UL: Benchmarking Diverse Agent-User Interactions for Tool-Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20536)
*Junzhi Chen,Harsh Trivedi,Jane Pan,Michael JQ Zhang,Tejas Srinivasan,Niranjan Balasubramanian,Ashish Sabharwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AppWorld-UL is a user-in-the-loop benchmark with 516 tasks across 9 apps, designed to evaluate agent–user interaction; emphasizes realistic user responses via constrained LLM simulation; current SOTA models perform poorly, underscoring benchmark difficulty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks inadequately capture diverse agent–user interactions in dynamic environments; there is a need to evaluate how agents interact with users to ask clarifications, request confirmations, and handle infeasibilities.

Method: Extend the AppWorld framework to 516 tasks across 9 popular apps (e.g., Amazon, Spotify); introduce ambiguities and constraints to require user interaction; simulate user responses with a constrained LLM; evaluate with scenario-level and compositional metrics and compare models.

Result: Claude Opus 4.7 attains 48.6% overall success, 35.7% on a harder compositional subset, and 21.3% on stricter scenario-level metrics; analysis shows correct user interaction is critical for success.

Conclusion: The benchmark is sufficiently challenging and can drive research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents by highlighting the importance of realistic agent–user interactions and compositional reasoning.

Abstract: Tool-use agents that address day-to-day digital tasks such as ordering groceries must not only operate applications, but also interact with the user, e.g., to ask clarification questions, prompt for confirmation, and inform the user when the instruction is infeasible. However, current benchmarks for evaluating agent-user interactions do not capture the diversity of such interactions. Further, they operate in small environments with few, often non-state-changing, APIs. To address this gap, we introduce AppWorld-UL, a ``user-in-the-loop'' benchmark of 516 challenging tasks requiring diverse agent-user interactions. Building upon the AppWorld framework with 9 popular simulated apps like Amazon and Spotify, we systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints that necessitate various types of agent-user interaction. User behavior is simulated by an LLM prompted to respond with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, offering more reliable simulation than the unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives used in prior work. Our evaluation reveals that a state-of-the-art LLM, Claude Opus 4.7, achieves only 48.6% success on AppWorld-UL, and only 35.7% on the harder, compositional subset. On the stricter, scenario-level metric, compositional task performance drops to only 21.3%. Our analysis reveals that correct user-interaction is crucial for success. This demonstrates the benchmark's difficulty and its potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

</details>


### [150] [StrideDiffusion: Accelerating Diffusion Models for Time-series Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20545)
*Du Yin,Estrid He,Julián Jerónimo Bañuelos,Yang Yang,Feng Hu,Yuchen Luo,Hao Xue,Stephan Sigg,Flora Salim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StrideDiffusion: a training-free, spectral-aware sampler for time-series diffusion models that adaptively selects denoising stride based on band-level activity (relative energy, log-power drift, phase velocity). It achieves large speedups (up to 18.9x) with comparable or improved quality across six unconditional benchmarks and 5-14x on conditional tasks, by exploiting spectral evolution to guide step size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models for time-series are accurate but slow due to many denoising steps. There is a key spectral heterogeneity: different frequency bands evolve at different rates during the reverse process. A training-free, spectral-aware sampler could dramatically accelerate inference without retraining.

Method: At each denoising step, StrideDiffusion analyzes spectral components: band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity. It decides on a finer stride when high-frequency bands are active and uses larger jumps when low-frequency structure dominates. The approach is training-free, relying on spectral activity signals. A bandwise stability analysis shows inactive frequency bands change linearly with the jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, supporting the step-size heuristic.

Result: Empirical evaluation on six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks shows 14-66 function evaluations vs traditional 500-1000 steps, achieving up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup while maintaining or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting, it yields 5-14x speedup with comparable predictive accuracy.

Conclusion: Spectral evolution provides a principled signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling. StrideDiffusion achieves substantial speedups without training and preserves quality; the approach is scalable and applicable to conditional tasks.

Abstract: Diffusion models have become competitive generators for time series, but their practical use is limited by the large number of sequential denoising steps required at inference time. Existing fast samplers typically use fixed or generic timestep schedules, overlooking a distinctive property of time-series diffusion: different spectral bands evolve at different rates during the reverse process. We introduce StrideDiffusion, a training-free spectral-aware sampler that adaptively selects the denoising stride from band-level activity. At each step, StrideDiffusion monitors relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity to identify whether high- frequency dynamics remain active or whether the trajectory is dominated by stable low-frequency structure. It then takes fine steps when rapidly varying bands are active and larger jumps once only coarse components remain. A bandwise stability analysis shows that inactive frequency bands change only linearly with the jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, providing a local justification for spectral activity as a step-size indicator. Across six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks, StrideDiffusion uses only 14-66 function evaluations instead of 500/1000 denoising steps, achieving up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup while preserving or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting, it further delivers 5-14x average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy. These results show that spectral evolution provides a practical and principled signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/stridediff-ts.

</details>


### [151] [CMI-Mem: Toward Generalizable Long-Term Memory Management via CMI-Augmented Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20553)
*Yubo Wang,Qiuyu Zhao,Zenghui Sun,Shichao Dong,Jinsong Lan,Xiaoyong Zhu,Haoyang Li,Bo Zheng,Lei Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RL-based memory manager CMIMem combines downstream QA accuracy with intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) as a hybrid reward to evaluate new inputs, reducing reliance on synthetic QA pairs and current memory state conditioning on sampled queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome dependence on LLM-generated synthetic QA pairs for memory valuation by introducing an information-theoretic intrinsic signal (CMI) that measures the contribution of new inputs to the memory state independently of any queried QA sample.

Method: Propose CMIMem, a lightweight reinforcement learning memory manager (4B) that optimizes a hybrid reward: downstream QA correctness plus intrinsic CMI. CMI assesses information added by new conversational inputs relative to current memory without conditioning on a sampled QA query, thereby complementing QA-grounded evaluation.

Result: The abstract claims that CMI provides an intrinsic, query-independent signal that complements QA grounding, potentially improving memory valuation. Public code and a model checkpoint are provided for reproducibility.

Conclusion: CMIMem offers an RL-based approach to memory management where memory updates are guided by both QA performance and intrinsic information contribution, reducing reliance on sampled QA queries and enabling a more information-theoretic assessment of memory content.

Abstract: Memory Manager models are pivotal in agent systems. Existing methods rely predominantly on LLM-judged synthetic question-answer (QA) pairs, making memory valuation dependent on sampled queries and the downstream reader. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{CMI-Mem}, a reinforcement learning(RL)-based lightweight memory manager model with a hybrid reward that combines downstream QA correctness and intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI). CMI evaluates the information contributed by new conversational inputs relative to the current memory state without conditioning on a sampled QA query, thereby complementing rather than replacing QA grounding. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/Wyb0627/CMIMem , and the CMI-Mem-4B model checkpoint is available at: https://www.modelscope.cn/models/wyb0627/CMIMem-4B

</details>


### [152] [AI-Driven Multi-Hop Relay Selection for Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimize Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20554)
*Giambattista Amati,Federica Mangiatordi,Simone Angelini,Emiliano Pallotti,Pierpaolo Salvo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A learning-to-optimise (L2O) approach using a graph neural network (GNN) approximates MILP-optimal multi-hop relay selection for NR-V2X in urban environments, achieving near-optimal connectivity with orders-of-magnitude faster inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-time, scalable relay selection for NR-V2X is needed in dense urban settings where limited RSU density and dynamic topology hinder single-hop links; MILP yields optimal decisions but is computationally intractable for large networks.

Method: Model vehicular states as attributed graphs (CAVs and RSUs as nodes; candidate links as edges with propagation-aware features). Use an offline MILP solver as oracle for supervision. Train an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) to imitate the MILP decisions, enabling near-constant, real-time inference for relay selection.

Result: On large-scale urban datasets from a SUMO–GEMV2 pipeline, the L2O approach achieves connectivity comparable to the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude.

Conclusion: The L2O framework enables cost-effective, scalable, real-time NR-V2X relay selection in smart city environments by leveraging existing vehicular assets and offering near-optimal performance with significantly lower latency.

Abstract: Reliable and low-latency NR-V2X communications are essential for smart mobility in dense urban environments. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) density, frequent non-line-of-sight conditions, and highly dynamic vehicular topologies often prevent many Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable single-hop connectivity. Although multi-hop relay-assisted communication can extend infrastructure coverage, selecting relay links in real time under practical flow, capacity, and connectivity constraints remains challenging.
  Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) yields optimal multi-hop relay decisions, but its computational complexity scales sharply with network density, limiting real-time applicability. To address this, we propose a Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time NR-V2X relay selection. Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs, where CAVs and RSUs are nodes and candidate radio links are enriched with propagation-aware features. An offline MILP oracle provides optimal supervision, while an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) approximates oracle decisions with near-constant inference latency. Experiments on large-scale urban datasets generated by an integrated SUMO--GEMV2 simulation pipeline show that the proposed approach achieves connectivity comparable to that of the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude.
