The framework enables cost-effective enhancement of urban V2X connectivity by leveraging existing vehicular assets and supporting scalable, real-time NR-V2X operation in smart city environments.

</details>


### [153] [KeySI: An Interaction Framework for Tuning Text Embeddings Based on Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20556)
*Yan Zhu,Y. Chen,Rebecca Faust*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KeySI is a keyword-based interactive framework that enables concept-level feedback to tune embeddings with reduced labeling effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained language models often miss domain-specific semantics; adapting them typically requires lots of labeled data and complex pipelines. Prior interactive approaches rely on document-level feedback, which forces users to inspect documents, hindering efficiency.

Method: KeySI framework: (1) curate representative keywords from a corpus, (2) visualize keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, (3) allow interactive grouping of keywords into concepts, (4) translate keyword groups into document-level supervision signals for subsequent tuning, (5) provide a prototype implementation with iterative refinement and user/system feedback. Evaluation includes a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments assessing intent capture and embedding alignment.

Result: The approach demonstrates effective capture of user intent and improved embedding alignment in experiments, with reduced need for manual document labeling and inspection.

Conclusion: Keyword-based concept feedback via KeySI offers a practical, efficient path to adapt embeddings to domain-specific semantics, lowering barriers to use and enabling iterative refinement through keyword-level interaction.

Abstract: In large-scale text analysis tasks, pre-trained language models are often used to embed text corpora for downstream analysis. However, such models may struggle to capture domain-specific semantics and adapting them typically requires large amounts of labeled data and technical expertise to implement training pipelines. Recent approaches have demonstrated how visual interactions in document projections can capture human feedback as training signals for model tuning. However, these methods operate on document-level feedback, which requires users to open and assess individual documents in order to provide effective feedback. In this paper, we propose KeySI, an interaction framework that enables feature-level feedback through keyword-based concept specification. Users specify feedback by organizing extracted keywords into groups representing concepts, which KeySI translates into document-level supervision for subsequent tuning. By operating on keywords as the primary interaction medium, KeySI reduces the need for manual document inspection and labeling and lowers the barrier to adapting embedding models. We present a prototype implementation that, given a corpus, curates representative keywords, visualizes keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, allows interactive specification of keyword groups, and supports iterative refinement through system feedback. We evaluate KeySI through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment.

</details>


### [154] [WaveformQA: Benchmarking LLM Temporal Reasoning on Digital Waveforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20638)
*Yichuan Liu,Daniel Cummings,Nick Vadlamudi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WaveformQA introduces an open-source benchmark (360 questions) to test LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms, showing improved reasoning with event-time JSON over VCD and highlighting context window limitations for complex questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap where LLMs excel at code generation but struggle with temporal reasoning over hardware waveforms; provide a reproducible, real-world-grounded benchmark to evaluate and accelerate research in this area.

Method: Programmatically generate questions across eight difficulty categories for waveforms derived from open-source designs; evaluate frontier LLMs on temporal reasoning tasks; compare representations (event-time JSON vs VCD); provide an extendable open-source framework for new categories and waveform sources.

Result: LLMs perform reasonably on simple queries but show degraded performance on complex temporal and multi-step questions due to limited context windows and reasoning challenges; event-time JSON representations improve LLM reasoning accuracy compared to VCD.

Conclusion: WaveformQA offers a practical, reproducible benchmark for temporal reasoning over digital waveforms and demonstrates that representation choices (event-time JSON) can significantly aid LLM reasoning; the framework supports rapid prototyping and extension for future research.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and reasoning, yet their ability to perform temporal reasoning over digital waveform data remains largely unexplored. Although reasoning over digital waveforms is a critical bottleneck in design verification, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate hardware description language (HDL) code generation and use waveforms only as supplementary context. This paper presents WaveformQA, an open-source question-answering benchmark for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. The benchmark comprises 360 questions with programmatically generated ground truths across eight categories of varying difficulty, including questions targeting multi-signal correlation and event ordering. Waveforms are generated from open-source design implementations, ensuring reproducibility and grounding the benchmark in real hardware behavior. Evaluation of frontier LLMs reveals that while models achieve reasonable accuracy on simple queries, performance degrades due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties on complex temporal and multi-step questions. In addition, we show that an event-time JSON representation of waveforms improves LLM reasoning accuracy versus the standardized value change dump (VCD) format. The open-source framework supports extending to new question categories and importing new waveform sources, enabling researchers to rapidly prototype temporal reasoning experiments.

</details>


### [155] [NVIDIA-labs OO Agents: Native Python Object-Oriented Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20709)
*Paul Furgale,Severin Klingler,James Nolan,Matt Staats,Gaia Di Lorenzo,Elisa Martinez Abad,Christian Schüller,Razvan Dinu,Alessio Devoto,Pascal Berard,Gal Kaplun,Elad Sarafian,Riccardo Roveri,Leon Derczynski,Ricardo Silveira Cabral*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NOOA presents a model-agnostic Python framework where an agent is a Python object; runtime action bodies are filled by an LLM loop, while deterministic Python code remains. This unifies agent development under standard Python abstractions and demonstrates the approach on established benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To streamline agent development by eliminating fragmented toolchains (prompts, tool schemas, callback code, workflows) and provide a single, testable, debuggable interface based on familiar Python programming constructs.

Method: Agent-as-object: methods are actions, fields are state, docstrings are prompts, and type annotations are contracts. Methods with '...' bodies are completed at runtime by an LLM-driven agent loop; regular bodies are deterministic. Exposed capabilities include context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, and validated LLM loops via Pythonic APIs; six model-facing ideas are combined on a single surface (typed I/O, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs).

Result: Current models can effectively use the NOOA interface in targeted capability tasks and agentic/reasoning benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, ARC-AGI-3).

Conclusion: NOOA offers a cohesive, testable, and model-agnostic framework that leverages standard Python abstractions to simplify and improve agent development, evaluation, and integration with LLM-driven loops.

Abstract: Traditional agent development is split across prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs. We present NVIDIA Object-Oriented Agents (NOOA), a model-agnostic Python framework for building reliable AI agents. NOOA takes a simpler approach: an agent is a Python object. Its methods are the actions the model can take, fields are its state, docstrings are its prompts, and its type annotations are contracts. A method whose code body consists of "..." is completed at runtime by an LLM-driven agent loop, while methods with normal bodies remain standard deterministic Python. This gives developers and agents the same interface, so agent behavior can be tested, traced, refactored, and improved just like other software.
  This paper makes three contributions. (1) We present the agent-as-a-Python-object programming model and the design principles behind it. Where Python has existing abstractions, we adopt them directly. Agent-specific capabilities--context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, and validated LLM loops--are exposed through simple Pythonic APIs, so both developers and agents share one familiar programming model. (2) We identify six model-facing ideas that NOOA is, to our knowledge, the first to combine on a single surface: typed input/output, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context and events. We find the community already converging on several of these ideas--often as experimental or partial features--and present the comparison to encourage further adoption. (3) We demonstrate that current models use this interface effectively, both in targeted capability tests and on agentic and reasoning benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 and ARC-AGI-3.

</details>


### [156] [ArbiGraph: Arbitrarily Scalable Verifiable Task Graphs for Evaluating Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20764)
*Pavel Golikov,Evgenii Opryshko,Gennady Pekhimenko,Mark C. Jeffrey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A benchmark generator, ARBIGRAPH, evaluates tool-assisted language agents on retaining, updating, composing, and discarding task-relevant context across extended reasoning workflows. It uses executable Python solvers and typed intermediate states to form controllable task graphs, enabling automatic verification. Evaluated on math, GSM-style word problems, and Python-tracing across four topologies; shows high isolated-task accuracy but significant degradation on dependent tasks (up to 33.3% drop), revealing failures unseen in single-task evaluations. Code and results at GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To expose failures of tool-assisted agents that standard single-task benchmarks miss by enabling controllable, verifiable long-horizon task graphs with explicit intermediate states.

Method: Represent each task as a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver; compose tasks through typed intermediate states (scalar/list); vary graph length, dependencies, distractor count, and value type; instantiate with math, GSM-style word problems, and Python-tracing tasks; evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B agent across four topologies; maintain exact automatic verification.

Result: High accuracy on isolated tasks but substantial degradation on complex dependent tasks; branching chains of dependent math tasks show up to 33.3% accuracy drop; ARBIGRAPH reveals failures not visible from single-task evaluation.

Conclusion: ARBIGRAPH provides a controllable, verifiable benchmark for tool-assisted reasoning that exposes long-horizon context-management failures; code, datasets, and results are available at the referenced GitHub repository.

Abstract: We introduce ARBIGRAPH, a benchmark generator for evaluating whether tool-assisted language agents can retain, update, compose, and discard task-relevant context across extended reasoning workflows. ARBIGRAPH represents each task as a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver, and composes tasks through typed intermediate states, instantiated here as scalar and list values. This design enables controllable task graphs whose length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value type can be varied while preserving exact automatic verification. We instantiate ARBIGRAPH with math, GSM-style word-problems, and Python-tracing task categories, and evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topologies. The results show high accuracy on isolated tasks but substantial degradation on more complex dependent tasks: accuracy drops by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks. This shows that ARBIGRAPH exposes failures that are not visible from single-task evaluation alone. Our code, generated datasets, and evaluation results are available at https://github.com/pavelgolikov/ArbiGraph.git

</details>


### [157] [The Human-AI Substitution Principle: When will you be replaced by AI in your organization?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20781)
*Bonny Banerjee,Shreya Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A hierarchical-organization model (HAT) analyzes when AI substitutes for human labor, revealing a substitution principle and conditions for abrupt transitions, hybrids, and flatter hierarchies; connects automation economics to organizational design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the timing and structure of human–AI labor substitution by formalizing asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI scaling, and to integrate automation economics with organizational design and governance.

Method: Develop an analytical HAT model for hierarchical organizations that encodes economic asymmetry; derive risk-adjusted costs, depth, deployment, and risk conditions; formulate the Human–AI Substitution Principle; analyze transitions, hybrid forms, and vulnerability across managerial levels.

Result: Derives a precise AI substitution condition; shows AI adoption can trigger abrupt workforce shifts, sustains hybrids without a minimum human fraction, and yields flatter hierarchies; identifies middle-management vulnerability and skill-threshold effects for highly skilled workers; provides a unified theory linking automation, design, governance, and planning.

Conclusion: The HAT framework unifies automation economics with organizational design and governance, offering structural criteria for AI-driven organizational transformation and workforce planning.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming organizations, raising a fundamental organizational and economic question: when will a human employee be replaced by AI? We present an analytical model for studying Human--AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations. A central feature of the HAT model is that it formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. The HAT model allows us to derive how risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk jointly determine when, where, why, and under what structural conditions human--AI replacement occurs. A key result is the Human--AI Substitution Principle, which provides a precise condition --- grounded in the formal asymmetry assumption --- under which AI replaces human labor. Building on this result, we show that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid human--AI organizations, including cases where risk heterogeneity sustains human and AI roles without requiring a minimum-human-fraction constraint, and flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control. The HAT model identifies structural conditions under which middle-management roles exhibit elevated vulnerability to automation, and shows that the vulnerability of highly skilled workers depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials. More broadly, the paper connects automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation.

</details>


### [158] [Refusal-Gated Decoding: Preserving Refusal Behavior Under High-Temperature Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20791)
*Phillip Howard,Xin Su,Allen Roush,Manikandan Ravikiran,Amir Abdullah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Efficient sequential decoding preserves refusal behavior under high-temperature sampling, achieving 91–99% preservation across three datasets with minimal latency, enabling diverse but safe LLM outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-temperature sampling increases diversity but weakens safety/refusal behaviour; need methods to maintain refusals while preserving high entropy.

Method: Proposed efficient sequential decoding approach that preserves a model's greedy-decoding refusal response at high temperatures with low additional latency; likely constrains or adjusts decoding to maintain refusals without slowing generation.

Result: Preserves 91-99% of greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets; high-temperature responses on safe prompts remain intact; overall efficiency gain.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasible maintenance of model safety under high-entropy sampling, enabling safe high-temperature generation for diverse outputs.

Abstract: High-temperature sampling is one of the primary mechanisms for increasing diversity in LLMs. Recent advances in truncation-based sampling techniques have helped mitigate drawbacks of high-temperature sampling such as neural text degeneration, thereby enabling greater diversity in LLM outputs without sacrificing coherence. However, increasing the entropy of the token probability distribution via high temperatures has also been shown to weaken model guardrails by reducing the model's refusal response in the presence of harmful prompts. Despite the potential benefits of high-temperature sampling and the importance of maintaining model safety, there is a lack of existing solutions for maintaining the refusal behavior of LLMs under a higher entropy regime. To address this gap, we systematically study how temperature influences refusal behavior in LLMs and propose an efficient sequential decoding approach which preserves a model's greedy decoding refusal response at high temperatures while incurring minimal additional latency. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach preserves 91-99% of the greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets without compromising the model's high-temperature response for safe prompts. Our work demonstrates how refusal behavior can be maintained in an efficient manner for applications which require high-temperature sampling.

</details>


### [159] [Can an AI System Be Creative? A Critical Perspective from Art and Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20796)
*Ivan Magrin-Chagnolleau*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI systems exhibit combinatorial creativity but are structurally incapable of creativity in its strongest sense (exploratory and transformational). The paper argues that serendipity and a subject-position are essential to creativity and are missing in AI, proposing a realistic, generative human–AI collaboration model. The paper itself demonstrates its thesis via a human–AI collaborative composition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether AI can achieve true creativity using Margaret Boden's framework (novelty, surprise, value; combinatorial, exploratory, transformational) and to explore how human–AI collaboration can realize a productive form of creativity.

Method: The analysis is grounded in Boden's framework, integrating electrical engineering and arts/philosophy perspectives. It employs theoretical argumentation and is illustrated by several concrete experiments, including a self-demonstrating instance where the paper is produced through human–AI collaboration.

Result: AI demonstrates genuine combinatorial creativity but is limited in exploratory creativity and fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. The main limitation identified is the absence of serendipity/accident and a subject-position to recognize and embrace such chance events. A practical, realistic model of human–AI creative collaboration is proposed, and the paper itself serves as a demonstration of this collaborative process.

Conclusion: Strong (transformational) creativity remains beyond current AI. However, a realistic, generative form of human–AI collaboration is viable and valuable. The work emphasizes the phenomenology of creativity (serendipity, subjectivity) and provides a framework for designing collaborative creative systems.

Abstract: This paper examines the question of whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems can be creative, approached from the dual perspective of a researcher trained in electrical engineering, pattern recognition, machine learning, and neural networks, who has also spent most of his life engaged in the arts as actor, stage and film director, writer, composer, and visual artist, and in philosophy. Drawing on Margaret Boden's foundational framework, both her three properties of creativity (novelty, surprise, and value) and her three types of creative processes (combinatorial, exploratory, and transformational), the paper argues that AI systems are structurally incapable of creativity in its strongest sense. While they exhibit genuine capability in the domain of combinatorial creativity, they are significantly bounded in exploratory creativity, and fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. The paper further argues that the most important limitation of current AI systems is not the absence of novelty per se, but the absence of any mechanism for serendipity, accident, or the unexpected, all of which play a central role in the phenomenology of creativity, and the absence of any subject position from which to recognize and welcome such chance events. The paper concludes by proposing a model of human, AI creative collaboration that is both realistic and generative, illustrated by several concrete experiments. The paper is itself a demonstration of the thesis it advances: it was composed through a deliberate human AI collaborative process, which is described in the methodological note that opens it.

</details>


### [160] [Profiling Lightweight Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20806)
*Tomohiro Harada,Enrique Alba,Gabriel Luque*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PTME-based precision-aware profiling for lightweight LLM inference: measure Precision, Time, peak Memory, and Energy (hardware-level) to reveal optimal trade-offs; proxies like size/FLOPs fail to predict precision; Pareto analysis yields non-dominated configurations for edge deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing efficiency evaluations rely on proxy descriptors (parameter count, FLOPs) that do not couple cost to task precision. A hardware-level, precision-aware framework is needed to guide deployment of lightweight LLMs under resource constraints.

Method: Develop and apply a PTME experimental framework that directly measures Precision, Time, Memory, and Energy on edge-class resource envelopes. Evaluate representative lightweight LLMs on desktop hardware with benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. Compare PTME-informed selections with traditional proxy-based choices. Use Pareto analysis to identify non-dominated configurations.

Result: Static proxies approximate inference cost but do not predict precision. Tightening resource envelopes raises cost without improving precision; execution time increases more than energy and penalizes larger models most. No single model dominates across all PTME dimensions; Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations unseen by accuracy/efficiency-only metrics. PTME profiling can guide deployment under varying resource envelopes.

Conclusion: PTME profiling uncovers configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost, enabling more informed model selection than size/FLOPs/latency/accuracy alone. It highlights trade-offs and actionable candidates for edge deployment.

Abstract: Lightweight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed locally on personal computers and are expected to play a growing role in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments. In such settings, energy consumption, execution time, and memory usage directly affect practical usability, yet existing evaluations of LLM efficiency largely rely on proxy descriptors such as parameter count or FLOPs, often decoupled from task precision. This paper introduces a PTME-based experimental framework for the precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, jointly measuring Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption through direct hardware-level measurements. The methodology is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs executed locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, using benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. We find that static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope increases cost without affecting precision, amplifying execution time more strongly than energy and penalizing larger models the most. Moreover, no single model dominates across all PTME dimensions, and a Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations that would be hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments, providing practical guidance for selecting models under different resource envelopes. These results show that selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can select the wrong deployment candidate; PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost.

</details>


### [161] [Enhancing Explainable Cardiac Diagnosis with Guide-Grounded Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20814)
*Hai-Nam Duy Vuong,Duy-Anh Bui,Trong-Nghia Nguyen,Kim-Ngan Thi Nguyen,Trang Mai Xuan,Tien-Cuong Nguyen,Van-Dem Pham,Thien Van Luong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Grounds ECG report generation with a fixed, distilled interpretation guide injected into a multimodal prompting pipeline, improving semantic quality and consistency of LLM-generated reports while preserving classification performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome limited interpretability and hallucination in CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM ECG reporting by tying outputs to established diagnostic criteria via a fixed knowledge block.

Method: CNN with Grad-CAM yields class probabilities and heatmaps from 12-lead ECGs; offline distillation of textbooks/guidelines into an ECG Interpretation Guide injected as a fixed knowledge block; an LLM takes the image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN fact pack, and the guide to generate structured, guideline-consistent diagnostic reports.

Result: On the PTB-XL test set, guide grounding improves semantic quality and perceived consistency of reports, while preserving competitive classification performance. Average BERTScore of generated impressions rose from 0.818 to 0.953 compared to a CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline.

Conclusion: Injecting a distilled interpretation guide into multimodal prompting reduces hallucinations, enhances clinical plausibility, and brings explainable cardiac diagnosis closer to deployment.

Abstract: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac as- sessment, yet clinical deployment of deep learning models remains con- strained by limited interpretability and the hallucination risk of large language models (LLMs). Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks can generate ECG reports, but their explanations are often only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, reducing trust- worthiness and reproducibility. We propose a guide-grounded multimodal framework that explicitly anchors report generation in curated clinical knowledge. A convolutional neural network (CNN) and Grad-CAM first produce class probabilities and class-specific heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guideline materials are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, which is injected as a fixed knowledge block for every sample. Conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the in- jected guide, a multimodal LLM generates structured diagnostic reports with guideline-consistent terminology and criteria usage. Experiments on the full PTB-XL test set demonstrate that guide grounding improves se- mantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports while pre- serving competitive classification performance. In particular, our method increases the average BERTScore of generated impressions from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicat- ing closer alignment with reference reports. These findings suggest that injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce hallucinations and enhance the clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing ex- plainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

</details>


### [162] [Efficient and Interpretable Body-Based Emotion Recognition with Lightweight Temporal Convolutional Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20820)
*Christian Arzate Cruz,Stefanos Gkikas,Houshyar Asadi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can offer an efficient and interpretable alternative to graph-based skeleton models for body-based emotion recognition, achieving competitive accuracy with drastically fewer parameters and lower latency. Upper-body motion is the strongest regional cue, though the usefulness of body regions varies by emotion; multiple interpretability methods reveal complementary insights into model behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address real-time body-based emotion recognition with lower computational cost and improved interpretability by moving from expensive graph-based skeleton models to lightweight temporal modeling.

Method: Evaluate a family of TCN models on the DIEM-A dataset, comparing against a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Conduct region-specific TCN analyses, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency to study body-region contributions and interpretability.

Result: G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, but TCN-Base remains within 1.58 accuracy points and 1.25 macro-F1 points of G-TSG while using 79.18% fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by ~12.5x. Upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone region cue; region usefulness varies across emotions. Different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior.

Conclusion: Lightweight TCNs can provide efficient, interpretable body-based emotion recognition with competitive performance and offer practical insights into motion cues contributing to classification.

Abstract: Body-based emotion recognition is important for real-time affective systems, but graph-based skeleton models can be computationally expensive. This paper studies whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can provide an efficient and interpretable alternative for body-based emotion classification. We evaluate a family of TCN models on DIEM-A and compare them with a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Although G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, TCN-Base remains within $1.58$ accuracy points and $1.25$ macro-F1 points while using $79.18\%$ fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by approximately $12.5\times$. We also analyze body-region contributions using region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency. The results show that upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone regional cue, that the usefulness of body regions varies across emotions, and that different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior. These findings suggest that lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while also providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification.

</details>


### [163] [Auditing Provenance Sensitivity in LLM Agent Action Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20827)
*Junchi Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Per-target authorization auditing shows untrusted evidence can sway LLM actions; even with source-authority cues, trusted/untrusted context diverges across tasks (stress-set results).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify and mitigate how untrusted, non-authorized evidence in mixed-context prompts affects LLM decision-making; design a target-specific authorization audit.

Method: Label context factors separately for each tool/argument target; primary test fixes task, proposition, position, and policy while varying only the proposition's source authority; assess behavior under weakened valid evidence and use context-subset interactions as a diagnostic; evaluate 450 controlled next-action tasks across multiple open-weight LLM families.

Result: Trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4% of competing cases vs 1.7% of supporting cases; under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition occurs at 2.4% (95% CI 2.1–3.0%); results are stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence; models respond to textual source-authority cues but untrusted evidence still influences actions.

Conclusion: Target-specific authorization audits reveal measurable influence of source authority on LLM actions and partial mitigation; untrusted evidence can still shape decisions, indicating the need for stronger grounding and auditing mechanisms.

Abstract: LLM agents choose tools and arguments from context that mixes user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, and untrusted text. Evidence can be relevant without being authorized to determine a decision, so a correct action need not be grounded only in permitted evidence. We introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Its primary test holds the task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while changing only the proposition's source authority. We then test behavior when valid evidence is weakened and use context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. Across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple open-weight LLM families, trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4 percent of competing cases versus 1.7 percent of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition is retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4 percent of comparisons, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 2.1 to 3.0 percent. These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.

</details>


### [164] [Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20848)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A behavioral audit framework evaluates medical LLMs' evidence-use in diagnosis, separating evidence interactions from failure judgments; findings show many evidence interactions are clinically plausible, and accuracy can mask evidence-use failures; advocates role-aware audits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diagnostic accuracy alone is insufficient to assess LLM reasoning; understanding how evidence informs diagnoses and how interactions among evidence affect decisions is crucial for clinically reliable models.

Method: Decompose patient information into evidence units; score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets; mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins; separate interaction discovery from failure assignment; evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase; use blinded, extensive review (e.g., 130-item sample) to assess validity of evidence use.

Result: Across datasets, most interaction strength is explained by faithful support and differential conflict/cancellation, suggesting many interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a blinded 5-reviewer, 130-item enriched sample focused on DDXPlus, invalid/shortcut-like cases concentrate when findings are negated/absent or locally-clinical evidence; accuracy may obscure candidate evidence-use failures.

Conclusion: Accuracy alone can hide evidence-use failures; role-aware audits are needed in medical LLM evaluation to properly assess how models use case evidence.

Abstract: Medical LLMs are often evaluated by whether they select the correct diagnosis, but diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used the case evidence appropriately. We present a behavioral audit of evidence use in medical diagnosis. For each case, we decompose patient information into evidence units, score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. Because medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions can reflect plausible differential diagnosis, while suspicious interactions require robustness checks and clinical review. We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. Across datasets, faithful support and differential conflict or cancellation account for most interaction strength, showing that many evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer 130-item enriched review sample, invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. These results show that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures and motivate role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

</details>


### [165] [Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20852)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A study of Code Monitor Red Teaming and CodeMonitorBench to detect hidden bugs after public test success; shows weak verifiers with scaffolding/adapted model families can catch some hidden issues but miss many at low false positives; adversarial pressure and evidence limits expose limitations; GLM-5.1 helps partially; need better inference for residuals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public tests alone do not guarantee specification correctness; investigate whether a weaker LLM verifier can identify residual hidden bugs once code passes public tests.

Method: Introduce a monitor-red-teaming protocol (Code Monitor Red Teaming) and instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench across function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Evaluate 71,000 generated candidates for public vs hidden test performance, varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and model capability; conduct adversarial public-test-overfit stress tests; test a GLM-5.1 verifier; perform an inferability audit of misses.

Result: Of 43,677 candidates that pass public tests, 23,081 fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family but miss most hidden bugs at a 5% false-positive rate. Adversarial overfit reduces verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates. GLM-5.1 recovers part of the gap under the same information boundary; inferability audit indicates remaining misses stem from verifier failures and M1 evidence limits.

Conclusion: Public tests are insufficient for guaranteeing safety; a monitor-based red-teaming approach reveals residual risks. Verifier scaffolding and model choice help but do not fully close the gap; improved interpretability and tighter evidence bounds are needed to reduce hidden-bug misses.

Abstract: Visible tests are a common gate for LLM-generated code, but passing them does not certify specification correctness. We study a deployment-like monitoring problem: after code has passed public tests, can a weaker LLM verifier identify the residual hidden bugs? We introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a monitor-red-teaming protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability. We instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench, spanning function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Across 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests and 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family, but still miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. As a robustness stress test, adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates in most cells. A GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the gap under the same evidence boundary; an inferability audit shows that remaining misses mix verifier failures with M1 evidence limits.

</details>


### [166] [Is Deep Research Reliable? Misleading Knowledge Induces False Conclusions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20891)
*Pengyu Zhu,Lijun Li,Longju Yang,Sen Su*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MisKnow-Agent demonstrates that misleading information can propagate through Deep Research workflows, causing false conclusions in final reports. Even with focused verification, long-horizon tasks are vulnerable; defenses help but do not fully prevent misclaims, underscoring the need for end-to-end evidence verification and correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess the reliability of LLM-based Deep Research agents in open information environments and whether misleading knowledge can be integrated into long-horizon reports.

Method: Introduce MisKnow-Agent to generate misleading instances with controllable authority and style, producing 5,933 quality-controlled instances on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Evaluate across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents and test defenses (pre-, post-, and combined) against false-conclusion adoption.

Result: Misleading knowledge exposure can induce false conclusions in final reports during long-horizon research. Focused corpus verification identifies misleading instances, but such instances can still be adopted in workflows. Verification gaps exist between corpus validation and workflow-level evidence use. Defenses reduce but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption.

Conclusion: Reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report generation.

Abstract: Deep Research agents extend LLM-based assistants into long-horizon workflows involving planning, retrieval, evidence synthesis, and report generation, yet their reliability in open information environments remains underexplored. A key concern is whether apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge encountered in such environments can propagate through these workflows and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports. To study this failure mode, we introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework for constructing and validating misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks. MisKnow-Agent generates misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances built on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Extensive experiments across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents show that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing a broad reliability vulnerability in current Deep Research agents. Although search-enabled verifier models consistently identify the retained instances as misleading during focused corpus validation, the same instances can still be adopted during long-horizon research, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. Finally, we evaluate pre- and post-research defenses, both individually and in combination, finding that all three configurations mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption. Our findings suggest that reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities.

</details>


### [167] [Source-Prior-Driven Selective Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion Model Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20913)
*Yi Xiong,Yuan-Yuan Cheng,Xiao-Ming Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A source-prior-driven selective adaptation framework that uses a static mask to identify parameters for targeted updates, improving adaptation to new domains/styles while preserving pretraining capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the adaptation–retention trade-off in fine-tuning large diffusion models by exploiting heterogeneous parameter sensitivity and cross-layer inconsistencies.

Method: 1) Learn a static parameter mask that selects parameters suitable for downstream adaptation. 2) Apply structured update strategies to the selected subset (e.g., constrained optimization, sparse/low-rank updates) to realize targeted fine-tuning.

Result: Empirical results show a superior adaptation–retention trade-off compared with strong baselines (full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient methods).

Conclusion: Source-prior-driven selective adaptation enables efficient fine-tuning of diffusion models with better preservation of general generative capabilities.

Abstract: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains or styles involves a trade-off: improving target-specific generation often degrades the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods typically handle this trade-off only implicitly. In this work, we propose a novel source-prior-driven selective adaptation method to efficiently fine-tune diffusion models, achieving a favorable trade-off. Our method relies on two key observations: (1) the loss of general generative capability is highly inconsistent across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters that have a relatively small impact on the model's general generative capability remain structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. Motivated by these observations, we first learn a static mask to explicitly identify parameters better suited for downstream adaptation, and then construct structured update strategies for the selected subset. Experiments show that our method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.

</details>


### [168] [Traceable Scholarship: Page Anchors and Ariadne's Thread for Humanistic Inquiry in the Age of Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20916)
*Deyu Jing*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Traceable Scholarship as a normative framework for AI-assisted humanistic research to ensure verifiability, introducing page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract, with a three-layer AIH-Infra implementation (Contexture, Open WebUI AIH-Infra, MCP Server) and a Kant Akademie-Ausgabe case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fluency of generative AI can mask lack of sources and evidence; need a normative condition to keep scholarship public, refutable, and source-aware in print, digital, and AI revolutions.

Method: Define normative framework (Traceable Scholarship) and architecture; specify constructs (page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, Scope Contract); present AIH-Infra stack; conduct Kant Akademie-Ausgabe case study to illustrate retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading.

Result: Formalizes traceability as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted scholarship; provides a reference implementation and demonstrates practical benefits for verifiability.

Conclusion: Traceability enables public, refutable humanistic research in the age of generative AI; it is a normative condition beyond software features.

Abstract: Generative AI lets large language models produce scholarly-looking text within seconds, yet fluency does not equal valid explanation. The deepest risk is not factual error alone but the appearance that an explanation is already established without clear sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. We liken the page anchor to Ariadne's thread: within the labyrinth of generative fluency, it is the thread that leads the scholar back to the source. This paper proposes Traceable Scholarship as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic research, situating it across the three revolutions of knowledge infrastructure: print, digital, and generative AI. We introduce page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract, and present AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation: Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). A case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base illustrates how traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. Traceability is not a software feature; it is the condition under which humanistic research can remain public and refutable in the age of generative AI.

</details>


### [169] [OPOD: On-Policy Omni Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20918)
*Tong Zhao,Yuyang Hu,Reed Li,Yu Lu,Haibo Shi,Yutao Zhu,Zhicheng Dou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: On-Policy Omni Distillation (OPOD) routes student outputs to modality-specific teachers (text, image, audio) to improve omni-modal models while maintaining cross-modal balance, outperforming pooled-data baselines across 12 benchmarks and three backbone sizes; able to train with dedicated teachers and discard them post-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal models trained on pooled data often underperform modality-specialized models due to interference between modalities. There is a need to leverage modality-specific expertise while preserving balanced cross-modal capabilities in a single omni-modal model.

Method: OPOD routes each student token to the corresponding text, image, or audio teacher. It only uses teacher guidance when the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student, allows independent modulation of each modality’s influence during training, and asks the routed teacher to assess both the final answer and the alignment of the reasoning with the correct answer. Training is evaluated across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes.

Result: OPOD achieves the best average score at all scales (70.8, 51.7, 46.2), surpassing the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On a 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a pooled multimodal baseline on all twelve benchmarks and ranks first or second on 11. The modality-specialist teachers are discarded after training, yielding a deployable omni-modal model that maintains cross-modal balance.

Conclusion: Coordinating modality-specific teachers via on-policy routing is an effective strategy to boost a shared omni-modal model without sacrificing cross-modal balance; OPOD demonstrates robust gains across scales and tasks and reduces intra-training interference by gating guidance and weighting modalities independently.

Abstract: Omni-modal models can handle text, images, and audio in one system, but improving all of these abilities together remains difficult. Training a single model on pooled multimodal data often fails to match models specialized for individual modalities. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a way to combine such specialists: the student generates a response, and a teacher evaluates that same response, so the student learns directly from behaviors it actually produces. Yet using several teachers can introduce competing guidance and improve one modality at the expense of another. We present On-Policy Omni Distillation (OPOD), which routes each student response to the matching text, image, or audio teacher. OPOD keeps teacher guidance only on tokens where the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student, adjusts the influence of each modality teacher independently during training, and asks the routed teacher to assess both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct answer. Across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average score at every scale, reaching 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2 and exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a counterpart post-trained jointly on pooled multimodal data on all twelve benchmarks, and ranks first or second on eleven even when the individual specialists are included. The specialists are discarded after training, leaving one deployable omni-modal model. These results show that coordinating modality-specific teachers is an effective way to improve a shared model while maintaining cross-modal balance.

</details>


### [170] [Representing Entity Importance in AI Knowledge Systems: A Dual-Signal Framework of Audience Evaluation and Structural Authority](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20925)
*Shen Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes an interpretable dual-signal representation for entity importance—audience-evaluation and structural-authority—and shows they are non-redundant; empirical validation on movie data indicating only weak association and limited overlap, arguing against collapsing to a single scalar for task-aware AI knowledge systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-scalar importance compression may discard distinctions critical for retrieval and reasoning; need to test whether separate audience and structural signals provide distinct, task-relevant information.

Method: Construct two signals for entities: audience-evaluation from IMDb ratings; structural-authority from PageRank on a knowledge graph built from Wikidata/Wikipedia links, with Wikidata alignment. Evaluate 482 entities and 13,690 directed edges; compute Spearman correlation; analyze top-K overlap.

Result: Found a weak but significant association (rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001); top-10 overlap 10%, top-100 overlap 34%; evidence of divergence; signals are non-redundant.

Conclusion: The dual-signal framework is not a ranking algorithm but a minimal, interpretable representation; supports task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct signals for context-specific selection/aggregation.

Abstract: AI knowledge systems require representations of entity importance for retrieval, recommendation, evidence selection, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Yet importance is often reduced to a single score derived from either human response or graph structure. Such compression may discard distinctions that matter when an AI system must choose among entities for different tasks. This study introduces an interpretable dual-signal representation in which each entity is characterized by an audience-evaluation dimension and a structural-authority dimension.
  The framework is evaluated using movie entities as an empirical validation domain. IMDb non-commercial datasets provide a rating-based audience ranking, Wikidata supports entity alignment, and English Wikipedia hyperlinks form the knowledge network on which PageRank estimates structural authority. Experiments on 482 entities and 13,690 directed relationships reveal a statistically significant but weak association between the two dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Their overlap is only 10% in the top 10 and 34% in the top 100, while entity-level divergence occurs in both directions.
  The results show that audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not automatically be collapsed into a single scalar notion of importance. The contribution is not a new ranking algorithm or learned embedding, but a minimal knowledge-representation framework and an empirical test of its dimensional necessity. The findings support task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct importance signals before applying context-specific selection or aggregation.

</details>


### [171] [SciExplore: Evaluating Autonomous Agents from Scientific Navigation to Information Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20926)
*Yinhao Tang,Youqing Fang,Yanan Sun,Wenran Liu,Weiming Zhang,Bin Liu,Kuikun Liu,Wenwei Zhang,Kai Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SciExplore is a benchmark with 103 expert-curated tasks across 10+ disciplines, evaluating scientific information-seeking and reasoning in LLMs/agents via four task types: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis; results show substantial performance gaps and degradation with task complexity, especially on structured synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the absence of benchmarks that reflect realistic scientific workflows requiring multi-source access and progressive reasoning from entities to domain-level synthesis.

Method: Construct four task types spanning 103 tasks across >10 disciplines; expert-curated; evaluate >10 SOTA LLMs/agents; assess abilities from entity-level reasoning to evidence-level grounding and domain synthesis.

Result: Models exhibit substantial performance gaps; accuracy declines as task complexity increases; extremely low accuracy on structured synthesis tasks.

Conclusion: Current LLMs/agents are inadequate for realistic scientific information-seeking; the benchmark exposes critical limitations and can guide future research toward more capable systems.

Abstract: Scientific research involves complex information-seeking and reasoning workflows across heterogeneous sources. However, existing benchmarks primarily emphasize general-domain retrieval or static scientific question answering, and therefore fail to assess key capabilities required in realistic scientific research workflows. We introduce SciExplore, a benchmark designed to evaluate scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities of LLMs and agents. SciExplore comprises four task types covering 103 expert-curated tasks across more than ten scientific disciplines: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis, which probe progressively higher-level abilities from entity-level reasoning and document-level identification to evidence-level grounding and domain-level synthesis. We evaluate over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents on SciExplore, revealing substantial performance gaps with performance degrading sharply as task complexity increases and extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks. These results highlight significant limitations of current models and agents in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.

</details>


### [172] [Clustered Edge Intelligence: Beyond Just Convergence of Edge Computing and AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20937)
*Chinmaya Kumar Dehury,Boris Sedlak,Alaa Saleh,Ilir Murturi,Lauri Loven,Satish Narayana Srirama,Praveen Kumar Donta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI), an intelligence-centric framework that treats intelligence as a first-class, shareable asset across the edge–cloud continuum, supported by a three-layer architecture and a set of enabling technologies and research dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Shifts from an information age to an age of intelligence: data will yield derived intelligence at the network edge; existing edge intelligence research focuses on resource management and lightweight models, but lacks an intelligence-centric framework where intelligence is a first-class, manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications.

Method: Conceptual design and architectural proposal: introduce a three-layer CEI architecture and analyze enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

Result: Definition of Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI) as a vision-based framework, a three-layer architecture, and a catalog of enabling technologies and research dimensions necessary to treat intelligence as a reusable asset across distributed edge and cloud resources.

Conclusion: CEI presents a forward-looking framework to govern, share, and manage derived intelligence across heterogeneous edge–cloud environments, outlining architecture and key research directions and signaling the need for standardization, interoperability, and practical realization.

Abstract: We are moving from an information age to the age of intelligence. A decade, or possibly less than that, data will not be the gold anymore rather the derived intelligence out of the data and the information we posses from the edge of the network. Existing Edge Intelligence research focuses mainly on two directions: using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices. However, existing edge computing research lacks an intelligence-centric framework in which derived intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications. To address these research gaps, we introduced Clustered Edge Intelligence, a visionary intelligence-centric approach. The aim of CEI is to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum. We present a three layer CEI architecture and examine enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

</details>


### [173] [From Scalars to Time Series: Rethinking Implicit Neural Representations for Time-Varying Volumetric Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20970)
*Weihan Zhang,Xuan Zhao,Yenwen Peng,Yuqi Chen,Jun Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Repurposes INRs for time-varying fields by using sequence-level supervision on spatial time series, removing the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling and enabling improved performance with lower training cost; MoE further enhances capacity for heterogeneous temporal dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense spatiotemporal sampling is computationally expensive and inefficient for time-varying fields. Representing data as spatially indexed time series allows leveraging temporal structure and reducing sampling, while preserving or improving reconstruction quality. The approach is compatible with various INR architectures and can benefit from mixture-of-experts (MoE) for diverse temporal dynamics.

Method: Represent data as a collection of spatially indexed time series. Train implicit neural representations using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location (learn each voxel/voxel-like location from its full temporal evolution) instead of coordinate-wise scalar samples. This reduces the need for dense sampling and aligns learning with temporal structure. The framework is compatible with standard INR architectures and can be augmented with mixture-of-experts to allocate capacity across locations with heterogeneous dynamics.

Result: Consistent improvement in reconstruction quality and a significant reduction in training cost across INR variants. When using MoE, the approach yields further improvements over both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, indicating stronger capacity allocation for heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

Conclusion: Per-location sequence supervision is an effective and efficient alternative to dense spatiotemporal sampling for time-varying INRs. The reformulation generalizes across INR architectures and, paired with MoE, provides superior reconstruction quality by better matching model capacity to temporal heterogeneity.

Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data are typically trained using dense sampling over spatiotemporal coordinates, where each observation corresponds to a single point in space and time. This coordinate-wise formulation requires extensive sampling during optimization, leading to high computational cost and inefficient use of temporal structure. In this work, we revisit this design choice and show that dense spatiotemporal sampling is not necessary for learning time-varying fields. Instead, we represent the data as a collection of spatially indexed time series and train INRs using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location, rather than coordinate-wise scalar samples. This reformulation eliminates the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling and instead learns each spatial location from its full temporal evolution in a structured manner. We demonstrate that this representation is compatible with a range of existing INR architectures and consistently improves reconstruction quality, while significantly reducing training cost. Furthermore, we show that this formulation can be combined with mixture-of-experts architectures, and that our MoE instantiation further improves reconstruction quality compared to both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, providing a stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

</details>


### [174] [Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20972)
*Swapnanil Saha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a two-tier memory model for coding agents where a harness-controlled, cue-anchored memory layer offloads incidental knowledge, yielding near-zero voluntary memory use and robust persistence across compactions in real tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-running agents rely on materials deliberately authored memories (documents, plans), but human expertise is often tacit and situation-specific. A harness-controlled, offloaded memory layer would preserve critical operational facts without burdening the agent designer’s memory-choosing step.

Method: Grounded in cognitive memory research (offloading, incidental encoding, event-based memory). Introduces a cue-anchored memory model with trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary. Evaluates via a controlled coding task: deterministic memory injections, zero false alarms, intra-session re-reads benefiting from stored content, and repeated-compaction decay tests comparing harness-owned vs. internal memory stores.

Result: Voluntary memory use nearly vanishes (0 ops in 114 turns) with pre-seeded store. Deterministic injections succeed with zero false alarms. 39% of intra-session reads reuse content seeded before compaction. Ten facts vanish after first summary but survive if stored in a harness-owned store across many compactions; deprived agent can reconstruct via harness’s session files. Facts injected by harness persist across all compactions; final summary carries none of the memory, indicating the need for a reliable, automatic memory channel.

Conclusion: Delivery, not storage, is the product: a harness-managed memory channel ensures reliable memory for long-running agents. The two-tier design, cue-anchored memories, and deterministic harness injections offer a pragmatic path to persistently usable memory with minimal agent cognitive load.

Abstract: Coding agents ship with one kind of memory: documents. Instruction files, plan artifacts, and auto-written memory directories are deliberately authored and deliberately retrieved: the agent must choose to write them and choose to read them back. Human expertise runs on a second tier that never gets written down: situationally-bound operational facts (gotchas, locations, local conventions) encoded as a side effect of the work and retrieved involuntarily when the situation cues them. We argue this second tier is the load-bearing one for long-running agents and must be a harness property, not an agent choice. We contribute: (1) a two-tier design theory grounded in the cognitive literature on memory offloading, incidental encoding, and event-based prospective memory, each mapped to an architectural requirement; (2) a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), evaluated deterministically by the harness, a composition no surveyed academic or shipped system provides; (3) a controlled evaluation on a real coding task showing that voluntary memory use is near zero even with a pre-seeded store (0 memory operations in 114 turns), that deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms, and that 39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content paid for before a compaction boundary; (4) a repeated-compaction decay probe: ten facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions, and the deprived agent greps the harness's own session files to rebuild them, while the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrive intact through all 138 compact-resumes as the final summary carries none. Delivery, not storage, is the product: the reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about.

</details>


### [175] [Beyond Independent Optimization: Compression, MoE Routing, and Quantization Interactions in Multimodal Edge Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20981)
*Jay Gor,Karm Dave,Akshita Abrol,Rajesh Gupta,Sudeep Tanwar,Zhengkui Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A comprehensive survey of efficiency challenges in multimodal LMs, emphasizing interconnected bottlenecks across visual token compression, routing, caching, and quantization, and proposing a unified, routing-aware view with a diagnostic and future directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient multimodal models are hindered not only by model size but by data-flow costs (token management, routing, caching, quantization) under real-world latency, memory, and energy constraints, demanding an integrated design perspective.

Method: Literature review and synthesis organized around interactions among components (compression, routing, KV-cache, quantization, hardware constraints). Proposes design trade-offs and a diagnostic (Temporal Routing Consistency) for video MoEs, plus open questions.

Result: Identifies that optimizations are interdependent; quantization, routing, caching affect each other; provides taxonomy of trade-offs (accuracy vs token budget, static vs adaptive compression, sparse routing vs expert collapse, low-bit vs modality degradation); sets up a framework and benchmarking call for routing-aware co-design.

Conclusion: Calls for routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence; presents Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic tool and highlights research directions.

Abstract: Efficient multimodal inference is increasingly constrained not only by model quality or FLOP count, but also by the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. This paper reviews recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal large language models, covering visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. We argue that these techniques cannot be treated as independent optimizations. Visual token compression alters downstream feature distributions and MoE routing decisions, routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity, quantized router logits influence expert assignment, KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence, and hardware constraints often transform computational savings into memory and communication bottlenecks. We organize the literature around these interactions and identify key design trade-offs, including accuracy versus token budget, static versus adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency versus expert collapse, and low-bit inference versus modality-specific degradation. Finally, we introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models and highlight open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

</details>


### [176] [GuardianAgentBench: Where Agents Fail and How to Guard Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20982)
*Vishal Ishwar Naik,Chenyu Xu,Donna Dong,Hussein Hassan,Abhishek Pradhan,Ofer Mendelevitch,Tallat Shafat,Humayun Irshad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GABench benchmarks autonomous LLM agents across 580 scenarios in six domains using three frameworks, revealing persistent safety limitations: strongest models reach 74.8% accuracy, two failure regimes (under-calling vs over-calling tools), performance declines with tool-set size and turn depth, and long-horizon planning bottlenecks. Guardrail interventions outperform system-prompt defenses, recovering 19.9% of failures at 0.5% FPR, indicating execution-time interventions improve safety without harming correct behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As autonomous LLM agents increasingly operate with tools and external environments, a robust, scalable safety evaluation is essential to identify failure modes and guide defense strategies that preserve correct behavior.

Method: Benchmarking study across 580 scenarios in six domains, evaluated on LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. Six state-of-the-art models tested. Multi-stage validation with five adversarial attack modes. Metrics include overall accuracy and analysis of tool-use patterns, with comparison of guardrail-based interventions versus system prompts.

Result: Strongest configuration achieves 74.8% overall accuracy. Two failure regimes observed: stronger models under-call required tools; weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades with larger tool-sets and deeper sequential turns; long-horizon planning is a major bottleneck. Guardrail implementation outperforms system-prompt defenses across all models, recovering 19.9% of failures at a 0.5% false positive rate.

Conclusion: Execution-time structural interventions (guardrails) enhance safety without disrupting correct behavior and are more effective than prompt-based defenses, though substantial safety gaps remain in automated tool-use for autonomous agents.

Abstract: As large language model agents increasingly operate autonomously with access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. We present GuardianAgentBench (GABench), a benchmark of 580 scenarios across six domains evaluated on three production-ready frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. The benchmark incorporates rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Experiments with six state-of-the-art models reveal that even the strongest configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy and expose two distinct failure regimes: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning proving the steeper bottleneck. Our guardrail implementation consistently outperforms system-prompt-based defenses across all models, recovering 19.9% of failures at a false positive rate of just 0.5%. These results demonstrate that execution-time structural intervention improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior.

</details>


### [177] [Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning: Attribution-Guided Repair and Knowledge Reuse for Structured Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20999)
*Zibin Lin,Shengli Zhang,Taotao Wang,Yihan Xia,Deen Ma,Guofu Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WML introduces Node–Mechanism Attribution and a six‑module WGSO loop for localized mechanism learning, enabling precise fault localization and selective reuse of external Skills; it achieves strong accuracy and efficiency across benchmarks and transfers to WikiTableQuestions, with code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address how to jointly locate a failure in a workflow, identify the responsible mechanism, and reuse third‑party Knowledge locally in frozen language-model agents.

Method: Node–Mechanism Attribution to identify failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit target; route single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects to L2 composition protocols. A six‑module Workflow‑Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop selects provenance‑ and scope‑aware third‑party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer‑side memory.

Result: On SpreadsheetBench, WML achieves 90.33 ± 1.53 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and 74.67 ± 3.51 with Qwen3.6‑Flash; without extra optimization, learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 ± 2.00 Denotation Accuracy and 83.00 ± 2.00 Denotation Accuracy (assuming the second refers to another metric). On Compiler‑Supported50, WML yields the highest hard‑PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution reduces tokens/calls vs direct SkillAgent while retaining most tasks. Code and artifacts are at the provided GitHub link.

Conclusion: WML provides a principled mechanism‑level debugging and knowledge‑reuse framework for frozen LMs, improving both accuracy and efficiency in workflow tasks. The approach demonstrates strong empirical gains and practical applicability, with open questions about ablations, scalability, and more diverse task settings.
