Abstract: Agent Skills package reusable procedural knowledge as external artifacts for frozen language-model agents, yet existing optimizers do not jointly resolve where a failure occurs in a workflow, which mechanism caused it, and how relevant knowledge from third-party Skills should be reused locally. We introduce Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning (WML). Its Node--Mechanism Attribution identifies the failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit target, routing single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop then selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory. On SpreadsheetBench, WML reaches 90.33 +/- 1.53 and 74.67 +/- 3.51 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and Qwen3.6-Flash, respectively; without additional optimization, the learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 +/- 2.00 and 83.00 +/- 2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML attains both the highest hard-PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution sharply reduces tokens and calls relative to a direct SkillAgent while retaining most of its successful tasks. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/xiaolin9595/workflow-localized-mechanism-learning.

</details>


### [178] [Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21000)
*Hyuk Lim,Seunghyun Yoon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Naju is a decoupled recurrent unit for long-sequence memory that improves retention and overwriting without stability penalties, outperforming Mamba and competitive with Transformer while preserving linear time/memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address opposing demands of memory retention and overwriting in long sequences; standard continuous-time SSM discretization harms memory dynamics; need a decoupled, stable update.

Method: Propose Naju with x_n = f_n ⊙ x_{n-1} + i_n ⊙ (B_n u_n); explicit discrete pole f_n (0<f_n<1) and independent write gain i_n; decouple to avoid |r|+w ≤ 1 constraint; analyze Schur-stability and fading-memory bounds; evaluate on diagnostic suite and standard benchmarks.

Result: Naju uniquely maintains strong retention and overwriting at 4x training length; outperforms Mamba baselines on principal comparisons; competitive with Transformer; preserves linear-time/memory scaling; shows strong performance across WikiText-103, Long Range Arena, and multi-query recall.

Conclusion: Decoupling write and forget gates in discrete-time memory units yields stable, efficient long-range memory with robust overwrite dynamics, offering a practical alternative to CT discretization and coupled recurrent designs.

Abstract: Long-sequence memory tracking places two opposing demands on a recurrent state: near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons, and active overwriting of stale ones. In our diagnostic suite, the strongest efficient baselines tend to solve only one side well. Continuous-time-parameterized state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba obtain their discrete recurrence by zero-order-hold discretization of a continuous-time system; we argue that this detour is unnecessary for memory tracking and parameterize the discrete transition directly. Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) factorizes the recurrent update, schematically $x_n = f_n\odot x_{n-1} + i_n\odot(B_n u_n)$, into an explicit discrete pole (a learned forget gate $f_n$), an independent write gain $i_n$, and input-dependent write/read maps. Since the sigmoid pole satisfies $0<f_n<1$, each frozen local coordinate is Schur-stable by construction, and the full time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound under uniform boundedness assumptions, with no stability regularizer. We formalize the key structural limitation of coupled designs: any non-expansive complementary single-gate recurrence ties the effective retention $r$ and write gain $w$ through $|r|+w\le 1$, so near-complete retention forces weak writing; decoupling $f_n$ from $i_n$ removes this constraint. Empirically, Naju is the only evaluated model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. Beyond the diagnostic suite, we evaluate Naju on WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall. Across these settings, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming the Mamba baselines in the principal comparisons while remaining competitive with the Transformer and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.

</details>


### [179] [Reexamining zero-shot summarization: Empirical investigation of trustworthiness of LLM-summarizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21010)
*Vasudha Bhatnagar,Purnima Bindal,Vikas Kumar,Raj Kumari Bahl*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Two-level diagnostic protocol to benchmark LLM-based zero-shot summarizers for stability and trustworthiness; introduces stability coefficient and stability index, with an empirical study showing inter-model variability across genres.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stochasticity in LLMs leads to unstable, potentially unreliable summaries in zero-shot settings, which is critical in educational contexts where accurate summarization matters.

Method: Level 1: document-level stability analysis over multiple LLM-generated summaries in a controlled environment; compute a stability coefficient; score each summary for semantic and factual alignment with the source. Level 2: stratified sampling from the corpus to estimate the stability index of the summarizer as a proxy for trustworthiness.

Result: Across three LLM-summarizers and three genres, significant differences in generation-level variability were observed across evaluation metrics, evidencing the stability problem and validating the proposed benchmarking protocol.

Conclusion: The study highlights stability as a key issue in LLM-based summarization and motivates developing robust, reliable, and trustworthy LLM-summarizers, with a practical benchmarking framework.

Abstract: Zero-shot summarization using Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced the abstractive summarization task by producing coherent and fluent summaries. However, underlying stochasticity of the large language models raises concerns about the stability and trustworthiness of the LLM-generated summaries. This issue has become increasingly important due to proliferation of LLM-generated summaries in educational settings, where students and researchers summarize complex academic materials in zero-shot manner.
  We propose a novel two-level diagnostic protocol for benchmarking LLM-summarizers based on the stability of the generated summaries. At the lower level, document-level stability analysis is performed over multiple LLM-summaries generated under controlled environment, and the stability coefficient is computed. Each generated summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the original document, enabling estimation of stability along more than one dimensions. At the next level, observations from a stratified sample of documents drawn from the corpus are consolidated to estimate the stability index of the LLM-summarizer, which is the proxy for its trustworthiness.
  Our empirical investigation of three LLM-summarizers across three genres of documents reveals statistically significant differences in the generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics. This study advances the LLM-summarization research by evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-summaries and motivates further research towards development of robust, reliable and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

</details>


### [180] [EmoAgent-R1: Towards Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21013)
*Lihuang Fang,Yuchen Zou,kebin Jin,Jinghui Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes EmoAgent-R1, a reinforcement learning-based dynamic agent specialization framework for multimodal emotion recognition (MER), featuring a cold-start training with synthetic data and a Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to handle sparse rewards; demonstrates improved emotion reasoning and training stability on MER benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed prompts in multimodal LLMs inadequately capture the dynamic, cross-modal emotion sources and reasoning required in MER; RL-based dynamic agent specialization aims to improve emotion perception, reasoning, and generalization while mitigating sparse-credit assignment issues.

Method: 1) Cold-start strategy: trains the MLLM with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data to bootstrap emotion recognition, reasoning, and routing. 2) RL fine-tuning: a two-step workflow with agent selection and agent specialization. 3) Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO): combines group-relative advantages with PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to convert sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, mitigating coarse-grained credit assignment in GRPO.

Result: Extensive MER benchmarks show EmoAgent-R1 achieves stronger emotion reasoning and improved optimization stability compared with baselines.

Conclusion: Dynamic agent specialization via reinforcement learning and the P-GRPO training objective effectively enhances MER performance and training stability, indicating promise for adaptive, multi-step agent designs in multimodal emotion understanding.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in multimodal emotion recognition (MER) tasks and lifted MER to a new level that is complex emotion understanding with advanced video understanding abilities and natural language description. However, existing MLLM-based methods often use a fixed prompt to perceive the emotions, ignoring the dynamicity and complexity of the emotion source in the multimodal inputs. To address these issues, we propose a novel Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization framework (\textbf{EmoAgent-R1}) to optimize the emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization abilities of an MLLM with dynamic agent specialization based on reinforcement learning. Specifically, we first adopt a cold start strategy to endow an MLLM with preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing ability by training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data. Then, we further train the MLLM with reinforcement learning to perceive emotions in a two-step agentic workflow with agent selection and agent specialization. To effectively train EmoAgent-R1, we propose a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to combine group-based relative advantages with a PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, mitigating the coarse-grained uniform credit assignment issue in GRPO. Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our EmoAgent-R1 in stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

</details>


### [181] [HiMe: Real-Time Self-Hosted Personal Agent Platform for Health Insights with Wearable Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21019)
*Wei Liu,Siya Qi,Linhai Zhang,Lorainne Tudor Car,Yulan He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HiMe is a locally deployable, privacy-first platform enabling real-time, personalized health insights from wearables via LLM agents, treating the database as a first-class component and optimizing effectiveness and efficiency for long-term user modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome limitations of rigid analytics and privacy risks in wearable health data by offering an open-source, privacy-preserving, real-time platform compatible with diverse wearables.

Method: Conceptual/design-level description of HiMe: privacy-first architecture, local deployment, real-time data processing, long-term user modeling, treating the database as a first-class citizen, Pareto-optimal optimization of effectiveness and efficiency, compatibility with wearable ecosystems.

Result: Abstract describes the platform and design principles; no empirical evaluation reported; demonstrates feasibility and potential for continuous, personalized health monitoring.

Conclusion: HiMe provides a practical, privacy-preserving path for Personal Health Agentic Analysis, enabling adaptive health insights in real time while preserving user privacy.

Abstract: Traditional approaches to wearable health signal analysis, such as smartwatches, are constrained by rigid analytical frameworks and limited personalisation. The emergence of LLM agents creates a new opportunity for Personal Health Agentic Analysis, where health insights can be generated adaptively and in context. However, currently there is no open-source locally deployable platform capable of processing personal health data in real time while preserving privacy. We present HiMe, a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform that is fully compatible with real-time health data ecosystems across a wide range of wearable devices. HiMe is guided by three design principles. The database is treated as a first-class component. Effectiveness and efficiency are jointly optimised to achieve a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance. Data are processed in real time while the user is modelled over the long term. Together, these principles make it practical for individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalised health monitoring for better wellbeing.

</details>


### [182] [Faster IndexTTS-2: Accelerating and Streaming Autoregressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis on GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21042)
*Muyang Du,Shuang Yu,Junjie Lai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Faster IndexTTS-2 accelerates all components of a state-of-the-art autoregressive TTS model (GPT, diffusion transformer, vocoder) on GPUs using TensorRT, enabling streaming and batched inference with significant speedups while preserving quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive TTS models offer high naturalness but suffer from slow, sequential inference; production deployment requires real-time latency, streaming, and efficient GPU utilization; IndexTTS-2’s speed limits hinder practical use.

Method: Optimize and accelerate all neural network components (GPT, flow-matching diffusion transformer, vocoder) with NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM; enable streaming synthesis and cross-component batched inference; adapt for GPU deployment and production workflows; evaluate on Seed-TTS English and Chinese benchmarks.

Result: End-to-end speedup up to 3.6×, with autoregressive GPT alone up to 5.0× speedup; minimal degradation in WER, speaker similarity, and naturalness on Seed-TTS English and Chinese benchmarks.

Conclusion: The work provides a practical blueprint for deploying autoregressive speech models in production by combining GPU-optimized components, streaming capabilities, and batching, achieving substantial latency reductions with limited quality loss.

Abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech models achieve strong naturalness but suffer from slow inference due to sequential token generation, limiting their deployment in production applications that require low latency. IndexTTS-2 is a state-of-the-art autoregressive TTS model consisting of a GPT, a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and a vocoder. Despite its high synthesis quality, its inference speed barely reaches real-time without streaming or batching support. We present Faster IndexTTS-2, which accelerates all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 for production deployment on GPUs using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. Faster IndexTTS-2 also enables streaming synthesis for latency-sensitive interactive applications, and batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization. Experiments on the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese demonstrate up to 5.0$\times$ speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6$\times$ end-to-end, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Our methodology provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs.

</details>


### [183] [Can Generative Recommendation Reach Cold Items? A Temporal Perspective on Semantic-ID Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21101)
*Jie Peng,Yanping Zheng,Zhewei Zhe,Bin Tong,Guan Wang,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SID-based generative recommendation is compositional but not fully open-ended; cold-start for unseen tokens/paths is challenging, with partial reach to future items via observed tokens/prefixes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To diagnose temporal open-token cold-start in SID-based generative recs under an absolute-time protocol and understand the token-level reachability of new items.

Method: Seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing; interpret SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing where early tokens select coarse regions and later tokens refine item-specific paths.

Result: Current SID models can reach some future items supported by observed tokens/prefixes but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths; cold-start is bounded by token-level invisibility and path gaps.

Conclusion: SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended; future work could explore more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context to improve open-ended item reachability.

Abstract: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation represents items as sequences of shared semantic tokens, enabling token recombination beyond isolated item IDs. However, closed-world recombination does not necessarily imply temporal open-token cold-start induction, where new items enter the item catalog with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. In this work, we revisit SID-based generative recommendation under an absolute-time temporal protocol that separates seen and unseen targets and diagnoses the cold item reachability at the token level. Through seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing, we show that current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. We further explain this boundary by interpreting SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths. These findings show that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended, and suggest future directions in more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context.

</details>


### [184] [AttriMem: Attribution-Guided Process Feedback for Agent Memory Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21106)
*Qinfeng Li,Yuntai Bao,Xinyan Yu,Hongze Chen,Wenqi Zhang,Xuhong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AttriMem trains memory-construction policies for LLM agents using attribution-guided local rewards in RL, improving long-horizon dialogue QA performance and training stability over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory management in LLM agents is driven by coarse task-level rewards which hinder fine-grained credit assignment for intermediate memory decisions. This limits cross-task adaptability and effective memory usage as interactions accumulate.

Method: AttriMem augments the global outcome reward with token-level contribution-based local rewards to guide memory construction via reinforcement learning, addressing the credit-assignment bottleneck with attribution-guided feedback.

Result: In long-horizon dialogue QA, AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL baselines; demonstrates generalization across benchmarks and answer models and stabilizes RL optimization.

Conclusion: Attribution-guided local feedback for memory construction enables better credit assignment, leading to improved performance, robustness, and cross-task adaptability for memory-aware LLM agents.

Abstract: Effective memory is crucial for LLM agents, yet constructing it effectively remains challenging. A memory-construction policy decides what information to extract, store, update, compress, or discard as interactions accumulate. Heuristic memory methods rely on subjective, task-specific rules, which can misalign with downstream objectives and limit cross-task adaptability. RL-based methods, by contrast, learn from task feedback but mainly use outcome- or module-level rewards. These coarse signals indicate task success but cannot identify which intermediate memory contents support the final answer, creating a fine-grained credit-assignment bottleneck. However, constructing such process feedback is prohibitively difficult because intermediate memory decisions lack unique ground-truth targets, while the appropriate credit varies with the agent's uncertain reasoning trajectory and therefore cannot be specified in advance. We propose AttriMem, an attribution-guided process-feedback framework for learning memory-construction policies with RL. AttriMem augments the global outcome reward with local rewards derived from token-level contributions to the final answer. Experiments on long-horizon dialogue question answering show that AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines, generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, stabilizes RL optimization.

</details>


### [185] [V-DEAL: Diagnosing Video Safety De-Calibration as an Understanding-Refusal Coupling Failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21151)
*Zhetong Zhang,Honghao Fu,Miao Xu,Yiwei Wang,Yujun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A diagnostic study reveals that Video LLMs are vulnerable to attack when harmful videos are paired with benign queries. The authors propose V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework analyzing perception, understanding, and internal representations to explain the vulnerability, and introduce a prompt-injection method that significantly mitigates attack success, offering a practical safety remedy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As Video LLMs move to real-world use, ensuring safety alignment is crucial. The paper investigates why models can be attacked despite apparently recognizing harmful content and seeks a diagnostic framework to pinpoint where failures occur (perception, understanding, or internal refusal) and practical mitigation.

Method: Develop V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework; evaluate six Video LLMs on three benchmarks; perform hidden-state analysis to compare visual vs textual understanding; invent a prompt-injection intervention method; compare to prior fine-tuning approaches.

Result: Harmful video content is recognized with >81% accuracy, yet ~48.33% attack success occurs when pairing harmful videos with benign queries; hidden-state analysis shows visual understanding has weaker refusal tendencies than textual; prompt injection reduces attack success by ~48.24 percentage points, achieving results comparable to fine-tuning-based methods.

Conclusion: V-DEAL offers a structured diagnostic lens to locate the roots of the vulnerability across perception, understanding, and internal refusals. The prompt-injection intervention provides a practical, low-cost mitigation that can significantly reduce attack success, highlighting the importance of robust prompting and internal refusal alignment for Video LLM safety.

Abstract: As Video Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, ensuring their safety alignment has become critical. Counterintuitively, we find that harmful videos paired with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates than the same videos paired with explicitly harmful queries. To understand the underlying mechanism of this vulnerability, we present V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework that jointly analyzes this failure across model behaviour, understanding, and internal representations. By progressively ruling out perception failure and quantifying the model's internal refusal tendency, V-DEAL provides a new diagnostic perspective for analyzing the underlying mechanism of the observed vulnerability. We tested six Video LLMs on three public benchmarks and observed that models correctly recognize harmful video content with over 81\% accuracy, yet the average attack success rate still reaches 48.33\% under the condition pairing harmful videos with benign queries. Hidden-state analysis further shows that visual understanding activates a weaker refusal tendency than textual understanding. Furthermore, we introduce a prompt injection intervention method that reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.24 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to prior fine-tuning-based methods, providing an effective and practical means to address such safety risks in Video LLMs.

</details>


### [186] [SafeStep: AI-powered Travel Assistance for Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21156)
*Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia Azul Debenedetti,David Gamez,Franco Such,Nik Kairinos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SafeStep is an AI-driven travel assistant for elderly with frailty/dementia; it uses a travel-graph that combines route planning with predictive modelling. For each journey stage, it generates failure scenarios via LLMs and the Anticip8 behavioral predictor, proposes targeted interventions, and estimates how interventions affect outcome probabilities to maximize successful arrival. Evaluated on travel-graph generation and a field study of 26 journeys; results show that using Anticip8 for failure prediction with GPT-based intervention evaluation provides the most reliable performance. User feedback indicates improved confidence and perceived safety, though interface usability needs improvement; the system could be extended to other domains such as mental health, career coaching, and addiction treatment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frail and dementia-affected elderly people have limited ability to travel in urban environments. There is a need for proactive, personalized support to improve safety, reliability, and confidence in travel by predicting potential failures and selecting interventions that increase the likelihood of reaching the destination.

Method: Develop a travel-graph representation that integrates route planning with predictive modelling. For each journey stage, generate personalized failure scenarios using a combination of large language models and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine; propose targeted interventions; estimate the impact of interventions on outcome probabilities; select interventions that maximize destination reach. Evaluation includes travel-graph generation experiments and a field study with 26 real-world journeys.

Result: Finding: combining Anticip8 for failure prediction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most reliable performance. User feedback indicates improved confidence and perceived safety, though interface usability needs improvement for the target demographic.

Conclusion: SafeStep demonstrates a viable AI-assisted travel system for frail/dementia-affected elderly, with potential applicability to other domains (e.g., mental health, career coaching, addiction treatment). Future work includes refinement and release of SafeStep.

Abstract: More than a million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, which severely compromise their ability to travel in urban environments. This paper presents SafeStep, an AI-driven travel system that assists elderly users with their journeys. At the core of SafeStep is a novel travel graph representation, which integrates route planning with predictive modelling. For each stage of a journey, the system (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using a combi-nation of LLMs and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (ii) proposes targeted interventions, and (iii) estimates the impact of interventions on out-come probabilities. This enables SafeStep to select interventions that maximize the likelihood of the person reaching their destination. SafeStep was evaluated through experiments on travel graph generation and a field study involving 26 real-world journeys. Results showed that combining Anticip8 for failure pre-diction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most re-liable performance. User feedback indicated that SafeStep improves confidence and perceived safety during travel, although interface usability needs to be im-proved for the target demographic. In the future, we would like to improve and release SafeStep. The AI system that was developed for SafeStep could be ap-plied in other areas, such as mental health, career coaching and addiction treatment.

</details>


### [187] [Safeguards for Speech2Speech LLM-Assistants: A Case Study in Automotive Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21180)
*Gregor Endler,Sebastian Kraus,Lukas Stappen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: End-to-end speech-to-speech (S2S) guardrails in automotive systems face prohibitive latency and non-determinism; transcript-based and tool-based guardrails fail to meet industrial deployment needs, with open challenges remaining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure safe, domain-specific safeguards for end-to-end S2S assistants in cars while preserving natural interaction and acceptable latency.

Method: Empirical evaluation of two guardrail approaches—transcript-based and tool-based—within an automotive S2S setup, measuring latency and tool-call determinism to assess industrial viability.

Result: Both guardrail strategies exhibit latency delays (0–1.4 seconds per answer) and issues like non-deterministic tool calls; neither is robust enough for widespread industrial deployment.

Conclusion: Open challenges persist for S2S guardrails in automotive contexts; further methodological or architectural advances are required to achieve reliable, low-latency, deterministic safeguards.

Abstract: Recent advances have introduced speech-to-speech (S2S) conversational assistants capable of producing natural-sounding interactions, including non-verbal cues like tonality and mood. In the automotive domain, this enables intuitive and humanlike in-car dialogue experiences. However, integrating these end-to-end assistants limits architectural options for programmable domain-specific safeguards. This paper discusses two implementation approaches for S2S guardrails: transcript-based and tool-based. Through an empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that both strategies are insufficient for industrial deployment in most cases due to prohibitive latency (delaying each answer by 0 to 1.4 seconds even for computationally cheap checks) and technical impediments (like potentially non-deterministic tool call behavior). Finally, we outline open challenges for S2S guardrails in the automotive context.

</details>


### [188] [Explaining Weather Bulletins via ILP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21184)
*Enrico Santi,Alessandro Dal Palù,Agostino Dovier,Talissa Dreossi,Andrea Formisano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ILP (FastLAS2) is used to learn interpretable hypotheses that explain symbol choices in weather bulletins, via an ASP-based pipeline from simulated meteorological data to natural-language explanations; the approach is generalizable across regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To combine symbolic learning with declarative meteorological knowledge and provide transparent, rationale-based explanations for the symbol annotations in forecast pictograms.

Method: Build a pipeline: generate simulated meteorological data and ground-truth bulletins (OSMER), extract data as ASP facts, form ILP examples, use FastLAS2 to induce explanatory hypotheses, translate them to natural language, and verify alignment with expert rationale; claim general applicability beyond the studied region.

Result: Proposes a feasible pipeline that yields interpretable hypotheses explaining weather forecast decisions and symbol choices; demonstrates generality.

Conclusion: The approach is general and transferable to bulletins from other sources and regions.

Abstract: Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) originated within the Logic Programming community in the Nineties as a framework for combining symbolic learning with declarative knowledge representation. Nowadays, mature ILP frameworks exist and they are capable of learning complex, non-monotonic hypotheses, thus broadening both the modeling capabilities and the scope of real-world applications of ILP. This work is primarily based on the FastLAS2 framework and aims to generate simple, interpretable hypotheses to help clarify the weather bulletins issued by OSMER FVG, the Regional Meteorological Observatory of the Italian region of Friuli Venezia-Giulia. In this paper we present a pipeline that, starting from simulated meteorological raw data and from OSMERs' bulletins (used as ground truth), extracts data as ASP facts and generates ILP examples. From such examples an explanatory hypothesis is then inferred via FastLAS2. Such a hypothesis (translated into natural language) explains the weather forecast issued by human experts, and in particular the rationale behind experts' choices of specific symbols in the bulletin pictogram (the symbol-annotated meteorological map of the forecast). The proposed approach is general, not specific to any particular region and it can equally be applied to bulletins from other sources and to different regions.

</details>


### [189] [Differentiable Logic Programming to Mitigate Reasoning Shortcuts in Neurosymbolic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21185)
*Akihiro Takemura,Katsumi Inoue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A matrix-based differentiable logic framework is proposed to mitigate reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems by unifying rules and constraints in a single matrix; one-to-one grounding reduces shortcuts on MNIST variants; architectural coupling is crucial.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neurosymbolic models show shortcut reasoning behaviors that undermine generalization and interpretability. The work aims to reduce constraint-satisfaction and cognition shortcuts by a unified matrix encoding and by studying gradient flow and grounding strategies.

Method: Introduce a matrix-based differentiable logic programming semantics that encodes rules and constraints in a single matrix. Analyze connections to fuzzy t-norms. Compare gradient-flow properties. Conduct MNIST-variant experiments emphasizing one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms. Evaluate how symbolic–neural coupling architecture affects shortcut mitigation.

Result: One-to-one grounding significantly reduces both constraint-satisfaction and cognition shortcuts compared to soft probabilistic baselines. Unified matrix encoding and careful architectural coupling improve shortcut mitigation. Gradient-flow properties vary with the chosen t-norm.

Conclusion: The coupling between symbolic knowledge and neural learning is critical for mitigating shortcuts. A unified matrix-based encoding provides a practical and effective approach to enforce constraints and mappings without relying on soft probability distributions.

Abstract: Neurosymbolic (NeSy) systems integrate neural networks with logical reasoning to achieve both generalization and interpretability, but recent work has shown they are susceptible to shortcut reasoning behaviors.  We propose a novel method using matrix-based differentiable logic programming to mitigate reasoning shortcuts in two phenomena: constraint satisfaction shortcuts, where constraints are satisfied without achieving the intended task, and cognition shortcuts, where biased data leads to semantically incorrect concept mappings despite logically sound inference. Building on recent matrix-based logic programming semantics, we introduce design elements to mitigate shortcuts, including a unified encoding of rules and constraints in a single matrix.  We also identify connections to fuzzy logic t-norms and empirically compare their gradient flow properties. Through carefully designed experiments on MNIST variants, we show that one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms significantly reduces both shortcut types compared to previous methods that rely on soft probability distributions.  We then confirm that architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning play a critical role in shortcut mitigation.

</details>


### [190] [Identifying Good Rules for Efficient SAT Encodings of Single-Constant Multiplication Using Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21188)
*Chufeng Jiang,Neng-Fa Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Neuro-symbolic SCM: a graph neural network predicts promising operator types for constant decompositions to prune the SAT encoding search, yielding large speedups and memory reductions while preserving near-optimal additions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SCM encoding is NP-hard; traditional dynamic-programming/SAT encodings are costly for large constants, hindering scalability.

Method: A graph neural network predicts operator-type choices during constant decomposition; confidence scores are used to prune no-good or unlikely branches during symbolic search, accelerating SCM SAT encoding.

Result: On unseen 17–32 bit constants, encoding time reduced by 1–2 orders of magnitude; memory usage reduced by >97%; branching reduced by an order of magnitude; additions remain near-optimal.

Conclusion: Learning-guided symbolic strategies can significantly improve SCM encoding scalability and efficiency; code and data are publicly available.

Abstract: The Single Constant Multiplication problem is a fundamental NP-hard optimization task in hardware design, which seeks to decompose a fixed constant using only additions, subtractions, and bit-shifts. Although dynamic programming methods can produce near-optimal SAT encodings for SCM, their encoding cost remains high for large constants. We propose a neuro-symbolic framework that accelerates SCM SAT encoding by identifying good rules for guiding operator selection during decomposition. Our approach employs a graph neural network model to predict promising operator types from constant decompositions, and exploits the resulting confidence scores to prune no-good choices in the symbolic search. Experimental results on unseen 17-32 bit constants demonstrate one to two orders of magnitude reductions in encoding time, over 97% reduction in memory usage, and an order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, while preserving near-optimal encoding quality in terms of additions. These results show that learning-guided symbolic strategies can significantly improve the scalability and efficiency of SCM encoding. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/Chufeng-Jiang/SCM_MLDP

</details>


### [191] [Bound-Founded Semantics for Answer Set Programming with Difference Constraints: Preliminary Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21201)
*Pedro Cabalar,Jorge Fandinno,Nicolas Rühling,Torsten Schaub,Sebastian Schellhorn,Philipp Wanko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a many-sorted Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb) to unify the semantics of ASP with linear constraints, and applies it to difference constraints to formalize constraint-atom foundedness, enabling a single framework for clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo and guiding future simplifications and integrations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hybrid ASP solvers for constraints currently rely on heterogeneous semantic foundations. A unified logical basis is needed to reason about equilibrium models across different semantics and to validate simplifications and integrations.

Method: Develop a many-sorted variant of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb), formalize the foundedness of numeric variables, characterize equilibrium models across alternative semantics, and compare how clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo justify constraint atoms within this framework.

Result: A single, coherent framework that formalizes the foundations of current systems like clingo[DL], enables rigorous analysis of program simplifications, and supports future integration of diverse semantic principles.

Conclusion: HTb provides a unified, flexible foundation for hybrid ASP with linear constraints, enabling rigorous semantic analysis, validation of simplifications, and the integration of future semantic variants.

Abstract: While the integration of linear constraints has significantly expanded the reach of Answer Set Programming (ASP), existing hybrid solvers often rely on disparate semantic underpinnings that lack a unified logical foundation. We address this gap by introducing a many-sorted variant of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb), providing a versatile framework capable of characterizing equilibrium models across a wide spectrum of alternative semantics for extensions of ASP with linear constraints. We apply this framework to the setting of difference constraints, focusing on the semantic characterization of clingo[DL]. Central to our approach is the formalization of foundedness for numeric variables. By investigating how different hybrid systems - such as clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo - justify constraint atoms, we uncover the semantic roots of their varying behaviors. This investigation results in a single, consistent framework that not only formalizes the foundations of current systems like clingo[DL] but also facilitates the rigorous study of program simplifications and the future integration of diverse semantic principles.

</details>


### [192] [A New Well-Supported Semantics for Description Logic Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21203)
*Spencer Killen,Jia-Huai You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new, stricter semantics for description logic programs is proposed, yielding a subset of the existing well-supported semantics. It preserves well-supportedness while keeping consistency NP-complete (not rising to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) and provides a reduct-based characterization via a fixpoint operator. The semantics are equivalent to the current one on a syntactic class and are meant to align more closely with traditional logic programming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address two limitations of current well-supported DL-program semantics: (i) the consistency problem becomes more complex (rising to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) and (ii) there is no reduct-based characterization.

Method: Introduce a stricter evaluation of ontological atoms, yielding a new well-supported notion. Develop a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation to characterize the semantics. Identify a syntactic class where the new semantics coincides with the current one. Formalize the semantics as a strict subset of the existing well-supported semantics.

Result: The new semantics keeps the consistency problem NP-complete. It is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics. There exists a syntactic class of DL-programs for which the new and the current semantics are equivalent.

Conclusion: The authors favor the new, stricter notion of well-supportedness due to its closer alignment with logic programming, while maintaining prior intuitions about well-supportedness and offering a reduct-based, fixpoint characterization.

Abstract: Description logic programs are a powerful formalism for combining rules with ontologies. The well-supported semantics for description logic programs ensures that no answer sets rely on cyclic dependencies. Most popular semantics for logic programming have this property of well-supportedness. We recognize two limitations of the current well-supported semantics for DL programs: its increased computational complexity for the consistency problem and its lack of a reduct transformation characterization.  In this work, we present a new semantics which evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than the current semantics. This keeps the complexity of its consistency problem NP-complete, rather than increasing it to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. Additionally, we identify a syntactic class of description logic programs for which our new semantics is equivalent to the current semantics. We characterize our semantics using a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation. Our new semantics is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics, so it maintains the prior notion  of well-supportedness while inducing its own stricter notion. We prefer our new notion of well-supportedness due to its similarities with logic programming.

</details>


### [193] [How Rules Represent Causal Knowledge: Causal Modeling with Probabilistic Logic Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21208)
*Kilian Rueckschloss,Felix Weitkaemper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Extends Pearl-style causal reasoning to probabilistic logic programming (PLP), introducing a non-temporal causal semantics with interventions; shows equivalence to P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog, with potential differences in non-stratified cases and other PLP formalisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pearl's framework, rooted in Bayesian networks and acyclic models, is not readily transferable to PLP. By aligning PLP with a non-temporal causal philosophy, the work broadens causal reasoning to a broader formalism and enables intervention semantics within PLP.

Method: Define a formal causal semantics for PLP, introduce intervention operators, implement the approach, and compare with existing P-log semantics. Establish equivalence with P-log for stratified ProbLog; analyze deviations in non-stratified or other PLP variants.

Result: The proposed causal semantics coincide with P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs; differences may arise in non-stratified cases and for other PLP formalisms.

Conclusion: Bringing Pearl-style causality into PLP enables intervention-based causal reasoning within probabilistic logic programs, with established alignment to P-log in the stratified regime and caveats about non-stratified cases and other PLP formalisms.

Abstract: Pearl famously argues that causal knowledge enables the prediction of intervention effects. By contrast, purely descriptive knowledge supports only conclusions drawn from observations. His theory of causality, however, is developed exclusively within Bayesian networks and causal models. Consequently, it is largely restricted to acyclic causal relationships, and transferring its ideas to other formalisms risks misinterpretation or inconsistency.
  This paper brings Pearl's approach to causality into probabilistic logic programming (PLP). To this end, such programs are aligned with philosophical foundations established in prior work that do not rely on temporal notions; that is, all relevant events are assumed to occur simultaneously. A formal causal semantics for these programs, together with a notion of intervention and an implementation, is proposed. It is shown that this semantics coincides with the P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs, while the two may differ in the non-stratified case and for other PLP formalisms.

</details>


### [194] [ICAE-Bench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Interactive Project Builders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21217)
*Zhongyuan Peng,Dan Huang,Chuyu Zhang,Caijun Xu,Changyi Xiao,Shibo Hong,David Lo,Lin Qiu,Xuezhi Cao,Jiyuan He,Yixin Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICAE-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating coding agents in interactive project-building settings, using real-repo ambiguity, a grounded User Agent, and multi-dimensional open-ended evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap between vibe-coding workflows and static benchmarks by enabling evaluation of agents that transform fuzzy product intents into working software through planning, tool use, and repository-level construction.

Method: Three key designs: (1) derive task ambiguity from precise real open-source repositories with executable behavior; (2) ground interaction via User Agent Data to reveal constraints without introducing new requirements or leaking implementation details; (3) assess open-ended repositories with standardized black-box tests and multi-dimensional diagnostics (functional correctness, semantic/API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, interaction quality).

Result: Introduces ICAE-Bench, a benchmarking framework that enables realistic, reproducible evaluation of interactive coding agents on real repositories, including a unified evaluation protocol and multi-dimensional metrics.

Conclusion: ICAE-Bench provides a fair, scalable platform to evaluate open-ended, interactive coding agents and encourages progress in vibe-coding workflows by aligning benchmarks with realistic user-agent interactions and repository-level challenges.

Abstract: The recent emergence of vibe-coding workflows is changing what coding agents are expected to do. Instead of merely completing code under fully specified instructions, agents are increasingly expected to transform incomplete product intent into working software by combining various abilities including planning, requirement clarification, tool use, debugging, and repository-level construction. Yet existing benchmarks have not fully caught up with this shift, evaluating agents on static, fully specified tasks.
  In this paper, we introduce ICAE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under interactive project-building settings. The basic idea is to start from a fuzzy product requirement, simulating the dynamic paradigm with an automated User Agent. To make this setting both realistic and evaluable, ICAE-Bench introduces three key designs. First, to avoid the ambiguity of unconstrained fuzzy requirements, each task derives ambiguity from a precise real open-source repository with executable behavior. Second, to ensure high-quality and reproducible user simulation, ICAE-Bench grounds interaction through User Agent Data, allowing the User Agent to reveal hidden constraints without inventing new requirements or leaking implementation artifacts. Third, to evaluate open-ended repositories fairly, ICAE-Bench uses standardized black-box tests together with multi-dimensional diagnostics, including functional correctness, semantic and API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, and interaction quality.

</details>


### [195] [Logic Programming Semantics for Causal Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21233)
*Felix Weitkämper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Stable models of positive logic programs match the eventual states from a neutral, undisturbed process; supported models match states reachable from any starting point, giving a temporal causal reading to logic programming semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap between logic programming semantics and dynamic causal processes in life sciences, providing a temporal, explanatory interpretation of stable and supported semantics.

Method: Theoretical analysis establishing formal correspondences between logic-programming semantics and the asymptotic states of causal processes, including a framework for interpreting logic programs as causal rules with temporal evolution.

Result: A precise mapping: stable models correspond to neutral-start, undisturbed processes; supported models correspond to states reachable from arbitrary initial conditions; introduces temporal causality into the causal-rule interpretation of logic programming semantics.

Conclusion: The work links logic programming semantics with causal-temporal reasoning, informing how to select semantics for causal rule languages and enriching the explanatory role of stable/support semantics in life-sciences modelling.

Abstract: Motivated by challenging modelling issues in the life sciences, we investigate the relationship between logic programming semantics and the eventual states of causal processes compatible with those logic programs. More precisely, we show that while stable models of positive logic programs correspond to the eventual states of processes commencing from a neutral state and continuing undisturbed indefinitely, supported models describe the eventual states reachable from arbitrary starting points. This also contributes to the discussion of the appropriate semantics for logic programming as a causal rule language, adding a temporal perspective to recent interpretations of the stable and supported model semantics from an explanatory viewpoint of causality.

</details>


### [196] [BasketEvent: Understanding Who Did What and When in Basketball Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21267)
*Yu Zhang,Jiayuan Rao,Haoning Wu,Weidi Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BasketEvent provides a player-grounded basketball event dataset with precise temporal annotations, and PlayNet is a player-centric reasoning model that tracks entities, reasons with interactions, and uses gated pooling to localize temporal evidence, achieving superior performance over video-level baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing basketball video understanding often treats spatial perception and semantic recognition separately, failing to ground events to players or locate their exact temporal boundaries within dynamic team play.

Method: BasketEvent: a dataset grounding event labels to responsible players and a subset of 1,000 samples with precise event intervals; PlayNet: a player-centric framework that tracks key entities, associates identities, models player–player, player–ball, and global court interactions, and aggregates sparse temporal evidence via gated pooling.

Result: Experiments show PlayNet significantly outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, demonstrating the value of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding.

Conclusion: Data, code, and models will be publicly available, enabling evaluation and further research in player-centric sports video understanding.

Abstract: Comprehensive basketball video understanding requires resolving not only what event occurs, but also who is responsible and when the key evidence appears. However, exist- ing methods typically treat spatial perception and semantic recognition as isolated tasks, failing to ground events to individual players or pinpoint their temporal boundaries within complex collective dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce BasketEvent, a player- centric basketball event understanding dataset curated from real NBA broadcasts. In BasketEvent, event labels are grounded to the responsible players, and a manually an- notated subset of 1,000 samples with precise event intervals is provided to evaluate tem- poral evidence localization. Based on this data, we propose PlayNet, a player-centric reasoning framework that maps basketball videos to player-level event predictions with temporal evidence. Concretely, PlayNet tracks key entities, associates player identities, and reasons about events by modeling player-player, player-ball, and global court inter- actions, while aggregating sparse temporal evidence via gated pooling. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that PlayNet significantly outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, proving the superiority of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding. Our data, code, and models will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [197] [An LLM-Driven Workflow for Automated Process Control Strategy Generation and Tuning from Dynamic Process Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21292)
*Ari Luna Rueda,Eike Cramer,Klaus Hellgardt,Mehmet Mercangöz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-driven, structured workflow for automated multi-variable control design with validation; on a gas-preheater benchmark, Bayesian-optimization tuning improves the closed-loop objective by ~26.5% over the initial workflow controller.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automate control-design from dynamic process models, enhance reproducibility, and enable automatic repair of failed artifacts via validation feedback.

Method: Constrained code-generation workflow with steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, MV-CV pairing, controller specification, closed-loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation, and Bayesian-optimization-based tuning; artifacts are executed and validated, with failures repaired via feedback; demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics; yields a decentralized PI with feedforward and an executable tuning environment.

Result: BO-based tuning reduces the closed-loop objective by ~26.5% relative to the initial controller, mainly improving pressure-loop transient performance; performance metric aggregates set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors; results quantify automated tuning stage rather than a manual controller; demonstrates feasibility of LLM-driven code-generation for executable control-design workflows but calls for validation on larger plant-wide benchmarks.

Conclusion: Structured LLM-based code generation can construct executable control-design workflows; promising approach with demonstrated gains and clear need for broader validation on larger benchmarks.

Abstract: We present a structured large-language-model-driven workflow for automated multi-variable control design from dynamic process models. The workflow decomposes the design task into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, manipulated-variable controlled-variable (MV-CV) pairing, controller specification, closed loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation and Bayesian-optimization (BO) based tuning. Generated artifacts are executed and validated before downstream tasks proceed, and failed artifacts are repaired using validation feedback. The proposed approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics. The generated workflow produces a physically consistent decentralized PI (proportional-integral) feedback-feedforward control structure and an executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed loop performance objective, which aggregates set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors for the controlled variables, by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller generated by the workflow, mainly through improved pressure-loop transient performance. This figure quantifies the automated tuning stage rather than a comparison against a manually designed controller. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using structured large-language-model-based code generation to construct executable control-design workflows, while also highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks.

</details>


### [198] [Expert Behavior Prior Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21302)
*Gong Gao,Weidong Zhao,Xianhui Liu,Ning Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EBP: online-learning with Q-guided CVAE priors learned from replay buffer, plus expert-policy guidance and gradient correction, yielding superior sample efficiency and stability vs offline-prior BPRL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline policy priors suffer from data scarcity/diversity; need adaptive, high-value priors learned from current experience to improve exploration and stability.

Method: Q-CVAE generates expert priors from online replay; EPG selects expert actions from a generated support set; PGC harmonizes Q-guidance with expert supervision during policy updates.

Result: Empirical evaluation on robotic (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial (DMControl) benchmarks shows EBP surpasses SOTA online RL in sample efficiency and convergence stability.

Conclusion: EBP demonstrates that expert priors learned online from replay can replace static offline datasets, enabling more reliable exploration and learning across tasks.

Abstract: Behavior prior reinforcement learning (BPRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to improve sample efficiency in online reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging policy priors derived from offline demonstrations. However, most existing BPRL methods rely on static offline datasets, which often suffer from low data diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality. This reliance restricts the effectiveness of policy priors, hindering both policy exploitation and stability during online training. Consequently, agents are prone to inefficient exploration and unstable learning dynamics. To address these limitations, we deviate from existing offline pre-training methods and propose an Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) algorithm. Specifically, we introduce a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) that learns to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer. This enables the generation of high-value actions for guiding policy updates without relying on pre-collected expert trajectories. To further enhance policy exploitation, we propose an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism that selects expert actions from a generative support set, and we integrate a policy gradient correction (PGC) module to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision, promoting stable and consistent policy improvement. Extensive experiments conducted on robotic control (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial control (DMControl) benchmarks demonstrate that EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms, achieving higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.

</details>


### [199] [Regulating autonomous and agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21345)
*Chris Reed,Alex Austria,Anmol Bharuka,Pragnitha Mandava,Khushiya Mujawar,Luka Shakhkulashvili*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Regulation must pivot from reactive oversight to proactive, cross-domain governance of autonomous AI by mapping four regimes and proposing adaptive solutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous and agentic AI challenges conventional regulatory assumptions: regulatee knowledge and control are dispersed across the AI supply chain, creating systemic risks that current models cannot address.

Method: Comparative analysis of four regulatory regimes—the UK regulation of content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, and the EU AI Act cross-sectoral regime—to identify challenges and propose regulator-adoptable solutions.

Result: Identifies key challenges posed by AI autonomy and offers actionable regulatory approaches aimed at shifting from retrospective oversight to ongoing, proactive risk management that can adapt to AI autonomy.

Conclusion: Regulators require fresh governance models and cross-regulatory coordination to effectively manage autonomous AI risks, enabling active, adaptive regulation rather than reactive oversight.

Abstract: Regulating activities where regulatees use autonomous and agentic AI is challenging. Regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control no longer hold true; much of that lies elsewhere in the AI supply chain which thus needs to be brought within the scope of regulation. Governance systems for autonomous AI cannot replicate existing governance models, but need a fresh approach. Retrospective supervisory oversight becomes ineffective as a risk management tool, and AI autonomy generates new systemic risks which require new solutions. This paper investigate four regulatory systems: UK regulation of content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, and the EU AI Act\'92s cross-sectoral regime. It analyses the challenges posed by autonomous and agentic AI and proposes potential solutions which regulators might adopt. These will transform regulation from a reactive process to an active one, and assist it in adapting to the challenges of AI autonomy.

</details>


### [200] [SPORD: A Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose Approach for Supply Chain Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21354)
*Jiayin He,Yutong Pan,Sen Yang,Ningxuan Kang,Yongzhi Qi,Jianshen Zhang,Wei Qi,Zuo-Jun Max Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A decoupled SPORD framework (Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose) implemented in JD.com's NetSim for e-commerce supply chains, yielding large speedups, scalable optimization, and improved executive trust; deployed at scale with measurable efficiency and environmental gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address three barriers in supply chain planning: operational fragmentation due to bespoke models, computational intractability from combinatorial scale, and poor implementation due to lack of trust by executives.

Method: Decouple simulation and optimization: simulation generates and evaluates all operationally valid candidate paths incorporating idiosyncratic business logic; optimization (integer programming) disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset. Accelerated by matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU simulation and a list scheduling algorithm, with a closed-loop intelligent diagnosis engine for feedback.

Result: Simulation achieves 10–100x speedups over serial methods; list scheduling reduces coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. Real-world deployment: NetSim optimized end-to-end services for >20,000 suppliers; cross-regional fulfillment rate changed from 6.1% to 4.9% (note: potential wording issue); monthly carbon reduction ~5,745 tCO2e.

Conclusion: SPORD shifts SPORD from mere monitoring to active planning; transparent outputs engage executives; modular NetSim enables future planning with configuration rather than reconstruction, offering scalable, trust-enabled optimization in e-commerce networks.

Abstract: For years, supply chain planning at e-commerce firms has operated as a collection of isolated projects. Each planning task from static network planning to dynamic warehouse assortment planning requires analysts to spend weeks building models from scratch, calibrating and persuading executives to act on outputs they cannot verify. Three barriers drive this: bespoke models proliferate because standardization is difficult (operational fragmentation); once unified, the combinatorial scale of millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes, and intricate routing logic exceeds what solvers can handle within a tight window (computational intractability); and a mathematically optimal solution still fails to be implemented if the executives do not trust it (implementation hurdle). To bridge this gap, we propose and implement the Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose method, deployed as JD.com's NetSim platform. The central insight is decoupling: simulation proposes by generating and evaluating the full set of operationally valid candidate paths-absorbing all idiosyncratic business logic, while an integer program disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset. Computationally, matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU accelerated simulation achieves a 10-100 times speedup over serial methods, and a list scheduling algorithm reduces coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. Operationally, we establish a closed loop via an intelligent diagnosis engine. Since 2025, NetSim has optimized end to-end services for over 20,000 suppliers, the cross-regional fulfillment rate dropped from 6.1% to 4.9%, and the average monthly carbon reduction is approximately 5,745 tCO2e. SPORD moves simulation from monitoring to active planning. The transparent outputs turn skeptical executives into engaged collaborators, and the modular architecture ensures that the next planning requires just configuration, not reconstruction.

</details>


### [201] [Towards Faithful Graph Explanations with Synergistic Edge Effects via Granular Balls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21381)
*Jiancu Chen,Shuyin Xia,Guan Wang,Degang Chen,Fan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SeeExplainer is a parameter-free GNN explainer that uses a granular-ball graph refinement to capture edge synergistic effects and explain instance-level decisions by perturbing a structural graph, outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge-wise perturbation explanations typically ignore synergistic interactions among edges, leading to incomplete or unstable edge importance for GNN explanations. There is a need for instance-level explanations that account for edge interactions.

Method: Introduce a granular-ball graph refinement that decomposes a graph into disjoint granular-balls of varying sizes and uses them as nodes to form a structural graph. Then perturb nodes and edges in this structural graph to generate explanatory subgraphs based on their contributions. The approach is parameter-free.

Result: Empirical evaluation on several graph classification datasets across different networks shows SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: The method effectively captures synergistic edge effects via the granular-ball structural graph, enabling superior, parameter-free instance-level explanations for GNNs.

Abstract: Instance-level explanations aim to reveal the rationale behind a model's decisions for a specific graph. Previous methods explain graph neural networks (GNNs) by selecting important edges to induce subgraphs, where edge importance is assessed by perturbing each edge and observing changes in the model predictions. However, they often neglect the synergistic effects among edges, which are crucial for accurately characterizing edge importance. To address this issue, we propose SeeExplainer, a parameter-free explainer to interpret GNNs. Specifically, we first introduce a granular-ball graph refinement mechanism that decomposes a graph into several disjoint granular-balls with no fixed size, and utilize them as nodes to construct a structural graph. This process can better capture the synergistic effects among edges. Then, we perturb nodes and edges in the structural graph to generate explanatory subgraphs based on their respective contributions. Experiments on several graph classification datasets of different networks show that SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [202] [Multimodal Pretraining for Generalizable EEG Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21384)
*Targol Bakhtiarvand,Jugal Kalita,Adham Atyabi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multimodal EEG foundation model integrates raw EEG, time-frequency, and text encoders in a shared embedding space, pre-trained with self-supervised objectives, achieving state-of-the-art seizure detection on CHB-MIT and good cross-subject/generalization with interpretable localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome dataset/task-specific EEG models by leveraging foundation-model paradigms and self-supervised learning, enabling broad applicability and cross-dataset adaptation in seizure detection.

Method: A multimodal architecture combining a Mamba-based raw EEG encoder, a ViT-style time-frequency encoder, and a lightweight text encoder, trained in a shared embedding space using masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses. Pretraining is followed by fine-tuning on CHB-MIT and other seizure datasets, with evaluation on standard splits and leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocols.

Result: On CHB-MIT standard split: single model AUROC 0.874; ensemble AUROC 0.878 (state-of-the-art). LOSO across 19 subjects yielded mean balanced accuracy 0.558. Across datasets/settings, the model showed robust seizure detection and adaptable cross-domain performance with interpretable seizure localization.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that a multimodal EEG foundation model can generalize across datasets and tasks, enable straightforward adaptation to new seizure detection scenarios, and provide interpretable localization, underscoring the value of multimodal self-supervised pretraining for EEG.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) models used for epilepsy are often limited to specific datasets and tasks. This limited approach can make it challenging to apply these models across different datasets or in various situations. However, recent studies in foundation models and self-supervised learning suggest that an adaptable EEG backbone could support a range of EEG related tasks. In this study, we have developed a multimodal EEG foundation model that combines a raw signal encoder based on the Mamba architecture, a Vision Transformer (ViT)-style encoder for time-frequency data, and a lightweight encoder for text, all within a shared embedding space. The pretraining process relies on several innovative techniques, such as masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses. These methods are designed to create rich, seizure-relevant representations without requiring labeled data. To assess the efficacy and generalization of our pretrained model, we fine-tuned it on the canonical CHB-MIT seizure detection benchmark and additional seizure detection datasets, and conducted extensive experiments comparing different model variants. On the standard CHB-MIT split, our best single model achieved an AUROC of 0.874, and an ensemble variant reached 0.878 AUROC, representing state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark. In addition to standard train-test splits, we evaluated performance under a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol, which is rarely reported in prior EEG seizure modeling work and highlights the difficulty of patient-independent seizure detection, with a mean LOSO balanced accuracy of 0.558 across 19 subjects. Across datasets and evaluation settings, our multimodal foundation model enabled robust seizure detection and straightforward adaptation to new seizure detection scenarios, while also supporting interpretable seizure localization.

</details>


### [203] [MSBraM: A Multi-scale Self-supervised Brain Foundation Model for Hierarchical EEG Dynamics Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21402)
*Tao Zhou,Jing Han,Lingyu Shu,Zixing Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSBraM introduces a two-stage, multi-scale self-supervised pretraining for EEG that learns hierarchical representations via a multi-scale neural tokenizer and curriculum masking, achieving state-of-the-art transfer across 12 datasets (10 tasks).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG signals have intrinsic multi-scale temporal structure; existing self-supervised models often fail to capture both local patterns and long-range dependencies, limiting cross-task generalization.

Method: Stage 1: multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG into semantic codes at multiple temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction. Stage 2: model is pretrained to predict masked codes using a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy that progressively integrates fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context.

Result: Pretrained on ~2,400 hours of EEG data; evaluated on 10 downstream tasks across 12 public datasets; MSBraM outperforms state-of-the-art pretrained models, showing strong generalization and transferability.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is crucial for effective EEG foundation models.

Abstract: Self-supervised foundation models have recently shown strong potential for electroencephalogram (EEG)-based analysis. However, existing approaches struggle to capture the inherently multi-scale temporal structure of EEG signals, where local neural patterns and long-range dependencies jointly encode task-relevant information. This limitation hampers cross-scale representation learning and generalization across diverse downstream tasks. To address this challenge, we propose MSBraM, a Multi-Scale self-supervised Brain foundation Model designed to learn hierarchical EEG representations. MSBraM follows a two-stage pretraining framework. First, a multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG signals into semantic codes at different temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction. Second, the model is pretrained to predict masked codes using a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy, progressively integrating fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context. We pretrain MSBraM on over 2,400 hours of EEG data and evaluate it across 10 downstream tasks on 12 public datasets. Extensive experiments show that MSBraM achieves superior performance on other state-of-the-art pretrained models, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability. These results indicate that explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is critical for effective EEG foundation models.

</details>


### [204] [Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21412)
*Bartolomeo Bogliolo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Euclid-MCP is an open-source MCP server enabling deterministic logic reasoning with a Prolog backend via an engine-agnostic Euclid-IR representation, enabling translate-run-inspect-repair loops for LLM-assisted inference with full proof traces; it improves reliability on larger problems and argues against semantic RAG for rule enforcement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the unreliability of LLMs in multi-step, safety- and compliance-critical reasoning and the lack of standardized, tool-augmented interfaces for neuro-symbolic systems; bridge LLMs with symbolic engines using a readable intermediate representation.

Method: Introduce Euclid-MCP server with SWI-Prolog backend and Euclid-IR, an Horn-clause logic IR that is easy for LLMs to generate and compile to Prolog or other backends; provide a compact translate-run-inspect-repair loop interface for LLM clients to delegate inference while preserving proof traces and derivation logs.

Result: Empirical evaluation on an IT security/compliance use case shows LLMs fail on larger knowledge bases due to hallucinations, while Euclid-MCP yields exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs; supports stable shared reasoning substrate for RAG and agentic systems, and demonstrates surpassing semantic RAG in rule enforcement contexts.

Conclusion: Euclid-MCP offers a standardized, open-source, engine-agnostic reasoning substrate that couples neural and symbolic components, enabling reliable, traceable inference for complex domains and serving as a foundation for tool-augmented agents and RAG systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language understanding and generation but remain unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning, especially in safety-critical or compliance-sensitive domains. Recent neuro-symbolic approaches address this gap by coupling neural models with external symbolic engines, yet most integrations are bespoke and lack a standardized interface for tool-augmented agents.
