This paper presents Euclid-MCP, an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog. Euclid-MCP introduces Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that is human-readable, easy for LLMs to generate, and straightforward to compile into Prolog or alternative backends. The server exposes a compact tool interface that supports a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while retaining full access to proof traces and derivation logs. We evaluate Euclid-MCP on a realistic IT security and compliance use case. Results show that while LLMs alone are sufficient on small knowledge bases, they hallucinate systematically on larger problems, whereas Euclid-MCP delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. We argue that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement, and that Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems.

</details>


### [205] [Logical Regression for Planning with Axioms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21414)
*Connor Little,Christian Muise*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes an approximation of logical regression in axiom-rich domains by restricting regression outcomes to minimal partial states, enabling robust, generalizable execution monitoring with significant variable reduction and strong recovery in dynamic settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Logical regression in planning becomes intractable with axioms; there is a need for scalable, robust mechanisms that produce compact state knowledge for execution monitoring and non-deterministic planning.

Method: Develop an approximation of regression that limits conditions to partial states, avoids recalculating axioms, and yields minimal partial states. Integrate this regression into an execution-monitoring framework and evaluate across multiple domains.

Result: Partial-state regression generalizes across domains, reducing the number of variables for monitoring by up to ~70%. The resulting monitor demonstrates robustness, recovering from unexpected changes in over 50% of trials across several domains.

Conclusion: Approximate regression over partial states is effective for execution monitoring in axiom-rich domains, offering scalable state information, better generalization, and practical robustness.

Abstract: In automated planning, logical regression is an operation that returns the most general condition necessary for an action to achieve a particular formula. It has many applications, such as allowing for more robust plan execution and providing compact policies for non-deterministic planning. Although relatively simple to calculate in basic planning settings, logical regression becomes significantly more complex when additional factors, such as axioms, are present. We introduce a methodology for approximating the logical regression of an action in a domain that includes axioms; an approximation that limits conditions to partial states. Our method produces minimal partial states while avoiding the recalculation of axioms. To demonstrate the impact of our methods, we embed our form of regression in an execution monitoring context, a well-established setting that can benefit greatly from logical regression. Our results show that this form of regression can dramatically generalize partial states across multiple domains, reducing the number of variables considered for execution monitoring by up to 70%, and demonstrate that the resulting execution monitor is robust enough to recover frequently in an environment with unexpected changes: several domains recover over 50% of the time in our tests.

</details>


### [206] [PATS: Policy-Aware Training Scaffolding for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21419)
*Yipeng Shi,Zhipeng Ma,Yue Wang,Qitai Tan,Yang Li,Peng Chen,Zhengzhou Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Pats is a policy-centric training scaffold for long-horizon RL with LLM agents that converts recent rollout data into evidence cards to adaptively guide subsequent rollouts, improving performance and reducing prompt tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weak policies in long-horizon RL produce repetitive failures and uninformative rollouts; existing skill-centric methods focus on skills rather than adaptive training-time support; there is a need for dynamic scaffolding that evolves with policy.

Method: Transform latest policy rollout groups into evidence cards; task-specific evaluation adjusts context used in future rollouts; provide concrete guidance to help weak policies complete tasks; revise or remove redundant context as policy improves; train with environmental rewards using standard RLVR; scaffold discarded at deployment.

Result: On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats outperforms strong baselines by up to 18.6%; across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens.

Conclusion: A dynamic, policy-centric training scaffold can adaptively guide policy learning, improve sample efficiency and performance, and reduce reliance on explicit guidance as the policy matures; the scaffold is discarded at deployment.

Abstract: In long-horizon LLM agent reinforcement learning, weak policies often repeat similar failures, producing uninformative rollout trajectories and limiting effective policy optimization. Existing skill-centric methods improve exploration by optimizing, filtering, or internalizing reusable skills. However, they remain centered on the skills themselves rather than being designed as adaptive training-time support for the evolving policy. To address this, we propose a policy-centric training paradigm that reframes skills as a dynamic training scaffold. Our framework, Pats, converts rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards and uses task-specific evaluation to adjust the context used in subsequent rollouts. Concrete guidance helps weak policies to complete challenging tasks. As policy improves, redundant context is revised or removed to reduce reliance on explicit guidance while preserving useful rollout variation. The policy is optimized with environmental rewards using standard RLVR, and the training scaffold is discarded at deployment. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.

</details>


### [207] [Bridging the Gap Between Plausibility and Admissibility: Constraint-Aware Flow Maps for Dynamic Graph Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21421)
*Michael Romei de Socio,Gian Luca Pozzato,Alessio Merlo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Post-sampling symbolic constraints can improve structural admissibility of diffusion-generated trajectories for dynamic graphs; hard filtering ensures validity but reduces sample size, while soft weighting preserves samples with less validity gain; structural inadmissibility is driven by dependency constraints and grows with graph complexity; overall, plausibility and admissibility are distinct reliability properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To distinguish and improve not just statistical plausibility but structural feasibility of generative trajectory models in dynamic, graph-structured systems by incorporating symbolic constraints after sampling.

Method: A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations. An external symbolic layer applies hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair to enforce structural constraints. Evaluated on two synthetic regimes (compact graph, medium-complexity dependency graph) using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration.

Result: In the compact regime, invalid mass is 0.002996 (almost fully admissible). In the medium-complexity regime, invalid mass rises to 0.155929. Hard filtering removes all invalid retained trajectories while preserving 84.4% of samples; soft weighting maintains effective sample size but yields limited validity gains. Dependency constraints account for nearly all inadmissibility. Conclusion: statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct; symbolic constraint handling becomes more valuable as graph complexity increases.

Conclusion: Symbolic post-sampling constraints can substantially improve structural reliability of generative graph trajectory models, especially as graph-structural complexity grows, by mainly addressing dependency-driven inadmissibility; a combination of hard filtering and constraint-aware design yields best trade-offs between validity and sample efficiency.

Abstract: Generative models can support decision-making under uncertainty by producing ensembles of plausible future system trajectories, but statistical plausibility does not ensure structural feasibility. This study investigates whether post-sampling symbolic constraints can improve the reliability of generative trajectory modeling in dynamic graph-structured systems. A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations, while an external symbolic layer applies hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair. The framework is evaluated on two controlled synthetic regimes: a compact graph and a medium-complexity dependency graph, using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration. In the compact regime, the model produces an invalid probability mass of 0.002996, indicating an almost entirely admissible trajectory manifold. Under the same architecture and training protocol, invalid mass increases to 0.155929 in the medium-complexity regime. Hard filtering removes all invalid retained trajectories while preserving 84.4% of generated samples, whereas soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields only limited validity gains. Family-level analysis shows that dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility. These results indicate that statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties and that symbolic constraint handling becomes more valuable as graph-structural complexity increases.

</details>


### [208] [Agent-Guided Relational Concept Discovery: Toward Interpretable Surgical Margin Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21437)
*Nooshin Maghsoodi,Amoon Jamzad,Robert Policelli,Mohammad Farahmand,Dilakshan Srikanthan,Martin Kaufmann,Kevin Y. M. Ren,Shaila Merchant,Sonal Varma,Ross Walker,Doug McKay,John Rudan,Gabor Fichtinger,Parvin Mousavi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Agent-Guided Concept Discovery (AGCD), a concept learning framework for REIMS-based surgical margin assessment that learns data-driven concepts without predefined labels, uses a reasoning agent for semantic refinement and adaptive weighting, and grounds concepts in a biochemical knowledge graph to align with metabolic relationships; shows improved balanced accuracy and sensitivity on Skin and Breast Cancer datasets and reduced false positives intraoperatively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical adoption is hindered by poor generalization to intraoperative operating room conditions and the black-box nature of deep models. Supervised concept-based approaches require concept labels that are difficult to obtain in complex mass spectrometry workflows.

Method: Agent-Guided Concept Discovery (AGCD) learns concepts directly from unlabeled spectra. A reasoning agent refines semantic descriptions of learned concepts and adaptively adjusts their weights based on diagnostic relevance. Concepts are grounded via a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure consistency with known metabolic relationships.

Result: Across Skin and Breast Cancer datasets, the model improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over a baseline. In an intraoperative representative case, it shows fewer false positives, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.

Conclusion: AGCD provides an interpretable, data-driven pathway to generalization for REIMS-based surgical margin assessment by discovering concepts without predefined labels and grounding them in metabolic knowledge, potentially aiding clinical adoption.

Abstract: Deep learning models can effectively use Rapid Evaporative Ionization Mass Spectrometry (REIMS) data for surgical margin assessment. However, their clinical adoption remains challenging due to limited generalization to operating room conditions. This difficulty arises because models are typically trained on labeled spectra collected from resected tissue samples, while they must operate on noisy, unlabeled data acquired directly during surgery. In addition, the black-box nature of deep learning models makes it difficult to understand and systematically improve their behavior. Concept-based learning offers a promising way to address these challenges by mapping raw measurements to human-understandable concepts. However, supervised concept-based approaches rely on concept annotations, which are difficult to obtain in complex mass spectrometry workflows. We propose Agent-Guided Concept Discovery, a framework that learns meaningful concepts directly from data without requiring predefined concept labels. During training, a reasoning agent refines semantic descriptions of the learned concepts and adaptively adjusts their weight based on diagnostic relevance. These concepts are further grounded using a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure consistency with known metabolic relationships. Across Skin and Breast Cancer datasets, our model improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over the baseline. In a representative intraoperative case, it shows fewer false positives, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.

</details>


### [209] [Detecting LLM-Generated Tokens in Human--LLM Coauthored Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21458)
*Yangjun Lu,Hongyi Zhou,Fabian Spill,Kai Ye,Chengchun Shi,Jin Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Token-level smoothing with adaptive Lepski bandwidth to localize LLM-generated content in mixed-authorship text, without token-level labels, with theoretical MSE guarantees and strong empirical performance, plus a public website.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need to locate LLM-generated portions within mixed-authorship documents; document-level detectors cannot identify local regions; token-level locality is essential for accountability and editing.

Method: Start from token-level detection scores; smooth adjacent token scores to reduce variability; apply an adaptive Lepski-type bandwidth rule based on local authorship structure; no token-level labeled data required for training.

Result: Approach achieves favorable mean square error in estimating the latent signal; strong empirical performance against baselines on synthetic and realistic datasets; publicly accessible website implementing the method.

Conclusion: Simple to implement; theoretically sound with MSE guarantees; practical utility for localizing LLM-generated content; validated empirically and deployed publicly.

Abstract: The rise of human-AI collaborative writing has created a growing need for fine-grained detection methods that support localizing likely LLM-generated content in mixed-authorship documents. Existing methods for detecting LLM-generated text mainly focus on document-level classification and cannot identify which parts of the text are generated by LLMs. This paper introduces a new method to address this urgent need. Our method operates at the token level, the natural unit of modern language models, and builds on existing token-level detection scores. The key idea is to smooth adjacent token scores to reduce their variability, while using an adaptive Lepski-type rule to select the bandwidth according to the local authorship structure. Our method is simple to implement and does not require token-level labeled data for training. Theoretically, we characterize this trade-off and show that the proposed method achieves favorable mean square error performance in estimating the underlying signal. Empirically, we demonstrate strong performance of our method against a wide range of baselines in both synthetic datasets and a realistic dataset. We deploy a publicly accessible website that implements the methods as well.

</details>


### [210] [AREX: Towards a Recursively Self-Improving Agent for Deep Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21461)
*Shuqi Lu,Chaofan Li,Kun Luo,Zhang Zhang,Hui Wang,Hongwang Xiao,Zheng Liu,Lei Xiong,Jiahao Wang,Sen Wang,Xiyan Jiang,Wanli Li,Yuyang Hu,Hongjin Qian,Bingyu Yan,Ziyi Xia,Yingxia Shao,Kang Liu,Zhicheng Dou,Di He,Chaozhuo Li,Qiwei Ye,Zhongyuan Wang,Zheng Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AREX introduces Recursively Self-Improving agents for deep research, alternating inner evidence gathering with an outer constraint-wise self-improvement loop, aided by a learned autonomous context-update tool to sustain long-horizon reasoning. It achieves strong performance on multiple benchmarks using smaller models and competition with larger ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address discovery-verification asymmetry in deep research: many constraints must be satisfied jointly, verification is tractable per constraint, while discovery is costly. Long-horizon tasks suffer from sparse rewards; an agent should iteratively improve its answers by verifying intermediate results to guide subsequent exploration.

Method: AREX alternates an inner loop that gathers evidence and constructs a provisional answer with an outer loop that audits the answer constraint-wise, identifies unresolved claims, and launches targeted follow-up research. It learns an autonomous context-update tool that compresses growing interaction history into a compact improvement state preserving verified evidence and unresolved constraints, enabling long-horizon RSI without external models. Training uses verified synthetic tasks and high-quality trajectories through agentic mid-training and long-horizon reinforcement learning. To handle sparse final rewards, AREX emphasizes decisive evidence acquisition steps and correction of erroneous directions. Implementations include a dense 4B model and a 122B-A10B mixture-of-experts model. Evaluation spans BrowseComp, WideSearch, DeepSearchQA, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and other reasoning/tool-use benchmarks, where AREX outperforms comparable-scale baselines and remains competitive with substantially larger models.

Result: AREX substantially outperforms baselines of similar scale and is competitive with much larger parameter models across a range of reasoning and tool-use benchmarks such as BrowseComp, WideSearch, DeepSearchQA, and Humanity's Last Exam.

Conclusion: A Recursively Self-Improving research paradigm, supported by a learned context-update mechanism, enables robust long-horizon reasoning and constrained multi-task discovery–verification, with strong empirical gains on diverse benchmarks and potential for scalable deployment with modestly sized models.

Abstract: Deep research requires agents to find answers that jointly satisfy multiple constraints. Discovering such answers is costly, whereas verifying a candidate can often be decomposed into tractable constraint-wise checks. This discovery--verification asymmetry suggests that a research agent should do more than simply search longer: it should recursively improve its current answer by verifying intermediate results and using the partially verified state to guide subsequent refinement. We introduce AREX, a family of Recursively Self-Improving (RSI) deep research agents. AREX alternates between an inner research loop that gathers evidence and constructs a provisional answer, and an outer self-improvement loop that audits the answer constraint-wise, identifies unresolved claims, and launches targeted follow-up research. To sustain RSI over long horizons, AREX learns an autonomous context-update tool that compresses growing interaction history into a compact improvement state preserving verified evidence and unresolved constraints, without relying on an external model. We train AREX on verified synthetic tasks and high-quality trajectories through agentic mid-training and long-horizon reinforcement learning. To mitigate sparse final rewards during long horizon learning, we emphasize key steps where decisive evidence is acquired or erroneous research directions are corrected. We instantiate a dense 4B model and a 122B-A10B Mixture-of-Experts model. Across BrowseComp, WideSearch, DeepSearchQA, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and other reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, AREX substantially outperforms comparable-scale baselines and remains competitive with models using substantially more activated parameters.

</details>


### [211] [Agentic coding without the cloud: evaluating open-weight large language models on longitudinal data preparation tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21482)
*Mack Nixon,Liam Wright,Yevgeniya Kovalchuk,Alison Fang-Wei Wu,Martin Danka,Andy Boyd,David Bann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Open-weight LLMs on consumer hardware show promise for AI-assisted data preparation under governance constraints, achieving high task completion on 20 tasks across 102 variables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Governance restrictions often prohibit sending data to external services. Local, open-weight models enable AI-assisted data preparation without data leaving the local environment.

Method: Introduces RRBench, an open-source framework with a curated ground-truth dataset from a British cohort study, defined tasks (e.g., category harmonization, multi-wave merging), and automated evaluation of LLM-produced R code and data outputs; benchmarks both consumer-grade open-weight LLMs and state-of-the-art models on 20 data-prep tasks.

Result: State-of-the-art models (31-35B) nearly saturated the benchmark with average task completion up to 87.9%; open-weight models on consumer hardware show considerable viability for governance-restricted data prep.

Conclusion: Open-weight models running locally can be a viable path for AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research; RRBench is publicly available to enable broader evaluation and adoption.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and agents are now widely used tools in code development, with data typically sent to third-party cloud-based models. Their adoption in research using personal data is constrained by governance requirements that typically prohibit data transmission to external services. Locally deployable open-weight models offer an alternative since sensitive data never leave the local environment. We introduce an open-source framework for evaluating the efficacy of AI agents powered by open-weight LLMs on one of the most persistent bottlenecks in research on longitudinal population studies: data preparation. The framework comprises: a curated ground-truth dataset (cleaning scripts preparing six sweeps of data from a British cohort study), task definitions encompassing tasks such as category harmonization and multi-wave merging, and automated routines for evaluating the LLM-produced R code and outputted data. We benchmark LLMs across the (consumer grade) deployment spectrum to assess their efficacy in 20 data preparation tasks (creation of 102 variables). Current state-of-the-art, 31-35B parameter models almost saturated our benchmark ("average task completion" up to 87.9%). The performance of open-weight LLMs running on consumer-grade hardware shows promise of a viable path toward AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research settings. Our framework is publicly available at: https://github.com/UCL-ARC/RRBench.

</details>


### [212] [Toward Continuous Assurance for the Democratization of AI Agent Creation in Industry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21495)
*Natan Levy,Harel Berger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Democratized AI agents risk silent, post-deployment degradation; a lightweight continuous-assurance framework with dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance is proposed, plus an initial auditor prototype and scenario-based tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As non-engineers create AI agents via low-code/no-code/conversational tools, dependencies (models, tools, data, prompts, schedules, services) can drift or fail, causing reliability issues that are hard to detect.

Method: Proposes a taxonomy of reliability challenges for citizen-created agents and designs a lightweight continuous-assurance framework comprising dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance. An initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessments illustrate translation of the taxonomy into concrete checks and remediation guidance.

Result: Conceptual framework with an operational component (auditor prototype) and scenario-based assessments that demonstrate how the framework yields actionable checks and remediation guidance.

Conclusion: A practical path to maintaining reliability of democratized AI agents by continuous assurance; future work should validate at scale, automate checks, and integrate governance with development environments.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly created inside organizations by non-engineering users through low-code, no-code, and conversational development environments. This democratization enables rapid local innovation, but it also creates a reliability gap: agents that appear to users as simple productivity artifacts may depend on changing models, tools, retrieval sources, permissions, prompts, schedules, and external services. These dependencies can cause silent degradation long after deployment, even when no user directly modifies the agent. This paper identifies the reliability challenge created by democratized AI agent creation and proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework for citizen-created organizational agents. The framework combines dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance to assess whether an agent remains operationally ready under expected conditions. We also present an initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment showing how the proposed taxonomy can be translated into practical checks and actionable remediation guidance.

</details>


### [213] [Agentic Context Management: Solving Agent Memory and Cost by Treating Them as Lifecycle and Architecture Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21503)
*Gaurav Dadhich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Agentic Context Management (ACM), a lifecycle-based approach to managing agent reasoning context beyond simple storage, comprising five primitives and a reference implementation with strong benchmark results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production AI agents accumulate context across conversations and tools, incurring high token costs and fidelity loss. Treating this as mere storage/retrieval is insufficient; need proactive, lifecycle-oriented management of what the agent remembers and uses across organizational contexts.

Method: Decomposes context management into five primitives—architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting & consolidation—and presents Maximem Synap as a multi-tenant implementation. Provides an economic analysis of token costs (quadratic growth, limitations of crude summarization) and demonstrates a reference system with specified configurations.

Result: Empirical claims: 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo under the described configuration. Argues that validated compaction preserves fidelity while achieving linear cost growth, and highlights dimensions not captured by existing benchmarks (latency, token efficiency, context-rot resistance).

Conclusion: ACM defines a holistic lifecycle for agent context, enabling scalable, provenance-preserving memory management across organizational scopes. It suggests directions for next benchmarks and practical deployments, focusing on efficiency, decision-level context, and organizational context.

Abstract: Production AI agents' failures are less often due to an inability to reason well and more often because they cannot manage what is in their reasoning context: conversation histories, large prompts, large tool definitions, and ballooning tool outputs. Agents drown in their own accumulating history while paying a token cost that grows every turn, producing missing recalls within and across conversations. The incumbent response treats this as a storage-and-retrieval problem. We argue that framing is too narrow. Actively managing what an agent holds in mind is a lifecycle, not merely a store: it spans deciding what to remember, extracting and structuring it, choosing the right store per data type, consolidating and forgetting while preserving provenance, deciding what is relevant now, anticipating what is needed next, and compacting context to a budget without losing what matters. In serious production this operates not over a single user but across an organizational scope hierarchy. We name this discipline Agentic Context Management (ACM) and decompose it into five primitives: architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting & consolidation. We then make the economic case: naive context accumulation grows token cost quadratically in conversation length, crude summarization buys linear cost at the price of an accuracy cliff, and only validated compaction achieves linear cost with preserved fidelity. We describe a reference implementation, Maximem Synap, that realizes the five primitives as a multi-tenant service and reports 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo under the configuration detailed in Section 6. We close with dimensions existing benchmarks do not yet capture, latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance, and the frontier of decision-level and organization-level context the category points toward.

</details>


### [214] [Same Dangerous Objective, Opposite Advice: Direct Exposure versus Multi-Agent Mediation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21518)
*Linjun Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Downstream LLMs can appear safer for the wrong reasons; upstream manipulation via multi-stage pipelines poses safety risks; highlights need for provenance and inspectability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To examine how alignment/safety depends on how instructions are presented and to reveal potential compositional manipulation risks in multi-stage AI workflows.

Method: Empirical test on OpenAI/alias GPT-5.6-SOL using 25 mirrored trade-off profiles. Compare direct exposure to a dangerous objective with downstream transforms (Id, Censor) that yield a constraint-rewritten, target-bearing intent, and a user-facing Superego that omits raw objective and manipulation clauses.

Result: Direct exposure to the dangerous objective yielded advice opposing the target; when transformed through Id/Censor into a target-bearing but opaque directive, the Superego produced advice aligned with the target. This suggests the model may detect or distrust manipulation and that a high-capability model can serve as the user-facing agent in a multi-stage pipeline while preserving the objective’s target direction. Endpoint-only access prevents inspection of upstream messages.

Conclusion: Pipeline-level safety is critical: even safe-looking downstream outputs can mask harmful upstream objectives. Raw directives, manipulation clauses, and provenance can be hidden from the downstream user, enabling manipulable objectives. Safeguards should emphasize provenance, inspectability, and constraint designs to prevent leakage and ensure alignment across all pipeline stages.

Abstract: Even a current high-capability LLM can appear safer when shown a dangerous objective directly than when other agents transform and relay its direction. Using OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol model alias, we test 25 pre-specified mirrored trade-off profiles. Direct exposure to an objective authorizing concealment, fabrication, and pressure produced advice net opposed to its target. After an Id and Censor transformed the same objective into affect and a constraint-rewritten, target-bearing intention, the user-facing Superego---which saw the preferred direction but not the raw objective, its manipulative clauses, or its source---produced advice net aligned with the target.
  This behavioral reverse shift is consistent with the model recognizing or distrusting the manipulative motive, although we do not identify its internal mechanism. The second result exposes a compositional safety gap: a current high-capability model can be used as the user-facing component of an automated, multi-stage workflow serving an explicitly manipulative objective. The workflow can keep the raw instruction, its manipulation-authorizing clauses, and its provenance outside the downstream model's context while preserving the objective's target direction. A user with endpoint-only access likewise cannot directly inspect those upstream messages including the objective.

</details>


### [215] [The Boundaries of Automation: A Theory of Persistent Human Participation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21547)
*Fares Fourati,Hinrich Schütze,Eyke Hüllermeier,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Automation limits are not solely about AI capability; humans may stay involved for technical complementarity, value of participation, and especially when targets emerge through interaction, yielding persistent human–AI co-construction that shapes design, evaluation, and ethics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reassess the default drive to automate by examining conditions under which human involvement persists even with highly capable AI, focusing on concepts of complementarity, developmental value, and emergent targets.

Method: Theoretical/conceptual analysis that identifies three grounding notions (technical/complementarity, normative/developmental, emergence) and defines human–AI co-construction as a persistent, constitutive process in certain activities.

Result: A framework in which three grounds justify ongoing human participation; in emergence-based settings, targets arise through interaction and human input becomes part of the produced outcome, not merely a means to improve performance.

Conclusion: The scope of automation is limited by whether human input is constitutive or merely supplementary; this has implications for how we design, evaluate, and ethically govern future AI systems, emphasizing co-construction in selected domains.

Abstract: The rapid progress of AI has intensified the long-standing pursuit of automation: replacing human participation with algorithms wherever possible. Implicit in this pursuit is the assumption that humans remain in the loop only because current AI systems are not yet sufficiently capable. This paper challenges that assumption. Rather than asking how far automation can extend, we ask where its conceptual limits lie and argue that human participation may persist even with highly capable AI systems for three distinct reasons. Technical or complementarity grounds arise when humans contribute capabilities or perspectives unavailable to AI. Normative or developmental grounds arise when participation itself is valuable for human agency or learning. Most importantly, emergence grounds arise from target emergence: in some activities, the target is not fully specified in advance but instead emerges through the interaction itself. In these cases, human participation is not merely a means of improving execution but is constitutive of the target being produced. Human--AI co-construction, understood as the joint production of outcomes by humans and AI systems, is therefore not simply a temporary response to imperfect AI, but a persistent feature of activities whose objectives emerge through participation. This perspective has important implications for the limits of automation and for the design, evaluation, and ethics of future AI systems.

</details>


### [216] [MIRROR: Learning from the Other View for Multi-Modal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21552)
*Wen Ye,Yuxiao Qu,Aviral Kumar,Xuezhe Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A study reveals that vision–language models show inconsistent reasoning across text, diagram, and combined views for geometry problems; introduces ODA-Data with multi-view problems and MIRROR, a reversal-KL self-supervised RL method that uses the best view as a teacher to align others, yielding improved accuracy and cross-modal consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the fragmented, view-dependent reasoning in VLMs where different modalities expose distinct reasoning paths and failure modes not leveraged by standard multimodal pretraining. The goal is to harness complementary information across views to improve robust multimodal geometry reasoning.

Method: Construct ODA-Data: a high-quality paired multimodal geometry dataset with text-dominant, image-dominant, and combined views for the same problems, plus training/evaluation splits for modality-dependent reasoning. Develop MIRROR (Modality-Informed Reciprocal Reasoning Optimization): for each problem, evaluate all views, select the best-performing view as a teacher, and train other views to imitate the teacher using a reverse-KL objective, via reinforcement learning-based self-supervision to improve cross-view reasoning.

Result: MIRROR outperforms standard reinforcement learning baselines on geometry reasoning benchmarks, producing more accurate and consistent behavior across modalities by leveraging complementary information exposed by different views.

Conclusion: Modality-aware self-supervision that leverages cross-view discrepancies can significantly enhance multimodal reasoning in VLMs. The ODA-Data dataset and MIRROR framework provide a practical path to more robust cross-modal understanding beyond single-view training.

Abstract: Unlike large language models (LLMs) that exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with visual reasoning, even on geometry problems that admit equivalent text, diagram, and combined diagram+text views. We show that these views often elicit different behaviors: a model may solve a problem from text but fail on the corresponding diagram, or succeed visually while failing textually. This inconsistency suggests that different views expose complementary reasoning paths and failure modes that standard multimodal post-training does not fully exploit. To study and exploit this phenomenon, we construct ODA-Data, a high-quality paired multimodal geometry dataset with text-dominant, image-dominant, and combined image+text views of the same problems, together with splits for training and evaluating modality-dependent reasoning behaviors. We then develop Modality-Informed Reciprocal Reasoning Optimization (MIRROR), a reinforcement learning approach for improving multimodal reasoning via self supervision. For each problem, MIRROR evaluates the model under all views, selects the best-performing view as a teacher, and trains other views with a reverse-KL objective towards the teacher. Across reasoning benchmarks that evaluate on geometry problems, MIRROR improves over standard RL and yields more accurate and consistent behavior across modalities

</details>


### [217] [OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21557)
*Xiao Yu,Baolin Peng,Ruize Xu,Hao Zou,Qianhui Wu,Hao Cheng,Wenlin Yao,Nikhil Singh,Zhou Yu,Jianfeng Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OpenForgeRL provides an open-source, end-to-end training framework for harness-based AI agents by proxying harness calls and running rollouts in isolated containers, enabling scalable training across diverse environments; it achieves strong benchmark results and reveals insights about harness learnability and RL's impact on reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Harness-based agents (e.g., Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) are powerful but hard to train end-to-end with standard SFT/RL stacks because their stateful, multi-process inference is not readily expressible in open training pipelines.

Method: Introduce a lightweight proxy that records harness model calls as training data for a standard RL codebase (veRL); deploy a Kubernetes-based orchestrator that runs each rollout in a separate remote container; decouple training and inference to enable scalable, end-to-end training on any harness and environment; evaluate across tool/claw-based and GUI browser-use agents, using hundreds to thousands of tasks.

Result: OpenForgeClaw achieves 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval, and 33.7 on QwenClawBench; OpenForgeGUI achieves 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager; both outperform open baselines of similar size on most benchmarks, with GUI performance matching or exceeding larger models.

Conclusion: Decoupling training and inference via OpenForgeRL enables end-to-end harness-based training and scalable evaluation across diverse environments. Harness choice heavily affects learnability; RL improves agentic reliability (self-verification, tool coverage, multi-step planning) but critical abilities like error recovery remain weak; the framework elucidates how to study and improve harness-driven agents.

Abstract: Modern AI agents rely on elaborate inference harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw to drive multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and access to external systems. While powerful, these complex harnesses also make agents hard to train end-to-end with open infrastructure, whose SFT/RL stacks cannot natively express stateful, multi-process harness inference. To address this, we present OpenForgeRL, an open-source framework for training harness-based agents end-to-end in diverse environments. OpenForgeRL achieves this with a lightweight proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as training data for a standard RL codebase (e.g., veRL), and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container, together enabling training on any harness in any environment at scale. By decoupling training and inference, OpenForgeRL allows researchers to easily train, study, and improve agents directly in the real harnesses and environments they are deployed with. We validate our framework across diverse, complex harnesses and environments, spanning tool/claw-based agents and multimodal GUI browser- and computer-use agents. Using only hundreds to a few thousand tasks, OpenForgeClaw reaches 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval and 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Both outperform open baselines of similar size on nearly all benchmarks, and in the GUI setting match or surpass models several times larger. Beyond benchmarks, we analyze how harness choice (e.g., ZeroClaw, OpenClaw, Codex) and RL shape agent behavior. We find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others, and that RL improves agentic reliability, such as self-verification, tool coverage, and completing multi-step plans, though critical abilities such as error recovery remain weak.

</details>


### [218] [Beyond Sycophancy: Structured Resistance and Compliance in LLM Moral Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21558)
*Baihui Wang,Bernard Koch*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Three studies show LLM judgment revision under social influence follows three dimensions: distance between incoming view and the model's initial position, source attribution of the view, and the coalition structure supporting it. Sycophancy is reframed as part of a broader belief-updating process, with implications for principled alignment in morally consequential interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond viewing sycophancy as a single failure mode and to develop a principled framework for distinguishing constructive belief revision from mere compliance, thereby improving alignment of morally relevant interactions.

Method: Three experiments manipulating incoming views across (i) psychological distance from the model's initial position, (ii) source attribution (whether views are framed as the model's own prior judgments or as external input), and (iii) coalition structure (group pressure) to observe effects on judgment revision across contexts.

Result: Judgment revision is structured along the three dimensions: models show greater receptivity to nearer positions, greater influence from views framed as the model's own prior judgments, and variable responsiveness to group pressure; sycophancy emerges as an aspect of the general belief-updating process under social influence.

Conclusion: The authors propose a framework to distinguish constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance, enabling safer and more morally aligned interactions by calibrating when social influence should inform judgments.

Abstract: Building socially calibrated large language models, which can learn from others without simply yielding to them, requires more than reducing sycophancy as a one-dimensional failure mode. Models must distinguish when to incorporate others' perspectives from when to maintain a well-grounded moral judgment. We study the broader resistance-compliance process governing this distinction. Across three studies, we show that models' judgment revision is structured along three dimensions that parallel classic phenomena in human social psychology: the distance between an incoming view and the model's initial position, the source attribution of that view, and the coalition structure supporting it. Models are generally more receptive to nearby positions, more influenced by views presented as their own prior judgments, and differently responsive to group pressure. These findings recast sycophancy as one expression of a broader judgment-updating process shaped by social influence. Our framework provides a principled basis for distinguishing constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance, thereby supporting better alignment in morally consequential interactions.

</details>


### [219] [Unsupervised Consensus-Based Anomaly Detection for Spatiotemporal Malaria Incidence in Ghana](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21559)
*T. Ansah-Narh,Y. Asare Afrane*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A consensus anomaly detection framework reveals spatial-temporal heterogeneity in Ghana's malaria transmission (2014-2023): burden and anomaly-frequency diverge across regions; Tamale shows high burden; Ashanti highest anomaly rates; anomalous months have large effect sizes; burden alone is insufficient for surveillance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve malaria surveillance by distinguishing prevalence from unusual transmission patterns to guide targeted investigations and control.

Method: Apply a consensus anomaly detection framework to monthly malaria data; identify atypical periods; quantify anomaly burden (cumulative cases during anomalies) and anomaly frequency (persistence of anomalies); compare atypical months to normal months using effect sizes (Cohen's d).

Result: Anomalies are spatially and temporally structured; Ashanti and Northern Regions show recurrent anomalies; Tamale, Kumasi, Accra are persistent hotspots; high-burden areas do not necessarily coincide with high anomaly frequency; anomalous months have Cohen's d = 3.252 for case counts and d > 1.2 for seasonal deviations; malaria burden alone is incomplete.

Conclusion: Distinguishing where malaria is prevalent from where transmission behaves unusually enhances surveillance, prioritization, and targeted control strategies.

Abstract: A consensus anomaly detection framework was applied to monthly malaria surveillance data from Ghana (2014-2023) to identify atypical transmission patterns. Anomalies were highly structured in space and time. Ashanti and Northern Regions accounted for most recurrent anomalies, with persistent hotspots at Tamale, Kumasi, and Accra. A key finding was the spatial distinction between anomaly burden (cumulative cases during anomalous periods) and anomaly frequency (persistence of unusual behaviour). Tamale had the highest burden during anomalies, whereas the highest anomaly rates clustered in Ashanti districts, showing that high-burden areas are not necessarily those with the most frequent anomalous transmission. Anomalous months formed a statistically distinct group, with much higher case counts (Cohen's $d = 3.252$) and large seasonal deviations ($d > 1.2$) compared with normal months. Malaria burden alone provides an incomplete picture of transmission dynamics. By distinguishing where malaria is most prevalent from where transmission behaves most unusually, this framework can strengthen surveillance, prioritise investigations, and support targeted control strategies.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [220] [DataPrep-Bench: Benchmarking LLMs as Training Data Preparators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20465)
*Hao Liang,Qifeng Cai,Yibo Lin,Jianzhuo Du,Qifeng Xia,Sizhe Qiu,Linzhuang Sun,Meiyi Qiang,Zhaoyang Han,Xiaochen Ma,Bohan Zeng,Ruichuan An,Conghui He,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes DataPrep-Bench, a unified end-to-end benchmark for LLM-driven data preparation with two capabilities (data construction and data quality evaluation), plus a data-construction skill and a distribution-based quality metric; demonstrates substantial gains and strong cross-model correlations across multiple domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is no unified benchmark to evaluate how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows prepare training data end-to-end, with a focus on downstream training utility rather than surface text properties.

Method: Introduce DataPrep-Bench with two complementary evaluation tracks. Data construction: methods transform identical raw sources into supervised data and are scored by downstream fine-tuning of a base model on their outputs alongside Dolly-15k; also release Data-Construction-Skill, a domain-aware agent that improves the Dolly baseline on Llama-3.1-8B Finance. Data quality evaluation: scoring functions are learned by their Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool, using the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based metric based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy.

Result: Data-Construction-Skill improves the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with top agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. DAS achieves strong cross-model correlation in four of six domains and, in Math, Science, and Medical, is the only metric with r > 0.70 across domains, outperforming prior quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators.

Conclusion: DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework to measure progress on both data-construction and data-quality evaluation as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation.

Abstract: The quality of training data fundamentally determines the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet no unified benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows actually prepare training data end to end. We view LLM-driven data preparation as comprising two complementary capabilities: data construction, which transforms raw sources into supervised training data, and data quality evaluation, which predicts the training value of candidate datasets before downstream training; throughout, "quality" refers to downstream training utility rather than surface-level textual properties. We introduce DataPrep-Bench, the first unified benchmark that jointly evaluates both capabilities under a shared downstream-grounded protocol over six domains and multiple base models. For data construction, methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; alongside this track we release Data-Construction-Skill, a skill-guided agent that lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. For data quality evaluation, scoring functions are scored by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool; we release the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator that uses MMD between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators. DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring progress on both capabilities as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation.

</details>


### [221] [PhantomFill: When the Form Demands an Answer, Language Models Invent One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20492)
*Rana Muhammad Usman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Format-driven constraints trigger fabrication; PhantomFill quantifies Coerced Fabrication Rate and Escape Utilization Rate; a single-schema fix is proposed to curb the issue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether requiring structured outputs (schemas, enums, minimum counts) causes ML model hallucinations and to establish a benchmark with deterministic scoring.

Method: Evaluate 13 models on identical prompts while varying the required output format (free text vs constrained JSON/enum fields). Inputs are designed to be unanswerable. Measure fabrication rates across configurations, analyze instruction suppression and model scale effects. Introduce PhantomFill benchmark with deterministic scoring and two metrics: Coerced Fabrication Rate and Escape Utilization Rate. Test a one-line schema fix.

Result: Required fields drive fabrication to near-universal levels (100% in ten of thirteen models). Open-weight models frequently ignore or resist constraints; some models override explicit prohibitions. Scaling within a model family does not remove fabrication risk. The study provides two reportable metrics (Coerced Fabrication Rate and Escape Utilization Rate) and demonstrates the pervasiveness of format-induced fabrication. The proposed fix is a one-line schema change; otherwise, failures are widespread across configurations.

Conclusion: Output formats shape model honesty; current training does not adequately inoculate models against schema-driven fabrication. PhantomFill offers a deterministic, comparable benchmark and underscores the need for schema-aware safeguards and evaluation.

Abstract: Language models in production do not write prose. They fill forms: JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates. We show that the form itself causes hallucination.
  We ask thirteen models the same question about the same input and change only the answer format. The inputs are built so the question cannot be answered: a viral post showing 12,400 likes but no visible replies, a support ticket whose call was never transcribed. In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly. It says there is no reply data, 98% of the time. Given a required JSON field for sentiment, the same model invents an answer 40 times out of 40. It fabricates the mood of crowds it never saw and quotes customers it never heard.
  The pattern holds with force. Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in ten of thirteen models. An explicit "insufficient evidence" option rescues only the frontier: all nine open-weight models ignore it. A direct instruction, do not infer sentiment, is overridden by the schema in four of six models. Resistance does not come with scale: within a single model family, the smallest model refuses, the mid-sized model fabricates, the largest refuses again. Honesty under format pressure is a training outcome that no one is measuring.
  The fabrication hides exactly where hedging is impossible: in required enums and minimum-count arrays, fields where no disclaimer fits. We release PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring and two reportable numbers: the Coerced Fabrication Rate and the Escape Utilization Rate. The fix we test is one line of schema. The failure we measure is everywhere.

</details>


### [222] [The Active Ingredient in Muon's Grokking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20512)
*Yufeng Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Orthogonalization via Newton-Schulz is the key driver of Muon's faster grokking on modular arithmetic; spectral-norm constraints alone do not explain the speedup and are unreliable. Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations speeds up but harms stability; spectral scaling can be dropped without cost. The study emphasizes reporting both first-crossing and sustained grok times and provides reproducibility through released code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To identify which mechanism—spectral-norm constraints or orthogonalized momentum—drives Muon's grokking speedup compared with AdamW, and to quantify stability across hyperparameters.

Method: Multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps with ablations separating orthogonalization from spectral constraints; mechanistic analysis of spectral-norm dynamics and embedding movement; vary Newton-Schulz iteration count (e.g., 5 to 1); assess stability across learning rates; evaluate impact of spectral scaling removal; report both first-crossing and sustained grok times; release full training/analysis code.

Result: The speedup is attributable to orthogonalization (Newton-Schulz iteration); spectral-only ablations are no faster than AdamW and unreliable. Orthogonalizers reach generalization at roughly 3x lower spectral norm, and when accounting for embedding movement, converge to a lower-norm solution. Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations from five to one accelerates threshold attainment but increases fragility with higher learning rates; five iterations offer a robust, learning-rate-robust choice. Spectral scaling can be dropped without measurable cost.

Conclusion: Under a stability-aware metric, faster grokking claims can invert; therefore, report both first-crossing and sustained grok times. Orthogonalized momentum is the key mechanism behind Muon's improved grokking speed, and the work provides guidance on hyperparameter choices and robustness. Reproducibility is supported by releasing code at the provided repository.

Abstract: The Muon optimizer reaches the grokking threshold on modular arithmetic faster than AdamW. Prior work attributes this to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but does not isolate which mechanism matters. To better understand Moun's behavior, we run multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps to decompose and stress-test the effect. First, an ablation shows the speedup comes from orthogonalization (the Newton-Schulz iteration): orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, whereas spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and is unreliable, and this verdict holds across learning rates. Second, a mechanistic analysis finds that orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at roughly 3x lower spectral norm and, controlling for how much the embedding actually moves, settle into a lower-norm solution rather than simply perturbing the embedding less. Third, reducing the Newton-Schulz iteration count from five to one accelerates reaching the threshold but makes the grokked solution fragile, prone to transient collapse, with fragility that grows with learning rate; a single iteration is fast and stable only at small learning rate, while the canonical five iterations are the learning-rate-robust choice. We also show spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. A methodological thread runs throughout: under a stability-aware metric, "faster" claims about grokking optimizers can invert, so we report both first-crossing and sustained-grok times. To support reproducibility, we release our full training and analysis code at https://github.com/louiswang524/muon-grokking-frontier

</details>


### [223] [Scaling Closed-Loop Feature Channel Configuration with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20516)
*Tolgay Atinc Uzun,Radu Timofte,Dmitry Ignatov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Scaled closed-loop, LLM-guided channel-configuration search leads to improved accuracy and parameter efficiency in a denser sampling regime; best model reaches 0.3676 accuracy with 11.8M params, revealing frequent non-power-of-two widths and regular channel-allocation patterns, suggesting the channel-search signal transfers to higher sampling density.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether the optimization behavior observed in sparse evaluations transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge with more generated networks.

Method: Scale the search to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle, yielding 2000 generated candidates across 8 cycles and 462 CIFAR-100 evaluations after filtering. Analyze cycle-level mean accuracy (and top-k means), assess parameter efficiency, and inspect channel-width distributions for regularities.

Result: Per-cycle mean accuracy shows a positive linear trend (slope 9.87e-4, p=0.043). The best accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676. Top-5 and top-10 cycle means also trend positively. The best model uses 11.8M parameters, versus 166.5M for the earlier high-performer. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates. Strong models share structured channel-allocation patterns: moderate early widths with expanded middle or later blocks.

Conclusion: The channel-search signal observed in the initial study transfers to the denser sampling regime, achieving higher accuracy with far fewer parameters and revealing architectural regularities to guide channel-width design.

Abstract: Promising initial results in closed-loop large-language-model-based channel-configuration search demonstrated that neural-network widths can be optimized directly through executable code generation and accuracy feedback. However, those results were obtained from a relatively sparse set of valid evaluations, leaving open whether the observed optimization behavior transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more generated networks are evaluated. To test this, the same search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. The analysis covers 2000 generated candidates from 8 complete cycles, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after task and metadata filtering. Per-cycle mean accuracy exhibits a positive linear trend with slope 9.87e-4 (p=0.043), while the high-performing frontier improves more strongly: the best observed accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676, and both the top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means exhibit positive trends. The scaled run also reveals improved parameter efficiency. The best model reaches 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters, compared with an early high-performing model at 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Beyond accuracy, the larger sample exposes architectural regularities that were difficult to assess from sparse observations. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates, and the strongest models share structured channel-allocation patterns characterized by moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks. These findings indicate that the channel-search signal observed in the initial study transfers

</details>


### [224] [Multimodal CoLRAG-TF: Triple-Filtered Retrieval for Complex PDFs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20517)
*Takato Yasuno*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A four-axis fusion retrieval framework for multimodal, multi-hop QA over heterogeneous PDFs, combining dense text embeddings, BM25, knowledge-graph triples, and image similarity; shows near-perfect recall and substantial multi-hop gains on Japanese disaster lesson PDFs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG over heterogeneous PDFs is hindered by multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and dispersed evidence requiring multi-hop reasoning; a robust, modular retrieval architecture is needed across modalities to improve reasoning and answer fidelity.

Method: Four-axis fusion architecture integrating dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity. Builds a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs using a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-based captioning. Extracts 11,414 OpenIE triples indexed with FAISS for fast lookup and hierarchical relevance propagation. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume -> chapter -> block) narrows search space; Bayesian optimization tunes fusion weights with triple axis dominant (α_triple = 0.44).

Result: On a 457-pair benchmark, Retrieval Recall = 0.9909 and a 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline with a vision LLM demonstrates applicability to visual inputs.

Conclusion: Triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured, robust reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework extendable beyond disaster-domain documents.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous PDF collections remains challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence. We present Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion architecture that integrates dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity for robust retrieval over complex documents. Our system constructs a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks extracted from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs, supported by a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-based caption generation. To enhance compositional reasoning, we extract 11,414 OpenIE triples and index them with FAISS, enabling sub-second triple lookup and hierarchical propagation of relevance signals. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume $\to$ chapter $\to$ block) narrows the search space before final fusion scoring. Bayesian optimization over fusion weights reveals that the triple axis must dominate ($α_\text{triple} = 0.44$) to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality. Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, Multimodal CoLRAG-TF achieves a Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6$\%$ improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM further demonstrates the applicability of the approach to visual inputs. These results show that triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework applicable beyond the disaster domain.

</details>


### [225] [Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20519)
*Andrei Cristian Popescu,Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde,Pietro Liò*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Decouples trajectory formation from exit policy in looped Transformers; investigates why adaptive depth fails: gate learning entangles stopping with supervision; finds fixed-prior depth supervision and post-hoc confidence readouts can match or surpass learned gates; reframes adaptive depth as joint trajectory-readout design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Looped Transformers use a shared recurrent block with a learned halting gate. The training objective ties the exit decision to per-depth loss weighting, entangling trajectory formation with debugging the model's stopping policy, complicating diagnosis of adaptive-depth performance.

Method: Empirically analyze adaptive depth via a trajectory–readout lens on controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic, binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B checkpoints. Compare fixed-prior depth supervision, learned gates, and post-hoc confidence readouts; evaluate gate training on frozen trajectories; assess throughput vs accuracy trade-offs on real hardware.

Result: Fixed-prior depth supervision yields trajectories with useful, difficulty-aware intermediate states. Simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or exceed learned linear/MLP gates. Gate training on joint trajectory tends to degrade performance due to trajectory-induced supervision. In Ouro-1.4B/2.6B, pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not universally Pareto-optimal; reductions in average exit depth translate to practical latency gains.

Conclusion: Adaptive depth should be treated as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, not gate learning alone. The trajectory induced by joint gate training is a key source of suboptimal adaptive-depth behavior. A diagnostic lens separating trajectory design from exit policy clarifies previous work and guides more robust, efficient adaptive-compute strategies.

Abstract: Looped Transformers increase test-time computation by repeatedly applying a shared recurrent block. Learned halting objectives in looped Transformers typically use a single exit distribution both as the inference-time stopping rule and as the training-time weighting of per-depth losses. This entangles exit selection with trajectory formation: the gate not only chooses which recurrent state to use, but also determines how strongly each intermediate state is supervised. Consequently, poor adaptive-compute performance can arise from the readout, the induced trajectory, or their interaction. We study adaptive depth in looped Transformers through this trajectory--readout lens, across controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic and binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B checkpoints. We find that fixed-prior depth supervision, which shapes the trajectory without an input-dependent halting policy, produces difficulty-aware trajectories whose intermediate states expose useful stopping signals, and that simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or outperform learned linear and MLP gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the failure: it appears to stem mainly from the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than from limited gate expressivity. The same pattern is present in Ouro evaluations, where pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal, and measured latency confirms that the resulting reductions in average exit depth translate into practical inference-time savings. Our systematic diagnostic evaluation reframes adaptive depth in looped Transformers as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, rather than gate learning alone, highlighting a distinction that prior learned-halting work has often left implicit.

</details>


### [226] [Generative Bayesian Filtering for State Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20521)
*Lei Cao,Sihang Feng,Jixin Yan,Tao Sun,Naichen Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GBF introduces a filtering framework that replaces restrictive observation models with pretrained conditional generative models (CVAE) to perform posterior sampling-based updates, yielding a score-based filtering procedure that leverages generative modeling and uncertainty estimation via ensembling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical filters rely on simple observation models (e.g., linear-Gaussian) that fail to capture nonlinear, heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor data. A flexible, learned observation model can improve state estimation and robustness.

Method: Integrate a CVAE-based likelihood into a Bayesian filtering recursion. The measurement update is treated as posterior sampling that combines the dynamical prior with the CVAE-induced likelihood. The problem is reformulated as a score-based sampling process, enabling the use of pretrained generative models and ensemble-based uncertainty quantification, enabling online inference.

Result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic data and real-world tasks (manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis) shows GBF achieves improved state estimation accuracy and robustness compared with baseline methods.

Conclusion: GBF demonstrates that combining conditional generative models with Bayesian filtering yields flexible, accurate, and well-calibrated state estimation in nonlinear, high-dimensional systems, with notable robustness and uncertainty quantification.

Abstract: The state of a dynamic system evolves over time, switching among several latent modes that govern its observable behavior. Filtering methods infer the latent state from observations. Classical filtering approaches, including Kalman filters, typically rely on simple observation models, such as linear-Gaussian models, that are incapable of characterizing the increasingly nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor signals. To tackle the challenge, we propose Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF), a filtering framework that replaces restrictive observation models with pretrained conditional generative models parametrized by conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE). For online inference, GBF performs a Bayesian prediction-update recursion in which the measurement update is formulated as a posterior sampling problem that combines the dynamical prior with the CVAE-induced likelihood. The resulting filtering problem is then transformed into a score-based sampling problem, which naturally inherits the flexibility from generative models and the uncertainty quantification capabilities from ensembling. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications involving manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis demonstrate that GBF improves state estimation accuracy and robustness relative to baseline approaches.

</details>


### [227] [Do Active SAE Feature Planes Carry More Holonomy? A Preregistered Reversal in Gemma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20522)
*Larry Richards*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Active SAE feature planes exhibit less holonomy than matched controls in Gemma 2 2B, falsifying the semantic-concentration prediction under preregistered analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test the semantic-concentration hypothesis by measuring holonomy across feature planes and determine whether active-feature planes concentrate holonomy as predicted.

Method: Measure holonomy on the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream via local-frame loops using a restricted-Jacobian transport rule; normalize by enclosed area. Preregistered design, thresholding, and verdict rules. Compare random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes; compute adjusted log contrast with 95% CI. Post-freeze diagnostics include area-law validation on a subset, regression-based center displacement bounds, and assessment of transport distortion as a mechanism/confound.

Result: Prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls; adjusted log contrast = -0.29439; 95% CI [-0.43989, -0.14889]. Magnitude-only explanation not supported; three-way ordering (random/mixed/active) undefined at matched magnitude due to common-support failure. Post-freeze diagnostics supported the area law on a small validation subset, bounded matched-center displacement, and identified transport distortion as a live mechanism or confound.

Conclusion: The finding constitutes a narrow, auditable operational reversal rather than a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The causal source remains open; candidate factors include activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear.

Abstract: This paper tests whether holonomy concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature planes in Gemma 2 2B, a concrete operationalization of the broader semantic-concentration prediction. Holonomy is measured at the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by carrying a local frame around small loops using the instrument's restricted-Jacobian transport rule, then normalizing the resulting rotation by enclosed area. The design, materiality threshold, analysis, and verdict rules were preregistered and frozen before the analysed measurements were inspected. The prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls, with an adjusted log contrast of -0.29439 and 95% interval [-0.43989, -0.14889]. A magnitude-only explanation was not supported in this design, while the three-way ordering across random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes was undefined at matched magnitude because common support failed. Post-freeze diagnostics at the same readout supported the area law on a small validation subset, bounded matched-center displacement under a simple paired regression, and identified transport distortion as a live mechanism or confound. The result is therefore a narrow, auditable operational reversal, not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear as live alternatives.

</details>


### [228] [Uncertainty-Aware Trust Estimation for Multi-LLM Systems via Structured Expert Judgement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20529)
*Jiawei Zheng,Jiazhen Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Uncertainty-aware Cooke-style weighting improves multi-LLM ensemble reliability in heterogeneous/adversarial settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address heterogeneity and varying uncertainty quality in LLM ensembles by estimating expert reliability based on probabilistic predictions, rather than assuming equal trust, enabling robust aggregation under uncertainty.

Method: Adapt Cooke-style structured expert judgment with context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability from probabilistic predictions; use Cooke log scoring to penalize overconfident incorrect predictions and reward well-calibrated experts; evaluate on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels.

Result: In homogeneous settings, aggregation methods perform similarly to baselines; in heterogeneous and contaminated panels, Cooke weighting provides a superior accuracy–reliability balance and remains robust when unreliable experts are present.

Conclusion: Uncertainty-aware trust calibration is essential for effective multi-LLM aggregation; Cooke-style weighting offers robustness to heterogeneity and adversarial behavior and should be incorporated into ensemble design.
