Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) ensembles are increasingly used to improve reliability by combining predictions from multiple LLMs. However, existing aggregation methods typically assume that all models are equally trustworthy, overlooking differences in uncertainty quality. This assumption is poorly suited to heterogeneous LLMs, whose reliability and capability vary significantly, making naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts. In this work, we formulate multi-LLM aggregation as a problem of uncertainty-aware trust estimation. We adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, using context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability based on the quality of its probabilistic predictions. Specifically, we employ Cooke-style log weighting, which penalises overconfident incorrect predictions and favours well-calibrated experts. We evaluate our approach on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels. Results show that while aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings, Cooke weighting becomes critical under heterogeneity and contamination. It achieves a superior accuracy-reliability balance and remains robust when unreliable experts are introduced. These findings suggest that Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty.

</details>


### [229] [CLOE: Christoffel Loss Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20530)
*Léa Billet,Louise Travé-Massuyès,Elodie Chanthery,Alexandre Gaffet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CLOE combines autoencoder-based dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function–based anomaly detector in latent space, introducing a loss that aligns representations with the normal data support and a principled thresholding method. It aims for scalable, low-tuning, high-dimensional anomaly detection and shows superior performance on high-dimensional tabular benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the scalability and tuning challenges of Christoffel Function–based anomaly detection in high-dimensional data by integrating it with a learnable latent representation that preserves the normal data support, while keeping a lightweight hyperparameter regime.

Method: Train an autoencoder to reduce dimensionality and apply a Christoffel Function–based detector in the latent space. Introduce a loss term guided by the Christoffel Function to shape latent representations toward the normal data support. Propose a principled thresholding procedure and an efficient scheme to tune a single remaining hyperparameter.

Result: Empirical evaluation on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks shows CLOE outperforming existing methods while maintaining the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function–based approaches.

Conclusion: CLOE delivers scalable, high-performance anomaly detection in high dimensions by synergistically combining autoencoder-based representation learning with Christoffel Function–based detection and a principled calibration process.

Abstract: Semi-supervised anomaly detection plays a key role in diverse fields such as process monitoring, healthcare, and finance. However, lightweight methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and typically require careful tuning of multiple hyperparameters. Among existing approaches, Christoffel Function--based methods are attractive due to their simplicity, requiring at most a single hyperparameter. They also benefit from a well-established theoretical foundation that yields several interesting results for data science. However, their main limitation is poor scalability to high-dimensional settings. In this paper, we introduce CLOE, a new method that combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function--based detector applied in the latent space. To better align representation learning with anomaly detection, we design a novel loss function that leverages the Christoffel Function to guide the autoencoder toward representations that better capture the support of the normal data distribution. We further propose a principled procedure to set the detection threshold and an efficient strategy to tune the single remaining hyperparameter. Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, while preserving the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function--based approaches.

</details>


### [230] [Position: Stop Reactively Patching Your Model Every Time and Start Proactive Test-Driven AI Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20532)
*Nadine Chang,Maying Shen,Jialiang Wang,Rafid Mahmood,Jose M. Alvarez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a proactive, test-driven maintenance flywheel for open-ended AI systems, introducing a test space to map feedback to objectives and claiming it achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations than reactive flywheels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reactive maintenance often ignores system-wide objectives, overlooks future edge cases, and suffers from long-tail data scarcity; a proactive approach aims to preempt errors and improve generalization.

Method: Introduce a 'test space' that links feedback data to task objectives and evolve the maintenance loop from reactive to proactive; provide mathematical proof of superior long-term scaling and reduced iterations for the proactive flywheel.

Result: Mathematically demonstrates that the proactive test-driven flywheel scales better over time and requires fewer iterations than a reactive flywheel.

Conclusion: Shifting to a proactive, test-driven maintenance paradigm with a defined test space yields more scalable, efficient, and robust AI systems compared to traditional reactive maintenance.

Abstract: Many modern AI systems are designed to operate under diverse, open-ended, use-cases. To help generalize deployed systems, many deployed-system maintenance pipelines use a reactive AI flywheel that observes emerging feedback from user behavior (errors) and patches the model accordingly. However, when used as the primary maintenance mechanism, these flywheels often ignore the broader context of these errors within the system's objectives, failing to preempt potential future edge cases, which leads to more unnecessary flywheel iterations. Also, it is statistically increasingly difficult to collect remaining errors due to the long-tail nature of open-world use-cases. This position paper argues that a proactive test-driven flywheel is required to address reactive flywheel's limitations and to approach a generalizable system. We advocate for creating a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives, evolving the flywheel from reactive to proactive. We augment our position by mathematically proving a proactive one achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations than the reactive flywheel.

</details>


### [231] [Grounding Investor Views: Neural Predicates in the Black-Litterman Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20533)
*Marcos Florencio*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A data-driven, interpretable framework replaces subjective view elicitation in Black-Litterman with a hierarchy of neural predicates that output probabilistic market stances, which map to the Black-Litterman matrices P, q, and Ω in an end-to-end differentiable model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the subjectivity and scalability of eliciting views and uncertainties in Black-Litterman by providing a formal, data-driven mechanism that yields calibrated view probabilities.

Method: Process structured financial analysis data through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates. Each predicate outputs probability distributions over market stances; these distributions are mapped to the Black-Litterman pick matrix P, view return vector q, and view uncertainty matrix Ω. View confidence is derived from predicate outputs, enabling a data-driven uncertainty quantification. The approach is interpretable (tracible to underlying data) and fully differentiable for end-to-end learning.

Result: The abstract presents a proposed framework; no empirical results are reported. It asserts interpretability (traceable to data) and differentiability (end-to-end learning) with a data-driven mechanism for view generation and uncertainty.

Conclusion: The work introduces a novel integration of neural predicates into Black-Litterman to automate and calibrate views and uncertainties, offering interpretability and differentiability to improve portfolio construction, while remaining to be demonstrated empirically.

Abstract: Portfolio construction under the Black-Litterman model requires investors to specify views on asset returns alongside explicit uncertainty estimates -- a process that remains largely subjective and difficult to scale. We propose a formal approach in which neural predicates serve as a structured, probabilistic mechanism for view generation. In our formulation, structured financial analysis data is processed through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates whose outputs -- probability distributions over market stances -- are mapped to the pick matrix $\mathbf{P}$, the view return vector $\mathbf{q}$, and the view uncertainty matrix $\boldsymbolΩ$ of the Black-Litterman model. View confidence is derived from predicate output distributions, providing a data-driven alternative to subjective uncertainty elicitation. The resulting approach is interpretable, in the sense that any portfolio weight can be traced back through the predicate's logical chain to the underlying data, and fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end learning.

</details>


### [232] [A Graph Neural Network approach to zero-shot Digital Twins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20535)
*Alicia Tierz,Icíar Alfaro,David González,Elías Cueto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A zero-shot digital twin framework that couples a metriplectic thermodynamics–informed graph neural solver with perception-driven data assimilation to enable real-time, geometry-agnostic simulations on unseen geometries, validated on viscoelastic beam deformation and viscous-fluid sloshing with ~25 ms/frame latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional predictive digital twins are geometrically rigid and require extensive retraining or fine-tuning whenever the physical domain or boundary conditions change, limiting generalization and real-time applicability.

Method: A Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture grounded in metriplectic thermodynamics to enforce local energy conservation and entropy production via graph message passing; an auxiliary GNN infers unobservable fields from sparse visual boundaries; continuous closed-loop data assimilation using deep segmentation plus sparse optical flow to track deformations and free-surface boundaries and correct the autoregressive simulation to curb drift; real-time implementation (~25 ms/frame) with potential AR projection of latent variables.

Result: The framework exhibits extreme generalization across two regimes—large viscoelastic beam deformations and nonlinear viscous fluid sloshing—on unseen geometries without retraining, maintaining physically consistent simulations within real-time latency and enabling latent-variable visualization through AR.

Conclusion: The proposed zero-shot digital twin platform integrates perception, physics-informed graph learning, and real-time data assimilation to yield geometry-agnostic, physically consistent simulations, effectively bridging sim-to-real for unseen geometries and enabling AR projection of latent variables.

Abstract: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins often remain geometrically rigid, requiring extensive retraining or fine-tuning whenever the underlying physical domain or boundary conditions change. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel framework for \textit{Zero-Shot Digital Twins} that seamlessly couples real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed reasoning engine. At the core of our architecture is the Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture, a Geometric Deep Learning solver grounded in a metriplectic thermodynamic formalism that enforces energy conservation and non-negative entropy production locally through graph message passing. The framework integrates an auxiliary Graph Neural Network to infer unobservable fields (such as stress tensors or velocity and energy distributions) directly from sparse initial visual boundaries, mitigating numerical start-up transients. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we implement a continuous closed-loop data assimilation mechanism; the pipeline tracks macroscopic deformations and free-surface fluid boundaries in real-time using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow, dynamically correcting the autoregressive simulation rollout and eliminating numerical drift. To test the validity of our approach, we demonstrate the extreme generalization capabilities of our approach across two disparate physical regimes: the large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and the non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. In both scenarios, the unified framework instantiates physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating well within real-time latency budgets (approximately 25 ms per frame) and enabling the direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.

</details>


### [233] [ReliableTableQA:How Much Supervision Does Reliability Annotation Need?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20537)
*Huei-Chung Hu,Hsin-Tai Wu,Koyo Kobayashi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReliableTableQA annotates the statistical reliability of tabular QA outputs, not just answerability, addressing UCAR (Unreliable Confident Answer Rate) with a 10-category reliability taxonomy, a data-efficient labeling pipeline generating 50k examples from a grammar over public retail schemas, and a controlled study showing SFT-based supervision suffices while GRPO adds little when SFT is adequate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In enterprise analytics, valid decision-making requires that computed table QA results have meaningful statistical support. Syntactically correct queries can produce unreliable estimates due to small samples, wide confidence intervals, multiple comparisons, or distribution-tails misalignment; current systems often report confident but unreliable results.

Method: (1) Propose a 10-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) for tabular QA outputs. (2) Build a program-first data pipeline generating 50k reliability-labeled examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified supervised FT/SFT and GRPO splits. (3) Conduct controlled experiments assessing how much supervision is needed to calibrate reliability annotations, comparing SFT-only, GRPO, and combinations across in-/out-of-distribution and hard-flag slices.

Result: With a small, schema-stratified SFT set (approximately 200 examples), reliability-flag F1 rises from 0.61 to 0.98, parse rate increases from 0.52 to 1.00, and UCAR drops to zero. The model generalizes to unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on hold-out H&M). GRPO provides marginal or no benefits when SFT is adequately trained; gains are limited to under-trained SFT scenarios (+0.06–0.16 exact-flag-set match) and disappear in hard-flag, strict exact-match, and OOD evaluations.

Conclusion: Reliability annotation for tabular QA is data-efficient: small, schema-aware supervision suffices to achieve high reliability calibration and generalization. Reinforcement learning via GRPO adds little once SFT is adequate; the work clarifies when retrieval/rl fine-tuning is beneficial and reframes reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem.

Abstract: We introduce ReliableTableQA, a framework for training an LLM to annotate the statistical reliability of tabular QA results, not whether the query is answerable, but whether the computed answer is statistically meaningful. In real enterprise analytics, a syntactically correct SQL query can return a value that is based on too small a sample, has an excessively wide confidence interval, or is too confounded to support action. Existing systems answer confidently in all such cases, a failure we quantify as the Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR). We contribute (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) covering hazards such as small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline that generates 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; and (3) a controlled study of how much supervision calibrated reliability annotation actually requires. We find that a small, schema-stratified SFT set is remarkably sufficient: 200 examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drive UCAR to zero, and yield a model that generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). Against this strong SFT baseline, GRPO, commonly assumed to be essential, helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples, in- and out-of-distribution) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, a null result we confirm across a hard compound-flag slice, a strict exact-match metric, and out-of-distribution evaluation. Our findings reframe reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem and delineate precisely when reinforcement fine-tuning does and does not pay off.

</details>


### [234] [Codec-Gauge: Learning Compression-Friendly Gauges for Transformer KV Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20538)
*Yitao Jiang,Yaoqing Yang,Luyang Zhao,Muhao Chen,Devin Balkcom*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A post-training KV-cache coordinate transform (Codec-Gauge) learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression/quantization backends to concentrate energy in low-frequency layouts, improving compression fidelity without retraining the model or changing weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context Transformer inference relies on KV-cache compression/quantization, which can degrade fidelity. Prior work shows channel basis affects backend preservation of behavior; goal is to improve compression fidelity post-training by learning cache-coordinate transforms.

Method: Introduce Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that applies small orthogonal channel transforms around compression/quantization backends. Optimize using a frequency-distribution objective combining a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to push KV energy to low-frequency codec-facing layouts. Evaluate on six models at 3/4/6 bits/value, using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring; compare to random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT baselines; show applicability to block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization; validate with a 27B model and long-context prompts and timing/storage measurements.

Result: Learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by 44.0% on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform several controls (random, Hadamard, DCT, PCA/KLT). They also improve quality preservation across block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments reproduce the trend on a 27B model and long-context tasks; storage and timing measurements validate the compressed-cache paths.

Conclusion: Cache-coordinate geometry is a practical post-training variable to improve compression fidelity for KV-cache based long-context inference, without altering model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

Abstract: Long-context Transformer inference increasingly relies on KV-cache compression or quantization. Prior rotation and transform-coding results suggest that the channel basis of each key/value vector affects how faithfully a fixed backend preserves model behavior. We introduce Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression and quantization backends. Its frequency-distribution objective combines a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. We evaluate actual compression and decompression using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring. Across six models at $3$, $4$, and $6$ bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by $44.0\%$ on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. The same gauges improve quality preservation for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments on a 27B model and long-context task prompts reproduce the quality trend, while serial storage and timing measurements validate the implemented compressed-cache paths. These results establish cache-coordinate geometry as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

</details>


### [235] [Leveraging Biokinetic Knowledge Priors for Data-Scarce Bioprocess Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20539)
*Kyunghoon Hur,Eunjung Jeon,Hyun Woo Kim,Gyubok Lee,Seongjun Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two priors for injecting biokinetic ODE knowledge into neural nets for bioprocess data are compared; both improve over baselines, and simulation pre-training is as effective as an architecture-embedded ODE, offering a simple data-efficient strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biomanufacturing data are scarce and costly; incorporating established biokinetic ODE knowledge into neural models could improve sample efficiency and generalization.

Method: Systematically compare a data-level prior (pre-train a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves) with an architecture-level prior (embed the ODE within the decoder); evaluate across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species.

Result: Both priors outperform no-prior baselines; the two priors are substitutable, with a generic simulation-trained decoder matching a fully bio-structured, real-data-trained decoder.

Conclusion: Simulation pre-training provides a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity, enabling effective incorporation of prior biokinetic knowledge.

Abstract: While deep learning has accelerated drug discovery, its impact on biomanufacturing has been considerably more limited. The reason is data scarcity. Bioreactor experiments are high-cost, take days to weeks, and are rarely shared in public form, leaving each research work with only a handful of experiments. The domain itself, however, is rich in prior knowledge. Biokinetic ordinary differential equation (ODE) models have described microbial growth for decades, yet how to inject this knowledge into a neural network has not been studied systematically. We present the first systematic study of how to inject this ODE knowledge into a neural network, comparing a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves against an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE inside the decoder. Both consistently outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. Our central finding is that the two are substitutable. A generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data. Simulation pre-training therefore offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.

</details>


### [236] [From Atoms to Entropy: Optimal Noise Allocation for Diffusion Training in the Convex Regime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20540)
*Luca Ambrogioni,Giulio Franzese,Alberto Foresti,Gabriel Raya,Bac Nguyen,Georgios Batzolis,Yuhta Takida,Naoki Murata,Chieh-Hsin Lai,Yuki Mitsufuji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Optimal diffusion-noise schedules are finite (atomic) in fully coupled training and follow a square-root entropy density in decoupled settings; empirically, finite-support schedules perform well on discrete domains and are competitive on continuous images.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current diffusion-noise schedules rely on heuristics; a principled asymptotic framework is needed to characterize optimal noise-level allocation across training.

Method: Develop a general statistical framework for asymptotic noise-level allocation. Prove atomic minimizers in the fully coupled regime under convex/PL assumptions. In an independent-learner regime, apply a random-matrix analysis with a feature-noise decoupling condition to derive a sqrt(entropy rate) sampling density. Validate on Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, and MNIST; compare with entropic proxy; extend to larger-scale experiments.

Result: In the coupled regime, the optimal training schedule concentrates on finitely many noise levels. In the decoupled regime, the sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate. The entropic proxy tracks the atomic optimum in neural networks and breaks down mainly in the fully coupled parametric case. Practically, square-root entropy scheduling improves efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

Conclusion: The framework explains when finite-support schedules arise and provides a practical, entropic scheduling heuristic that improves training efficiency in discrete domains and competes well on continuous images; full schedule optimization remains challenging in large-scale, fully coupled settings.

Abstract: How should a diffusion model decide which noise levels to train on, and how much? Despite the importance of this choice, current noise schedules are based largely on heuristics or empirical tuning. Here, we develop a general statistical framework for studying asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation in diffusion training. Our first main result concerns the fully coupled regime, where information can spread between different time points. Under convexity or Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type assumptions, we show that the optimized training schedule admits an atomic minimizer, concentrated on finitely many noise levels. Our second main result specializes this framework to an idealized independent-learner regime, intended to model temporal specialization in neural networks. Under an additional feature-noise decoupling condition, a random-matrix analysis leads to an information-theoretic proxy: the decoupled sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate, the rate at which conditional entropy grows along the forward process. We test these predictions in controlled settings where the coupled objective can be optimized directly, including Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, and MNIST. In these settings, the optimized schedules are consistently finite-support, while the smooth entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural-network models and breaks down mainly in the fully coupled parametric case, as the theory suggests. We then evaluate the entropic schedule in larger-scale experiments, where full schedule optimization is currently intractable. The results indicate that square-root entropy scheduling can substantially improve training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with standard EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

</details>


### [237] [HypNO: A Graph-Based Neural Operator with Physics-Informed Message Passing for Hyperbolic Conservation Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20541)
*Dimitrije Ždrale,Cassie An Jeng,Katie Wang,Sonia Vanier,Alexandre Bayen,Hossein Nick Zinat Matin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HypNO is a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws that enforces upwinding and entropy on a space-time finite-volume graph, yielding accurate, shock-aware predictions on LWR and ARZ traffic models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hyperbolic PDEs with shocks pose challenges for operator learning; existing neural operators struggle with discontinuities and global transport. A physics-informed, graph-based operator could better capture upwind behavior and entropy conditions.

Method: Build a space-time graph of finite-volume cells; apply adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks; train to map initial data to solution snapshots.

Result: HypNO accurately predicts solution snapshots across diverse initial conditions and captures shocks and discontinuities in LWR and ARZ traffic models, a stress test for operator learning.

Conclusion: A robust, shock-aware neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws, with strong performance on traffic-flow models and potential applicability to similar hyperbolic systems.

Abstract: We introduce HypNO, a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws. HypNO operates directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells and uses adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks. We benchmark the architecture on the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) and Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) traffic-flow models, a stress test for operator-learning methods because of their simultaneous global transport and shock formation. HypNO predicts solution snapshots accurately across a range of initial conditions while capturing the shocks and discontinuities of the solution.

</details>


### [238] [Improving Access to Essential Medicines via Decision-Aware Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20542)
*Angel Tsai-Hsuan Chung,Jatu Abdulai,Patrick Bayoh,Lawrence Sandi,Francis Smart,Hamsa Bastani,Osbert Bastani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A decision-aware, multi-task learning ML framework for essential medicines allocation in LMICs improves consumption by ~19% in treated districts and scales nationwide to 2M women/children; demonstrates feasibility and potential for low-cost, equitable resource allocation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Resource scarcity and poor data in LMICs hinder efficient medicine allocation; need data-driven tools that are sample-efficient and equity-conscious.

Method: Develop a decision-aware ML framework with multi-task learning and catalytic priors; collaborate with government; staggered nationwide deployment; econometric evaluation.

Result: Estimated 19% increase in consumption in treated districts; nationwide scale to ~2 million beneficiaries; demonstrates efficiency and potential for low-cost global health impact.

Conclusion: ML methods can improve efficiency and equity in essential medicine allocation in resource-constrained settings; approach shows practical deployment and scalability.

Abstract: A critical challenge in healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is the efficient and equitable allocation of scarce resources, particularly essential medicines. This problem is complicated by limited high-quality data, which restricts the applicability of traditional data-driven techniques. We propose a novel decision-aware machine learning framework for essential medicines allocation, which additionally leverages multi-task learning to ensure sample efficiency and catalytic priors to ensure equitable allocation. In collaboration with the Sierra Leone national government, we performed a staggered, nationwide deployment of our system as a decision support tool. Our econometric evaluation finds an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts, demonstrating its efficacy at improving access to essential medicines. Our tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, covering an estimated 2 million women and children under five. Our work demonstrates how machine learning methods can improve efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings.

</details>


### [239] [When RLVR Shrinks the Reasoning Boundary: Diagnosing Pass@k Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20543)
*Todd Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper diagnoses pass@k inversion in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), showing that optimizing for verifier checks can erase rare but recoverable boundary prompts. It introduces Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) as a simple method to preserve base-solvable trajectories while sharpening prompts. Empirical results across Omni-MATH-Test and MATH500 indicate PBA improves Pass@1 and high-budget coverage versus GRPO, with a diagnostic regime showing the risk pattern. The work argues for considering not just optimization strength but the safety of prompts, and posits broader relevance to verifier-guided optimization in vision-language agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why verifiable-reward-based RL can deteriorate long-run coverage (pass@k inversion) despite improving one-shot accuracy, and to propose a lightweight mitigation that preserves rare but valid solutions, particularly at decision boundaries.

Method: 1) Conceptual framing: two-mode (absence-of-evidence) explanation for loss of rare boundary trajectories under RLVR. 2) Propose Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA): use sufficiently frozen-base evidence to sharpen prompts and anchor risky prompts to the base distribution. 3) Empirical evaluation across three training seeds on Omni-MATH-Test with MATH500 as a high-coverage validation benchmark; a 3000-prompt regime-controlled diagnostic study. 4) Use mathematical verifiers as a controlled testbed for verifier-guided optimization, and discuss applicability to ECCV-style vision-language agents.

Result: PBA yields higher Pass@1 and improved high-budget coverage compared with matched GRPO. Across seeds, ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories; diagnostic results align with the predicted absence-of-evidence mechanism.

Conclusion: Reasoning post-training must consider which prompts are safe to optimize, not only how strongly to optimize. The observed pass@k inversion risk generalizes to verifier-driven checks in other domains; safe-optimization strategies like PBA or similar anchoring are needed to maintain base-level coverage while benefiting from verifier guidance.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve one-sample accuracy while making a model worse under repeated sampling. We study this pass@k inversion: after training, the policy may solve fewer distinct problems than its base model at large $k$. The failure concentrates on boundary prompts, where the base model contains rare correct trajectories that are recoverable by sampling but too sparse to reliably appear in finite RLVR rollout groups. We argue that a two-mode account explains this as an absence-of-evidence failure: rare correct trajectories may disappear before RLVR samples and reinforces them often enough. The main contribution is this diagnostic and mechanistic framing. Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) is a deliberately simple proof-of-concept: sharpen prompts with sufficient frozen-base correct evidence, and anchor risky prompts to the base distribution. Across three training seeds on Omni-MATH-Test, with MATH500 as a secondary high-coverage validation benchmark, PBA improves both \PassK{1} and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO. A 3000-prompt regime-controlled diagnostic study is consistent across seeds with the expected signature: ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories. We use mathematical verifiers as a controlled testbed for verifier-guided optimization; the same pass@k inversion risk applies to ECCV-relevant vision-language agents when repeated visual, spatial, or chart-reasoning attempts are checked by external tools or verifiers. Reasoning post-training should decide not only how strongly to optimize, but which prompts are safe to optimize.

</details>


### [240] [Conflict Resolution under Degraded Surveillance in Air Corridors Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20547)
*Esrat Farhana Dulia,Syed Arbab Mohd Shihab,Caleb Adams,Ruben Del Rosario*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DQN-based MARL framework for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous AAM in a 3D corridor; evaluates safety under degraded surveillance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safe Advanced Air Mobility requires robust, scalable conflict resolution when surveillance is noisy, delayed, or incomplete; current methods may fail under degraded observations; need simulation-driven assessment of performance and trade-offs.

Method: Deep Q-Network based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with decentralized control. Separate policies trained for two aircraft categories using only local observations and a 14-action space (course maintenance, turns, vertical maneuvering, landing, speed control). Simulation includes category-specific dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay/dropout, wind, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty.

Result: Evaluated over 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation; loss of separation frequency/duration rise with density and separation thresholds, but most events resolve within 1 s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain motion ~79% of the time. Conflict actions: turning 33%, maintain motion 29%, speed control 25%, vertical maneuvers 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations show safety-capacity trade-offs. Framework enables simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution under degraded surveillance.

Conclusion: The framework provides a scalable, data-driven tool for benchmarking and optimizing conflict-resolution strategies in Safe AAM under realistic imperfections in surveillance and actuation, facilitating Pareto analyses of safety versus corridor capacity.

Abstract: Safe Advanced Air Mobility operations require aircraft to maintain separation when surveillance information is noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable. This study develops a Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous small unmanned aerial vehicles and electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft operating within a structured three-dimensional corridor. Separate policies are trained for the two aircraft categories using local observations and a 14-action space that includes maintaining course, turning, vertical maneuvering, landing, and speed control. The simulation incorporates aircraft-specific dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty. The trained policies are evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds. Loss-of-separation frequency and duration generally increase with traffic density and separation requirements, although most events are resolved within 1s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain their motion approximately 79% of the time. During conflicts, turning accounts for 33% of actions, followed by maintaining motion at 29%, speed control at 25%, and vertical maneuvers at 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity. The framework supports the simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions.

</details>


### [241] [SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20548)
*Mikail Khona,Aditya Vavre,Boxiang Wang,Deyu Fu,Hao Wu,Mike Chrzanowski,Bryan Catanzaro,Dheevatsa Mudigere,Jeff Pool,Michael Lightstone,Mohammad Shoeybi,Mostofa Patwary,Nima Tajbakhsh,Tijmen Blankevoort*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Higher-order optimizers (Muon, SOAP) can outperform AdamW at scale with targeted algorithmic and system enhancements; the authors adapt preconditioned gradient methods to address instability and cost in large-scale LLM pretraining, propose per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning, and implement a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM. They perform a unified study with update-RMS matching, evaluate orthogonalization quality, and release code for reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome instability, numerical challenges, and high computational cost of higher-order preconditioners (like Muon and SOAP) in large-scale language model pretraining, enabling faster convergence and stable training at very large batch sizes.

Method: Adapt and enhance preconditioned gradient methods by (1) identifying instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes, (2) introducing per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning, (3) conducting a unified empirical study comparing SOAP, Muon, and AdamW with update-RMS matching for fair LR transfer, (4) empirically evaluating Muon's orthogonalization quality, (5) developing a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM that avoids approximations in optimizer computations, and (6) adding system-level optimizations to speed up training at scale; releasing an implementation with Emergent Optimizers codebase.

Result: SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW in multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens, maintaining stability at batch sizes up to 100M tokens where AdamW degrades; the layer-wise optimizer enables efficient large-scale training with balanced memory and communication, without compromising optimizer accuracy; a publicly available codebase is provided for reproducibility.

Conclusion: Higher-order optimizers can deliver superior convergence and stability at scale with proper algorithmic refinements (QR orthogonalization, robust preconditioning) and system-aware implementations; these methods merit consideration for large-scale LLM pretraining, and the released code supports broader adoption and experimentation.

Abstract: Higher-order optimizers such as Muon and SOAP offer faster convergence than AdamW, but their computational cost and numerical stability challenges have limited adoption at scale. In this work, we adapt and enhance preconditioned gradient methods to overcome the practical challenges of large-scale LLM pretraining. We first identify instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes and propose algorithmic modifications including per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning strategies that eliminate loss spikes and enable stable training in these regimes. We then present a unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, and AdamW using update-RMS matching to ensure fair learning rate transfer across optimizers. As part of this analysis, we empirically evaluate the orthogonalization quality of Muon. Our experiments on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens reveal that SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at the scales we tested. Notably, at batch sizes of up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, these optimizers maintain training stability and quality while AdamW degrades. To enable efficient training at large scale, we introduce a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM. Our implementation balances memory and hides communication while avoiding approximations to the optimizer computations, thus retaining their convergence benefits. Additionally, we identify and build specific system-level improvements to further accelerate our layer-wise implementation. To support the research community, we release a codebase that contains emerging algorithms for optimization: https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Emerging-Optimizers

</details>


### [242] [SevDiff: Severity-Conditioned Diffusion for Long-Tail Conflict Trajectory Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20549)
*Eni Solomon Laughter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SevDiff is a severity-conditioned diffusion model that takes a target TTC value as a scalar input and generates V2V interaction trajectories whose realized TTC matches the target with high precision, enabling controllable synthesis of conflict events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address severe data imbalance in ADAS evaluation by enabling controllable generation of rare conflict events; existing methods condition on scene-level properties but cannot enforce a specific TTC target.

Method: Propose SevDiff, a diffusion probabilistic model conditioned on a scalar target TTC. Train on 468 interaction windows from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (~1k vehicles, ~822k observations after smoothing). Generate paired vehicle trajectories with a hit-rate metric assessing TTC target adherence. Analyze physical plausibility across 12 kinematic features (out-of-range rate, negative values).

Result: Achieves 100% hit-rate within ±0.5s for TTC targets 0.5–1.5s; 97–99% for 2.0–2.5s; 39% at 5.0s. Generated kinematics are plausible: max out-of-range rate 4.7% across 12 features; no negative speed/gap values in >96.5% of samples. Hit-rate pattern aligns with conditioning signal strength relative to training prior.

Conclusion: SevDiff provides precise, controllable generation of conflict severity in vehicle interactions, enabling robust evaluation of ADAS under rare but critical events; its conditioning behavior offers a interpretable precision metric rather than a binary pass/fail.

Abstract: Trajectory datasets used in ADAS evaluation are heavily biased toward routine driving; genuine vehicle-to-vehicle conflict events are rare, and the rarer the event, the higher the cost when an ADAS system fails to handle it. Existing generative approaches address this imbalance by conditioning on scene-level properties - spatial goals, agent structure, or natural-language adversarial objectives - but none can accept a target Time-to-Collision (TTC) value as input and be held to producing it within a measurable error. This paper introduces SevDiff, a severity-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that accepts a requested minimum TTC value as a scalar conditioning signal and generates paired vehicle interaction trajectories whose realized conflict severity matches the request, evaluated through a hit-rate metric. Trained on 468 interaction windows extracted from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations after smoothing), SevDiff achieves 100% hit-rate within +/-0.5 s for TTC targets of 0.5-1.5 s and 97-99% at 2.0-2.5 s, with graceful degradation to 39% at TTC = 5.0 s. Generated kinematic features are physically plausible, with a maximum out-of-range rate of 4.7% across 12 features and no negative speed or gap values in more than 96.5% of samples. The hit-rate degradation pattern is physically interpretable as the strength of the conditioning signal relative to the training prior, making it a precision characterization of the generator rather than a pass/fail result.

</details>


### [243] [Beyond SBDD: Geometric Deep Learning in Polypharmacology and Multi-target Drug Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20550)
*Tianming Han,Zhijie Pan,Wenchi Ge,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Geometric deep learning (GDL) is proposed as a unifying, structure-driven framework for rational polypharmacology, with a survey of architectures and applications for multi-target drug design and generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The traditional one-drug-one-target approach is insufficient for multifactorial diseases due to compensatory pathways and resistance; rational, geometry-aware multi-target design remains computationally challenging.

Method: Systematic survey of GDL architectures (invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models) on non-Euclidean molecular data; analysis along three dimensions: shared binding pockets via geometric embeddings, multi-target bioactivity via heterogeneous graph fusion, and de novo dual-target ligand generation; evaluation of diffusion-based, structure-conditioned generative algorithms with reinforcement learning; emphasis on multimodal omics integration and geometric benchmarking infrastructures.

Result: Synthesizes recent methodological advances and presents a paradigm shift from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacology; provides a structured guide for navigating next-generation structure-based drug design for multi-target therapeutics.

Conclusion: Geometric deep learning can integrate diverse geometric and omics data to enable rational, polypharmacological molecular design; future work should advance structure-conditioned generative models, robust validation on benchmarking tasks, and standardized evaluation pipelines.

Abstract: The traditional "one drug, one target" paradigm of structure-based drug design (SBDD) frequently proves inadequate for treating multifactorial diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders, owing to compensatory signaling pathways and the emergence of drug resistance. While polypharmacology offers a synergistic therapeutic strategy, the rational design of ligands capable of simultaneously satisfying the geometric constraints imposed by multiple targets remains a major computational bottleneck. This review positions geometric deep learning (GDL) as a powerful integrative approach to overcome these limitations. We systematically survey GDL architectures ranging from invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models that harness non-Euclidean molecular data to capture intrinsic three-dimensional (3D) structural interdependencies. We critically analyze GDL applications across three core dimensions, including the characterization of shared binding pockets via geometric embeddings, multi-target bioactivity prediction through heterogeneous graph fusion, and de novo generation of dual-target ligands. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging structure-conditioned generative algorithms that integrate diffusion models with reinforcement learning to autonomously resolve complex geometric conflicts between competing binding sites. Furthermore, we evaluate the pivotal role of multimodal omics integration and specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures in validating these models. By synthesizing these methodological advances, this review elucidates the paradigm shift in drug discovery from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, thereby providing a clear, structured guide for navigating the complexities of next-generation therapeutics.

</details>


### [244] [SenCos-GEM: SENet-Calibrated and Law-of-Cosines-Constrained Geometry-Enhanced Molecular Representation for Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20551)
*Tianming Han,Li Zhang,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SenCos-GEM introduces an explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework for 3D GNNs, using physics-guided geometric consistency (law of cosines), SE-based adapters, and a FiLM+SENet dual-modulation head, achieving state-of-the-art performance on 3D-sensitive MoleculeNet tasks and improved robustness to conformational perturbations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SSL/3D-GNN methods for molecular property prediction lack explicit physical constraints, are sensitive to geometric noise from coarse force fields, and ignore dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, leading to potential forgetting and negative transfer.

Method: Propose SenCos-GEM with (1) a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to produce high-fidelity, invariant 3D priors; (2) lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules as task-specific adapters; (3) a dual-modulation prediction head combining Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet for dynamic feature recalibration.

Result: Demonstrates competitive performance across MoleculeNet classification/regression tasks; achieves new SOTA on 3D conformation-sensitive tasks (FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, QM9) with relative RMSE reductions of 12.9%, 5.3%, and MAE reduction of 8.2%; improved discrimination of stereoisomers and conformational perturbations, indicating robust spatial modeling.

Conclusion: SenCos-GEM represents a significant advance in molecular property prediction by tightly integrating physics-informed geometry constraints with dynamic adaptation mechanisms, yielding robust 3D-aware representations and improved predictive accuracy.

Abstract: Effective molecular representation learning is crucial for accurate molecular property prediction. Recently, numerous self-supervised learning (SSL) approaches leveraging 3D GNNs have been developed to capture comprehensive 3D structural information for drug discovery. However, existing methods lack explicit physical constraints and are highly susceptible to geometric noise induced by coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training.Furthermore, they overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. To address these limitations, we introduce SenCos-GEM, a novel explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that incorporates SENet-calibrated and law-of-cosines-constrained enhancements. SenCos-GEM employs a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity and mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors. In addition, lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules are integrated into the backbone as task-specific adapters, while a dual-modulation prediction head combines Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms to enable dynamic feature recalibration. SenCos-GEM demonstrates highly competitive performance across diverse classification and regression tasks on MoleculeNet benchmark, establishing new state-of-the-art results specifically on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks, such as FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9, achieving relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE), 5.3% (RMSE), and 8.2% (MAE), respectively. Moreover, our model exhibits superior capability in distinguishing stereoisomers and discriminating conformational perturbations, underscoring its robust spatial modeling performance. Collectively, SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction.

</details>


### [245] [Thermodynamic Weight Decay: Exploring Grokking Acceleration via Attention Specific Heat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20552)
*Chitraansh Pandey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces CvAdamW, an online adaptive weight-decay method that uses the variance of attention logits (treated as a specific heat Cv) to detect a phase transition preceding grokking; adapts training to accelerate generalization within a fixed budget; demonstrates grokking on modular addition (a+b mod 97) where baselines fail, with a scale-invariant reformulation that reduces hyperparameter dependence; validated across 10 seeds with favorable statistics; code and data are public.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grokking—delayed generalization long after memorization—occurs unpredictably and wastes compute. By linking attention thermodynamics to phase transitions and providing a proportional intervention (dynamic weight decay), the work aims to detect precursors of impending generalization and reliably accelerate it within a fixed compute budget.

Method: Treat attention-logit variance as a thermodynamic specific heat Cv. Monitor Cv online; when a peak indicating a phase transition is detected, inject energy by dynamically scaling weight decay (CvAdamW). Address three failure modes (initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, slingshot blinding) with a memorization gate and an EMA-based shock absorber. Introduce a scale-invariant z-score reformulation to remove task-specific hyperparameters. Evaluate on a+b mod 97, using paired seeds (10 seeds) and 4000-epoch budgets; compare with baseline; report paired statistics (p-values, effect sizes, bootstrap CIs).

Result: Cv peaks before grokking; CvAdamW enables grokking at epoch 2802 within a 4000-epoch budget where baseline fails. Cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen’s d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8/10 seeds. Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds on this task. Code and data are public.

Conclusion: Neural networks exhibit precursors to impending generalization transitions detectable via a thermodynamics-inspired signal. A proportional, physics-motivated intervention (CvAdamW) can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget, with results replicated across seeds and supported by statistical analysis.

Abstract: Grokking -- the delayed generalization of neural networks long after they have memorized their training data -- wastes thousands of training epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. Building on the recent result that Transformer attention is formally isomorphic to a thermodynamic system, we treat the variance of attention logits as a specific heat Cv and show that its peak reliably precedes the generalization transition. We introduce CvAdamW, a drop-in AdamW variant that monitors Cv online and injects thermal energy by dynamically scaling weight decay when a phase transition is detected. Through a strictly iterative development process we identify three failure modes -- initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, and slingshot blinding -- and resolve them with a memorization gate and an exponential-moving-average shock absorber. On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW enables grokking at epoch 2802 in a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. We further propose a scale-invariant z-score reformulation that removes task-specific hyperparameters, and evaluate it across 10 paired seeds. A paired analysis shows the cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds; on this single task Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds. Our results indicate that neural networks may expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions, and that a physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget. Code and data are public.

</details>


### [246] [Double-Scoring: Reliable Extraction of Strong Lottery Tickets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20555)
*Bryce A. Christopherson,Jack Baretz,Darian Colgrove,Salah Dandan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Double-scoring augments edge-popup with an enlarged score space to enable stronger lottery-ticket extraction without layerwise sparsity tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Strong lottery tickets are theoretically possible in overparameterized random networks, but extracting them reliably is hindered by the need to search sparsity at each layer; a more flexible, robust method is needed.

Method: Introduce double-scoring: optimize over augmented score tensors instead of performing layerwise sparsity search. Prove that fixed-density masks in augmented space can realize all original-coordinate masks; interpret the approach as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. Conduct controlled experiments comparing against fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines and against rewound sparse-training topologies, with ablations to understand the source of gains.

Result: Significant improvements in strong-ticket extraction over baselines; better performance and robustness than rewound sparse-training and pruning-at-initialization; reduced sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters; gains attributed to augmented score-space competition rather than merely more trainable scores.

Conclusion: Augmented score-space (double-scoring) provides a more reliable and effective mechanism for extracting strong lottery tickets, clarifying the role of sparsity search and enabling robust, initialization-free sparse subnetworks.

Abstract: The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that large random neural networks contain sparse subnetworks that can match the performance of dense models after comparable training. A stronger version asserts that sufficiently overparameterized random networks contain subnetworks that are already accurate before any weight training. Existing theory establishes that such strong lottery tickets exist, but reliable extraction remains difficult. We revisit edge-popup, a frozen-weight score-training method for extracting strong tickets, and identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck. We introduce double-scoring, an augmented score-space parameterization that replaces a layerwise sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors. We prove that fixed-density masking in an augmented score space preserves access to all original-coordinate masks, and we show that the resulting method can be interpreted as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. In controlled experiments, double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines, improves on the performance of rewound sparse-training topologies, and exhibits markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations show that the gain is not merely due to additional trainable score parameters, but is tied to the augmented score-space competition that induces the effective original sparsity.

</details>


### [247] [Monkey King Bang: A Unified Scientific Multimodal Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20557)
*Hesen Chen,Xinyu Su,Xiaomeng Yang,Yuetan Lin,Zixiong Yang,Junyi An,Fenglei Cao,Yifeng Jiao,Yunqi Zhang,Yuan Cheng,Zhiyu Tan,Hao Li,Libo Wu,Yuan Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A unified multimodal model (MKB) for cross-domain scientific understanding and generation, using a shared Transformer backbone with modality-tailored encoders/decoders; spans six domains; native outputs; two-stage modality-then-language training; competitive benchmarks and high-fidelity outputs; maintains backbone capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of domain-specific or text-token‑only scientific AI by enabling joint understanding, reasoning, and native-output generation across diverse scientific modalities with a single shared backbone.

Method: A modular architecture with a shared Transformer backbone and modality-specific encoders, adapters, and decoders. Six domains: DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, and medical images. Native modalities include biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, and segmentation masks. Training uses a two-stage curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality components to the frozen backbone; Stage 2 consolidates with the language backbone using mixed scientific/general corpora.

Result: MKB achieves competitive performance on biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely preserves the general capabilities of the Qwen3-VL backbone.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates feasibility of a shared-backbone, modality-tailored architecture for cross-domain scientific multimodal reasoning and generation, offering a promising foundation for future cross-domain Science AI.

Abstract: Scientific discovery is increasingly shifting from isolated disciplines to multi-domain reasoning, and AI for science faces a similar transition. Existing systems are either specialised for individual domains or unify scientific data mainly through text tokenisation and prompt-based interfaces, limiting their ability to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, and support joint understanding, reasoning, and generation across scientific domains. We introduce MKB, a unified scientific multimodal model for both understanding and generation, built around a shared Transformer backbone and modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders. MKB covers six scientific branches, including DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, and medical images, and supports native outputs such as biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, and segmentation masks. Training follows a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with the frozen backbone, and Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora. Experiments show that MKB achieves competitive scientific understanding across biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed paradigm, suggesting that shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components can provide a promising foundation for future cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration. The model and code are publicly available at https://github.com/Shanghai-Academy-of-AI-For-Science/MKB and https://huggingface.co/sais-org/MKB.

</details>


### [248] [StabilityBench: Benchmarking Instability in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20558)
*Emma Kondrup,Zachary Yang,Anne Imouza,Reihaneh Rabbany*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: StabilityBench turns single-turn benchmarks into multi-turn interactions with realistic user simulations to reveal instability in LLMs; StabilityBench-Mini offers a scalable variant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static, single-turn benchmarks fail to capture real-world conversational variability and high-stakes risks in AI assistants, necessitating a principled, model-agnostic evaluation operator.

Method: Introduce StabilityBench that converts benchmarks into multi-turn histories and injects demographic proxy or sycophantic user simulations while preserving task intent; evaluate across four benchmarks and nine LLMs; propose StabilityBench-Mini as a cost-efficient, size-preserving variant.

Result: LLM performance degrades under the injected interactions, with substantial drops on three of four benchmarks, highlighting the limitations of static evaluations.

Conclusion: Static benchmarks are insufficient for real-world assessment; StabilityBench and StabilityBench-Mini provide practical tools for more realistic, robust evaluation across domains.

Abstract: AI Assistants are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, such as healthcare or government services. Yet their real-world behavior remains poorly understood due to strong context dependence. Current evaluation protocols follow a defense-in-depth paradigm with compounding layers of safeguards, ranging from traditional benchmarks to live or adversarial testing. Such benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, limiting their ability to capture real-world variability in conversational settings. We propose StabilityBench, a principled, general and model-agnostic benchmark operator that transforms single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn interaction histories. StabilityBench augments existing benchmarks by injecting realistic user simulations, through demographic proxies or sycophantic baits, while preserving original task intent. We apply StabilityBench to four benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, health question-answering and safety, and evaluate nine large language models under these conditions. Our results show that model performance is consistently unstable under these injections, with considerable performance degradations on three out of four benchmarks studied. These highlight important limitations of static evaluations and motivate more realistic evaluation settings. To this end, we propose StabilityBench-Mini: a size-preserving variant of StabilityBench that samples across diversification axes, enabling more realistic evaluation without increasing costs.

</details>


### [249] [Joint Utilization of Geospatial and census proxies for Autoencoder-Assisted Downscaling (JUGAAD) of socioeconomic indicators in India](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20559)
*Aditya Dutt,Paul Gader,Aditya Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JuGAAD is a deep-learning downscaling framework that fuses census and survey data with autoencoder latent representations to predict high-resolution poverty and food security indicators in India, validated against district NSSO data with strong accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome scale mismatch between coarse, infrequent survey indicators and fine-grained census/geospatial data, enabling high-resolution socioeconomic mapping for policy decisions in developing countries.

Method: A three-step process: (1) aggregate census and geospatial data into intermediate village-cluster tessellations to smooth noise and handle boundary changes; (2) use an autoencoder to compress high-dimensional NSSO data into a low-dimensional latent representation; (3) train a regression model to map upscaled census and geospatial features to the latent space, then apply the learned mapping to fine-grained census data to generate high-resolution predictions; validation is performed by comparing predictions against ground-truth district NSSO indicators.

Result: The framework yields high-resolution socioeconomic predictions that align closely with district-level NSSO indicators, demonstrating strong predictive accuracy at finer scales than the original survey data.

Conclusion: JuGAAD demonstrates a viable path for cross-scale socio-economic downscaling, enabling more granular monitoring of poverty and food security; the approach holds potential for generalization to similar settings with comparable data ecosystems and could inform policy planning at sub-district levels.

Abstract: Monitoring poverty and food security indicators is imperative for addressing socioeconomic challenges in developing nations. A limitation is mismatches in scale between data sources: census data provide geographic coverage, while socioeconomic indicators are derived from infrequently conducted surveys at coarse resolutions, posing a methodological challenge. This study introduces a deep learning framework, JuGAAD, using Indian census and survey data from 2001 and 2011 as a case study. We employ a three-step process: census and geospatial data are averaged into intermediate village-cluster-scale tessellations to reduce noise and regularize administrative boundary changes; an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data into a low-dimensional latent representation; and a regression model maps upscaled census and geospatial data to this representation. This function is applied to fine-grained census data to generate high-resolution predictions, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators. Results confirm the methodology predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine scales with strong accuracy.

</details>


### [250] [Chronofy: A Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture for Information Validity in Time-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20560)
*Muntaser Syed,Marius Silaghi,Sheikh Abujar,Sharun Akter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Chronofy introduces a three-layer neuro-symbolic Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) to embed temporal validity into RAG, reducing temporal hallucination and enabling principled data re-acquisition; validated on temporal KG forecasting and temporal QA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporal provenance of retrieved facts matters in RAG, but existing systems treat all retrieved knowledge as equally valid, leading to temporal hallucination when older or outdated facts influence outputs.

Method: Layer 1: temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings to structurally separate fact age; Layer 2: learnable exponential decay in graph-based retrieval with decay coefficients β_j anchored by Bayesian decision theory (≈ 2× latent mean-reversion rate); Layer 3: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to assess temporal validity of retrieved knowledge and enforce the possibilistic weakest-link bound on final output confidence.

Result: Chronofy improves retrieval precision and reduces temporal hallucination on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks and the TimE temporal QA benchmark; the framework enables principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient and shows robustness across domain-specific sensitivity analyses.

Conclusion: Explicit modeling of temporal decay across representation, retrieval, and reasoning enhances temporal grounding in RAG systems and provides a principled mechanism to manage outdated information and trigger data re-acquisition.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems retrieve and integrate external knowledge to ground large language model (LLM) outputs. However, current RAG architectures treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of temporal provenance, leading to temporal hallucination, where plausible but obsolete facts corrupt the output. A clinical lab reading from yesterday is actionable; the same reading from six months ago is noise. We present Chronofy, a three-layer neuro-symbolic framework implementing the Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) that embeds temporal validity directly into the representation, retrieval, and reasoning layers of RAG systems. Layer 1 reserves a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings to make fact age structurally irremovable from the representation. Layer 2 integrates learnable exponential decay functions into graph-based retrieval, where the decay coefficient $β_j$ is grounded in Bayesian decision theory as an approximation of twice the latent process mean-reversion rate. Layer 3 applies Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions to evaluate the temporal validity of retrieved knowledge, not LLM output confidence, and enforces the possibilistic weakest-link principle to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain. We evaluate Chronofy on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and a domain-specific sensitivity analysis, demonstrating that explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

</details>


### [251] [CT-Merging: Consensus Directions and Task-Level Scaling for LoRA Adapter Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20561)
*Keumseo Ryum,Joonhyuk Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CT-Merging is a LoRA-aware model-merging algorithm that constructs a common subspace from task SVDs and uses per-task RMS coefficient scales to form a unified multi-task adapter, improving accuracy over prior SVD-based merging methods on DC-Merge benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the mismatch between inherited transfer coefficients on a fixed merged basis and the task-induced updates, and to reduce reliance on raw SVD magnitudes while enabling efficient deployment of a single multi-task adapter.

Method: Iteratively derive a common basis by leveraging repeated support across task SVD subspaces; compute consensus directions via average task subspace projectors; assign task-level RMS coefficient scales to the final update, instead of using the raw task SVD magnitudes.

Result: CT-Merging achieves higher average normalized accuracy on the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark than state-of-the-art merging methods; it also outperforms DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

Conclusion: CT-Merging provides more accurate and robust multi-task adapters by aligning shared directions with consensus subspaces and scaling task contributions, outperforming existing SVD-based merging approaches across evaluated ViT backbones.

Abstract: LoRA adapters provide an efficient way to specialize a pretrained model for many downstream tasks, but deploying one adapter per task requires adapter storage and task selection at inference time. Model merging addresses this issue by combining independently trained adapters into one multi-task adapter. Recent SVD-based LoRA merging methods mainly focus on constructing shared or task specific directions, while the coefficients assigned to the final directions are often directly from the original task SVD. On a fixed merged basis, inherited coefficients preserve component order with high rank correlation, yet their magnitudes differ substantially from the coefficients induced by the task updates. To address this mismatch, we propose CT-Merging, a LoRA-aware merging algorithm that estimates consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales in the final update. CT-Merging uses repeated support across task SVD subspaces to construct the common basis, while reducing reliance on rank wise SVD magnitudes after direction construction. On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy compared to state-of-the-art merging methods and further improves over DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

</details>


### [252] [AI-Driven Surrogate Models for Predicting Electrode-Scale Discharge Behavior in Lithium-Ion Batteries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20577)
*Mengda Xing,Jean-Marie Lagniez,Alejandro Franco*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Swin3D Transformer–based surrogate predicts spatiotemporal LIB discharge dynamics from volumetric data, using Gaussian Positional Encoding and a Temporal Encoding module; it outperforms point-cloud baselines and offers orders-of-magnitude speedups for high-throughput battery design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics-based LIB electrode-scale simulations are extremely costly; there is a need for accurate, scalable surrogates that can capture complex microstructural geometry and nonlinear time evolution to accelerate design and optimization.

Method: Develop a Swin3D Transformer–based surrogate pipeline. Introduce Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE) to encode electrode microstructure geometry, and a dedicated Temporal Encoding module to handle nonlinear time evolution. Train on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset and compare against state-of-the-art point-cloud baselines for spatiotemporal prediction.

Result: The approach achieves higher prediction accuracy than baselines and reduces computational overhead by orders of magnitude, enabling scalable high-throughput simulations.

Conclusion: Gaussian positional embedding and temporal encoding within a Swin3D framework yield an effective and efficient surrogate for LIB discharge dynamics, supporting rapid battery design and optimization.
