Abstract: Physics-based simulations are essential for understanding the electrode-scale discharge behavior of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) but suffer from prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce a novel deep learning surrogate pipeline based on the Swin3D Transformer to predict spatiotemporal discharge dynamics directly from volumetric data. Our approach integrates two key innovations: Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE), which enhances spatial feature representation by adapting to the complex geometry of electrode microstructures, and a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear timeseries evolution. Experimental validation on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset demonstrates that our pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method reduces the computational overhead by orders of magnitude, providing a scalable and efficient framework for high-throughput battery design and optimization.

</details>


### [253] [Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21488)
*Gil Lifshits,Igal Bilik,Gilad Katz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MAPS introduces a Master-Agent Proto-plan System where a central Master emits a compact proto-plan embedding used by decentralized workers to coordinate autonomous vehicles; demonstrated on HighwayEnv across 72 intersection configurations with improved efficiency and strong zero-shot generalization (94% success from 3 to 5 agents).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, and rigid agent designs in MARL for unsignalized intersections; need scalable, generalizable coordination.

Method: Hierarchical DRL: Master agent outputs continuous proto-plan embedding; Worker agents fuse embedding with local observations to perform control; training decouples strategic intent from execution; evaluated in HighwayEnv.

Result: Collision-free navigation, reduced average travel time; outperforms baselines; proto-plans show robustness; 94% zero-shot generalization to five-agent scenarios.

Conclusion: Proto-plan-based hierarchical learning is a promising framework for coordinating multiple AVs; enables scalable coordination and generalization across agent counts.

Abstract: Coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections remains a critical challenge for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems, which typically struggle with combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, or rigid agent designs. We propose Master-Agent Proto-plan System (MAPS), a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture in which a centralized Master agent generates a compact, continuous embedding, denoted as proto-plan, that encodes a global coordination strategy. Decentralized Worker agents integrate this embedding with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution and enabling independent optimization of each module.
  As a proof-of-concept evaluation of this coordination mechanism, we test MAPS across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv. MAPS achieves collision-free navigation while significantly reducing average travel time, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The learned proto-plans further exhibit robust generalization: a system trained with three agents achieves a 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot to five-agent scenarios, confirming that proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination.

</details>


### [254] [Fisher Widths: Local Learning Geometry and Anisotropic Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20578)
*Vu Khac Ky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces primal Fisher width w_G and inverse-Fisher width w_{G^{-1}}, analyzes their complementary roles in learning and recovery on statistical manifolds, proves a sharp product bound w_G(T) w_{G^{-1}}(T) ≥ w(T)^2, and provides two-sided estimates for statistical dimension and support-sensitive recovery under Fisher geometry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds through Fisher-based geometries, bridging learning and sparse recovery under Fisher regularity and anisotropic Gaussian measurements.

Method: Define w_G(T)=w(G^{1/2}T) and w_{G^{-1}}(T)=w(G^{-1/2}T); study Fisher balls and their scales; derive learning bounds for Fisher-regular losses (w_G(H_r)/√n on small Fisher balls); analyze recovery with anisotropic Gaussian measurements via inverse Fisher width; obtain two-sided estimates for statistical dimension and establish support-sensitive recovery with curvature-based ordering; prove product inequality w_G(T) w_{G^{-1}}(T) ≥ w(T)^2.

Result: Learning side: the scale w_G(H_r)/√n is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls for Fisher-regular losses. Recovery side: inverse-Fisher width yields a two-sided bound for the statistical dimension, with support-sensitive recovery and a natural ordering of supports by curvature. Global relation: w_G(T) w_{G^{-1}}(T) ≥ w(T)^2 on common compact coordinate sets, showing Fisher anisotropy can shift, but not reduce, complexity on both geometries.

Conclusion: Fisher anisotropy mediates complexity transfer between primal and inverse geometries without eliminating Euclidean-scale difficulty; the framework unifies learning and recovery on statistical manifolds and clarifies how curvature and measurement anisotropy shape width-based complexity.

Abstract: We study Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds through a pair of functionals: the primal Fisher width $w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T)$, induced by the Fisher metric, and the inverse-Fisher width $w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T)$, induced by the inverse Fisher metric. The two widths play complementary statistical roles.
  On the learning side, the Fisher width measures the size of local parameter fluctuations in the geometry induced by the Fisher information. For Fisher-regular losses, we prove that the scale \(w_G(H_r)/\sqrt n\) is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls.
  On the recovery side, the inverse-Fisher width captures the effect of anisotropic Gaussian measurements whose covariance is determined by the inverse Fisher information. For sparse recovery, the resulting geometry depends not only on sparsity but also on the position of the active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum. We obtain a two-sided estimate for the corresponding statistical dimension, together with support-sensitive recovery estimates and a natural ordering of supports with different curvature profiles.
  Finally, we establish a sharp relation between the primal and inverse-Fisher widths. On any common compact coordinate set $T$, they satisfy \[ w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T)\geq w(T)^2. \] Thus, Fisher anisotropy may transfer complexity from one geometry to the other, but cannot reduce both widths relative to the Euclidean scale.

</details>


### [255] [Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20582)
*Frederik Hauke,Patrick Wienholt,Christiane Kuhl,Dyke Ferber,Jakob Nikolas Kather,Sven Nebelung,Daniel Truhn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MC dropout yields an epistemic uncertainty signal for a multi-task chest X-ray classifier, improving error-detection AUROC (0.74→0.77) and reducing confident misdiagnoses when presented as a binary error-risk flag; the benefit depends on how uncertainty is communicated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical image ML often lacks reliable confidence estimates, hindering use in ambiguous/atypical cases; epistemic uncertainty can flag potential errors to support decision-making.

Method: Apply Monte Carlo dropout to a multi-task chest radiograph classifier (eight findings; 137,593 training images). Evaluate uncertainty as a signal of generalisation across training-set scales and test its utility in downstream decision support via a 2x2 factorial experiment.

Result: Adding the uncertainty signal raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 (ΔAUROC = +0.023, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]). In a 2x2 factorial test, a decision-support agent used the uncertainty only as a binary error-risk flag, reducing confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%.

Conclusion: Epistemic uncertainty estimation provides decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its practical value depends on how uncertainty is communicated to downstream agents.

Abstract: Machine learning models for medical image analysis typically lack a reliable measure of confidence, limiting their use in ambiguous or atypical cases. Here we show that Monte Carlo dropout, applied to a multi-task chest-radiograph classifier (eight thoracic findings, 137,593 training images), provides an epistemic uncertainty signal that tracks generalisation across training-set scales and flags confident yet error-prone predictions. Adding this signal to the point prediction raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 ($Δ$AUROC +0.023, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]). In a controlled 2x2 factorial experiment, a clinical-decision-support agent exploited this uncertainty only when it was delivered as a binary error-risk flag rather than as raw scores, cutting confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%. Epistemic uncertainty estimation thus carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its value for downstream agents depends on how it is communicated.

</details>


### [256] [Exact ReLU realization of affine one-dimensional refinement iterates via residual memory and offset frames](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20586)
*Boldsaikhan Bolorkhuu,Tsogtgerel Gantumur*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Finite affine refinements with vector-valued data admit exact fixed-width ReLU realizations of depth O(n) for M≥3; a residual memory controller enables backward replay of the affine forcing, with extensions to forcing terms and various recursive constructions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Realize affine refinement operators efficiently in ReLU networks with provable depth bounds and exactness, handling vector-valued data and piecewise-linear forcing.

Method: Introduce a residual memory controller that converts noninvertible residual dynamics into an injective skew-product, enabling exact backward replay for Horner-type evaluation of the forcing sum. Use offset frames to separate forcing atoms from residual seams, and exploit complementary loop readouts for exact state recovery. Address branch-selection ambiguity where the affine state vanishes. For M≥3, apply to arbitrary compactly supported CPL forcing; for M=2, apply to ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. Extend stage-dependency to forcing terms lying in a fixed finite-dimensional CPL span and obtain linear-depth upgrades for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert-/Morton-type recursive constructions.

Result: Constructive proof that every finite affine iterate W^nγ has an exact fixed-width ReLU realization with depth O(n) when M≥3. For M≥3, holds for arbitrary compactly supported CPL forcing; for M=2, seam-separated forcing. Also provides a stage-dependent extension for forcing in a fixed finite-dimensional CPL span and yields linear-depth upgrades for several recursive constructions (open-curve, finite-state, Hilbert- and Morton-type).

Conclusion: The paper delivers a practical, provably efficient ReLU realization framework for vector-valued affine refinements, introducing a residual memory controller to enable exact backward replay and offering broad applicability to forcing terms and multiple recursive architectures.

Abstract: We study vector-valued affine refinement operators of the form [
(Wγ)(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} A_jγ(Mt-j)+B(t), ]
with finitely supported matrix mask and compactly supported continuous piecewise linear input and forcing data. Building on the homogeneous realization theorem for (B\equiv 0), we prove that, for (M\ge 3), every finite affine iterate (W^nγ) admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization whose depth is (O(n)).
  The main new ingredient is a residual memory controller. It replaces the noninvertible residual dynamics by an injective skew-product and permits exact backward replay of the residual states required by a Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Offset frames align the forcing atoms away from residual seams, allowing complementary loop readouts to recover their values exactly. The remaining branch-selection ambiguity occurs only where the accumulated affine state has already vanished.
  For (M\ge 3), the result applies to arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing terms. For (M=2), the same construction applies to ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. We also prove a stage-dependent extension for forcing terms in a fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear span and record the resulting linear-depth upgrade for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.

</details>


### [257] [Detecting Neural Network Failures through Spectral Analysis of Internal Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20590)
*Arunan J*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Spectral drift in internal activations reveals failure signals invisible at the output; a lightweight detector (SDNN) uses multi-scale spectral features to detect misclassifications with strong AUROC gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Output confidence alone is insufficient for reliability; internal spectral dynamics offer diagnostic, early failure indicators within DNNs.

Method: Compute spectral features across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments; train a lightweight detector with curriculum learning over progressively harder distributions (natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, adversarial perturbations); overhead ~5% parameters.

Result: On CIFAR-10, SDNN achieves 79.0 ± 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially surpassing confidence-based baselines (MaxSoftmax 50.5%, Energy Score 52.9%) by ~25–30 percentage points. Ablations show wavelet decomposition and statistical features contribute consistently; STFT's role is inconclusive.

Conclusion: Spectral analysis of internal activations is a promising avenue for neural network reliability, yielding diagnostic information not captured by output-based approaches and warranting further exploration of spectral detectors in NN safety and reliability.

Abstract: Neural network misclassifications exhibit characteristic spectral instability in internal activations that is invisible at the output layer. This phenomenon is identified and formalized as Spectral Drift -- the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations -- with empirical validation showing that failures exhibit significantly higher drift than correct predictions (1.9% increase, p<0.001). This spectral signature emerges during internal processing but becomes masked in final outputs, explaining why confidence-based detection methods struggle.
  This work introduces Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), a framework that monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features. A lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) learns to identify failure-indicative patterns via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.
  Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that SDNN achieves 79.0 +/- 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming confidence-based baselines including MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by approximately 25-30 percentage points. Ablation studies reveal that wavelet decomposition and statistical features make consistent contributions, while STFT's role remains unclear. This work establishes spectral analysis of internal activations as a promising direction for neural network reliability, revealing diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches.

</details>


### [258] [STeMP: Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20592)
*Jan Linnenbrink,Jakub Nowosad,Marvin Ludwig,Anna Frederike Jablotschkin,Fabian Schumacher,Teja Kattenborn,Hanna Meyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces STeMP, a standardized protocol for transparent reporting of spatio-temporal ML modelling, with three sections (Overview, Model, Prediction) and an accompanying R-package and web app to fill the protocol; aims to improve trust, comparability, and guide modelling decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatio-temporal ML models are highly sensitive to training data characteristics and cross-validation choices, and there is currently a lack of standardized reporting protocols, hindering transparency and comparability.

Method: Proposal of the Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol (STeMP) with a three-section structure: Overview (metadata), Model (predictors, evaluation, software), and Prediction. Hosted on GitHub; implemented as an R-package with a web application to fill the protocol manually or semi-automatically from modelling objects; includes warnings for common pitfalls and supports reviewer assessment.

Result: Definition and availability of the STeMP protocol; an R-package and web app to facilitate protocol adoption and automated checks; community-driven via GitHub to incorporate contributions and feedback.

Conclusion: STeMP fills a critical gap in spatio-temporal modelling reporting, promoting transparency, reproducibility, and cross-study comparability, and providing practical guidance during modelling and review.

Abstract: Spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling is an important tool in environmental research. However, machine-learning models are highly sensitive to both the characteristics of the training data, such as its distribution, and methodological choices, including the cross-validation strategy. Each decision has impact and implications on the model itself as well as the estimation of the model quality and applicability for certain purposes. Taking into account the large role of machine-learning based maps of the environment in science and their transfer into practice, transparent reporting of spatio-temporal models, ideally using standardized model protocols, is essential to enable trust, transparency and comparability. However, such protocols are currently lacking for spatio-temporal modelling.
  We propose STeMP (Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol) to fill this gap by serving two purposes: standardized reporting to understand the model functioning as well as providing guidance during the modelling process by pointing at critical decisions and parameters. The protocol is structured in three sections: Overview, Model and Prediction. The Overview section contains metadata, while the Model and Prediction sections go into detail, describing predictors, evaluation and software, and further relevant elements of the modelling workflow.
  The protocol definition is hosted on GitHub and accompanied by an R-package (https://github.com/LOEK-RS/STeMP). The R-package contains a web application that can be used to fill the protocol either manually or in a semi-automated way from provided modelling objects. Warnings are returned from the protocol when common pitfalls are encountered, which may help authors as a guide through the modelling process but also support reviewers in the assessment of modelling studies. Via GitHub, incorporation of contributions and feedback from the community is encouraged.

</details>


### [259] [When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20594)
*Tong Zhang,Junhao Hu,Yun Peng,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Four empirical findings link training budget, weight sharing, and curricula to the emergent algorithm in weight-tied looped transformers, with a computable frontier v and a principled halting rule. Architecture priors, not expressivity, select the algorithm; circuit-complexity walls mispredict learnability on group problems; warm-starting and curricula transfer algorithms across seeds, while input schedules enforcing seriality hinder performance. A convergence-time metric tau(n,i) causalizes dynamics and aids OOD prediction; results replicate on an easy-to-hard benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine when a weight-tied looped transformer implements a concrete algorithm and how training budget, architecture, and curricula shape emergent computation on structured tasks (group word problems).

Method: Controlled experiments with a weight-tied looped transformer (T repetitions), varying budget, depth, and sharing; introduce convergence-time tau(n,i) and damage cones to causally test dynamics; seed across multiple trials; compare standard and operator-first curricula; evaluate both easy-to-hard benchmarks and OOD generalization.

Result: Four findings: (1) A linear computation frontier v ~ n_train/T_train; speed ≤ contract; SGD selects the frontier; test-time loops salvage late positions; halting rule T* = ceil(n/vhat). (2) Architecture priors determine the algorithm: standard-depth transformers ~ parallel scans; weight tying shifts to serial frontier; at same depth/params untied models extrapolate poorly and fail A5; (3) Walls do not align with circuit complexity; NC1-completeness costs nothing; group-order effects (S5) can block joint learning; operator-first curricula dissolve walls. (4) Mechanisms are portable, not mandated: warm-starting transfers algorithms across seeds; re-pricing speed with budgets; imposing serial input schedules defeats free training. The head instrument tau(n,i) causally tracks v via damage cones; in-distribution head measurements predict OOD fate where tail metrics fail. Replicates on public easy-to-hard benchmark.

Conclusion: Emergent algorithms in weight-tied looped transformers are governed by training budget, architectural priors, and curricula. Standard metrics miss these dynamics; the convergence-time metric provides causal insight and helps predict OOD outcomes. Results generalize across seeds and benchmarks, with warm-starting as a practical transfer mechanism and curricula shaping the learnable frontier.

Abstract: When does a weight-tied looped transformer -- one block applied T times -- implement an actual algorithm? We answer with four findings from controlled populations on group word problems. (1) The budget law: free training installs a linear computation frontier, a mechanism that solves v positions per loop, whose speed is priced by the training contract: v ~ n_train/T_train (exponent 0.98 +/- 0.04, R^2=0.99), exactly unity under T=n training. SGD selects a frontier matching the minimum the contract demands; granting more test-time loops than ever trained rescues late positions at fixed input length, yielding a principled halting rule T* = ceil(n / v-hat). (2) Architecture prior, not expressivity, picks the algorithm: standard-depth transformers learn parallel scans on this family; weight tying flips the selection to the serial frontier, even when positional addressing for a log-depth scan is supplied. At matched depth and parameters, untied models extrapolate worst and fail to learn A5 at all. (3) The walls are not where circuit complexity says: NC1-completeness costs nothing (A5 generalizes fully), while group order does (S5's 120x120 operator deadlocks joint learning) -- and an operator-first curriculum dissolves the wall in every seed. (4) Mechanisms are portable, not mandatable: warm-starting across budget contracts transfers the algorithm in every seed, re-pricing its speed, while imposing seriality through the input schedule fails where free training succeeds. These results are invisible to standard instruments, which provably saturate at the fixed points trained loops converge to. We introduce a head instrument, the convergence-time scaling tau(n,i), validate it causally via damage cones whose slope reproduces v, and show in-distribution head measurements predict out-of-distribution fate where tail metrics do not. Results replicate on the public easy-to-hard benchmark.

</details>


### [260] [Are Single-Token Sparse Autoencoder Features Causally Necessary? Layer-Depth and SAE-Family Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20596)
*Seonglae Cho,Zekun Wu,Kleyton Da Costa,Rishi Kalra,Ilham Wicaksono,Adriano Koshiyama*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Single-token SAE features reveal that causal roles vary across training regimes; cross-family stability is weak and training method drives interpretability more than activation function or scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether a feature's causal role is stable across SAE families by analyzing sparse, single-token features across multiple models and SAE designs using zero-ablation.

Method: Analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families with zero-ablation at full layer depth; identify single-token features; measure their localization in decoder space; perform ablations; apply Benjamini-Hochberg significance; compare across families; assess rank recovery and activation-function controls.

Result: Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers; ablations produce significant logit reductions in 178/208 conditions; depth controls downstream cascade vs direct effects; cross-family causal differences exceed within-family effects; GemmaScope and BatchTopK are causally anchored, LlamaScope locally redundant; target token rank recovers to within 2x baseline in 96-98% after ablation; activation-function tests can reverse sign within same model; training recipe remains a residual candidate.

Conclusion: Cross-family interpretability claims depend on training methodology rather than activation function or scale.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are used to interpret and steer large language models, yet whether a feature's causal role is stable across SAE families remains untested. Single-token features that activate on one vocabulary item provide the diagnostic case where ground truth permits direct comparison. We analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families using zero-ablation at full layer depth. Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers (Layer 0 in GPT2-Small; L0-L4 in Gemma). Ablating them yields Benjamini-Hochberg-significant logit reductions in 178 of 208 full-layer conditions, with depth controlling whether damage cascades downstream or shapes the output directly. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: on the same base model, GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored, while LlamaScope features are locally redundant. The target token's rank recovers to within 2x baseline 96-98% of the time after the same ablation, and a controlled activation-function comparison reverses sign within the same model, leaving training recipe as the residual candidate. Cross-family interpretability claims are therefore sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale.

</details>


### [261] [One Round Is All You Need: Analytic Federated Learning for Task-Heterogeneous Multi-Label Medical Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20641)
*Afsaneh Mahanipour,Hana Khamfroush*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analytic federated learning for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity; uses closed-form operations to achieve rapid convergence (≤2 rounds) and outperforms state-of-the-art FedMLP while reducing communication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Task heterogeneity in FL where clients have only annotations for a subset of labels causes false-negative bias and slow convergence; gradient-based methods are inefficient; need principled closed-form approach.

Method: Three closed-form operations: 1) balanced label projection to neutralize class-imbalance across clients; 2) per-class absolute aggregation to build ridge-regression classifier per disease category from clients' sufficient statistics; 3) optional analytic pseudo-label refinement by propagating knowledge from a teacher to non-annotating clients; only two communication rounds.

Result: On ChestXray14 with four increasing missing-class configurations, achieves up to 18.44 BACC and 13.24 AUC improvements over FedMLP; reduces communication rounds.

Conclusion: The proposed analytic FL framework effectively handles task heterogeneity in multi-label medical imaging, offering fast convergence, reduced communication, and improved accuracy.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple clinical institutions to collaboratively train a shared disease classifier without centralizing patient data. In practice, however, each institution annotates only the pathologies within its area of expertise, so the federation operates under task heterogeneity: each client holds labels for a strict subset of the target disease categories while the remaining classes are entirely unobserved at that site. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail under this setting because they require hundreds of communication rounds to converge and because missing class labels introduce systematic false-negative bias that the model cannot correct without a principled mechanism. We propose an analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity. The proposed method replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations: a balanced label projection that neutralizes class-imbalance bias by normalizing positive and negative contributions to equal total mass; a per-class absolute aggregation law that independently assembles the optimal ridge-regression classifier for each disease category from the sufficient statistics uploaded by its annotating clients; and an optional analytic pseudo-label refinement round that propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to non-annotating clients. The entire procedure requires at most two communication rounds, irrespective of the degree of task heterogeneity or the number of participating clients. Experiments on ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art federated multi-label method FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points, while reducing the communication.

</details>


### [262] [Scaling Interpretable Transformers with Parity Bottleneck Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20652)
*Andrew Mack,Kraig Yuheng Tou,Mark Henry,Zhengxun Wu,Lauren Greenspan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ParityTransformer introduces a scalable, sparse, interpretable bottleneck (DPB) at each layer, enabling design-for-interpretability with competitive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Over-complete, per-layer bottlenecks for interpretability are memory/compute prohibitive; aim to make interpretable representations inherent to model computation.

Method: Replace learned over-complete bases with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary via Deep Parity Bottlenecks; implement a hierarchical sparse bottleneck using a multi-level mixture-of-experts, optimized for hardware efficiency.

Result: Par ityTransformers match or exceed post-hoc SAE performance on sparse probing tasks and outperform on feature absorption, steering, and fine-grained causal interventions; computation engages only surviving sparse features, making representations native to the forward pass.

Conclusion: This work advances towards training models with interpretable internal representations by design rather than via post-hoc probes.

Abstract: Language models are thought to exhibit the phenomenon of superposition, representing many more features than dimensions in their residual streams. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to recover such features post-hoc, but training models that are interpretable by construction has remained impractical, as a per-layer over-complete bottleneck is prohibitively expensive in both memory and compute. To overcome this issue, we introduce the ParityTransformer, a GPT-2-scale architecture whose intermediate representations are efficient and wide / sparse by design. At each layer, a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) replaces a learned over-complete basis with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary, providing a deterministic incoherence guarantee and eliminating the memory requirements that have prevented per-layer interpretable bottlenecks at scale. A DPB is a hierarchically structured sparse bottleneck which efficiently enforces sparsity using a multi-level mixture-of-experts approach: a hardware-aware implementation that closes the cost gap between activation sparse and dense training to a manageable interpretability tax. Empirically, ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks, while out-performing on measures of feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Because subsequent computation acts only on features that survive the sparse bottleneck, the ParityTransformer's features are native to the model's forwards pass by construction, addressing the question of whether SAEs probe features the model actually uses during computation. We see this as a step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post hoc.

</details>


### [263] [SalesLoop: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Sales Lead Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20655)
*Chenyu Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SalesLoop uses reinforcement learning to close the loop between CRM lead ranking and business outcomes, addressing offline-online metric mismatch, objective misalignment, and temporal drift through a performance-aware reward and a discriminative listwise objective (Discriminative GRPO). It yields notable offline ranking gains (NDCG@K +7.9%, P@K +15.8%) and production improvements (lift +4.7% and +8.7% in a 160-day real-world trial) including improved recall and higher conversion rates for high-intent leads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a persistent gap between offline evaluation metrics and production performance in CRM lead ranking. This gap arises from (i) metric mismatch between offline success measures and real business outcomes, (ii) misalignment between pointwise/offline objectives and listwise/online ranking goals, and (iii) distribution drift over time in production data.

Method: Introduce SalesLoop, a reinforcement learning framework with a closed feedback loop between model predictions and business outcomes. Key components include (1) a performance-aware reward that encodes conversion outcomes weighted by ranking position and conversion velocity, and (2) Discriminative GRPO, a listwise optimization objective that adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization to discriminative ranking models.

Result: In offline evaluation, NDCG@K improves by 7.9% and P@K by 15.8% over the strongest static baseline. In 160-day production A/B testing with 16.5 million leads and 280 sales specialists across two provincial markets, cumulative lift is +4.7% (p=0.047) and +8.7% (p=0.002). Production ranking backbone achieves top-10% recall of 44.1% and surfaces high-intent leads at 2.3x conversion rate relative to specialist baselines.

Conclusion: SalesLoop demonstrates effective closed-loop learning for CRM lead ranking, achieving meaningful offline and in-production gains, and validating the viability of a reinforcement learning approach for optimizing business outcomes in large-scale CRM deployments.

Abstract: Lead ranking in Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems faces a persistent challenge: models achieving high offline accuracy often underperform in production. We identify three fundamental gaps responsible for this disconnect: offline-online metric mismatch, pointwise-listwise objective misalignment, and temporal distribution drift. To address these gaps, we propose SalesLoop, a reinforcement learning framework that establishes a closed feedback loop between model predictions and real-world business outcomes. Our approach introduces (1) a performance-aware reward that encodes conversion outcomes weighted by ranking position and conversion velocity, and (2) Discriminative GRPO, a listwise optimization objective that adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization to discriminative ranking models.
  SalesLoop improves NDCG@K by +7.9\% and P@K by +15.8\% over the strongest static baseline. A 160-day production A/B test at a New Energy Vehicle manufacturer, spanning 16.5M leads and 280 sales specialists across two provincial markets, validates statistically significant cumulative lift of +4.7\% ($p=0.047$) and +8.7\% ($p=0.002$). In production, the ranking backbone achieves Top-10\% recall of 44.1\% and surfaces high-intent leads at $2.3\times$ the conversion rate of specialist baselines.

</details>


### [264] [Adaptive Multi-Horizon Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20656)
*Manoosh Samiei,Doina Precup,Paul Masset*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adaptive multi-horizon temporal discounting for RL; adaptively selects and combines multiple horizons to handle changing rewards and continual task switches, improving adaptability and parameter efficiency in MiniGrid.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed discounting imposes a single planning horizon, which limits performance in nonstationary environments. Biological agents exhibit flexible discounting across timescales, suggesting multi-horizon planning is advantageous for adaptation.

Method: Introduce a multi-horizon RL framework that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, removing the need for manual discount-factor tuning and enabling robust adaptation in continual learning settings with task switches.

Result: Empirical demonstrations in MiniGrid environments, including continual settings with three sequentially changing tasks, show that the approach identifies effective discount factors across tasks and improves adaptability and parameter efficiency.

Conclusion: Adaptive temporal discounting enhances robustness and adaptability in RL, with implications for both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems, particularly in continual and nonstationary environments.

Abstract: Effective decision-making in complex and changing environments requires balancing short-term and long-term consequences. In reinforcement learning (RL), this trade-off is typically controlled through a fixed discount factor, which imposes a single exponentially discounted temporal horizon. However, biological agents exhibit flexible and adaptive temporal discounting, suggesting that effective planning requires multiple timescales. Here, we propose a multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, enabling robust adaptation to changes in reward structure without manual discount-factor tuning. This flexibility makes the method particularly suitable for continual learning scenarios involving task switches and varying environmental configurations. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach identifies effective discount factors across a range of MiniGrid environments, including continual settings composed of three sequentially changing tasks. These results suggest that adaptive temporal discounting can improve parameter efficiency and enhance adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems.

</details>


### [265] [End-to-End Learning of Safe Optimal Feedback Control in High Dimensions with Control Barrier Function Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20674)
*Xingjian Li,Kelvin Kan,Deepanshu Verma,Krishna Kumar,Stanley Osher,Samy Wu Fung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Scalable end-to-end training of high-dimensional CBF-constrained controllers via operator splitting and Jacobian-Free Backpropagation, enabling hard safety for QP-based safety filters in systems up to 1200 states and 400 controls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome computational and differentiation bottlenecks when embedding control barrier function (CBF) safety filters into end-to-end learning, which previously restricted methods to low-dimensional systems.

Method: Combine operator splitting with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation to differentiate through a quadratic-program-based safety filter within end-to-end training; provide nonsmooth analysis-based theoretical justification.

Result: Empirically validated on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state dimensions up to 1200 and control dimensions up to 400, demonstrating scalability and preservation of hard safety constraints.

Conclusion: Enables scalable, provably safe end-to-end training of high-dimensional systems using CBFs, extending applicability of safety-critical learning to large-scale problems.

Abstract: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional semi-global feedback controllers under hard safety constraints enforced by control barrier functions (CBFs). Incorporating CBFs into end-to-end policy training requires embedding a quadratic-program-based safety filter as an optimization layer, but computational and differentiation bottlenecks have largely restricted prior approaches to low-dimensional systems, typically with at most 16 state dimensions. We address this limitation by combining operator splitting with the recently developed Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) method to enable scalable end-to-end training while preserving hard safety guarantees through the CBF safety filter. We justify this training methodology theoretically using nonsmooth analysis techniques and demonstrate its effectiveness on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state and control dimensions up to 1200 and 400, respectively.

</details>


### [266] [Explanation-Based Runtime Verification for Trustworthy ML-driven Optical Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20675)
*Omran Ayoub,Carlos Natalino,Ali Al Housseini,Felix Foschum,Philipp Morger,Tiziano Leidi,David Hock,Paolo Monti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes explanation-based runtime verification to audit ML decisions in optical networks using XAI explanations; can intercept erroneous decisions by checking coherence and physics grounding, while preserving high automation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ML-driven control in optical networks risks service degradation if decisions are flawed; need runtime guarantees and transparency.

Method: Uses explainable AI to generate explanations of predictions; assesses explanation coherence and physics-grounding consistency at runtime; defers or rejects uncertain decisions; evaluated on a lightpath QoT (quality of transmission) classification use case.

Result: Intercepted a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving a high automation rate.

Conclusion: Explanation-based verification improves reliability of ML-driven network control with minimal impact on automation; promising for safer, scalable optical network automation.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) models are increasingly integrated into optical network automation frameworks to support tasks such as failure management, performance monitoring and resource allocation. In these environments, ML-driven predictions may be directly coupled with control-plane actions where incorrect decisions can immediately impact service quality, resource efficiency, and network stability. As automation levels increase, ensuring the reliability of individual decisions at deployment time becomes a critical requirement. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques have emerged to improve transparency by highlighting the factors influencing ML predictions. In addition to identifying influential features, they provide insights into the underlying reasoning process of the model, revealing how different input variables contribute to the final outcome and how feature interactions shape the decision boundary. In this work, we introduce explanation-based runtime verification, an approach that exploits model explanations to assess the soundness of individual ML decisions before they are executed in the network control loop. The proposed approach evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency at runtime, enabling the system to defer or reject decisions flagged as uncertain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a representative use case of lightpath quality of transmission classification. Experimental results show that explanation-based verification can intercept a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving high automation rate.

</details>


### [267] [Attribution Markets: A Fisher-Market Formulation for Fractional Credit Assignment Between Planned Tasks and Performed Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20694)
*Salavat Ishbulatov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bridges planned task budgets and performed actions with a quasi-linear Fisher market, introducing market instruments and a concave completion utility; analyzes convergence via a fixed point, handles noise with entropy-regularization, and validates reproducibility and relevance to attribution and optimal transport.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To fix drift between planned effort budgets and logged actions in personal/organizational planning, avoiding false stalls and improving alignment between plans and execution.

Method: Model as a Fisher market with budget-constrained buyers (planned tasks) and divisible goods (performed actions). Valuations are fused from text/structure/temporal signals. Introduce seller reserve price and buyer cash option to ensure conservation, hard budget caps, and a junk-filter theorem. Extend with a concave completion utility that discounts progress near plan. Prove existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under diagonal-dominance. Empirically validate on random/adversarial instances. Use a de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark with affinity-noise to reveal sensitivity to sharp equilibria. Propose a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization unifying Fisher-market and entropy-regularized optimal transport, plus a noise-adaptive regularization rule. Report reproducibility parameters and discuss limitations; connect to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

Result: Theoretical guarantees: conservation, hard budget cap, and junk-filter hold as theorems. Existence of a satiation-threshold fixed point with local uniqueness under a diagonal-dominance condition. Empirical results show a noise-vs-entropy trade-off: zero-entropy equilibrium is highly sensitive to affinity noise, while entropy-regularized OT yields a smoother, more robust solution. A unified entropy-regularized framework and noise-adaptive regularization strength are proposed. Reproducibility parameters provided; limitations acknowledged; practical relevance to attribution and transport.

Conclusion: The work presents a novel market-based bridge between planned and performed work, with provable properties and practical safeguards. It situates the approach within attribution and transport literatures, offers a unifying entropy-regularized model to mitigate sensitivity to noise, and candidly discusses limitations and reproducibility. Future work may explore broader empirical validation and sensitivity analyses.

Abstract: Personal and organizational planning systems maintain two records that drift apart: what was planned (a task's effort budget) and what was done (a logged action's duration and description). Existing systems bridge them with an exclusive, all-or-nothing link that strands genuinely related but unlinked effort and reports false stalls on active goals. We formulate the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market: planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers, performed actions are divisible goods, and a fused text/structural/temporal signal sets each buyer's valuation. Two market instruments - a seller reserve price and a buyer cash option - yield conservation, a hard budget cap, and a provable junk filter as theorems. We extend the market with a concave completion utility discounting progress as a task nears its plan; standard convergence theory for the market's algorithm does not transfer here, resolved by a satiation-threshold fixed point with existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under an explicit diagonal-dominance condition, validated empirically on random and adversarial instances. A de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark - observed affinity corrupted independently of the scored ground truth - surfaces a genuine weak spot: the market's sharp, zero-entropy equilibrium is more sensitive to affinity noise than entropy-regularized optimal transport's permanently smoothed one. We resolve this with a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization unifying the two, plus a noise-adaptive rule for its regularization strength. We report full reproducibility parameters, discuss limitations candidly, and relate the result to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

</details>


### [268] [CEDAR: Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20696)
*Mohammad Fesanghary*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CEDAR is a sparse, constraint-based method for lagged causal edge discovery in autoregressive time series, screening cross-variable lags with AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation, then using two targeted conditional-independence tests per lag, with a maximal-one-lag-per-ordered-pair rule, followed by stable MCI pruning and optional deterministic C-nodes for trend-like nonstationarity. It achieves O(d^2) CI tests post-screening and preserves edge-level interpretability, performing best with scarce data and lag-1 self-dynamics; richer conditioning becomes preferable as data or complexity grows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable interpretable and scalable identification of lagged causal edges in sparse autoregressive time series, particularly under limited data, while controlling for autoregressive structure and confounding through targeted independence tests.

Method: Screen candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation. For each significant lag candidate, apply two targeted conditional-independence tests and allow at most one lag per ordered pair. Apply a stable MCI pruning step to remove indirect edges. Optionally include deterministic C-nodes to adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. In sparse regimes with few surviving lags, the method uses O(d^2) CI tests after screening while preserving edge-level interpretability.

Result: The abstract claims that CEDAR achieves O(d^2) CI tests after screening in sparse regimes and preserves edge-level interpretability. It positions CEDAR as most effective when data are scarce and lag-1 dynamics dominate, with guidance that richer conditioning sets are preferable as T grows or when higher-order or simultaneous multi-lag effects are present.

Conclusion: CEDAR offers a scalable, interpretable framework for lagged causal discovery under sparsity and limited data, with explicit mechanisms (AR(1) residualization, distance-correlation screening, targeted CI tests, MCI pruning, and optional C-nodes) to control for autoregression, nonstationarity, and indirect effects; its advantages diminish as network density or autoregressive order increases, suggesting that richer conditioning schemes or alternative methods may be preferred in those settings.

Abstract: We propose CEDAR (Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes), a constraint-based method for lagged causal edge discovery in sparse autoregressive time series. CEDAR screens candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation, then applies two targeted conditional-independence tests per significant cross-variable lag candidate and accepts at most one lag per ordered pair. A stable MCI pruning step removes indirect edges, and optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. In sparse regimes where few lags survive screening, CEDAR requires $O(d^2)$ CI tests after screening while retaining edge-level interpretability. CEDAR is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics; methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable as $T$ grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

</details>


### [269] [Perspective Latents as an Architectural Condition for Causal Emergence in Active Inference Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20708)
*Hongju Pae*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In an active inference agent, Φ_r localizes to the slow global latent g in reward-free settings, and overall Φ_r magnitude is architecture-driven and decreases with training; learning effects appear only at the atom level, where decoupling changes sign and downward causation modulates regime-specific adjustments, arguing against Φ_r as a simple scalar of learned integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess whether information-theoretic measures of causal emergence (Φ_r) align with reward-free predictive organization in active inference, by contrasting a fast perception latent z with a slow latent g, and examining how Φ_r distributes and evolves without reward signals.

Method: Analyze an active inference agent with a fast perception latent z and a slow global latent g (driven by prediction error; decoupled from policy gradients) in a reward-free regime-switching environment. Compute integrated information decomposition to quantify Φ_r and examine atom-level contributions and directional influences (upward/downward causation).

Result: Under reward-free regime-switching, Φ_r concentrates in g; the aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The learning signal becomes evident only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips Φ_r's contribution from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental changes, while downward causation accounts for regime-dependent adjustments.

Conclusion: g is the architectural locus of Φ_r-relevant temporal organization in the active inference agent; scalar Φ_r should not be read as a direct index of learned integration, and detailed (atom-level) analysis is necessary to capture learning-related information dynamics.

Abstract: A recent line of work measures causal emergence in reinforcement learning agents through Integrated Information Decomposition, reporting that $Φ_r$ grows with training and tracks reward improvement. For active inference, this raises the question of how reward-free predictive organization relates to such information-theoretic signatures. I test this within an active inference agent whose architecture separates a fast perception latent $z$ from a slow global latent $g$, where $g$ is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. In a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol, $Φ_r$ concentrates in $g$; its aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The substantive effect of learning becomes legible only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries the regime-dependent adjustment. These results identify $g$ as the architectural locus of $Φ_r$-relevant temporal organization in an active inference agent, and argue against reading scalar $Φ_r$ as a direct index of learned integration.

</details>


### [270] [LLMs Get Lost in Evolving User Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20734)
*Jihoon Tack,Philippe Laban,Jennifer Neville*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Static single-turn proficiency does not predict performance when user intent evolves in multi-turn conversations; a framework reveals a gap in tracking evolving intent and robust collaboration with agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate LLMs in realistic interactive settings where user intent unfolds over dialogue, addressing the mismatch between static benchmarks and dynamic collaboration; enable reuse of existing benchmarks without new annotations.

Method: Develop a framework that transforms static tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations with evolving, incrementally revealed and revised user intent, while preserving original evaluation protocols; test across multiple tasks and model families.

Result: Across tasks and models, strong static performance does not transfer to evolving-intent settings; substantial performance drops observed; across model families, indicating a fundamental gap in intent-tracking and action accordingly.

Conclusion: Current LLMs do not faithfully track evolving user intent; dynamic evaluation reveals capabilities not captured by static tests; advancing collaborative AI requires models and evaluation methods that handle evolving intent and mid-conversation redirection.

Abstract: As LLMs become more capable, they are increasingly deployed as collaborative agents, taking on user-delegated tasks through iterative interaction. Yet genuine interaction is inherently dynamic: users rarely specify their intent upfront, instead disclosing, revising, and reshaping it as the conversation unfolds. Despite this, LLMs are still predominantly evaluated or trained in single-turn, fully-specified settings, leaving open a fundamental question: how well do LLMs track and act on user intent as it evolves over the course of a conversation? To study this, we introduce a framework that transforms static, single-turn tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations in which the user's intent evolves across turns--incrementally revealed, revised, and at times redirected mid-conversation--while preserving each task's original evaluation protocol, enabling existing benchmarks to be reused as controlled testbeds without new annotation. Across multiple tasks, we surface a consistent phenomenon: strong static-setting performance does not transfer to the evolving-intent setting, with substantial drops across model families. Our findings point to a fundamental gap: today's LLMs do not yet faithfully track and act on the user's evolving intent, a capability invisible to static evaluation yet critical for future collaborative agents.

</details>


### [271] [Cardinality-Decomposed Loss: Matching Training Objectives to Relation Structure in Heterogeneous Recommendation Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20737)
*Parul Maheshwari,Amulya Paruchuri,Yiqing Zou,Alireza Sahami Shirazi,Farhad Farahani,Prakhar Mehrotra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cardinality-decomposed loss (CDL) combines Cross Entropy and BPR to handle one-to-one attribute edges and one-to-many user-item relations in heterogeneous bipartite GNNs, improving attribute embedding discriminability and balancing ranking with attribute signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BPR-focused training causes attribute embeddings to collapse and deteriorates downstream user embeddings; a unified loss fails to respect varying edge cardinalities, hindering representation quality.

Method: Introduce CDL that decomposes loss by edge cardinality, applying CE to one-to-one attribute relations and BPR to one-to-many relations; demonstrate CE-BPR optimization conflict in a shared encoder; evaluate on five datasets with varying configurations, using a tunable lambda to balance objectives; perform a lambda-sweep to relate performance to semantic alignment and topology leakage.

Result: CDL yields more discriminable attribute embeddings across datasets; ranking gains (NDCG) appear when attributes carry meaningful preference signals and may decline when correlation is weak; a lambda-sweep reveals dataset behavior is governed by semantic alignment and topology leakage.

Conclusion: Cardinality-aware objectives improve representation quality in heterogeneous GNNs by aligning losses with relation cardinalities; CDL provides a tunable framework to balance attribute discrimination and ranking, with performance governed by how well attributes align with preferences and how much the graph topology already encodes them.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks trained on heterogenous bipartite graphs form a common basis in recommendation systems. These graphs often express relations that vary in cardinality, for example, user-item preferences are one-to-many and user-attribute features are one-to-one. Traditionally, a unique loss function is applied for all of the network components which is often Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR). While BPR works well for the recommendation task, we find that it causes attribute embeddings to collapse to near-random geometry -- a silent failure that leaves standard ranking metrics largely unaffected and therefore invisible to conventional evaluation. This in turn pollutes user node embeddings, which are shaped by both edge types simultaneously, hurting downstream tasks like personalization, segmentation, etc. Here we propose a Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL) that combines both Cross Entropy (CE) and BPR to enable the model to collectively optimize for relations across cardinalities. We confirm this CE-BPR conflict by showing the two losses compete in the shared encoder's parameter space. We evaluate CDL on five datasets spanning two structural configurations -- one-to-one attributes on user nodes (MovieLens-1M, Last.fm-360K, PayPal Audience Factory, BookCrossing) and on item nodes (Yelp) -- and find that CDL consistently improves discriminability in attribute embeddings. We also show that ranking (NDCG) improves when attributes carry meaningful preference signal, but conflicts with it when the correlation is weak. We use a lambda parameter to navigate this trade-off, and a lambda-sweep reveals that dataset behavior is governed by two graph properties -- semantic alignment and topology leakage. Semantic alignment measures whether the attribute predicts preferences, while topology leakage measures whether the graph's connectivity already encodes it.

</details>


### [272] [Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion for Trustworthy Multi-Omics Multimodal Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20742)
*Mohammad Raahemi,Ali Sekhavati,Alireza Maleki,Hamid Nasiri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion (ACE) enhances multimodal fusion by generating supplementary modalities from intra-modality correlations and using a dual-level confidence mechanism to reweight modalities and provide a global trust score, improving classification and confidence calibration on multi-omics data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal models struggle with noisy/uninformative streams and lack robust, trustable confidence measures, hindering deployment in safety-critical/clinical settings.

Method: ACE introduces two components: (i) intra-modality correlation-based augmentation to expand the multimodal space with complementary modalities, and (ii) a dual-level confidence system that (a) adaptively reweighs each modality by reliability before fusion, and (b) estimates a global trust score for the final decision.

Result: ACE achieves superior classification performance and confidence calibration compared with state-of-the-art methods on four multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, ROSMAP). It yields more stable and robust fusion, facilitating multimodal learning in high-stakes problems.

Conclusion: ACE provides a trustworthy, robust fusion framework for multimodal learning in clinical contexts by augmenting the modality space and incorporating dual-level confidence, improving both predictive accuracy and decision confidence.

Abstract: Multimodal learning is a robust approach to improve predictive performance in applications such as medical prognosis. However, the clinical applicability of models that use multimodal learning is hampered by their poor performance under noisy or uninformative data streams. Present fusion approaches often lack robust mechanisms for the dynamic assessment of data quality and for the provision of a trustable confidence score on the final prediction. This dissuades their deployment in safety-critical settings. To address these limitations, we introduce Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion (ACE), a novel framework to enhance the trustworthiness of multimodal fusion models. ACE first enhances the multimodal space by generating new, complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations. It then employs a dual-level confidence mechanism that (1) adaptively reweighs all modalities by their reliability before fusion and (2) estimates a global trust score over the fused, final decision. To evaluate ACE, we used four challenging multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, and ROSMAP). ACE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in both classification performance and confidence calibration. Our framework provides a more stable and robust data fusion method that facilitates the use of multimodal learning in addressing high-stakes problems.

</details>


### [273] [GaugeQuant: Online Learning of Quantization-Optimal Bases from LLM Symmetries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20757)
*Miguel P. Bento,João Seabra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GaugeQuant introduces a LogSumExp loss term during training to break Transformer symmetries and select a rotation-basis, reducing activation outliers and improving quantized LMs without calibration data; achieves notable perplexity improvements on LLaMA-2 7B under W4 quantization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address internal continuous symmetries of Transformers that preserve outputs but impair activation statistics under quantization, leading to degraded performance in low-bit quantized models.

Method: In-training objective adds a LogSumExp term to the loss to favor a basis with smaller activation outliers; a stop-gradient operator ensures only rotation matrices are updated, leaving the language modeling objective intact; requires no calibration data and adds negligible training overhead.

Result: Perplexity on LLaMA-2 7B improves from 8.22 to 6.73 under W4A4 and from 11.16 to 5.45 under W4A16; code is available at the provided repository.

Conclusion: The approach yields competitive gains relative to post-training quantization methods that rely on frozen models and calibration data, offering a calibration-free, training-efficient path to better quantized language models.

Abstract: Transformers are known to have internal continuous symmetries that leave outputs invariant, while modifying quantization. GaugeQuant leverages this in-training by introducing a LogSumExp term to the loss that breaks the symmetries, thus selecting a basis that minimizes activation outliers. A stop-gradient operator ensures that only rotation matrices are updated, yielding the language modeling objective completely unaltered. Our requires no specific calibration data, no quantization simulation, and adds negligible training overhead. With the LLaMA-2 7B model under W4A4 quantization with group size 128, perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73, competing with post-training methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets. Under W4A16, perplexity drops from 11.16 to 5.45. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/gauge-quant.

</details>


### [274] [Memory-Computation Tradeoffs in Semi Amortized Parametric Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20769)
*Shijie Pan,Agustin Castellano,Zeyu Shen,Enrique Mallada*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how much offline memory is needed to achieve a target accuracy when online computation is limited, within amortized parametric optimization using K steps of projected gradient descent with a learned warm start from stored solutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand fundamental memory-online computation tradeoffs in learning-enabled decision systems, and to quantify how offline data can accelerate online optimization under a fixed online budget.

Method: Offline phase stores a finite memory of solved problem instances; online phase retrieves a warm start and performs K steps of projected gradient descent on a smooth convex parametric problem over a compact domain. A nonparametric predictor built from stored solutions is used. The authors derive upper and lower bounds on the memory needed to achieve ε-accuracy for μ-strongly convex objectives, and near-matching bounds with a phase transition for β-growth convex objectives (β>2). They provide a general proof framework linking acceleration memory to online convergence rate and Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map, and validate predictions via parameterized ridge regression experiments.

Result: For μ-strongly convex objectives, matching upper and lower bounds on memory guarantee ε-accuracy under fixed K; for β-growth convex objectives (β>2), near-matching bounds and a phase transition where added memory stops helping beyond a certain K. The framework quantifies memory cost of acceleration and identifies the two driving quantities. Experiments on parameterized ridge regression confirm the memory–computation–accuracy tradeoffs.

Conclusion: Offline memory can be systematically leveraged to accelerate online optimization, with explicit bounds that relate online convergence and solution map sensitivity to the required memory. The results reveal fundamental tradeoffs and a practical framework for designing amortized optimization systems.

Abstract: Learning-enabled decision systems often use offline data or computation to reduce online compute cost. Despite the empirical success of such approaches, there is limited general understanding of how much offline information is needed to achieve a desired accuracy under a fixed online computation budget. We study this question through the lens of amortized parametric optimization: an offline phase stores a finite memory of solved problem instances, and an online phase produces a solution to a new instance by retrieving a warm start and applying $K$ steps of projected gradient descent. We analyze this setup for smooth convex parametric optimization over a compact domain, using a nonparametric predictor built from the stored offline solutions. For $μ$-strongly convex objectives, we establish matching upper and lower bounds on the memory required to guarantee $\varepsilon$-accuracy under a fixed online iteration budget $K$. For convex objectives satisfying a $β$-growth condition ($β>2$), we obtain near-matching bounds and identify a phase transition in $K$ beyond which additional memory provides no benefit. We further provide a general proof framework that (i) explicitly quantifies the memory cost of acceleration---how much offline memory is required to achieve a prescribed speedup over the unaided online optimizer---and (ii) identifies two key quantities driving this cost: the convergence rate of the online optimizer and the Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map to the problem parameter. Experiments on parameterized ridge regression confirm the predicted memory--computation--accuracy tradeoffs.

</details>


### [275] [Toward Mechanistic Interpretability of an AI Foundation Model Fine-Tuned for Atmospheric Chemistry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20778)
*Jason Y. Hu,Ivan Higuera-Mendieta,Patrick Obin Sturm,Makoto M. Kelp*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Aurora, a chemistry-tuned weather foundation model, shows partial learning of atmospheric chemistry: it reproduces a first-order ozone response to NOx but fails to enforce chemical constraints, produces chemically inconsistent species combinations, and its internal representations are dominated by pretraining meteorology with little chemistry-specific structure; sparse autoencoders reveal components causally affecting chemistry forecasts that do not map cleanly to discrete atmospheric processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether AI-driven atmospheric chemistry forecasts learn genuine physical/chemical mechanisms from reanalysis data or rely on statistical regularities, and establish a framework to evaluate internal mechanisms beyond forecast accuracy for policy-relevant use.

Method: Impose controlled chemical perturbations on FM forecasts and test against known photochemical relationships; analyze internal representations; apply sparse autoencoders to identify internal components that influence the chemical forecast and examine their mapping to atmospheric processes.

Result: Aurora captures a first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen but does not enforce chemical constraints; it yields chemically inconsistent combinations of related species and tends to relax localized emission features toward background; representations remain meteorology-centered from pretraining with little chemistry-specific structure; sparse autoencoders uncover internal components that causally control the chemical forecast but do not map cleanly to individual atmospheric processes.

Conclusion: As composition forecasts gain policy relevance, evaluation should extend beyond skill metrics to inspect internal mechanisms; a framework is provided to test whether AI forecasts truly learn atmospheric chemistry from data, highlighting potential gaps between learned associations and physically-consistent chemistry.

Abstract: Weather forecasting foundation models (FMs) are increasingly fine-tuned to predict air quality, offering fast global pollution forecasts at lower computational cost than conventional chemical transport models. These FMs are typically trained on reanalysis data and generate forecasts through autoregressive rollout. They do not explicitly represent governing physical or chemical processes. Therefore, high forecast skill does not reveal whether a model has learned physical mechanisms or exploits statistical regularities in its training data. Here, we present the first study of what a FM fine-tuned for atmospheric chemistry has learned by examining Microsoft's Aurora model. We impose controlled chemical perturbations on its forecasts and test them against known photochemical relationships. We then examine the internal representations that generate these forecasts. We find that Aurora captures a first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen but does not enforce the chemical constraints that a process-based model encodes. It generates chemically inconsistent combinations of related species and relaxes localized emission features such as wildfire plumes toward background. Internally, its representations remain largely organized around the meteorology inherited during pretraining, with little structure specific to chemistry. Using sparse autoencoders, we identify internal components that causally control the chemical forecast but do not map cleanly onto individual atmospheric processes. This work provides a framework for testing whether AI forecasting systems learn atmospheric chemistry from reanalysis data. As these models are increasingly positioned to inform environmental policy decisions, we argue that composition forecasts should also be judged by their internal mechanisms rather than by benchmark skill alone.

</details>


### [276] [Synthetic minority data is redundant or invalid: a data-dependent validity theory and a de-biased test](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20787)
*Ahmad B. Hassanat,Ahmad S. Tarawneh,Ghada A. Altarawneh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper de-biases the standard validity check for synthetic minority oversampling, showing that current methods fail to provide reliable validity or information gain; a held-out data test reveals 96–99% underestimation of invalidity, and no method across 91 techniques clears both validity and feature gain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Challenge the widespread reliance on synthetic minority oversampling (e.g., SMOTE) by exposing bias in the standard validation approach and determining whether synthetic data truly adds information under realistic, held-out evaluations.

Method: Introduce a de-biased validity estimator that scores synthetic samples against held-out real data, then empirically evaluate 91 methods across three classifiers and diverse medicine/finance datasets; compare against the classical check; force open-data audit as a pip-installable test.

Result: Classical validation underestimates invalidity in 96–99% of method-by-imbalance-ratio cells; de-biased estimate aligns with true invalidity; validity is data-dependent and limited by class overlap; oversampling provides negligible gains and often harms calibration; no method clears both validity and information gain, even a generator tailored to pass the old test.

Conclusion: Synthetic minority data must demonstrate data-grounded validity and information gain; the authors publish an auditable test and shift the burden of proof onto oversampling methods, suggesting that oversampling is unnecessary when classes are well-separated and invalid when they overlap.

Abstract: For two decades, the standard remedy for class-imbalanced learning has been to fabricate synthetic minority examples, and the standard evidence of their validity has been a check that cannot fail: synthetic points are scored against the very data that generated them. We de-bias the check. Validity becomes a population quantity -- the probability that a synthetic point truly belongs to the minority class -- with a consistent estimator that scores synthetic points against withheld real data. Where held-out ground truth is available, the classical test underestimates true invalidity in 96-99% of method-by-imbalance-ratio cells, while the de-biased estimator tracks it closely. We prove validity is a property of the data, not the method: class overlap sets an invalidity floor no faithful generator escapes, making oversampling redundant where classes separate and invalid where they overlap. Across 91 methods, three classifiers, and datasets spanning medicine and finance -- including a generator engineered to pass the classical check -- none clears both bars: gains over the best trivial baseline are noise-thin (median below 0.01 F1, a decision threshold's reach), and most damage calibration. We release the audit as a pip-installable test and flip the burden of proof: synthetic minority data must now demonstrate, on the data at hand, both validity and information gain.

</details>


### [277] [Memoir: Should a Model Write to Its Memory While It Thinks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20792)
*Jaber Jaber,Osama Jaber*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Coupled memory rewriting in Memoir incurs a learning-speed penalty under fixed budget compared to a read-only variant; no observed degradation of the energy signal; kernel restructuring improves forward-time; results shown on a finite-task recall benchmark; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
