Method: 1) Prove impossibility: any procedure using only inside-candidate labels cannot certify non-trivial missed mass. 2) Prove a matching finite-corpus lower bound: to certify fewer than m misses with high probability when none are present, one must inspect ≈ N0/m labels from the excluded pool. 3) Develop an exact finite-sample toolkit using binomial and hypergeometric inversion, including a two-pool design to convert missed mass bounds to recall, certificates for nested candidate families, and stress-test certificates against perturbations. 4) Ensure guarantees hold when the candidate generator or the pre-specified family and the audit rule are fixed before labels are examined.

Result: Established that excluded-pool auditing is minimax-rate-optimal for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime, with a finite-sample lower bound of Ω(N0/m) labels. Delivered an exact finite-sample toolkit that yields missed-mass certificates, converts to recall, certifies nested generator families, and provides stress-test certificates, all under a fixed-design discipline.

Conclusion: The framework enables defensible, pre-specified design choices with finite-sample guarantees, linking missed-mass control to observable review burden and enabling stress-tested certification across candidate generators.

Abstract: An initial high-recall stage in an empirical pipeline decides which items pass to later review, labelling, or modelling, and relevant items it misses are lost to every subsequent stage. We study how many audit labels are needed to certify, with finite-sample validity, that this missed relevant mass is small, and our main results characterise the label complexity of this problem. We first show that no procedure using only labels from inside the candidate set can certify any non-trivial bound on the missed mass: the audit must sample the excluded pool, the only region where unrecovered relevant items can lie. We then prove a matching finite-corpus lower bound. Any valid audit that certifies fewer than $m$ missed relevant items with high probability when none are present, even if adaptive and permitted to label the entire included pool, must inspect on the order of $N_0/m$ excluded-pool labels. Excluded-pool auditing is therefore minimax rate-optimal, not merely convenient, for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime. Building on this characterisation, we develop an exact finite-sample toolkit, using binomial and hypergeometric inversion rather than asymptotic approximation, that certifies missed mass, converts it to recall through a two-pool design, certifies pre-specified families of nested candidate generators simultaneously, and produces stress-test certificates against declared perturbation mechanisms. These certificates can be paired with observable review burden to select the least burdensome pre-specified candidate generator meeting a missed-mass target. Every guarantee holds under one discipline: the candidate generator, or the pre-specified family from which it is selected, and the audit rule are fixed before the certification labels are examined.

</details>


### [326] [Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21535)
*Alagappan Valliappan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Windowed-MTP: bounding the draft's KV attention with a StreamingLLM-style sliding window and attention sink yields 28–44% per-decode-step cost reductions across 1M context, without harming output distribution, by reclaiming unread draft KV with a constant working set.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding hinges on cheap draft heads (MTP/NEXTN) but their full-attention KV reads escalate with context length. At million-token contexts, the draft's read cost dominates, undermining speculation's benefit, especially with hybrid/linear attention. A fixed-size, windowed approach is needed to keep draft cost sublinear and maintain verification.

Method: Introduce a streaming sliding-window approach (Windowed-MTP) that restricts the draft's attention to a fixed-size KV window and uses an attention sink for the draft: verification remains with the full-attention target. Training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction; unread draft KV entries are reclaimed via a compact ring buffer. This bounds the draft KV working set to a constant (dropping ~99% of KV at 1M context).

Result: On three architectures (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, Windowed-MTP cut per-decode-step cost for the native MTP draft by 28% to 44%, yielding proportional end-to-end latency improvements at matched acceptance. The mechanism preserves the target's verified output distribution, and unread draft KV (7.7–11% of total KV at 1M) is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer with no cost to acceptance or quality.

Conclusion: Windowed-MTP provides a training-free, drop-in, lossless improvement for speculative decoding in long-context LLMs by constraining the draft's KV attention. It yields meaningful latency/memory savings at 1M context and scales with context length, while preserving the accuracy of the verified outputs.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a cheap draft propose tokens that a target verifies in parallel. Frontier models increasingly ship a built-in Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP/NEXTN) draft head under the assumption that the draft is negligibly cheap. At million-token context this breaks: an MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, so its read grows linearly with context and comes to dominate the draft cost -- precisely where speculation is most valuable. The effect compounds with draft length (a deep native draft can turn net-negative, slower than no speculation) and sharpens under hybrid/linear-attention targets, where cheaper verification leaves the draft's full-attention read exposed. We apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP), leaving full-attention verification intact. It is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction: the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which are accepted. It bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M. Across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, windowing cuts the per-decode-step cost over the shipping native MTP draft by +28% to +44%, an input-invariant margin that widens with context. Since per-token latency is this cost divided by acceptance length, at matched acceptance end-to-end decode latency improves by the same amount, and more where windowing also lifts acceptance, while preserving the target's verified output distribution. Finally, the unread draft KV -- 7.7-11% of total KV at 1M -- is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer at no acceptance or quality cost.

</details>


### [327] [Zero-Flow Two-Sample Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21542)
*Yakun Wang,Leyang Wang,Song Liu,Taiji Suzuki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces ZF2ST, a two-sample test based on zero-flow discrepancy; learns local misalignment via a learned witness, with regression-based and power-maximization variants, achieving strong power with calibrated Type-I error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of fixed-kernel tests and purely discriminative adversarial approaches by decoupling witness learning from hypothesis evaluation, enabling flexible neural networks with valid statistical calibration for two-sample testing.

Method: Define a zero-flow discrepancy metric capturing local misalignment between samples from two distributions. Train a witness function through regression or a power-maximization objective, then perform hypothesis testing with calibration. The learning and testing steps are separated to leverage neural nets while maintaining statistical validity.

Result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic and image datasets demonstrates strong testing power for structured distributional changes and well-calibrated Type-I error.

Conclusion: ZF2ST provides a flexible, calibrated two-sample testing framework that can harness neural witnesses, particularly effective for structured distributional differences.

Abstract: We propose a new approach to two-sample testing for deciding whether two sets of samples are drawn from the same distribution. The test is built on a statistical discrepancy based on the zero-flow criterion, termed zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD). We prove the validity of ZFD and propose a practical testing procedure, termed the zero-flow two-sample test (ZF2ST). The key idea is to learn how samples from the two distributions are locally misaligned and use the resulting directional pattern as evidence of distributional difference. By separating witness learning from hypothesis evaluation, ZF2ST can use flexible neural networks while maintaining valid statistical calibration. We develop both regression-based and power-maximized approaches for learning the witness. Experiments on synthetic and image datasets demonstrate that ZF2ST can achieve strong testing power for structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error.

</details>


### [328] [X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21550)
*Dongjie Fu,Di Cao,Xize Cheng,Zihan Zhang,Wenxu Jia,Yifu Chen,Shengpeng Ji,Yu Zhang,Tao Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cross-modal on-policy distillation (X^3-OPD) transfers reasoning from a text teacher to an audio-language student via a three-tier symmetric corpus, boosting audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while preserving generalization under domain shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridging the gap between audio-language models and text-based LLMs in deep logical reasoning by addressing the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data and leveraging a powerful textual teacher.

Method: Train a student to generate reasoning trajectories conditioned on its acoustic perception (on-policy distillation) while a textual teacher provides token-level guidance using matched inputs and verified answers. Build a three-tier symmetric corpus: textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning with paralinguistic cues.

Result: Empirical evaluation on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR shows substantial improvements in audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality, with the model retaining capabilities under domain shift.

Conclusion: Cross-modal distillation can extend reasoning beyond textual content to non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context; X^3-OPD demonstrates effective transfer of reasoning capabilities and robustness across domains.

Abstract: While large audio-language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this gap, we propose X$^3$-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student. During training, the student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. We further construct a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This design extends cross-modal distillation beyond textually recoverable content to reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context. Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR demonstrate that X$^3$-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

</details>


### [329] [Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21561)
*Aaron Feller,Kris Deibler,Maxim Secor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EnsembleEGNN encodes molecular conformational ensembles via per-conformer EGNN embeddings pooled with Set Attention; pretrained on cyclic peptide ensembles improves property prediction, outperforming sequence-only baselines, and further gains when co-trained with a BERT sequence encoder.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecules exist as conformational ensembles; single conformer representations lose thermodynamic information. Incorporating ensemble structure and dynamics should improve predictive accuracy for properties sensitive to conformation, especially in cyclic peptides where conformational ensembles are crucial.

Method: Architecture encodes each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network layers; a Set Attention Block pools per-conformer embeddings into an ensemble representation. Pretraining on CREMP with a multi-task self-supervised objective (masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, pairwise distance reconstruction). Evaluation on CREMP-CycPeptMPDB: compare training from scratch vs pretrained; compare to a sequence-only BERT baseline; also co-train EnsembleEGNN with BERT end-to-end.

Result: From-scratch training on CREMP-CycPeptMPDB yields near-zero predictive power (R^2=0.005). Pretraining yields R^2=0.477 and Pearson r=0.699, beating the sequence-only BERT baseline (R^2=0.439, r=0.667). Co-training with the BERT sequence encoder improves to R^2=0.538 and r=0.737.

Conclusion: Encoding conformational ensembles into a thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction, outperforming single-conformer and sequence-only approaches; ensemble-aware pretraining plus end-to-end fusion with sequence models yields the best performance.

Abstract: Molecular property prediction from structure often uses a single representative conformation, even though many molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. We introduce EnsembleEGNN, a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes an ensemble by first encoding each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pooling the resulting conformer representations with a Set Attention Block. We pretrain the model on CREMP, a cyclic peptide ensemble dataset, using a multi-task self-supervised objective combining masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. On the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB dataset, training EnsembleEGNN from scratch fails entirely ($R^2=0.005$). However, the pretrained model reaches $R^2=0.477$ and Pearson $r=0.699$, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline ($R^2=0.439$, Pearson $r=0.667$). When EnsembleEGNN is co-trained end-to-end with the BERT sequence encoder, the hybrid model improves further to $R^2=0.538$ and Pearson $r=0.737$. These results demonstrate that encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

</details>


### [330] [Beyond Sufficiency: Time Series Explanation with Counterfactual Necessity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21573)
*Hongnan Ma,Yiwei Shi,Mengyue Yang,Weiru Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TimePNS introduces a necessity-aware, two-stage framework for time-series explanations that combines a sufficiency mask with counterfactual interventions to identify and emphasize essential subsequences while suppressing non-essential ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing explanations optimized for sufficiency may highlight spurious subsequences that are not truly necessary for the model's decision. There is a need for explanations that capture both sufficiency and necessity to ensure reliability and robustness of time-series predictions.

Method: Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process together with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II applies counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, guiding a temporal gate to refine the mask by suppressing non-essential components and highlighting counterfactually necessary ones.

Result: Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world time-series datasets show that TimePNS improves the accuracy of identifying decision-critical subsequences and achieves better trade-offs between sufficiency and necessity compared to strong baselines.

Conclusion: TimePNS provides a principled, counterfactual-based approach to time-series explanations that explicitly models necessity, yielding more faithful and robust explanations of model decisions.

Abstract: Faithful explanations of time-series classifiers should identify subsequences that are not only sufficient to preserve a black-box model's prediction, but also necessary for maintaining it. However, existing sufficiency-oriented methods can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support the prediction without being essential to the model's decision. We introduce \textbf{TimePNS}, a necessity-aware framework for time-series explanation. Inspired by Pearl's counterfactual notion of necessity, TimePNS assesses whether a temporal factor is necessary by intervening on it and measuring whether the original prediction is disrupted. The framework adopts a two-stage design. Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process together with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial explanation by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones. Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

</details>


### [331] [Expanding Flow Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21585)
*Sophia Tang,Pranam Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows) and Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs) enable flow-based generation with increasing dimensionality, accommodating variable output size in continuous and discrete domains by expanding state via conditional noise and a two-step expand/transport decomposition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional normalizing flows and related models assume fixed dimensionality/output size. This limits controllable generation for variable-length sequences and graphs. EFlows/EFMs aim to unify fixed-canvas flows with progressive dimensional expansion, enabling learned output-size as a degree of freedom.

Method: Introduce expanding interpolants that grow state by augmenting with conditional noise. Define expand operators (state-space augmentation conditioned on current state) and transport maps (pushing expanded state along the interpolant). Compose these to form a single map that expands and denoises. Extend to the discrete simplex for variable-size graphs and sequences.

Result: A principled, general framework for variable-output-size generation in both continuous and discrete domains; reduces to fixed-canvas flows when the expand operator is the identity; enables variable-size graph/sequence generation via the discrete extension.

Conclusion: EFlows and EFMs provide a unified approach to learnable output-size as a controllable parameter, with potential applicability to flexible graph and sequence generation and to settings where the canvas size is not predetermined.

Abstract: Flow-based generative models have enabled remarkable progress in fast and controllable generation across continuous and discrete state spaces, yet existing parameterizations are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths. Here, we introduce Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality along an expanding interpolant that grows the state by augmenting it with conditional noise. Building on this construction, we propose Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), a new class of flow maps that distill the expanding interpolant into efficient few-step generative models. Each EFM factors the map between any two timesteps into two learnable operations: an expand operator, which augments the state space with new coordinates or tokens conditioned on the current state, and a transport map, which pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant. Composing these operators yields a single map that jointly expands and denoises the state, recovering existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as the special case in which the expand operator is the identity. We further extend the framework to the discrete simplex, enabling variable-size graph generation and variable-length sequence generation. Across both continuous and discrete modalities, we establish EFlows and EFMs as a principled framework for settings in which output size is itself a learned, controllable degree of freedom.

</details>


<div id='cs.RO'></div>

# cs.RO [[Back]](#toc)

### [332] [HERMES: Heterogeneous Edge-Relational Multi-Head Embedded SSM Attention for Traffic Conflict Prediction at Signalized Intersections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20505)
*Md Monzurul Islam,Subasish Das*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes HERMES, a heterogeneous edge-relational graph neural network incorporating SSM-informed multi-head attention for scene-level traffic conflict classification, achieving state-of-the-art metrics and transferable performance across sites.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches flatten scenes or ignore heterogeneous interaction structures, limiting proactive safety assessment and transferability across locations.

Method: Model vehicles and pedestrians as heterogeneous nodes with relation-specific edges (vehicle-vehicle, vehicle-pedestrian, pedestrian-pedestrian) using continuous kinematic and surrogate-safety descriptors. Introduce relation-specific attention, dynamic node-edge updates, safety-aware graph pooling, and temporal sequence learning within a heterogeneous scene-graph framework to estimate scene-level conflict probability.

Result: Evaluated on 109,028 trajectory-derived sequences from a signalized urban intersection and tested on an independent dataset. Enhanced HERMES achieved AUC-ROC 0.9898±0.0013, AUC-PR 0.9412±0.0067, F1 0.8449±0.0103; at 5% false-alarm rate, detected 95.7% of conflict sequences, outperforming Transformer and XGBoost. Zero-shot evaluation yielded AUC-ROC 0.9752 and AUC-PR 0.7829; joint source-target training improved target-site performance.

Conclusion: Preserving heterogeneous interaction topology, safety-informed edge semantics, and short-term temporal evolution improves scene-level conflict classification and supports transferable roadside safety monitoring at signalized intersections.

Abstract: Surrogate safety measures (SSMs) enable proactive traffic safety assessment, but many existing methods evaluate pairwise interactions independently or flatten multi-agent scenes into fixed feature vectors, limiting their ability to represent heterogeneous interaction structure and evolving scene-level risk. This study formulates traffic conflict assessment as temporal heterogeneous scene-graph classification and proposes HERMES, a heterogeneous edge-relational graph neural network with SSM-informed multi-head attention. Vehicles and pedestrians are represented as heterogeneous nodes, while vehicle-vehicle, vehicle-pedestrian, and pedestrian-pedestrian interactions are encoded as relation-specific edges with continuous kinematic and surrogate-safety descriptors. Relation-specific attention, dynamic node-edge updates, safety-aware graph pooling, and temporal sequence learning are jointly used to estimate scene-level conflict probability. HERMES was evaluated using 109,028 trajectory-derived sequences from a signalized urban intersection and tested on an independently collected comparable intersection dataset. Enhanced HERMES achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9898 +/- 0.0013, an AUC-PR of 0.9412 +/- 0.0067, and an F1 score of 0.8449 +/- 0.0103. At a 5% false-alarm rate, it detected 95.7% of conflict sequences, outperforming the strongest Transformer baseline and XGBoost. In zero-shot external evaluation, HERMES achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9752 and an AUC-PR of 0.7829. Joint source-target training further improved target-site performance with limited target-site data. These findings show that preserving heterogeneous interaction topology, safety-informed edge semantics, and short-term temporal evolution improves scene-level conflict classification and supports transferable roadside safety monitoring at signalized intersections.

</details>


### [333] [PhysCoRe: Physics-Corrected Residual World Models for Material-Aware Deformable Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20653)
*Haocheng Yin,Shuohan Tao,Yongsheng Chen,Lu Gan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PhysCoRe integrates a differentiable MPM simulator with a material-refinement network (MfM) and a residual dynamics network (RfD) to predict deformable-object manipulation; it supports online material identification and uncertainty-guided exploration, achieving superior prediction accuracy on real sequences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses slow, non-generalizable per-object parameter fitting and poor generalization of end-to-end models by grounding prediction in physics while retaining data-driven corrections and online adaptation; enables uncertainty-aware exploration for deformable object manipulation.

Method: Couples a differentiable MPM simulator with two feed-forward networks: MfM infers per-particle elasticity from visual observations to ground the simulator in object-specific physics; RfD learns a residual correction to the simulator's dynamics to capture model bias. Online material identification on novel objects and uncertainty estimates steer exploration.

Result: On real deformable-object manipulation sequences, PhysCoRe outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in prediction accuracy; its per-geometry confidence distribution provides a reliable signal for future confidence-guided exploration.

Conclusion: A physics-informed residual world model that combines an interpretable physics simulator with learned corrections and online material identification, yielding improved generalization and actionable uncertainty for deformable-object manipulation.

Abstract: Predicting how deformable objects evolve under robotic manipulation is a longstanding challenge. Existing approaches typically rely on per-object optimization to fit material parameters, which can be slow and cannot generalize, while end-to-end learned alternatives extrapolate poorly and often violate basic physical structure. We present PhysCoRe, a physics-corrected residual world model that couples a differentiable Material Point Method (MPM) simulator with two feed-forward neural networks. A material refinement module, Material from Motion (MfM), infers per-particle elasticity from visual observations, grounding the simulator in object-specific physics. A residual correction module, Residual from Dynamics (RfD), learns the discrepancy and predicts corrections to the simulator's internal dynamics, absorbing systematic biases that the analytical model cannot capture. This design also supports online material identification on novel objects. MfM adapts from limited interactions, and its predictive uncertainty steers further exploration toward the regions where its estimate is least confident. Experiments on real deformable-object manipulation sequences show that PhysCoRe outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in prediction accuracy, and that its predicted confidence forms a reliable distribution across the object's geometry, providing a natural signal for future confidence-guided exploration.

</details>


### [334] [Scalable Low-Cost Laboratory Automation: A Digital Twin-Integrated Robotic Platform for Autonomous Liquid Handling (RAINBOTTM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20662)
*Mohamed Rami Ayeche,Souhil Sid,Ahyen Mostofa,Rehaan Hussain,Ali Shayesteh,Fadwa El Mellouhi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Open, low-cost liquid-handling robot (RAINBOT) built from a consumer 3D printer; features a browser-based digital twin and inverse-design integration; validated with color-mixing proof-of-concept; hardware cost ~$1300.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lower barriers to automated experimentation by reducing cost, increasing transparency, and enabling remote supervision, addressing the constraints of proprietary, expensive systems.

Method: 1) Replace printer extruder with a single-channel pipette; actuate via the printer's XY‑Z gantry and two compact linear actuators for plunger and tip ejection, controlled by Python. 2) Implement a browser-based digital twin for bidirectional synchronization of kinematics and pipetting states, enabling remote monitoring and emergency stop. 3) Validate with colorimetric mixing using an integrated color sensor; couple to CEID framework for inverse-design guided experimentation with human oversight.

Result: Successful sequential aqueous color exchanges; color sensor quantifies mixtures; red–yellow–blue responses align with expected mixing within a mean absolute error of 2 percentage points. Demonstrated real-time tracking and remote supervision; cost under $1300, about an order of magnitude cheaper than entry-level commercial systems.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a feasible, open-hardware pathway for self-driving laboratory automation by integrating inexpensive hardware, a digital twin, and goal-directed design; establishes a scalable, reproducible framework for remote, transparent experimentation.

Abstract: Laboratory automation accelerates discovery, yet its adoption is constrained by the high cost, proprietary design, and limited remote supervisability of commercial liquid-handling systems. This work presents RAINBOT\textsuperscript{TM}, a low-cost, openly reproducible liquid-handling robot built by converting a consumer-grade Cartesian 3D printer (Elegoo Neptune 4 Max). The printer extruder is replaced by a precision single-channel pipette actuated through the printer's own G-code-driven X--Y--Z gantry, with plunger and tip-eject motions effected by two compact linear actuators under Python control. To make experiments transparent and remotely supervisable, a browser-based digital twin is implemented to synchronise bidirectionally with the physical platform, mirroring kinematics and pipetting states in real time and exposing remote monitoring, intervention, and an emergency stop from any web browser. As a proof of concept, RAINBOT\textsuperscript{TM} performed sequential exchanges of differently coloured aqueous solutions while an integrated colour sensor quantified the resulting mixtures; measured red, yellow, and blue (RYB) responses agreed with expected mixing behaviour to within a mean absolute error of two percentage points, validating correct execution and real-time tracking. Closing the loop, the platform is coupled to the CEID\textsuperscript{TM} (Cooperative Explorer for Inverse Design) framework, which recasts experimentation from iterative manual guessing into a goal-directed inverse-design search while keeping a human in the loop. The complete hardware costs under US\$1300, which is roughly an order of magnitude below entry-level commercial handlers, thereby establishing an accessible physical--virtual framework for self-driving laboratory automation.

</details>


### [335] [Safe and Scalable Multi-Drone Payload Transport via CBF-based Reinforcement Learning with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20665)
*Jaeyoun Choi,Oswin So,Songyuan Zhang,Cooper Taylor,Chuchu Fan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A learning-based, fully distributed framework for safe and scalable multi-drone payload transport using a 2D abstraction, domain randomization, and DGPPO, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and generalization across team sizes and dynamic obstacles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address unsafe and inefficient coordination in complex, coupled drone-payload dynamics, where existing methods struggle with safety, scalability, and adaptability in dynamic/unstructured environments.

Method: Introduce a minimal 2D abstraction preserving task-relevant drone-payload coupling. Apply domain randomization over team size and physical parameters. Train a fully distributed policy via Discrete Graph Control Barrier Function Proximal Policy Optimization (DGPPO) for robust safety-aware coordination. Achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without fine-tuning; evaluate on single policy across varying teams and in multi-group hardware with moving obstacles.

Result: The learned policy generalizes across team sizes and task scenarios in real-world tests. In multi-group experiments, the policy safely operates in dynamic environments with other drone teams as moving obstacles, demonstrating robustness and scalability.

Conclusion: The proposed 2D-abstracted, learning-based framework provides safe, scalable, and generalizable multi-drone payload transportation suitable for real-world deployment in dynamic environments.

Abstract: Multi-drone payload transportation has emerged as a promising research paradigm with potential applications in construction, logistics, and disaster response. However, the complex coupled dynamics among drones, cables, and payloads pose significant challenges, and existing approaches remain limited in safety and scalability, particularly in dynamic and unstructured environments. In this work, we propose a learning-based framework for safe and scalable multi-drone cooperative payload transport. We introduce a minimal 2D abstraction that preserves the task-relevant drone-payload coupling required for coordination and safety, while remaining computationally efficient for large-scale learning. Using domain randomization over team size and physical parameters, we train a fully distributed policy via Discrete Graph Control Barrier Function Proximal Policy Optimization (DGPPO), enabling robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without fine-tuning. Extensive real-world evaluations demonstrate that a single learned policy generalizes across varying team sizes and task scenarios. Furthermore, multi-group hardware experiments show that the same policy can safely operate in dynamic environments, where other drone teams act as moving obstacles. These results indicate that the proposed framework enables efficient, safe, and scalable multi-drone payload transportation with strong generalization to complex real-world conditions.

</details>


### [336] [Towards Capability-Aware Traversability Navigation for Unstructured Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20679)
*Gianluca Capezzuto,Felipe Tommaselli,Matheus P. Angarola,Ricardo V. Godoy,Marcelo Becker*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Capability-Aware Traversability (CAT) embeds robot embodiment in the spatial feature space to ensure terrain traversability predictions respect platform constraints, outperforming morphology-agnostic baselines across multiple metrics and deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traversability is embodiment-dependent: the same terrain can be traversable for one robot and unsafe for another. Prior methods rely on late-stage trajectory filtering, failing to encode platform constraints in learned representations.

Method: Introduce SPADE-based spatial conditioning to inject per-robot traversability vectors into semantic terrain maps; ground supervision masks in physical trajectories via an interactive annotation pipeline; use per-robot prototypes to capture capability; evaluate on both human-annotated and trajectory-aligned datasets; deploy on legged quad and wheeled skid-steer for hardware-embedded operation.

Result: CAT outperforms all ranking-based metrics: AUROC +11.0% on physically executed trajectories and AUPRC +15.8% on human traces versus strongest baseline. Ablations show the importance of spatial conditioning and per-robot prototypes. Demonstrations achieve embodiment-aware obstacle avoidance on embedded hardware at 4.8 Hz across two robot platforms.

Conclusion: Embedding embodiment into the representation through spatial conditioning and robot-specific prototypes enables capability-aware traversability estimation, improving both predictive ranking metrics and real-time obstacle avoidance across morphologies; the approach supports efficient deployment on embedded hardware.

Abstract: Estimating traversability in unstructured environments requires conditioning on robot embodiment, as the same terrain can be traversable for one platform and unsafe for another. Existing methods often transfer predictions across morphologies through late-stage trajectory filtering rather than encoding platform constraints in the learned representation. We propose Capability-Aware Traversability (CAT), a framework that embeds physical limits directly into the spatial feature space. CAT grounds dense supervision masks in physical trajectories through an interactive annotation pipeline and modulates semantic terrain maps with robot-specific traversability vectors through Spatially-Adaptive Denormalization (SPADE) blocks. Across human-annotated and trajectory-aligned datasets, CAT leads all ranking-based metrics, improving AUROC by 11.0% on physically executed trajectories and AUPRC by 15.8% on human traces over the strongest baseline. Ablations show that spatial conditioning and per-robot prototypes produce capability sensitivity beyond generic path prediction. Deployments on a legged quadruped and a wheeled skid-steer demonstrate embodiment-aware obstacle avoidance on embedded hardware at 4.8 Hz.

</details>


### [337] [FELT: Generating Tactile Signals from Vision for Visuo-Tactile Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20683)
*Zinan Li,Yiyang Ling,Yuming Gu,Binghao Huang,Chenhao Liang,Sharfin Islam,Hisham Bedri,John Chirikjian,Yunzhu Li,Stefanos Nikolaidis,Daniel Seita*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: FELT learns to generate per-finger tactile signals from RGB using a frozen visual encoder and lightweight decoders, enabling visuo-tactile policies with less tactile data by producing either tactile images or latent features; separate left/right branches capture asymmetric contact patterns, and inference uses RGB only, improving performance on four tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tactile data is scarce and hard to collect due to fragile sensors and standardization issues, hindering robust visuo-tactile policy learning; leveraging RGB to synthesize tactile signals can reduce data collection needs and broaden applicability.

Method: A large frozen visual encoder feeds a lightweight query decoder that decodes tactile signals per finger. Separate branches handle left and right tactile sensor panels to respect physical topology and asymmetric contact. At inference, only RGB is required; FELT can output either generated tactile images or latent tactile features for use by the policy, augmenting vision-only data.

Result: On four contact-rich manipulation tasks, FELT improves policy success over vision-only baselines. Both generated tactile images and latent tactile features help; notably, latent features require no real tactile sensor during training or deployment.

Conclusion: FELT offers a practical route to reduce tactile data requirements in visuo-tactile learning by translating RGB input into tactile representations, with flexible deployment (images or latent features) and a design that respects sensor topology, yielding improved manipulation performance.

Abstract: The sense of touch is central to manipulation, especially when vision is occluded or ambiguous. Although combining vision and touch improves manipulation, learning robust visuo-tactile policies requires substantial tactile data. Such data remains scarcer than visual data, because tactile sensors are fragile, specialized, and hard to standardize. To address this, we present Feature-Extracted Latent Tactile (FELT), a learning-based framework that synthesizes per-finger pressure tactile images from RGB observations, reducing the need for tactile-equipped data collection. FELT uses a large frozen visual encoder and a lightweight query decoder to predict tactile signals in a single feed-forward pass. To respect the physical topology of dual-finger tactile sensors, FELT decodes the left and right tactile sensor panels through separate branches, capturing the asymmetric contact patterns during interactions such as wiping, insertion, and in-hand rotation. At inference time, FELT only requires RGB data, allowing us to augment existing vision-only data with tactile observations, either as generated tactile images or as latent tactile features. Experiments on four contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate that both generated tactile images and latent tactile features improve policy success over vision-only baselines, with latent feature requiring no real tactile sensor during policy training or deployment. Supplementary material is available on our anonymous website: https://felt-tactile.github.io/.

</details>


### [338] [Decentralized UAV Swarms for Ground Target Protection in GPS- and Communication-Denied Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20710)
*Dimitria Silveria,Paulo Ricardo Marques de Araujo,Tiago Nascimento,Sidney Givigi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GPS-denied autonomous UAV swarms for ground-target protection using relative measurements, decentralized encirclement, and Kalman filters; validated on real robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In modern warfare, defense systems must operate without GPS or inter-UAV communications; existing methods rely on UAV-to-UAV communication and GPS which may be unavailable in contested environments.

Method: Develop Kalman filters to estimate states of unknown targets and swarm UAV positions using only relative measurements; design a decentralized swarm encirclement strategy adaptive to target motion; validate with real robots in GPS-denied conditions.

Result: Extensive real-robot validation showing effectiveness in detecting, encircling, and intercepting hostile UAVs.

Conclusion: Decentralized encirclement in GPS-denied environments can effectively protect ground targets from UAV threats, offering a viable alternative to GPS-based coordination.

Abstract: The presence of UAVs in military operations has recently increased, also increasing the demand for defense systems against UAV attacks. UAVs can also be used as countermeasures. Most available methods rely on UAV-to-UAV communication and global positioning. However, such resources may not be available in modern warfare scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a pipeline for ground-target protection against UAV attacks that employs autonomous swarms of UAVs. We assume a communication- and GPS-denied environment in which the UAVs use onboard sensors to track the target and coordinate as a swarm. We developed Kalman filters to estimate the states of unknown targets and the positions of UAVs in the swarm using only relative measurements. Also, our strategy is to encircle the target of interest to maximize coverage. To achieve that, we propose a decentralized swarm encirclement technique that adapts to the target's motion. Our approach was extensively validated using real robots, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting, encircling, and intercepting hostile UAVs.

</details>


### [339] [Self-Supervised Bio-Inspired Robotic Trajectory Planning with Obstacle Avoidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20743)
*Miroslav Krupa,Miroslav Cibula,Kristína Malinovská*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Neuro-inspired self-supervised trajectory planning using forward/inverse models; demonstrates feasibility in obstacle environments but reveals exploitation of the supervisory signal; proposes training regimes to mitigate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the computational cost of sampling-based planners and the limitations of model-learning approaches (sample inefficiency and limited generalisation) by using a self-supervised framework that relies on bounded forward passes and internal supervision.

Method: A neuro-inspired self-supervised framework where forward and inverse models serve as internal supervisors for trajectory planning; tested in environments with obstacles; analyzes learning dynamics and proposes additional training regimes.

Result: Empirical results confirm feasibility of the approach; however, the planner tends to exploit the learning signal from forward/inverse models. The work also evaluates mitigation strategies and additional training regimes.

Conclusion: The proposed self-supervised framework is promising for efficient trajectory planning but requires addressing shortcut exploitation of supervision signals; the added training regimes show potential mitigation and guide future refinement.

Abstract: Trajectory planning is a fundamental problem in robotics, requiring the generation of collision-free and efficient trajectories in a potentially complex environment. While sampling-based planners remain the dominant approach, they are often computationally expensive, particularly in high-dimensional spaces and obstacle-rich environments. Methods based on model learning offer a promising alternative, enabling efficient planning through a bounded number of forward passes through a neural trajectory planner, but commonly suffer from low sample efficiency or limited generalisation due to their reliance on exploration or expert demonstrations. This follow-up work tests our neuro-inspired self-supervised learning framework for trajectory planning that leverages forward and inverse models as the internal supervisory mechanism in an environment that contains an obstacle. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the approach while revealing a tendency of our planner to exploit the learning signal provided by the forward and inverse models. To address this issue, additional training regimes and mitigation strategies are proposed and evaluated.

</details>


### [340] [A real-time RGB-D perception pipeline for autonomous impact hammers in mining: self-filtering, rock segmentation and rock-breaking poses generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20748)
*Martín Gallegos,Francisco Leiva,Patricio Loncomilla,Michelle Cortés,Javier Ruiz-del-Solar*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-time RGB-D perception pipeline enables autonomous operation of hydraulic impact hammers by jointly generating rock-breaking poses and a robot-free 3D workspace, using image-based segmentation and geometric point cloud processing on embedded hardware at ~10 Hz with ~675 ms latency, validated in scaled experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underground impact hammers are typically teleoperated, limiting efficiency; automating perception is a key step toward real-time autonomous operation in mining robotics.

Method: Combines image-based instance segmentation with geometric point cloud processing to produce operationally feasible rock-breaking poses and a robot-free 3D workspace representation; implemented on embedded hardware and running at ~10 Hz with ~675 ms end-to-end latency, enabling closed-loop control.

Result: Demonstrates real-time capability and suitability for autonomous hammer operation in a representative scaled scenario through experimental validation.

Conclusion: The proposed pipeline represents a viable step toward autonomous hydraulic impact hammer operation, enabling real-time closed-loop execution and providing a foundation for integrated control; further real-world validation and controller integration are anticipated.

Abstract: Impact hammers, also known as rock-breakers, are essential machines in mining operations, where they perform secondary reduction. In underground mining, these machines are typically teleoperated, limiting operational efficiency. This paper presents a real-time RGB-D perception pipeline as a step towards automating the operation of hydraulic impact hammers used in mining. The proposed system simultaneously generates operationally feasible rock-breaking poses and a robot-free 3D representation of the workspace. The proposed approach combines image-based instance segmentation with geometric point cloud processing, and operates on embedded hardware at approximately 10 Hz with a total latency of around 675 ms, enabling responsive closed-loop behavior when integrated with a control system. Experimental results in a representative scaled scenario demonstrate that the proposed system is suitable for real-time autonomous impact hammer operation.

</details>


### [341] [Emergent Compositional Skills in Mixture-of-Experts VLAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20771)
*Shlok Shah,Rhiaan Jhaveri,Tharun Kumar Tiruppali Kalidoss,Chirayu Nimonkar,Ishaan Javali*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: End-to-end learning of compositional robot policies from demonstrations using a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) head; emergent reusable primitives and routing enable high-level sequencing without explicit task decomposition; MoE performance matches monolithic baselines while showing interpretable specialization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve modular, interpretable robot policies by learning from data alone, without pre-specified task hierarchies, and to see if the router can learn high-level sequencing while experts capture reusable low-level skills.

Method: Train a (VLA) network with a simplified Mixture-of-Experts action head on expert demonstrations; a router selects among multiple experts, encouraging emergence of reusable, distinct low-level behaviors.

Result: Learned experts are heavily reused across tasks and correspond to qualitatively distinct low-level behaviors; the router appears to perform high-level sequencing; MoE matches the performance of a monolithic baseline and exhibits meaningful expert specialization.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates emergent modularity and interpretability in robot policies purely from data, with Mixture-of-Experts serving as compositional primitives and the router enabling task-wide sequencing without explicit decomposition.

Abstract: We consider the problem of learning compositional robot policies end-to-end from expert demonstrations, without any pre-specified notion of task decomposition or hierarchy. We ask whether a VLA trained with a simplified Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) action head can emergently learn to decompose tasks into reusable, interpretable primitives. We find that learned experts are heavily reused across tasks and consistently correspond to qualitatively distinct low-level behaviors, suggesting that the router implicitly learns to perform high-level sequencing while experts serve as compositional primitives. Our MoE matches the task performance of a monolithic baseline while demonstrating meaningful expert specialization, a step toward modular, interpretable robot policies that emerge from data alone.

</details>


### [342] [Socially Consistent Multi-Robot Navigation Using Decoupled Planning and Trajectory Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20772)
*Matthew M. Sato,Kincho H. Law*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A partially decentralized framework for multi-robot navigation that enforces long-horizon social consistency by (1) embedding social norms into a modified A* path planner and (2) using the resulting social-path graph to coordinate trajectories via a mixed-integer convex program.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve predictable, socially compliant, and scalable multi-robot navigation in human-centric environments by reducing dependence on local, short-horizon planning and alleviating planner burden through socially informed global path planning.

Method: 1) Modify A* to incorporate macroscopic social norms into the planning cost, producing socially aware routes. 2) Share planned paths among robots to form a social graph of established routes, promoting path consistency and reducing future planning effort. 3) Use the emergent structure of these paths to cast multi-robot trajectory coordination as a mixed-integer convex program that computes conflict-free trajectories and supports dynamic task assignment.

Result: Enforcing social consistency at the path-planning stage yields predictable, socially compliant robot motions and simplifies the subsequent multi-robot coordination problem, with apparent scalability to large fleets.

Conclusion: Long-horizon predictability and social compliance can be achieved by decoupling global path planning from trajectory coordination and by embedding social norms into planning; the approach scales with fleet size and reduces coordination complexity.

Abstract: The successful integration of mobile robots in human-centric environments requires navigation that is not only safe and efficient, but also predictable and aligned with social conventions, key precursors for human comfort and acceptance. While significant research addresses short-term human-aware planning, these methods often lack mechanisms for ensuring consistent and predictable behaviors across long horizons. Without socially aware long-term planners, local planners are overburdened, resulting in inefficient and locally reactive movements that undermine predictability. This paper introduces a partially decentralized framework that generates predictable and socially consistent multi-robot motion by decoupling global path planning from trajectory coordination. First, we propose a modified A* planner that embeds macroscopic social norms into the planner cost function. Planned paths are shared across mobile robots to collaboratively build a social graph of established routes, which enforces path consistency and reduces future planning effort. Second, we leverage the emergent structure of the socially constrained paths to formulate the multi-robot trajectory coordination problem as a mixed-integer convex program. The convex program enables efficient computation of conflict- free trajectories, scaling effectively to large fleets and supporting dynamic task assignment. Our results demonstrate that enforcing social consistency at the path planning stage produces predictable, socially compliant mobile robot paths and simplifies the otherwise complex problem of multi-robot coordination.

</details>


### [343] [Robostral Navigate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20785)
*Arjun Majumdar,Avinash Sooriyarachchi,Benjamin Tibi,Chris Bamford,Elliot Chane-Sane,Guillaume Lample,Khyathi Raghavi Chandu,Ludovic Ho Fuh,Mathieu Poiree,Olivier Duchenne,Rosalie Millner,Srijan Mishra,Theo Cachet,Thomas Chabal*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Robostral Navigate: an 8B vision-language model that navigates using only monocular RGB images to predict waypoints, achieving state-of-the-art results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE while employing a training-efficient, scalable recipe.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable scalable, sensor-agnostic navigation that generalizes across robot embodiments and minimizes hardware and data collection costs by avoiding depth sensors, multi-camera rigs, or pre-built maps.

Method: An 8B vision-language model trained on 2.4 million trajectories across 350k simulated scenes. It operates in image space, predicting the next target location by pointing within the current camera frame. A tree-based attention mask prevents conditioning on prior ground-truth actions. Reinforcement learning improves exploration/recovery. A prefix-caching training recipe packs entire episodes into single sequences, reducing tokens by 22x and training time from months to days.

Result: On Room-to-Room and RxR-CE benchmarks, Robostral Navigate achieves state-of-the-art performance: 77.4% success rate on R2R-CE (beats monocular baselines by 10.5 points and depth/multi-camera baselines by 5.3), and 75.1% on RxR-CE (outperforming all monocular baselines).

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates scalable, camera-intrinsic-robust navigation with a single RGB camera, enabling cross-embodiment deployment across wheeled, legged, and aerial robots, aided by a data-efficient, scalable training regimen.

Abstract: Deploying navigation systems at scale requires a recipe that minimizes sensor assumptions, generalizes across robot embodiments, and trains efficiently. Yet, today's best systems depend on depth sensors, multi-camera rigs, or pre-built maps, limiting the hardware they support and increasing deployment cost. We introduce Robostral Navigate, an 8B vision-language model built around this scalability objective. The model consumes only a stream of monocular RGB images - the most ubiquitous sensor across robotic platforms and predicts waypoints by pointing to the next target location in the current camera view. Operating purely in image space, rather than robot-specific coordinates, makes the policy naturally robust to changes in camera intrinsics and scene scale, enabling deployment across wheeled, legged, and aerial robots without recalibration. We generate 2.4 million trajectories across 350k simulated scenes to reduce the reliance on real-world data collection and scale easily. We further introduce a prefix-caching training recipe that packs entire episodes into single training sequences, reducing training tokens by 22x and cutting training time from months to days. A tree-based attention mask prevents conditioning on previous ground-truth actions, encouraging visually grounded action prediction, and reinforcement learning is used to further improve exploration and recovery capabilities. On the Room-to-Room and Room-Across-Room in Continuous Environments (R2R-CE and RxR-CE) benchmarks, Robostral Navigate sets a new state of the art. On R2R-CE, it achieves a 77.4% success rate, surpassing the best monocular method by 10.5 points and the strongest depth- or multi-camera system by 5.3 points despite using only a single RGB camera. On RxR-CE, it reaches 75.1% success rate, outperforming all monocular baselines.

</details>


### [344] [URF: A Unified Robot Control-Policy Framework for Stable Contact Aware Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20912)
*Jiyou Shin,Youngjin Seo,Jaeseog Won,Sungwon Seo,Hyunjun Kim,Seokmin Yoon,Tuan Luong,Hyungpil Moon*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: URF unifies policy learning with adaptive control by predicting a virtual target, stiffness, and an impedance-admittance switch to decide controller mode, supervised by force-derived labels; shows improved task success and safer contact in box-flipping and line-pressing tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigid-contact manipulation with purely learned actions can fail due to mismatch with low-level controllers; separating policy and controller causes instability, excessive loading, or tool damage. A unified approach that also predicts how to execute actions (controller mode) could improve performance and safety.

Method: A Unified Robot Control-Policy Framework (URF) takes multimodal observations and outputs: (1) a virtual target, (2) a stiffness matrix, and (3) an impedance-admittance switch ratio. The switch ratio governs when the controller behaves like admittance control (for accurate tracking) versus impedance control (for safe rigid contact). Ground-truth stiffness is unavailable from demonstrations; switch labels are constructed from measured contact forces to supervise controller-mode prediction. Evaluation on box-flipping and line-pressing tasks.

Result: URF achieves higher task success rates and reduces failure modes seen with admittance-only execution, such as rapid force buildup, large force oscillations, tool breakage, and safety stops.

Conclusion: Incorporating controller behavior prediction alongside compliant actions yields more contact-aware policies and improves robustness and safety in manipulation tasks involving rigid contact.

Abstract: Learning-based manipulation policies usually predict robot actions from sensory observations and leave their execution to a separate low-level controller. In rigid contact, this separation can be problematic: the same motion to a virtual target or compliant motion command can lead to unstable contact, tracking error, excessive loading, or tool damage, depending on the low-level controller. In this paper, we propose a \textit{Unified Robot Control-Policy Framework} (URF), which connects compliant action prediction with unified impedance-admittance control. Given multimodal observations, URF predicts a virtual target, a stiffness matrix, and an impedance-admittance switch ratio. The switch ratio determines when the controller should behave more like admittance control for accurate motion tracking and when it should move toward impedance control for safer rigid contact. Because demonstration data do not provide ground-truth environment stiffness, we construct switch-ratio labels from measured contact forces and use them to supervise controller-mode prediction. Across box-flipping and line-pressing tasks, URF achieves higher task success rates while reducing failure modes observed with admittance-only execution, including rapid force buildup, large force oscillations, tool breakage, and robot safety stops. These results suggest that contact-aware policies benefit from predicting not only compliant actions but also the controller behavior used to execute them. Project page: https://jiyou384.github.io/urf_project_page/

</details>


### [345] [Deep Reinforcement-Learning-Guided Model Predictive Control for Preventing Overtakes in Autonomous Racing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20973)
*Yufei Xi,Yijie Liao,Tulga Ersal*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Hierarchical RL-guided MPC for defensive blocking in autonomous racing using Soft Actor-Critic in Frenet domain to generate geometry-aware defensive references embedded as spatial regularization under friction constraints; sim on Thunderhill West shows improved defense (overtake time up, opponent progress down) with real-time capable solve.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address defensive blocking rather than lap-time minimization, treating defensive control as spatial occupancy regulation under dynamic limits to prevent faster opponents from overtaking while maintaining high-performance driving.

Method: A two-layer approach: a Soft Actor-Critic strategic layer in the Frenet domain proposes defensive references; these references are integrated into a nonlinear MPC as spatial regularization, subject to tire friction constraints, enabling geometry-aware defense. The framework operates in real time with a reported mean solve time.

Result: In simulation on Thunderhill West: average overtake time increases from 8.8 s to 14.6 s; opponent progress is significantly reduced; the ego vehicle uses 83.4% of available tire force; mean solve time 33.3 ms (std 13.9 ms).

Conclusion: The framework effectively implements defensive blocking via spatial occupancy regulation with real-time capable optimization, achieving substantial improvement in overtaking resistance while maintaining high vehicle utilization and real-time performance.

Abstract: This paper addresses defensive blocking in autonomous racing, where a vehicle must prevent a faster opponent from overtaking while operating near its dynamic limits. Different from lap-time minimization, we formulate defense as a spatial occupancy regulation problem via a hierarchical reinforcement-learning guided model predictive control framework. A Soft Actor-Critic strategic layer operates in the Frenet domain to generate geometry-aware defensive references, which are embedded into the nonlinear model predictive control formulation as spatial regularization under friction constraints. Evaluated on the Thunderhill West circuit in simulation, the framework increases average overtake time from 8.8 s to 14.6 s while significantly reducing opponent progress. Meanwhile, it allows the vehicle to utilize 83.4% of available tire force. The framework achieves a 33.3 ms mean solve time (13.9 ms std), supporting real-time high-speed adversarial interaction.

</details>


### [346] [Distributed Model-Based Diffusion For Scalable Multi-Robot Trajectory Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20992)
*Haejoon Lee,Xinyi Wang,Taekyung Kim,Dimitra Panagou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Distributed Model-Based Diffusion (DMBD) extends diffusion-based trajectory optimization to multi-robot systems by decomposing the reverse diffusion into local conditional processes. A central server aggregates broadcasts of other robots' trajectories, enabling each robot to denoise within its own subspace while conditioning on others. This yields scalable, sub-second coordination in diverse tasks and outperforms baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate the curse of dimensionality and the need for global access to all robots' dynamics/constraints in centralized multi-robot diffusion, enabling scalable, decentralized optimization.

Method: A distributed server-robot framework that splits the reverse diffusion into local conditional reverse diffusions. Each robot denoises in its control subspace and conditions on current trajectory estimates of other robots, which the server aggregates and broadcasts. Iterative, parallelizable updates drive the joint trajectory toward coordination objectives.

Result: Extensive simulations (goal swapping, multi-floor coverage, parking, rush-hour) demonstrate strong scalability, solving many challenging coordination tasks in sub-seconds and significantly outperforming existing baselines.

Conclusion: DMBD provides a scalable, distributed diffusion-based approach for multi-robot trajectory optimization, balancing local autonomous denoising with global coordination via server aggregation, and outperforming baselines in diverse scenarios.

Abstract: Trajectory optimization for multi-robot systems remains a critical challenge, particularly when navigating highly non-convex, non-linear, and non-differentiable environments. While Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) has recently emerged as a promising sampling-based optimization paradigm for single-robot trajectory generation, extending it to multi-robot systems results in a centralized, high-dimensional inference problem that (i) suffers from poor sample efficiency due to the curse of dimensionality and (ii) requires global access to all robots' dynamics, constraints, and objectives. To address this, we propose Distributed Model-Based Diffusion (DMBD), a distributed server-robot framework that decomposes the reverse diffusion process into local conditional reverse diffusion processes. This decomposition enables each robot to iteratively perform denoising independently within its own control subspace while conditioning on the current trajectory estimates of the other robots that are aggregated and broadcast by the server. Extensive simulations in goal swapping, multi-floor coverage, parking, and rush-hour scenarios demonstrate that DMBD achieves strong scalability, solving many challenging coordination tasks in sub-seconds and significantly outperforming existing baselines.

</details>


### [347] [TableVerse: A Large-scale Tabletop Dataset with Real-world Grounded Layouts for Generalizable Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21017)
*Boyuan Wang,Yue Zhang,Xutao Xue,Xueyu Song,Yu Sun*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A Real2Sim pipeline (TableVerse) reconstructs real-world unscripted images into high-fidelity, simulation-ready tabletop environments with accurate scale and stable physics, plus automated task-conditioned trajectories, resulting in TableVerse-100K: 100k environments with manipulation demonstrations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the data bottleneck in generalizable robotic manipulation by moving from imaginative synthetic layouts to deterministic, real-world-informed scenes reconstructed from internet imagery, ensuring physical plausibility and realistic clutter.

Method: A fully automated Real2Sim pipeline that converts unstructured, in-the-wild images into high-fidelity, metric-tabletop simulations with authentic topology and verified stability, paired with an automated trajectory generation framework to produce high-quality, collision-free pick-and-place demos, culminating in TableVerse-100K dataset of 100k environments and demonstrations.

Result: Creation of TableVerse-100K: 100,000 physically consistent tabletop environments with interactive manipulation trajectories, capturing diverse asset compositions and realistic spatial distributions, enabling scalable high-fidelity data for learning robotic manipulation.

Conclusion: TableVerse-100K provides a scalable, high-fidelity data foundation for future research in generalizable robotic manipulation, addressing the gap between real-world cluttered scenes and simulation-ready data.

Abstract: The development of generalizable robotic manipulation policies is inherently bounded by the availability of large-scale, high-fidelity scene data. While recent automated synthesis methods attempt to bridge this gap via text-to-layout hallucination or simplified procedural generation, they frequently suffer from physical implausibility and fail to capture the complex, dense clutter of actual human environments. In this paper, we introduce TableVerse, a fully automated Real2Sim pipeline that shifts the paradigm from imaginative layout generation to deterministic reconstruction from unstructured, in-the-wild image data. Our framework seamlessly processes unscripted internet media into high-fidelity, simulation-ready tabletop environments with accurate metric scales, authentic topologies, and verified mechanical stability. Furthermore, an automated task-conditioned trajectory generation framework is integrated to synthesize high-quality, collision-free pick-and-place demonstrations. Leveraging this complete pipeline, we construct the TableVerse-100K Dataset, a large-scale corpus comprising 100,000 unique, physically consistent environments paired with interactive manipulation trajectories. By capturing diverse asset compositions, realistic spatial distributions, and high-quality demonstrations, TableVerse-100K establishes a highly scalable and high-fidelity data foundation, providing significant value to facilitate future research in generalizable robotic manipulation tasks.

</details>


### [348] [ZONDA: Zero-shot Object Navigation with Dynamic Avoidance in Multi-floor Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21025)
*Shaomin Liang,Xuanhong Liao,Shiyao Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ZONDA enables zero-shot cross-floor object navigation with dynamic pedestrian avoidance using heuristic multi-floor planning, multi-view target verification, and dynamic pedestrian tracking; shows improved performance on a real biped robot and HM3D/MP3D simulations, with robustness in HM3D-DYNA under dynamic conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing object navigation methods are limited to static, single-floor environments, lacking cross-floor topologies and dynamic obstacles, hindering real-world deployment.

Method: Three components: (i) Heuristic multi-floor planning from height-difference traversable maps to enable stair traversal and cross-floor exploration without a platform-specific learned controller; (ii) Multi-view target verification using a vision-language model to cross-check observations at multiple scales and reduce false positives; (iii) Dynamic pedestrian avoidance by explicitly tracking and predicting moving pedestrians to generate anticipatory behaviors. Zero-shot and platform-agnostic.

Result: Empirical evaluation on a real Direct Drive Tech TITA biped robot and extensive simulations on HM3D and MP3D show significant performance gains; ZONDA maintains robust navigation on the dynamic HM3D-DYNA benchmark compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that a combination of heuristic multi-floor planning, cross-modal target verification, and dynamic pedestrian anticipation enables zero-shot object navigation in cross-floor, dynamic environments, suggesting practical deployment potential and avenues for future enhancements.

Abstract: In Object Goal Navigation task, existing methods are typically restricted to static and single-floor environments, ignoring cross-floor topologies and dynamic pedestrian, which limits their real-world deployment. To address these limitations, we propose ZONDA, a zero-shot object navigation with dynamic avoidance framework. In particular, ZONDA integrates three core components: (i) Heuristic multi-floor planning: from height-difference traversable maps, enables stair traversal and cross-floor exploration without a platform-specific learned controller; (ii) Multi-view target verification: cross-checks multi-scale observations with a vision-language model, significantly reducing false positives; and (iii) Dynamic pedestrian avoidance: explicitly tracks and predicts moving pedestrians to generate anticipatory behaviors. Evaluated on a real Direct Drive Tech TITA biped robot and extensive simulations on HM3D and MP3D, ZONDA achieves significantly improved results. Moreover, ZONDA can maintain robust navigation on the dynamic benchmark HM3D-DYNA compared to the existing baseline.

</details>


### [349] [A Real-Time Generalized Nash Equilibrium Framework for Interaction-Aware Autonomous Driving in Mixed Traffic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21043)
*Nouhed Naidja,Mohamed-Cherif Rahal,Steve Pechberti,Stéphane Font,Guillaume Sandou,Marc Revilloud*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes a Generalized Nash Equilibrium (GNEP) framework for AV decision-making in mixed traffic, solved in real-time by a PSO-based solver, validated on a Renault Zoe with a human driver, achieving convergence under 50 ms and generating human-like trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-standing challenge in AV navigation arises from the interdependence of AV actions and unpredictable human driver responses. Existing decoupled optimization can fail to guarantee safety and feasibility under dynamic interaction.

Method: Formulates driving interaction as a Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problem with shared safety and geometric constraints. Develops a dedicated Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)–based solver to solve the non-convex GNEP in real time. Validates the architecture on a test track with a real autonomous Renault Zoe engaging a human driver.

Result: The PSO-based solver converges in under 50 ms in benchmarks. The framework produces comfortable, human-like trajectories and handles critical interactions on the track, demonstrating operational feasibility.

Conclusion: A GNEP-based decision-making framework with a PSO solver can enable safe, efficient, and human-like navigation in mixed-traffic scenarios, with real-time feasibility demonstrated on hardware.

Abstract: Safe and efficient navigation in mixed-traffic environments remains a critical challenge for Autonomous Vehicles (AVs), primarily due to the complex interdependence between the AV's decisions and the unpredictable reactions of human drivers. This paper introduces a comprehensive decision-making framework that formulates the driving interaction as a Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problem (GNEP). Unlike decoupled optimization approaches, this framework explicitly models shared safety and geometric constraints, ensuring that the feasibility of the AV's strategy is dynamically linked to the opponent's actions. To solve this non-convex problem in real-time, we propose a dedicated solver based on Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). The complete architecture was validated on a test track using a real autonomous Renault Zoé interacting with a human driver. Experimental results demonstrate the system's ability to handle critical scenarios by generating comfortable, human-like trajectories. Benchmarks confirm the solver's operational feasibility, achieving convergence in under 50 ms.

</details>


### [350] [GuidedAttention: Interpretable and Correctable Visual Attention for OOD-Robust Robot Manipulation via Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21049)
*Masaki Murooka,Ryoichi Nakajo,Keisuke Shirai,Tomohiro Motoda,Hanbit Oh,Ryo Hanai,Yukiyasu Domae*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces GuidedAttention, an interpretable visuomotor framework that uses predicted task-relevant attention keypoints as an intermediate representation to condition a diffusion-based policy. Users can inspect and optionally correct keypoints at rollout start; corrections are propagated by a tracking module during execution, yielding improved manipulation performance especially under distribution shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end visuomotor policies offer little visibility into visual attention, hindering interpretability and correction. An interpretable, correctable attention mechanism can enhance transparency, debugging, and robustness, particularly under positional and appearance out-of-distribution conditions.

Method: Predict task-relevant attention keypoints from camera images. Condition a diffusion-based action policy on these keypoints. At rollout initialization, allow users to inspect and optionally correct selected keypoints. Use a tracking module to propagate the corrected attention across execution.

Result: GuidedAttention demonstrates consistent improvements in robotic manipulation in both simulation and real-world experiments, with notable gains under positional and appearance OOD conditions.

Conclusion: Explicit, interpretable attention as an intermediate representation with user-correctable mechanisms improves performance and robustness of visuomotor imitation, offering a transparent and adaptable framework for robot control.

Abstract: End-to-end visuomotor policies provide little opportunity for humans to understand or correct the policy's visual attention. We propose GuidedAttention, a visuomotor imitation learning framework that introduces interpretable and correctable visual attention as an explicit intermediate representation. Task-relevant attention keypoints are predicted from camera images and condition a diffusion-based action policy. Users can inspect and optionally correct selected keypoints once at rollout initialization, after which the corrected attention is automatically propagated throughout execution by a tracking module. Experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate that GuidedAttention consistently improves robot manipulation performance, particularly under positional and appearance out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions.

</details>


### [351] [Human-Inspired Framework for Robotic Craniotomy: Integrating Multimodal Fusion and Adaptive Trajectory Adjustment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21058)
*Renzhen Le,Xiao Zhang,Di Wu,Yuanyu Wei,Jiachen Zhu,Zhenzhi Ying,Pengfei Zhang,Liming Shu*

Main category: cs.RO
